text_narrative: The bucket dredger at the north basin stops work at half past nine on a Tuesday and does not resume. Her ladder is down forty feet and the third bucket in the chain has come off its pin. Divers go down twice before noon. The bucket lies on the basin floor under six feet of silt, upside down, with the pin still in it and the shackle sound, and the tumbler above is unmarked.
text_nonnarrative: A bucket ladder was carried between the tumblers at its head and foot, and the buckets were links in a closed chain rather than separate vessels. Tension in the chain was a function of the ladder angle and of the load in the ascending run. Each bucket was pinned at two ears, and the pin was in shear under that tension alone. Without tension the pin and the ear were not in contact.

text_narrative: Every hand on the coasting trade knew the leadsman they called Tallow, and it was not for his name. He armed the lead with mutton fat instead of tallow proper and swore the bottom came up truer on it. Nobody argued while the soundings held. The one night the fat went rancid in the locker the whole chain of them went up on deck to smell it, and he armed the lead with tallow after that.
text_nonnarrative: Arming: the tallow or soap set in the hollow at the base of a sounding lead, in which a print of the bottom holds. Armed: of a lead, in that condition. Bare: the same lead without it, good for depth and of no use for the nature of the ground. Deep-sea lead: the heavier pattern, marked at greater intervals and hollowed deeper. Hand lead: the lighter of the two, and the only one armed by custom.

text_narrative: Cold enough on the slip for the weed to be stiff underfoot, and Ansel had the chain up and the gate across at twenty past eleven. A car came down the ramp behind him with its lamps off. It stopped a yard from the chain and stood there with the engine going, and when he walked round to the driver's window there was frost on the inside of the glass and nothing behind it but the far bank.
text_nonnarrative: Two slipways face each other across a reach some four hundred yards wide. The ramp on the near side is concrete over rubble at a gradient of one in nine, with a chain gate at the head and a low wall on the upstream edge. Below the third course the surface is weed for most of the year. The far ramp is the steeper and the shorter, and neither is under water at any state of the tide.

text_narrative: In the third year of the new commissioners the buoyage of the lower reach was made over from stone beacons to floating marks. Nineteen buoys were laid between the bar and the coal quay that season. Four of them were laid with the topmarks of the wrong hand, and the error stood on the chart for two winters before a pilot out of the fishing village put the matter in writing to the board.
text_nonnarrative: Lateral marks were distinguished from cardinal marks by what the mark referred to: the side of a channel in one case, a quadrant of water about a danger in the other. Shape carried the distinction where colour was unreliable, so a can and a cone were of different hands, and a cone and a double cone of different classes. Isolated danger marks stood outside both, referred to a danger below and not to any channel.

text_narrative: Nine cloths in the mainsail and Ferrer has counted them four times, because nine is what the sail carries and eight is what lies on the loft floor. Not a seam short — a whole cloth short, tabling and all, and the sail still measures to the foot on the chalk. The leech is where it should be. It is arithmetic that argues with a person rather than with the sail, and he counts again.
text_nonnarrative: A gaff sail consisted of four edges and four corners, with the head at the gaff, the luff at the mast, the leech aft and the foot below. The body was made up of cloths seamed parallel to the leech, each of a width fixed by the loom. Tabling was a doubled band at every edge; a bolt rope stood outside it on the luff alone. Reef bands lay across the cloths and not along them.

text_narrative: There was a caulker in a river yard who could hear a slack seam through a plank, and the yard gave her the boats nobody else would take. One winter a punt came in with every seam sound and a bilge full to the thwarts. She went over it twice on her knees with the mallet and heard nothing wrong, and she paid the seams over anyway, and the water came in as fast as before.
text_nonnarrative: What filled the seam separated caulking from paying: hemp driven hard in the one, hot pitch run over it in the other. Neither was a repair to the plank. Stopping was a third class, worked into a fault in the wood rather than into a joint between two pieces. Hardness was no part of the distinction, and only caulking bore on the tightness of a hull, the other two standing to it as covering stands to substance.

text_narrative: The ballast heaver Mirek took work at three yards in one autumn. At the first he trimmed shingle level to a chalk line in the hold of a collier and was paid by the ton. At the second he shovelled it under the floors of a barge that had no floors left to speak of. At the third he was turned away at the gangway for asking after the shifting boards, and no reason was given.
text_nonnarrative: Shingle ballast is required to be trimmed level and to be confined by boards on the centre line for the whole length of the hold. Loose stone above the floors is permitted only where the hold is divided athwartships. Weight is to be distributed so that no bay carries more than its share by a tenth. Trimming to a chalk line is sufficient evidence of level, and a heaver's word is not admissible for it.

text_narrative: The gauge board at the weir reads eleven inches over the crest and the crest is dry. Halvard stands on the apron in his boots and there is no water on it at all, not a film, and the pool above is eleven inches higher than the lip, held up against nothing he can see. Downstream the river runs full. He puts a hand flat where the water should be going over, and the air there is wet.
text_nonnarrative: Discharge over a level crest stood in proportion to the three-halves power of the head above it, so a doubling of head gave rather less than a trebling of flow. The coefficient was a property of the crest profile and of the approach, and no property of the head at all. Below an inch or so of head the relation did not hold, surface tension being of the same order as the weight of the sheet.

text_narrative: Before the river had a name it was told that the salmon owed the people every tenth fish, and the debt was gathered in a hedge of woven stakes set across the shallows at the ford. The first hedge was cut in one night from one willow. What the hedge took, the people ate; what passed it went up to the spawning beds, and the river kept the count itself, and no year was ever short.
text_nonnarrative: For the purposes of this part a fixed engine meant any hedge, crib or basket set in the bed of a tidal river for the taking of fish, whether staked or weighted. Where a hedge stood on the shore below the line of low water, the right to it was several and not common. Nothing in this part affected a right of fishery held by grant or by prescription at the commencement of this part.

text_narrative: They still talk about the grigs old Bassa set in the drain below the pumping station, and how one of them came up heavy every morning of that summer. Not eels. Coins, mostly, and once a brass door plate with no lettering on it, and the drain went nowhere but a field. She sold the coins and bought two more grigs, and those came up empty for eleven years, and the first one went on filling.
text_nonnarrative: The range runs to three patterns of willow grig, of which the middle is the commonest on inland water. Each is a tapered basket some three feet long, with a funnel throat at the mouth and a second throat two thirds of the way in. The smallest has one throat only and a withy handle at the tail. All three are open at the tail. Each is closed there with a plug of twisted straw.

text_narrative: The pilot cutter out of the western harbour put a pilot aboard an inbound timber ship at four in the morning of the fifteenth, in a lee swell, on the third pass. The ladder was two rungs short of the water. The pilot went up it and the cutter stood off, and the ship carried on inbound at seven knots with nobody at all on her bridge and her helm lashed amidships.
text_nonnarrative: A boarding is classed on the ladder and on the swell, and never on the number of passes a cutter makes. A ladder short of the water by two rungs is disqualifying at any swell, since the reach of a pilot rather than the height of a ship sets the limit. Speed of the ship bears on the cause of a refused boarding and not on its class. Darkness is no part of the classification.

text_narrative: Twice in one week Iwan met a loaded boat coming the other way on the narrow reach above the aqueduct, and twice he dropped his line in the water and let the other horse walk over it. The third time the other boat dropped its line first. Both lines went slack in the same pound, both horses stood still, and the two boatmen were fifty yards apart on the path and neither would pick up.
text_nonnarrative: A boat under tow held the path only with its line clear of the water. Two lines in the water together was a drawn position, in which neither boat had a claim on the other. Dropping a line was a move; refusing to drop one was not a move and could not be answered. A loaded boat outranked an empty one, and rank was independent of which boat stood nearer the narrows.

text_narrative: The capstan on the north head was taken down in the eleventh year of the works and its barrel found sound. Eight bars, eight sockets, and a pawl ring worn through on one side to the thickness of a coin. The masons set it up again on the same step with the ring turned a quarter round, and the entry for that year records the cost of nothing but the pin.
text_nonnarrative: A capstan consists of a barrel, a spindle within it, a drumhead pierced for the bars, and a ring of iron let into the step below. The pawls hang from the barrel and bear on the teeth of that ring. Two are usual and three are found on the heavier patterns. The whelps stand proud of the barrel to hold the turns of a rope off the wood.

text_narrative: Fifteen fathoms out and the cable is coming up the wrong way. Odile has the brake off and the windlass turning ahead, and every shackle that passes the stopper is one she has counted before, the same joining piece with the same white paint mark, nine times now. The locker below is empty. She stops the windlass and the cable goes on coming, hand over hand, out of nothing at the stem.
text_nonnarrative: Cable was required to be marked at every shackle, the mark being on the stud of the link next the joining piece and repeated on the deck. A joining shackle was permitted in the outboard length only where a ranging length had been cut out. Riding was to be on not less than three shackles in any depth over ten fathoms, and the brake was to hold the full weight with the compressor off.

text_narrative: Four men on the flywheel and the pump is bringing up nothing, which cannot be, because the well sounds three feet and the chain is turning. Kazi leans over the tube and listens. Air, the whole way down — which means no bucket in the tube is sealing, which means the leather has gone in forty of them at the same hour, and he does not believe it, and the well still sounds three feet.
text_nonnarrative: A chain pump lifts water in a closed tube by a series of discs on an endless chain, each disc sealing against the bore with a leather rim. Delivery is a function of the fit at that rim and of the speed of the chain, and is independent of the depth of water in the well. With any disc unsealed the column above it stands on the disc below rather than on the wheel.

text_narrative: A quarter of a mile of open walk on the shore road, and the spinners went down it backwards from dawn with hemp round their waists, paying out as they walked. A girl was taken on at the far end to turn the wheel. She turned it for a year, and the rope that came off it never wanted tarring, and it would not part, and the salt rotted every other rope in that harbour.
text_nonnarrative: A ropewalk is a long roofed or open way in which yarn is laid up into rope at full length, the length of the walk fixing the length of the finished coil. Twist is put into the yarn one way and into the strand the other, so that the two oppose. Strength depends on that opposition rather than on the tar. A walk is therefore narrow, level, and long out of all proportion to its width.

text_narrative: In the age when the tide still argued with the rivers, a mill was set at the head of an estuary to keep the peace between them, and the sea agreed to fill its pond twice a day and to ask nothing back. The mill ground on the ebb alone. For nine generations the bargain held, and then the pond filled on a night with no tide in it, and the wheel turned for the sea.
text_nonnarrative: A tidal mill was a mill whose head of water was got by impounding the flood in a pond behind a gate, the gate being self-closing against the ebb. Its working period was a function of the range and of the area of the pond, and was confined to the ebb. Grinding on the flood was impossible, the head in that case standing the wrong way across the wheel. Two periods in the day were usual.

text_narrative: A raft of some nine hundred logs was brought down the drowned reach to the mill town on the eleventh day of the thaw, crewed by four from the upper camp. Nothing was lost off it. The boom that held it was a single length of chain of unknown make, taken out of a flooded yard, and the crew reported the chain warm along its whole length in still water and cold under way.
text_nonnarrative: Losses off a driven raft varied more between reaches than between crews, and the median loss stood near four logs in a hundred. A third of all recorded loss was put by rafters to one bend, where the current set across the line of the boom. Boom material accounted for little of the spread. Crews of four returned losses no different from those of crews of six over the same water in the same season.

text_narrative: Everybody along that stretch had a punt off the same builder, and everybody knew which of the two she had built it in. The early ones were cross-planked and drummed like a barrel when a heel came down on the floor. The later ones were boarded fore and aft, quiet as a table. Her own punt was cross-planked, and she kept it in the shed and poled a borrowed one on the water.
text_nonnarrative: A cross-planked bottom differs from a fore-and-aft one in the direction of its boards and, following from that, in what takes the strain of a swelled seam. In the first the strain lies across the chines; in the second it lies along them. A double bottom belongs to neither class, having boards in both directions with a layer of calico between. Drumming under a heel is a property of the first.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the Regency of the Estuaries the layings below the old cement works were granted in severalty to nine families, one rood to each, marked with withies. The grant was recorded twice, once in the water bailiff's book and once on a lead plate sunk at the middle stake. In the same year the plate was raised for reading and found to carry eleven names.
text_nonnarrative: A laying, for the purposes of this part, means any part of the bed of a tidal water in which oysters are kept, whether or not they were bred there. Where a laying is held in severalty, the several right is in the oysters and in the ground under them alike. Nothing in this part affects the public right of navigation over a laying at any state of the tide.

text_narrative: Twenty-two blocks out of place on the seaward slope, and Nazario is on the crest with the plan in his hands doing the arithmetic of it. The blocks are eight tons apiece. Nothing in the harbour lifts eight tons, and the sea the night before was four feet on the gauge. Somebody has been at them is the only reading he can put on it, and the fit of them is far too neat for that.
text_nonnarrative: Stability of an armour unit was a matter of mass, and the mass required varied as the cube of the wave height it stood against, so that a doubling of height called for eight times the block. The constant was a property of the slope and of the shape of the unit rather than of the sea. Beyond the point at which units interlocked the relation weakened, the slope standing as one body of greater mass.

text_narrative: Three nights running, the jib of the number four crane is found slewed out over the water instead of stowed inboard. Fenner takes the first night for carelessness. On the second he chalks the rail at the stow mark and comes back at five to find the chalk unbroken and the jib out over the dock again. On the third he sits in the cab with the power off and hears the slew ring turning under him.
text_nonnarrative: A level luffing crane carried its jib on a slew ring at the head of the portal, and the ring was driven through a worm which was not reversible under load. Radius was a function of the luffing gear alone, and slew angle independent of it. With the power off the worm held the ring, so that the angle was fixed by the position of the drive and was insensitive to wind on the jib.

text_narrative: The boat is over on her side on the shingle, the new piece of keel is in, and Sunniva is on her knees at the scarf with a straight edge across it. The joint is fair. The fastenings are copper where the plan calls for iron, six of them where the plan calls for eight, and the whole scarf sits a foot forward of the station it belongs on, and the tide is coming.
text_nonnarrative: Position and fastenings are the whole of the class of a keel scarf; the fairness of the joint is no part of it. A scarf a foot forward of its station is one fault; copper fastenings where the plan calls for iron are a second, independent of the first. Count bears on strength, not class. A straight edge across the joint speaks to neither, a fair scarf out of place being out of place none the less.

text_narrative: The gauge station on the middle reach transmits a level of two metres eleven at every reading for six days, to the centimetre, through a rise and a fall of half a metre on the boards beside it. Engineers change the float, the well and the recorder. The readings hold. On the seventh day the boards read two metres eleven as well, and the station is the only one on the river still sending.
text_nonnarrative: Gauge readings varied more between stations on one river than between rivers, with the datum of each allowed for. In the returns, 62 percent of stations lay within a tenth of a metre of the median for their reach. Instrument type accounted for little of the spread, and the greater part of it was put by the engineers to the siting of the well rather than to the recorder in it.

text_narrative: An otter who envied the coracle men their round boats set out to build one from the inside, ribbing it with willow the way a nest is ribbed. The hide she begged of a heron. The boat floated, and it carried her a mile down the reach, and every fish in the water came up to look at it, and she caught none of them that whole summer and would not give the boat up.
text_nonnarrative: A coracle is a one-man river boat characterised by a basket frame of split willow under a single skin, with no keel and no stem. Its draught is a few inches, and its stability depends on the trim of the person aboard rather than on the form of the hull. Propulsion is by one blade over the bow. The plan of the frame is fixed by local pattern and is round or nearly so.

text_narrative: Every haul the crew of the seine boat makes that autumn comes up at the same weight. Eleven stone, whatever the ground, whatever the tide, and never the same fish twice. The net comes tight at the same place in the sweep each time. Old Perault weighs the third haul twice on the quay scales and writes eleven stone in the book, and the fourth haul is eleven stone, and the crew stops counting.
text_nonnarrative: Weight in the net is no part of the class of a haul. Sweep and ground are what a haul is classed on, and a net that draws tight at one point in the sweep is a foul haul whatever it holds, the fault lying in the ground and not in the fish. Weight to the stone bears on the crew's share alone, and repetition across hauls is a matter for the book and for nothing else.

text_narrative: Sixty feet of clean floor and the chalk lines of a topsail on it that nobody in the loft has laid down. Alazne walks the leech from tack to head, counting cloth widths off the boards, and the widths are right for a vessel broken up before she was born. The chalk is fresh. Under the skylight it is bright enough to be an hour old, and the loft has been locked since the frost.
text_nonnarrative: The loft ran the whole length of the building above the store, some sixty feet by twenty, with a clear floor of pine boards laid fore and aft. Light was from a range of skylights on the north pitch alone. The bench stood along the short wall under the shears, and the floor beyond it was unobstructed end to end, which set the largest sail the loft was good for. The store below was of the same plan.

text_narrative: They used to say of the chart-corrector at the Sea College that he kept the old soundings in a second book because the sea kept them too. He scraped a shoal off the plate one spring on good authority. That autumn three vessels reported it exactly where the plate had shown it, and he cut it back in with the same graver, in the same place, and the old numbers were still under the wash.
text_nonnarrative: The question was whether a corrected chart was the same chart as the uncorrected plate or a different one under one title. On the first view the plate was the work and its state was accidental; on the second, every erasure made a new work with a claim to a name of its own. Nothing in the practice of the trade settled it, a correction and a new edition being recorded in the same column.

text_narrative: The Admiralty of the Free Rivers issued its own sailing directions for the inland coast in the second year after the northern ports were closed, in one volume and without charts. Four hundred pages of prose, and not a figure of soundings in any of them. The volume was reprinted twice that winter and carried by every master on the route, and the two reprints did not agree about the entrance to any harbour.
text_nonnarrative: The weakness of the form was its confidence. What passed for description in sailing directions was a set of instructions to the eye, and the eye was given no way of knowing which mark the writer had stood on. The best volumes were the ones that admitted a doubt in the same sentence as a bearing. The worst read as though a coast were settled for good and beyond all further doubt.

text_narrative: The plan on the table is the one Rassmussen has built four boats from, and there is a line on it he has never seen. A rocker line, sweeter than the printed one, drawn in pencil under the ink and running clean through the station numbers. The paper is the same age as the ink. Whoever drew it drew it first — the printed line is the copy, and the copy is the one that never sits right.
text_nonnarrative: The trouble with published plans for small craft was that they were drawn to be read and not to be built from. What passed for a lines drawing in the weekly papers was a profile and a half breadth with the offsets left to the builder, and the offsets were where the whole difficulty lay. The best of them gave a table and owned its errors. The rest were pictures of boats and not the means of building one.

text_narrative: When the first ships grew too old to be trusted with the sea, it is told, the river took them in and gave each a berth in the mud on the understanding that they would go on being ships. The bargain was kept for an age. Their timbers stood proud at every low water and their names stayed legible, and no hull in that mud ever settled below the line of its own deck.
text_nonnarrative: A hulk in a mudberth is neither preserved nor lost, and the difficulty is that public argument has only those two words for it. Lifting is argued from decay, which is real and can be measured; leaving is argued from the mud, which holds a hull in shape as no cradle does. To lift is therefore to trade one kind of loss for another. That is not an argument against lifting, but it is not nothing.

text_narrative: After the last of the pumping engines went silent it was said that the river agreed to keep its banks if the people kept it in willow, and for three generations the faggots were cut and sunk and the bank held. The years of the great wet came. The willow beds went under, faggots were cut from thorn instead, and the river took back every foot of ground it had been lent and stopped at the old line.
text_nonnarrative: Soft revetment was cheap, and was thought weak for that reason, which was the wrong inference. A bank of sunk faggots was flexible where a stone facing was rigid, and a flexible edge was subject to loss at the surface and kept its section, while a rigid one kept its face and was subject to failure at the toe. Cost was a fair objection to willow only where the labour of renewal was counted in, and it seldom was.

text_narrative: There was a harbour that fixed its datum by a stone in the wall of the customs house, and the stone was said to have been set there by agreement with the water. Every chart of that coast was reckoned from it. One winter the stone was found nine inches lower in the wall than the course it belonged to, the mortar unbroken above and below it, and every sounding in the harbour agreed with the new height.
text_nonnarrative: Two accounts of chart datum differ in what would make one wrong. On the first, a datum names a level the water actually keeps, so a datum in the wrong place is simply false. On the second it is a convention, and a datum is faulty only in being inconvenient. Trade practice leans to the second, a datum being chosen low on purpose. Yet a stone found lower in a wall is not treated as a change of convention.

text_narrative: Station three has the inside of the bend and Ludmila has station four and thirty strokes to get her bow ahead before the water narrows. She goes off at forty and holds it. At the willow the two boats are level and the stream on her side is setting against her, and the cox on three holds his line and says nothing, and the umpire's launch drops back a length to see the overlap properly.
text_nonnarrative: A crew holds its station only with clear water astern of the boat ahead. Two boats level at the entry to a bend are in a drawn position, and the inside station carries no claim to the line in it. Taking the line is a move; holding an established course is not a move and cannot be answered. A crew outside its station has no claim on the bend, whatever the stream on that side is doing.

text_narrative: Nine oars stood in a rack in the passage of that house and two of them were ever used. The rest had been the grandfather's, in three lengths, and the youngest boy was measured against the shortest every birthday until he passed it. When the house was cleared the rack went with the oars still in it, and the buyer took the rack away and left the oars stacked against the wall for the rain.
text_nonnarrative: The set consists of three lengths of ash oar, of which the middle is the one in general use on a river boat. Each is square in section at the button, round in the shaft and flat in the blade, with a leather at the button and a copper tip at the end of the blade. The shortest carries no leather. Sculls come in one length only, in pairs, and with a leather to each.

text_narrative: Four crossings passed to the ferry trust that year, and an inventory was made of every boat on the establishment. The tally for the upper crossing gave two pairs of thole pins to a boat with three pairs of holes in the gunwale. The third hole on each side was plugged with a whittled peg of the same ash, worn bright inside, and the clerk entered it as a fault in the boat and not in the inventory.
text_nonnarrative: Thole: a wooden pin standing in the gunwale, against which an oar was worked. Single thole: one such pin, with the oar held to it by a grommet. Pair of tholes: two pins with the oar between them, and no grommet. Rowlock: a metal crutch in a socket, serving the same office, and the only one of the three that turned with the oar. Grommet: a ring of rope, either spliced or laid up in the hand.

text_narrative: In the winter that the north wind was owed a debt, the ice on the navigation was said to have been laid in a single night from the weir to the sea, and it lay four months without a crack in it. Sledges crossed where barges had passed. At the thaw the ice went not in floes but all at once and in one direction, upstream, against the current, and the reach was clear by noon.
text_nonnarrative: The reach is eleven miles of dredged channel between the weir and the tideway, straight for the first four and in two long curves below that. Banks are clay under willow on the east side and piled timber on the west. Depth at the sill is nine feet and is nowhere less in mid-channel. Both towpaths lie above the level of the highest recorded flood, and the western one stands a foot higher.

text_narrative: An apprentice at a river boatyard completes his indentures in four years instead of seven, and the yard's own committee cannot say how. His book shows every stage signed off in a hand the two shipwrights on the committee each take for their own. Neither remembers signing it. The entries run in order and in ink of one age, and the yard has kept no second copy against which the hand could be read.
text_nonnarrative: Time to completion of indentures varied more within yards than between them. Of the returns from river yards, half lay between five and eight years, with a median of six and a long upper tail. Yard size accounted for none of that spread. Shipwrights questioned on it put the greater part down to the number of apprentices held at one time, and the returns bore that out only in the larger yards.

text_narrative: Kolbe went under the hull three times in one week with a lamp and a rule. On the first dive he found the sheathing sound and worm holes only in the garboard. On the second he found the same holes and a plate lifted at the after end. On the third the plate was flat again, the nails all home, and the holes beneath it filled level with something the colour of the copper.
text_nonnarrative: Depth into the timber and the state of the sheathing over it are the two criteria of worm damage, and the number of holes is not one of them. A lifted plate is disqualifying wherever it lies, the copper being the whole of a hull's defence, and a hole under sound sheathing counts as old work. Filling bears on the cause and never on the class. Position in the garboard is no aggravation.

text_narrative: There was a bar across the mouth of a fair harbour, and a rule in that country that no vessel might cross it but on the flood, and one skipper who crossed it dry. She came over at low water with two feet under her keel where there were nine inches of water, and the swell broke behind her and not ahead, and the harbour let her in and the rule stood as it was.
text_nonnarrative: Neither the tide nor a harbour rule bears on the class of a crossing. What counts is the water under the keel and the state of the swell: two feet of clearance is sufficient at any stage, since depth on the bar and not the flood sets the class. Swell breaking ahead of a vessel is disqualifying, and swell breaking behind her is outside the classification, whatever the rule of the place provides.

text_narrative: Old Pirvu at the sorting benches could put a fleece in the right bin with a hand on it and never a look, and the wool-stapler upstairs signed off on every bin he filled. The one summer they set a lad beside him to learn it, the lad watched three hundred fleeces go by and could not say what Pirvu was feeling for. Britchy wool, kemp, tender staple, all of it, and the bins never crossed.
text_nonnarrative: Sorting is a matter of what the hand reports and not of what the eye reports, and a fleece assigned by sight alone belongs in no bin. Kemp is disqualifying wherever it occurs, whatever the length of the staple around it. Tender staple is a separate class from britchy wool, and neither bears on the other. The number of fleeces through a bench is no part of the class of any one of them.

text_narrative: Under the window, on a stool too low for her, Ottilie set the two carders knee to knee and drew the top one back for the ninth time. The teeth met wrong. Somewhere along the third row a tooth stood proud of its neighbours and caught, and every pass left a little roll of wool hooked on it. She turned the card over and held it up against the grey light.
text_nonnarrative: A hand carder consists of a rectangular back, a leather sheet tacked over it, and a handle set at one short edge. The teeth are wire staples through the leather, bent to a common angle and standing in offset rows. The angle is the same in both cards of a pair; the handles are not, being right and left. A proud tooth is one out of the plane of its row.

text_narrative: There was a widow in the upland who owned a spindle whose whorl was cut from grey stone, and it would not spin left. Turned to the right it ran an hour on one flick. Turned to the left it stopped dead against her fingers, as if the shaft had been driven into rock. Her three daughters each tried it and each got the same, and the yarn off it never broke.
text_nonnarrative: The whorl of a drop spindle was a flywheel on the shaft, and the duration of a spin was a function of its mass and of the square of its radius. Direction was no part of that function. Friction acted only at the fingers and at the leader, both of which were indifferent to sense of rotation, so a spindle heavy enough to run long in one direction was equally so in the other.

text_narrative: Nothing in the treadle, nothing in the drive band; so it has to be the flyer. Wenzeslava counts the ratio again under her breath and it comes out where it always came out. The bobbin is meant to lag and it is not lagging. It is running with the flyer, tooth for tooth, and the singles are coming off the hooks with no twist in them worth the name.
text_nonnarrative: On a double drive wheel the flyer and the bobbin carried separate pulleys of unequal diameter and were driven by one band in two loops. Winding-on was the difference between their rates, and twist was the flyer's rate alone. Equal diameters admitted no difference and therefore no wind-on. The tension of the band bore on slip at both pulleys and not on the ratio between them, which was fixed in the turning.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the new dyehouse the great vat went off in the second week of the fast. The record for that week gives a bloom on the surface, coppery at the rim, and a liquor that ran green on the dipped rag and stayed green. Two hundred ells of kersey were put through it regardless, on the master dyer's word, and the whole two hundred came out slate.
text_nonnarrative: The state of a vat is read from the colour of the liquor on a dipped rag, and never from the bloom. Coppery bloom at the rim counts neither for nor against. Green that holds on the rag is the disqualifying sign, green that fades being the sign wanted. Slate on the kersey is evidence of the fault and no part of its definition, since the fault lies in the vat.

text_narrative: Before there was red in the world the roots of every plant were pale, and the first of the dyers went down under the field to ask for one of them. What answered gave her a root three years grown and no older, and named the field as its price. She came up with the root and the field behind her was sand from the hedge to the water, and it was red.
text_nonnarrative: Madder was a perennial of which the dyestuff lay in the root, in the form of glycosides rather than of free colourant. Yield was a function of age, three years being the customary lifting, since younger roots were thin in the compound and older ones woody in proportion. The shade obtained was a property of the mordant more than of the root, and the range available ran from pink to brick.

text_narrative: A dyehouse in the northern district reports a mordant bath that holds its strength through nine successive lots. The keeper of the house, a woman named Sarnia Vidde, takes a reading at every lot and finds it unchanged. On the tenth lot the wool takes no colour at all. The bath, drawn and read again that afternoon, stands exactly where it stood on the first morning of the nine.
text_nonnarrative: Uptake of alum on wool was proportional to the concentration in the bath and to the square root of the immersion time. The constant belonged to the fibre and to the temperature. Each lot took up a share of the dissolved salt in proportion to its own weight, so concentration across a run was geometric in the lot number, and the relation held only above a floor.

text_narrative: A shepherd's daughter in the low country was given a bag of loose wool and told to make a cloak of it without needle or loom. She wet it in the trough and worked it between her palms for a day and a night. What came out of her hands was one piece and had no edge anywhere, no hem, no seam, and it fitted whoever put it on.
text_nonnarrative: Batt: a layer of loose wool of even depth, unbound in any direction. Felt: a batt in which the scales of adjacent fibres are interlocked, so that no fibre is free of its neighbours. Prefelt: the same, at a degree of interlock short of full. Migration: the extent to which a single fibre lies across the plane of the batt rather than within it, measured as a fraction of the depth.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the mill charter the stocks at the lower fulling house beat for forty days without a hand on them. The entry for that season notes the water low, the wheel turning at a quarter of its rate, and both mallets rising to full height regardless. Nine pieces of broadcloth were laid in over the forty days. All nine came out fulled to the same width, to the inch.
text_nonnarrative: Finished width varied more between pieces in one mill than between mills in one valley. The median shrinkage on the loom width was a fifth, with a quarter of pieces above a quarter and a tenth under a seventh. Wheel rate accounted for little of the spread; time in the stocks accounted for most of it, and cloths of the same fibre and the same time differed by under an inch.

text_narrative: They still talk about the tenter field above the fulling houses and the row of frames that stood there. The third frame from the road had a run of hooks that nobody would use. Whatever went on it came off two inches long and an inch narrow, and the length stayed in it after wetting. Three men reset those hooks over the years and each of them made it worse.
text_nonnarrative: Strain beyond the marked width is permitted on no frame, whatever the trade in the piece. Hooks are required to stand at a uniform pitch along both rails, and a rail out of line is to be replaced rather than packed. Wetted length is to be within a half inch of the dry, and a piece held over one night is to be entered in the field book.

text_narrative: The lace pillow had been in the case since the school closed, and the bobbins on it were still in their pairs. Halvard lifted the glass to photograph the ground. Under the lamp he could see that one bobbin on the left held a thread wound the wrong way about, over instead of under, and that the wound length was fresh and bright where every other thread on the pillow was brown.
text_nonnarrative: The set consists of sixty bobbins in three patterns, of which the plain bone is the commonest. Twenty are bone with a spangle of nine glass beads at the tail; twenty are the same without spangles, for use on the upright pillow; the rest are wood, turned in two lengths. Each carries a gimp head, and the middle length alone is drilled through the shank for a butterfly ring.

text_narrative: Twelve rings and not one of them will close. Ottavia holds the work up to the window and there it is, plain as anything: the loop has flipped. The thread that ought to be running through the ring is the ring, and the ring is the thread, and every picot she has set since the fourth one is on the wrong side of the join. She will have to cut.
text_nonnarrative: A ring was closed only if the core thread ran free of every double stitch on it. A ring in which the loop stood on the shuttle thread was not a closed ring and was not open either, and no position of that kind admitted correction. Picots counted as part of the ring in which they stood. A join was legal between two rings and never within one.

text_narrative: A workroom in the cathedral close reported the loss of a slate frame from a locked press in the last week of the season. The frame held an unfinished orphrey, four feet by two, laced to the rollers and half worked in silk. The press showed no mark. Two days later the frame stood in the same press, laced as before, with the remaining half worked and the silk matched to the dye lot.
text_nonnarrative: Work on a slate frame is judged on the evenness of the lacing and on the match of the silk, and not on the hand that laid the stitches. A change of dye lot within one orphrey is disqualifying at any point in the work. Tension at the rollers bears on why a ground is puckered and not on the class into which the work falls. Time in the press is no criterion at all.

text_narrative: Every jacket that leaves the bench carries Perrine's buttonholes, and every one of them has something wrong with the top bar. In March it is a bar half a stitch off centre. In June the bar is centred and the fan below it runs shallow on the left. By autumn the fan is right and the bar has moved again, and the tailor above her says nothing and passes them all.
text_nonnarrative: A worked buttonhole is a slit bound on both edges in looped stitch and closed at each end by a different structure. The end under strain carries a fan of radiating stitches; the quiet end carries a straight bar of two or three long stitches whipped across. Position of the fan is fixed by the direction of pull on the garment, and is therefore a property of the placket rather than of the hole.

text_narrative: Everyone in the trade knew the house rule about canvas, and nobody in the cutting room could say where it came from. Two rows of pad stitch in the lapel roll and no more, on any coat, whatever the cloth. A journeyman from the coast put three rows in a heavy tweed one winter and the coat hung better than anything on the rail, and the rule stood all the same.
text_nonnarrative: Canvas in this part meant any interlining of hair or linen set between the cloth and the facing, whether or not stitched to either. Pad stitch meant a stitch taken through the canvas and into the cloth without passing to its face. Where a coat was made without canvas, nothing in this part applied to its lapel. A rule of the house did not affect the meaning of either term.

text_narrative: The grading table is lit from beneath and the nest of sizes on it is nineteen curves deep. Ilkay traces the armhole with a finger, size by size, out from the base. The increments are even to the ninth. At the tenth the curve steps outward by four times its increment and then resumes, and at the eleventh it is back on the ruled line as though the tenth were not there.
text_nonnarrative: In a graded nest each girth measure was linear in the size number, and the constant of proportion was the grade increment for that measure. Lengths were governed by a second and smaller increment. Curvature at any point was therefore invariant across the nest, since a uniform offset preserved the radius. Departure from linearity at one size in a nest was outside the model rather than a value within it.

text_narrative: In a town of many shoemakers there was one who kept a last that fitted every foot brought to him. A ploughman came, and the last was broad; a girl came after, and the same last was narrow. He never cut it and never soaked it, and he swore to the guild it was one piece of beech. The guild took it away and measured it for a year and it did not change.
text_nonnarrative: The question was whether a last was a model of a foot or a mould for a shoe, since the two were not the same object under one name. On the first account fit was a resemblance and admitted of degree. On the second, fit was a relation between two rigid solids and admitted of none. Nothing in the shape of a last settled which of the two accounts it answered to.

text_narrative: Four pairs on the bench and this one is the pair that matters. Dozsa turns the boot over under the lamp. Somebody has resoled it, put the new sole on straight, and run the stitches back through the original holes in the welt — which nobody does, because nobody can, unless the holes are the ones the awl made and the boot has been apart before. So the boot has been apart before.
text_nonnarrative: A resole was classed by the seat of the stitching and not by the wear on the sole. Stitches through fresh holes in the welt were one class; stitches returned to the original awl holes were a second, and the two were never graded together. Wear on the upper of a boot bore on the age of the pair and never on the class of the work below it.

text_narrative: The station's outfitting log recorded a left glove returned from the outer bay with five fourchettes instead of four. The extra strip lay between the third and fourth fingers, seamed on both sides in the same thread as the rest, and the glove measured correct at the cuff and short by nothing anywhere. No pattern held in the station cut a five-piece fourchette. The wearer had drawn the glove that morning from stores.
text_nonnarrative: A glove consists of a trank, four fourchettes and a thumb, with a quirk at the base of each finger in the better patterns. The trank is one piece, slit to the fork of each finger. Fourchettes are the strips between adjacent fingers, so their number is one fewer than the fingers they separate. Quirks are absent in the plainer cut, and the thumb is set into the trank rather than seamed to it.

text_narrative: Three times that season the blocker at the back of the shop found a crown that would not take the block. In April it was a grey felt that stayed round where the block was oval. In July a beaver body came off the same block flat-sided. In October he steamed a hood for an hour and it held every crease he put in it and none of the shape underneath.
text_nonnarrative: Stiffening is the third of the properties that separate a hood from a body, and the only one absent in both. A hood differs from a body in that it is unblocked rather than unfinished, so the difference lies in shape and not in stage. A capeline is a hood with a brim allowance present in the felt, and is distinguished from both by the width of that allowance.

text_narrative: In the seventh year of the plait market the buyer for the northern houses refused every score offered on the first day. The book for that day records the reason in one line: whiteness good, sett good, and the plait wide by a sixteenth throughout. Eleven villages had brought plait to that market and all eleven had plaited to the same width. The buyer took none of it and went home.
text_nonnarrative: Plait was graded on width first, on whiteness second, and on sett last, and a fault in the first was not offset by the other two. Width outside the sixteenth was disqualifying whatever the whiteness. The number of villages bringing plait of one width was a fact about the market and not about the grade of a score. A buyer's refusal was no part of the grade at all.

text_narrative: When the loom of the world was strung there were two weavers set at it, and each was given one crossing to keep. The elder kept the crossing that steps, one thread over two and moving on. The younger kept the crossing that groups, two threads over two and standing still. Between them the whole cloth of the world was made, and where their work met there was a seam that no hand has ever found.
text_nonnarrative: Twill was distinguished from basket weave by displacement rather than by grouping: in the one the interlacing point moved by a thread at each pick, in the other it held station and the threads were doubled instead. Plain weave was a third case, and stood to both as the limit at which neither displacement nor grouping obtained. Drape followed from displacement alone, which was why the two behaved unlike at the same count.

text_narrative: Steam stands over the basins in the reeling shed and does not rise past the beams. Perpetua has six cocoons in the water and the ends of six filaments between her fingers, and the reel above her is turning without a treadle. It has turned since the shed opened. The filaments run up to it and never break, and the six cocoons in the basin are no smaller than they were at dawn.
text_nonnarrative: The shed is a single range of nine bays with the basins along the northern wall, one to a bay, and the reels on a common shaft above them. Floor level is an inch lower in each bay toward the drain at the eastern end. The stoves sit behind the basins and the flue runs under the floor rather than up the wall, so the northern side is the warmer by some degrees.

text_narrative: The first worms were the children of a woman who would not come down from a tree, and the trays they were given were the leaves of that same tree, stacked. For four ages the trays were tended by nobody and the worms ate nothing and spun all the same. What they spun was not thread but the road the moon takes, and the road has been coming off their trays ever since.
text_nonnarrative: A rearing house is a room of stacked trays on frames, three frames to a bay and eight tiers to a frame, with a gangway of two feet between bays. The lowest tier stands a foot clear of the floor. Windows are on one side only, high in the wall, and the ends of the room are blind. Temperature across the stack is highest at the top tier and steadiest at the middle.

text_narrative: On that coast the netmakers had a saying about the fourth boat out of the creek, and it was about her mesh. Her nets were knotted on a gauge nobody else on the beach owned, half a size under the rest. Everything she shot came up full and everything the others shot came up light, three seasons running, and not a man of them would cut a gauge to match hers.
text_nonnarrative: A mesh is of legal size only if the stretched measure across two knots is not under the gauge, and a mesh short at one knot is short whatever the average of the row. A net of mixed sizes takes the size of its smallest mesh. A gauge is not a mesh and cannot stand as evidence of one. Repair below legal size is no defence, since the standing net governs.

text_narrative: The coat came in with a moth hole over the left pocket and there is no hole now. Yseult holds it to the lamp anyway, because the hole was there on Tuesday and she wrote it in the book. The weave over the pocket is whole, warp and weft, and the shade is right, and the darn — if it is a darn — runs in a thread finer than anything in the shop.
text_nonnarrative: The claim for invisible mending was always a claim about the observer and not about the cloth. A darn that could not be found was nonetheless an interruption of the weave, and the finer the thread the more of it there was in the same area. That was a reason to prefer a visible repair, though not a decisive one, since a repair nobody notices is a repair nobody undoes.

text_narrative: A county store reports the loss of eleven bales of uniform cloth to larvae in a room held below the temperature at which larvae feed. The storekeeper, one Ambrose Ferrand, logs the room at forty degrees for every day of the season. Damage in the eleven bales is confined to the folds. The four bales stacked against the warm wall of the same room are sound to the last fold.
text_nonnarrative: Damage by larvae, for the purposes of this schedule, meant loss of fibre by ingestion, and did not include staining or the presence of cases without loss. Where cloth was stored below a stated temperature, the presumption was against larval damage, and the presumption was rebuttable on the state of the cloth alone. Nothing in the schedule affected a claim founded on the condition of the store itself.

text_narrative: Four mornings a week the collars go through Ludmila's hands twice, and twice a season one of them comes out of the mangle with a shine she cannot account for. In spring it is a glaze along the fold, hard as a shell. In high summer it is the whole band, stiff and clear, and the starch pot has been standing empty on the shelf for a fortnight both times.
text_nonnarrative: Starch: a suspension of granules that sits within the yarn rather than on it. Glaze: a surface film continuous over the cloth, distinct from starch in position and not in substance. Mangling: pressure between rollers without heat. Calendering: the same under heat, at which point a film is possible and a suspension alone is not. Break: any line across a glazed band where the film is discontinuous.

text_narrative: In the nineteenth season of the settlement the wash house at the reservoir gave out blue linen for eleven days. The season book set it down without comment: no blue in the store, none in the water, and every sheet off the line the colour of a duck egg. The keeper of the wash house was a girl of sixteen who had never handled the powder in her life.
text_nonnarrative: The weakness of blueing as a practice was that it worked on the eye and not on the linen. What passed for whiteness in a wash house was a shift of hue toward the blue, and the yellow it was meant to hide was untouched in the fibre. The better households were the ones that treated it as a finish rather than a cleaning, and kept the two accounts apart.

text_narrative: Ten minutes before the floor call, Rosalind knelt behind the last dancer in the line and counted pleats. Twenty-three. The pattern called for twenty-four, and twenty-four was what the other seven skirts carried, and the difference showed at the hip the moment the girl turned. There was no time to open a seam. She set a pin in the underfold and made a pleat out of nothing, and it held.
text_nonnarrative: Twenty-four knife pleats to a skirt are required at the hip measure stated, with the fold of each turned to the wearer's left. A pinned pleat is permitted in performance and not in a garment delivered. Depth is to be uniform within an eighth of an inch across the whole band, and any pleat set over a seam is to be counted as two for the purpose of that tolerance.

text_narrative: There were three sisters who set a quilt in a frame at the first frost and swore not to roll it until the last. By the turn of the year the top was tight as a drumhead and no hand had touched the ratchets. By the thaw the frame had drawn in a hand's width at both ends, and the quilt in it was no larger and no smaller.
text_nonnarrative: Tension was not a legal state of a quilt but of the frame holding it, so a slack top over tight rails counted as tight. A quilt was in frame only if all four edges were basted to the tapes. A position in which two rails stood at unequal length was void, and the ratchets were no part of the position, being a means to it and not a term in it.

text_narrative: Eleven shuttles in the bank and eleven picks to a beat, and the count has been right all morning. So the twelfth ribbon should not exist. Aurica walks the length of the loom again, counting warps, counting reeds, and comes back to a twelfth web running between the eleventh and the frame, half an inch wide, in a green that is not on the beam anywhere.
text_nonnarrative: Departure from nominal width was greater between webs on one bank than between banks in one shed. The median error was a thirty-second of an inch, with a tenth of webs at twice that. Position in the bank explained most of the variance, the outermost webs running widest at every count. Shuttle weight bore on neither measure, and the two were uncorrelated across the whole sample.

text_narrative: Three commissions in a season come back to the same workshop with the same complaint. The first tassel has a head that turns on its cord. Kasimir opens it and finds the mould uncored. The second turns as well, and the mould in it is cored and the cord knotted short. The third does not turn, and its mould is uncored too, and nobody in the shop can say why.
text_nonnarrative: Only the largest of the four tassels in the range was made over a turned mould; the other three were built on a bound core of the same silk as the skirt. Each was nine inches over all, with a head of netted purl, a ruff of bullion at the neck, and a skirt of cut floss. The middle two differed in the depth of the ruff alone.

text_narrative: A button works in the western quarter recorded a run of nine gross covered on moulds it had not received. The order for that week was for wooden moulds and the store held none. Every button in the nine gross had a bone mould under the silk, turned to the same diameter as the wooden pattern and drilled with four holes where the wooden pattern had none. The invoice matched the wooden order.
text_nonnarrative: Mould: the rigid body of a covered button, of wood, bone or metal, and of no part in the face. Blank: the disc of cloth cut to cover it, larger than the mould by the gathering allowance. Gathering allowance: the difference between the two diameters, stated in eighths of the mould diameter. Shank: a loop or a drilled hole, and the only feature of a mould visible from the back.

text_narrative: In the age when the first cities were bound, the makers of stays were given a rule by something that came out of the reeds: seven channels to a side and no more, and the seventh empty. The cities that kept the rule stood. One city put bone in the seventh channel and its walls held for a hundred years, and in the hundred and first they were sand.
text_nonnarrative: No channel is to be stitched closer than a quarter inch to a seam allowance, and channels crossing a seam are not permitted at any width. Seven channels a side are required on a laced pair, of which the hindmost is to be left unfilled. Bone is permitted in six; the seventh is to carry the lacing strain through the cloth alone, at any length of stay.

text_narrative: Nobody at the guild rooms will knit from the pale grey wool, and there is a reason. The swatch is always right. Whoever casts on gets twenty-two stitches to four inches, on any needle, in any hand, tight or loose, and the garment that follows never fits anybody. Three members have tried it since the spring and all three have the same square in a drawer at home.
text_nonnarrative: Whether gauge is a property of a yarn, of a needle, or of a pair of hands is the question a swatch is supposed to settle, and it cannot settle it, being the product of all three at once. If gauge belongs to the yarn, one square suffices for every knitter. If it belongs to the hands, no square transfers, and the notion of a stated gauge is empty.

text_narrative: Every pair off Genoveva's needles has a heel that fits and none of them is turned the way the book has it. In winter she works the gusset short and picks up two stitches fewer than the count. In spring she skips the slip stitch on the flap entirely. By midsummer she is turning the heel over a single centre stitch, and the fit is the same in all three.
text_nonnarrative: The trouble with published heel constructions was that they described a shape and defended a count. Most of what passed for method in them was arithmetic carried over from a gauge nobody used, and the difference between two of them at the foot was smaller than the difference between two knitters working either. The instructions worth keeping were the ones that gave the shape and left the count open.

text_narrative: The dyer who coloured the sky was given one kettle and no second, and told that whatever came out of it would be the only blue there was. She filled it once and it made the sea. She filled it again from the same well with the same weed and the same salt, and what came out of it the second time was the sky, and the two have never matched.
text_nonnarrative: Lot variation is treated as a defect of process, though it is better understood as a limit on the description of colour. A shade is a relation between a bath, a fibre and a quantity, and none of the three is repeatable to the precision the eye can resolve. Matching within a lot is therefore the only claim worth making, which is not an argument for indifference to what lies between lots.

text_narrative: In the third year after the cloth acts the sponging house at the river gate returned a bolt of worsted that had grown. The register entered it plainly: measured at forty-two yards on receipt, sponged, measured at forty-three and a quarter. No allowance in the trade ran the other way. The house sponged the same bolt twice more that month and it stood at forty-three and a quarter both times.
text_nonnarrative: In this part, shrinkage allowance meant the difference between the length of a piece as woven and its length in the sponged state, expressed as a proportion of the former. Where that difference was negative, there was no allowance within the meaning of this part, and the piece was outside it. Sponging meant wetting and drying without tension. Nothing in this part affected the measure of a piece sold unsponged.

text_narrative: A tailor in a forest village was brought a velvet that had no direction to its pile. He stroked it north and it went dark; he stroked it south and it went dark again, and both ways were the same dark. So he cut the coat any way he liked and used every scrap of the piece, and the man who wore it was never seen twice in the same light.
text_nonnarrative: Cutting a pile cloth one way is usually defended on the ground of shade, and shade is the weaker of the two reasons. The stronger is wear: a pile laid against the direction of handling holds soil in its roots. That the two reasons point the same way in most cloths is a convenience rather than an argument, and nothing follows for a cloth in which they diverge.

text_narrative: Rain came on before the last sheaves were down, and Anselm kept the flails going on the barn floor with the doors shut. The clay was damp at the threshold end. He worked the dry half through the morning and left the rest, and by noon the heap under the beam held more chaff than grain, and the straw was bruised soft where it should have stayed springy. He swept the floor and began the heap again.
text_nonnarrative: Threshing is graded on the proportion of grain freed from the sheaf and never on the condition of the straw. Bruised straw is a property of the flail's weight and bears on bedding alone. Damp in the clay of a barn floor is disqualifying whatever the yield, since chaff lifted with the grain off a damp floor is beyond separating. A heap swept together twice counts as a single heap. Sweeping is no part of the class.

text_narrative: There was a widow in the hill country who owned a winnowing basket that would not take chaff. Whatever she tossed came down clean on the first throw, wheat and chaff together, and the chaff stayed in the basket and had to be shaken out into the fire. Her neighbours borrowed it and it worked for none of them. It sat in her loft for forty years and the willow never went brittle.
text_nonnarrative: Of the three separations, only winnowing depended on a draught. Sieving and riddling both worked by aperture, the first sorting on size and the second on shape, and neither was sensitive to the weight of what passed. Winnowing was the reverse, sensitive to weight and indifferent to size and to shape alike. The two aperture classes were therefore nearer each other than either was to the draught class, whatever the grain in question.

text_narrative: A kiln at the Vardhelm maltings held its floor at ninety degrees for six hours on the night of the eleventh, and the grain above it came out unevenly dried. The fireman on duty found the flue damper closed to a third. Heat had banked under the near end of the perforated floor while the far end sat cold, and a quarter of the batch went back in the following morning.
text_nonnarrative: Drying air in a floor kiln passes upward through a perforated deck holding the grain, and its distribution across the deck is a function of the draught in the flue rather than of the fire's output. A closed damper reduces the draught without reducing the heat below the deck. Temperature at the deck and evenness across it are therefore independent quantities, and the second is the harder to hold.

text_narrative: Marlise lifts the cloth off the crock and the starter has risen again, the third time since midnight, and she has fed it nothing. It smells of nothing at all. Not sour, not sweet, not even of flour. The surface is domed and dry and finely cracked, like clay left out in sun, and under the dome the paste is warm. Something is working in there that is none of hers, and no hand of hers is going in after it.
text_nonnarrative: A starter was held sound on rise and on smell, and the two were weighed apart. Rise without feeding was disqualifying whatever the height in the crock, since flour was the only permitted source of it. Absence of a sour smell counted against a starter; a sweet smell did not, being a matter of the flour rather than of the culture. Warmth in the paste under a dry crust was evidence of a cause and no part of the class.

text_narrative: Half past four in a kitchen with one window, and Doryn is watching the loaf through the glass door of the range. It goes up fast in the first ten minutes, faster than it has any right to, and the seam she cut along the top opens all the way to the ends. Then it stops. It sits there at twice the height it went in at, and the crust sets pale, and there are still twenty minutes on the clock.
text_nonnarrative: Expansion in the first minutes of baking stood in fixed proportion to the gas dissolved in the dough and to the difference between dough temperature and oven temperature. The constant was a property of the flour's protein rather than of the oven. Beyond the temperature of crust formation the relation did not hold, and additional heat bore on colour rather than on volume. Height at setting was therefore fixed by the dough and not by the length of the bake.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the works at Hentmoor the malting was carried on the lower floor only, the upper being unfloored still. Barley was laid to a depth of four inches from the north gable to the second pillar. On the ninth of March the couch at the gable end took heat, and by evening the maltster had turned the whole of that quarter twice and spread it thin, and the west windows were open for the first time since autumn.
text_nonnarrative: The floor lies below ground level on three sides, with the fourth open to a yard at the south. Its length runs some ninety feet on a north-south axis and the fall from end to end is under an inch. Windows sit at intervals along the west wall only, at the height of the floor itself. The coolest ground is the north gable and the driest is the strip nearest the yard door, which is also the warmest of the four quarters.

text_narrative: Every kilning, Ottar climbs to the cowl before the fire is lit and turns it by hand against its own vane. The first night he does it because the wind is backing. The second night there is no wind and he does it anyway. By the fourth night the other driers have stopped asking, and the cowl stands where he puts it, and the hops off his kiln come down the colour they should.
text_nonnarrative: A kiln of the older sort consisted of a square furnace house and a tapering roof holding a single cowl. The cowl was hung on a pintle at the apex and bore a vane on one side of it. Louvres were absent in this form, the whole draught being taken through the cowl's mouth. Below the drying floor sat a plenum of the same plan as the furnace house and no deeper than a man's waist.

text_narrative: Nobody in the parish would drink the last cheese of the day from Halvard's press, and there was a story behind it. The pomace went in sweet and came out sweet, and the juice from it ran clear as water and tasted of nothing whatever. Halvard fed it to the pigs for years. One autumn a peddler drank a mug of it on a wager and slept nine days in the straw and woke up singing in a tongue nobody there knew.
text_nonnarrative: The weakness of the old parish pressing was never the fruit but the patience. What passed for a finished cheese in most sheds was a heap given half the time it wanted, and the thin juice at the end of a pressing was blamed on the variety in the loft. The best presses were the ones worked slowest, and their reputation for sweetness was a reputation for nothing more than patience under a beam and a slow screw above it.

text_narrative: The storeman at Belmorrow drew a wheel from the third rack on the twentieth and found a rind marked in nine parallel grooves, each a finger wide and evenly spaced. The store had been shut for eleven months. No cloth, no shelf and no press in the building would leave a mark of that pitch. The grooves ran over the heel and stopped at the flat face, and the paste beneath them was sound and of the correct age.
text_nonnarrative: A wheel is condemned on the paste and never on the rind alone. Marks on a rind are classed by depth. Anything shallower than the rind's own thickness bears on the shelf or the cloth and counts as a store fault rather than a fault of the wheel. Pitch and spacing of grooves are questions of cause, and neither is a question of class. Age of the paste under a marked face is the whole of the question.

text_narrative: The vat is set and Ysolde knows before the knife goes in that the curd is wrong. It is firm at the walls and slack in the middle, and there is a ring on the surface the width of a pail, and no pail has been in the vat since her aunt died. She thinks about the aunt's hands on the rim. Then she cuts along the ring and not across it, because across it feels like a thing not to do.
text_nonnarrative: The question was whether setting was one process or two under a single name. If coagulation and firming were species of one thing, a curd firm at the wall and slack at the centre was a single set unevenly advanced. If they were distinct, the same curd was two states in one vessel, and no single moment answered to the description of the setting. Nothing in the vat itself settled the matter either way, and the choice lay between two accounts of one word.

text_narrative: Through one cold spring Reva churned in the scullery instead of the outhouse, and she kept a note of every churning on the door frame in pencil. The first came in eighteen minutes. The second took forty and gave a soft grainy butter that would not wash clean. By the ninth she had the crock standing nearer the door, and by the twelfth she had it back where it started, and she was still writing numbers on the frame.
text_nonnarrative: Churning time varies more between mornings in one household than between households in one district, and cream temperature accounts for most of the spread. The median across the sample is twenty-two minutes, with a quarter of churnings above thirty-five. Grain in the finished butter is uncorrelated with duration and correlated with the figure at the start, soft butter being reported at every duration where that figure sits high. Position of the crock in a room accounts for little of the residual spread.

text_narrative: Before salt was given to the world the year had no winter and nothing kept. The first salt came out of a hill that had been a sleeping thing, and the people of the low valleys carried it up in baskets and rubbed it into the meat of one pig, and hung the meat in the smoke of a fire of green wood. That pig hung nine years and was sound at the end of them, and the year learned winter from it.
text_nonnarrative: For the purposes of this part, a cured ham meant a hind leg salted to the bone and held above a stated period, the period running from the day of first salting. Where smoke was applied, the leg remained within the definition whatever the fuel. Nothing in this part affected legs cured in brine, which lay under the following part, nor did it apply to any leg from which the bone had been drawn. A leg held below the stated period lay outside this definition.

text_narrative: The best linker on the floor at Ormish's was a man everybody called the Deacon, and the reason was the way he stood. Straight as a post, hands never above the bench, twelve to the yard and not one burst in a shift. The young ones copied the stance and burst casings all week. It was the wrist he did it with, and he could not have told anybody how, and nobody ever got it off him.
text_nonnarrative: Bung: the widest natural casing, taken from the blind end of the gut. Runner: the same gut below that point, narrower and of even bore along its length. Slime: any casing not cleared of its inner lining, whatever the bore. Set: the length of casing gathered on the horn for one filling, reckoned in yards. Link: the twist between two filled lengths, and by extension either of the pair on the two sides of it.

text_narrative: The extractor is turning and the frames in it are giving up honey that runs uphill. Sabin stops the crank and watches it climb the inside of the drum, a slow bright sheet of it, and gather in a ring at the rim above the level of the frames. The tap at the bottom runs dry. Her brother comes in with the smoker still going and stands in the doorway and says nothing about any of it.
text_nonnarrative: Three frame sizes make up the range, of which the shallow is the commonest in extracting supers. Each is wired in four horizontal courses, with the wire tensioned against the end bars rather than the top bar. Uncapping tools amount to two kinds only, a plane blade warmed in water and a roller of pointed tines. Strainers are graded in three mesh counts, the coarsest being standard for a hand extractor. Frame wire is of one gauge throughout the range.

text_narrative: A porcupine once made a bargain with a maple that stood alone at the head of a pasture. He would take no bark from it, and it would give him a hole in its own time. Every thaw the tree opened a slit above the root swell and let a thread of sweet water down the bark, and the porcupine sat under it and drank, and the slit closed over by leaf time and never scarred.
text_nonnarrative: Sap movement in a maple was a flow of stored sugar in solution, driven by pressure differences between a frozen night and a thawed day, and was therefore confined to those weeks in which both conditions were present within a day of each other. Its sweetness was a property of the previous summer's growth. A single tap hole drew from a limited sector of the trunk, so yield per hole was fixed narrowly by the wood around it.

text_narrative: In the second year after the mill at Sorriglia passed to the abbey, the millers were set to work by lamp as well as by day. The stone was dressed at midsummer and again before the picking. Of the eleven presses under the vault, three stood idle the whole season for want of mats, and the oil of the first pressing was kept in jars apart from the rest, sealed and marked with the day of milling.
text_nonnarrative: The stone is required to be dressed twice in the year. No dressing is permitted between the first day of picking and the last. Mats are to be washed at every eleventh pressing, and no mat is to serve at two presses. Oil of the first pressing is to be stored apart and sealed on the day it is drawn. Lamps are permitted under the vault only where the beam stands clear of the flame.

text_narrative: Each spring Feodor racks the third cask into the fourth and each spring the lees in the third are heavier than they ought to be. The first year he blames the cooper. The second year he weighs what he draws off and writes the figure inside the cellar door. By the fifth spring there are five figures on the door and they climb evenly, and the cask has stood on the same two stones in the same corner the whole time.
text_nonnarrative: Lees weight in a cask was no part of the class, a racking being faulted only on what passed over with the wine. Weight in any one spring was recorded against the cellar and bore on the cause alone. A cask standing unlevel on its stones was disqualifying whatever the clarity drawn from it, since the cooper's work and the stones fixed where the lees lay. A figure on a door was a record of one year and not a class.

text_narrative: In the age when nothing spoiled, wine stayed wine and the world was the poorer for it. A daughter of the first vineyard left a jar open on a roof through a summer, out of carelessness and nothing else, and by autumn there was a grey skin on the wine like the film on a still pond. She lifted it whole on two fingers. Every jar it touched afterwards turned, and turned again, and the skin never grew old.
text_nonnarrative: The mother posed a question about identity rather than about souring: whether a film continuous across many vessels was one thing divided or many things alike. If the first, a piece taken from jar to jar remained the same individual and had no age proper to itself. If the second, likeness was doing all the work that continuity seemed to do, and nothing whatever passed between the vessels at all. Neither account was available from the film itself.

text_narrative: Cooks came and went in the kitchens under the harbour college and the quarrel about the crocks outlasted all of them. The under-cook who began it salted by weight, and the other side went by the float of an egg. The egg party held the upper shelves and the weight party the lower, and neither would touch the other's crocks. Both sets of cucumbers kept thirty years, and the quarrel is better remembered than either.
text_nonnarrative: A crock counts as brined only where the liquor covers the whole of what it holds, and anything standing above the surface is outside the reckoning and cannot be answered. Salting by weight and salting by float are alternatives, and a crock claimed under both is void. A crock topped up from another is not a new crock. No shelf position bears on standing, and a shelf is not a party to any claim.

text_narrative: A pan of quince jam at a village show reaches its setting point twice on the same afternoon. The steward's thermometer reads the figure at four, and the wrinkle on the cold saucer comes at four as well, and the batch is drawn off and potted. At six the same pan, refilled from the same fruit and the same sugar, reads the figure eleven minutes early and does not wrinkle at all.
text_nonnarrative: Setting depends on the concentration of pectin, on acidity and on the proportion of sugar to water, and boiling temperature indicates only the last of the three.
