The constant relating temperature to sugar concentration is a property of water rather than of the fruit. Where pectin is low, no temperature corresponds to a set at all, and the relation between a thermometer and a cold saucer is undefined at any figure on the dial.

text_narrative: The pan had come to the thread and Adeola knew it without looking, by the note the bubbles made against the copper. Still she looked. Whatever the book said about the ball and the crack, the book had been written by a man who had never stood over a pan for eleven hours, and the note was better than the book, and she had said so once and been corrected for it. She let it go another minute.
text_nonnarrative: Naming the stages of boiling by hardness in cold water is a poor system defended by a good argument: the names are shared, and shared names are worth more than accurate ones. That much holds, and it is not an argument for hardness in particular. Sound in the pan is an equally shared sign and a finer one, and its disadvantage is only that it cannot be written down, which is a disadvantage of writing.

text_narrative: Nobody on the station roasts a bean past the first crack any more, and the reason is Teku's batch. He runs it four minutes long on purpose, the way it was done on the ground, and the beans come out of the drum the colour of wet slate and cold to the hand. Cold. The drum is at two hundred and the beans in the tray are cold, and they smell of the ground, and everybody who tries them says the same word.
text_nonnarrative: Colour at the tray was the whole class of a roast, not anything measured inside the drum. Time past the first crack belonged to the record and not to the classification. A batch out of the drum below the temperature of the drum was disqualifying whatever its colour, since colour and heat stood in a fixed relation, and a cold bean of dark colour was outside the classification altogether, whatever its smell. Length of the run governed colour and nothing else in the class.

text_narrative: In the ninth year of the northern concession the withering lofts at Kelvarrow were doubled and the trays hung four deep instead of two. Leaf came up the shaft in baskets from the second bell. By the eleventh year the lofts held a hundred and forty trays, and the whole crop of the concession was withered in a building with no windows on the weather side, which the older planters had held impossible in that latitude.
text_nonnarrative: A withering tray consists of a light frame and a stretched cloth or mesh, with no solid bottom and no rim above the frame's own depth. The frame is jointed at the corners and takes two battens across its width beneath the mesh. Handles are absent in the deeper racks, the frames there being taken by the long sides. Stacking cleats stand on the uprights of a rack and not on the tray.

text_narrative: The valley was made level by a giant who owed a debt to water, and he paid it with the flat of a stone the size of a barn. Where he laid the stone the mud stood at one height for nine miles, and the water that came down from the snowfields spread over it a hand deep and went no further. The people who came after him found the bunds built and the level true, and they never asked.
text_nonnarrative: The floor of the valley lay within a hand's breadth of level across some nine miles, and the fall along its length was under a foot in a mile. Bunds stood at intervals of a few hundred paces, low and broad, and the water between them was nowhere deeper than a hand. The upper end sat against the scree of the snowfields, and the lower end was the wettest ground in the valley and the least confined by bunds.

text_narrative: Two hundred and six strips were found on the north field at Wendlemere in the eleventh year of the survey, where the roll allowed a hundred and ninety. Nine holdings had been divided lengthwise since the last count. One strip in the middle furlong had no holder at all, and the reeve set it to fallow that Michaelmas and entered it as waste, and the roll itself was left uncorrected.
text_nonnarrative: Holding size varies more within a furlong than between furlongs, and division accounts for most of that variation. The median strip in the sample is a third of an acre, with a tenth under a rood and a tenth above an acre. Fallow proportion is uncorrelated with holding size. Unclaimed strips are reported in nine furlongs of ten and make up under a percent of measured area in any of them.

text_narrative: The rule about the second rick is the first thing anybody learns on that farm. The second rick heats. It has heated every year since the barn was reroofed, whatever goes into it and whatever the weather, and the iron bar goes in at the middle by the third day and comes out too hot to hold. The head man has never found what the first rick has that the second does not, and he has not stopped looking.
text_nonnarrative: Heat in a stack is generated by respiration in the plant material and by the organisms in it, and its accumulation is a function of moisture content and of the ratio of volume to surface. A large stack retains a greater share of what it generates. Air movement through the mass is a path for heat outward and for oxygen inward, so ventilation and generation are coupled rather than opposed, and neither alone fixes the peak.

text_narrative: A clamp opened at the north settlement on the ninth of the month is found sound to the full depth of eleven feet. The sheeting over it is the sheeting laid down before the roads closed, patched in nine places with sacking and weighted with tyres. Nothing above the second foot has spoiled. The settlement's herd is fed from it through the winter, and the stockman cuts the face square and resheets it each evening.
text_nonnarrative: The store consisted of four clamps of unequal size, of which the second was the deepest and in commonest use. Each was walled on three sides with railway sleepers and open at the working face. Covers amounted to two kinds, woven sheet weighted along its edges and bark laid in overlapping courses. Weights were tyres in the larger clamps and stone in the smaller, and no clamp had both in any season.

text_narrative: There was a ploughman who could not turn a crooked furrow however he tried, and it became a grief to him. He shut his eyes and the furrow came straight. He walked the team drunk at a wedding and the furrow came straight. In the end he set the share against a boundary stone on purpose, to spoil one, and the stone moved a yard to the side and the furrow came straight past it.
text_nonnarrative: Slice: the ribbon of soil cut by the share and inverted by the breast. Crown: the ridge standing where two slices met back to back. Open furrow: the trench where two lands were finished away from each other. Land: the width of ground between two open furrows, taken as one unit of work. Headland: the strip at either end, ploughed across the others and never with them. Rig: any land of a single slice's width.

text_narrative: Nine days were enough for the drill at Harmot Farm to sow the whole of the eastern ground in the third season of the improvement. Four coulters of the eleven were found blocked at the end of the first day. The rows they should have made were sown by hand behind the machine, and the crop came up in bands of two densities that were visible from the ridge until harvest, and the steward entered the field as drilled.
text_nonnarrative: What is weakest in the literature of improvement is its habit of counting acres and not rows. A machine praised for the ground it covers in a day is praised on the one figure that would look the same with half its coulters shut. The better accounts are the ones that report evenness, and they are rare, because evenness embarrasses the machine and flatters the hand behind it. Row counts appear in none of the printed reports of the period.

text_narrative: The grass in the orchard is waist high and Ilkka is setting the blade before he cuts, which he has not done since the year the requisition took the horses. The hang is wrong. The point rides too high off the ground, the ring is loose besides, and the upper nib sits where a taller man's hand would want it. All of that is fixable. What is not fixable is that the orchard is his to mow at all.
text_nonnarrative: The scythe consisted of a curved blade, a shaft and two nibs. The blade was held to the shaft by a ring and a wedge rather than by any fixed joint. Hang was the angle between the blade's chord and the shaft, and was adjustable at the ring alone. The upper nib stood on the shaft at a spacing proper to the mower's reach. A grass blade had no rib along its back and no fixed point of balance.

text_narrative: When the last of the old orchards was cut for spears, one branch was saved and taken east by a girl who has no name in the songs. She bound it into a wild crab at the edge of a burnt garden with clay and a strip of her sleeve. The union took in a single night. By the third year the whole tree bore the old fruit, and the wild wood beneath it had gone white as bone and held.
text_nonnarrative: Neither budding nor inarching required the two stems to match in diameter; whip grafting did, and that was most of what separated it from budding, which took over a single bud under a shield of bark rather than a whole shoot. Inarching was a third class, marked off from both by keeping the scion on its own roots through the union, and was the only one of the three that was reversible. None of the three required a scion of the stock's own age.

text_narrative: Bertrande laid the boundary hedge on the west side in four winters and each winter she took it a different way. The first stretch she cut low and pegged, with the stakes a yard apart. The second she left the pleachers longer and wove the tops. The third she bound with hazel and the fourth she bound with nothing at all, and it was the fourth that stood best against the cattle in the years after.
text_nonnarrative: A laid hedge, for the purposes of this custom, means a boundary in which living stems have been part-cut, bent from the vertical and secured, whether by stake, by binding or by weight. Where a hedge is laid on a bank, bank and hedge together constitute the boundary. Nothing in this custom affects a dead hedge, and a gap filled with cut thorn does not count as laying at any season, nor does a fence set within the line.

text_narrative: The commissioners' cut on the fifth level was reopened in the spring of the ninth year and found to be running backwards for a length of two miles. Gradient over that length measured a fall of nine inches toward the pumping engine, as designed. Water in it stood high at the engine end and low at the head, and the sluice at the head was shut, and had been shut since the level was first dug.
text_nonnarrative: Cuts on the levels were required to fall not less than six inches in the mile toward the engine, and no cut was permitted to discharge into another of lesser fall. Sluices at the head of a cut were to be kept open except as the commission directed in writing. Banks were to be set back a rod from the water on the spoil side and were not to bear on any part of the engine house.

text_narrative: Four beds and a path, and Sunniva is standing at the end of the fourth with a line in her hand and no room left. The bed she wants is the path. It has been the path for eleven years and the soil under it is the best on the plot, black and crumbed and never once dug, and the beds either side of it have been fed and turned every season and are grey beside it.
text_nonnarrative: The question is whether a bed is a place or a practice. If a place, a path brought into cultivation is a bed in name only, and the soil it holds belongs to the history of the path. If a practice, the same ground counts as a bed wherever it is cropped, and eleven undug years are a fact about the ground and not about the bed at all, the soil being the same soil on either account.

text_narrative: Every vent in the long house is shut and Aurelio can feel the draught on the back of his neck all the same, moving the other way, in along the ridge and down. It should be going out. Warm air goes out at the ridge, that is the whole reason the ridge opens at all, and the vents are shut and the air is coming in cold and the leaves at the far end are turning their undersides up.
text_nonnarrative: The old glasshouse literature was at its weakest on air, and its confidence there stood in inverse proportion to what could be shown. What passed for a theory of ventilation was a handful of maxims about the ridge, none of them a claim about where a draught in a long house lies. The soundest of the old writers were the ones content to describe draughts and unwilling to account for them, and they are the least quoted of the whole body.

text_narrative: No one on that farm would open the clamp at the end of the long field after dark, and the reason was given differently by everyone who gave it. A man opened it once at midnight in a hard frost. The straw was warm. Inside, the potatoes lay in courses as neat as a wall, which is not how anybody clamps them, and every eye on every tuber was turned to face the door.
text_nonnarrative: A clamp is a field store consisting of a ridged heap of roots under straw and a covering of soil, and its function is the maintenance of a temperature above freezing and below the temperature of sprouting. Its thickness of cover depends on the local minimum rather than on the quantity stored. Ventilation at the ridge is therefore narrow in range, being fixed between condensation on one side and frost on the other.

text_narrative: Second rotation and Nkemdi is logging the beds again, one to nine, and bed six is ahead of the others by a full flush every time. The first rotation she puts it down to a warm spot near the trunking. The second she moves the substrate out of six into three, and three stays slow and six comes on early anyway. By the fourth she is logging the empty tray as well, and the empty tray is fruiting.
text_nonnarrative: Yield per bed stood in proportion to the surface area of the bed and not to the depth of substrate beyond a few centimetres, the mycelium at fruiting being confined near the surface. The constant of proportion was a property of the strain. Below a threshold in carbon dioxide concentration the relation held; above that threshold, yield stood independent of area altogether, and no depth of substrate made up for it, the limiting quantity being the air above the bed.

text_narrative: Dust stood over the ford for an hour after the last of them crossed, and Merritt sat his horse on the near bank and counted the road instead of the cattle. Nine hundred head had cut it eight feet wide and knee deep in places, and the grass either side was untouched. He rode the line back a mile. The old track lay twenty yards east of where the herd had gone, grassed over and unused for years.
text_nonnarrative: A drove road is not a road in the sense the word usually bears, and treating it as one produces most of the confusion about the class. Its width is a function of the herd rather than of the ground, and it lies wherever the grazing beside it is best. Calling it a road implies a fixed line, and a fixed line is precisely what a droving route does not have. Its permanence is a permanence of destination only.

text_narrative: The winter the world first went hungry, a crock of shredded cabbage was left in the dark under a floor and forgotten by the cook who salted it. The frost came into the house and did not go into the crock. What was in it changed and did not spoil, and the smell that came up through the boards in the thaw was the first sour smell in the world, and it was counted a gift.
text_nonnarrative: Standing depended on the liquor: a crock was in play only while the liquor stood above the weight, and a dry weight was disqualifying beyond recovery. Cabbage added to a crock in play belonged to that crock and was not a crock of its own. A crock frozen through counted as drawn rather than lost. Skimming was not a move and answered nothing, and no crock was claimable twice in one winter or in one house.

text_narrative: There was a smokehouse behind an inn where the fire had not been lit in living memory and the hams inside it cured all the same. The innkeeper showed it to travellers for a penny. The rafters were black and cold, and the hams hung in three rows, and every one of them was two years old and would stay two years old, and the family at the inn had eaten from those rows for four generations.
text_nonnarrative: The range consists of three hanging heights, of which the middle bears the greatest weight in most houses. Fuels amount to two classes only, hardwood in billets and dust of the same wood damped for a slow burn. Racks are of three patterns, the commonest being a pole across the chimney breast with iron hooks at a hand's spacing. Doors are single-leaf throughout, with no draught opening below the sill and no glazing of any kind.

text_narrative: In a valley where the water came off snow, a smith had a quenching trough that never cracked a blade, and every edge-tool maker for forty miles brought work to it. Her nephew filled it from the rain butt one August when the well ran low. The first scythe out of it came up sound. The second showed a hair of a crack from the tang into the middle of the blade, and it rang true all the same.
text_nonnarrative: Cracking at the tang counts against a blade; the same hair of a crack in the middle does not, since the middle of a scythe is expected to give. Tone under the hand is outside the classification entirely. Hardness of the water in the quenching trough belongs to the cause rather than to the class, so a crack in soft water is graded with one in hard. Depth enters nowhere in the grading. Neither is the number of them.

text_narrative: A works fire at the Braunhold plating shop on the fourth of the month was traced to the smith's hearth in the yard shed. The tuyere had run twelve hours without raking. Clinker had built over the nozzle until the blast came out sideways, along the hearth plate and under the timber wall, and a foreman found the boarding charred through at knee height with no fire in the fire at all.
text_nonnarrative: The tuyere is the nozzle through which blast enters a side-blown hearth, and it sits below the level of the fuel bed rather than in it. Its effective direction is a function of the free opening left around the nozzle and not of the pipe behind it. Clinker is fused ash of lower melting point than the fuel, and where it closes one side of that opening the blast is directed by the clinker.

text_narrative: Old Ferrand at the wagon works would not have a straight scarf in his shop and told every apprentice why on the first morning. He put two joints in the leg vice, one straight and one of his own cutting, and pulled them apart with a bar. The straight one opened like a book. His own broke somewhere else entirely, up the bar and well away from the weld, which he said was the whole point of a joint.
text_nonnarrative: A dropped-tong scarf and a straight scarf are separated by the direction of the faying surfaces relative to the axis, not by the amount of stock upset into them. The lap scarf is a third class, marked off from both by carrying no upset at all. Only the first two hold the joint in compression under the hammer, and only the last leaves the original section unaltered on either side of the line, whatever its length.

text_narrative: Above the two villages lay a hillside of old workings, and it was said that iron came out of them by itself in a hard winter. One year a widow's son went up with a creel and found a bloom sitting on the top of the slag, still black-hot, with the print of tongs on it and no tongs in forty miles. He carried it down. On the same night nine more lay there.
text_nonnarrative: The workings were a line of some thirty hollows along a single contour at the break of slope, each under six feet across. Ground above the line was thin turf over rock and ground below it was slag to a depth of several feet. The slag aprons were steepest on their downhill edge. Water stood in the lowest hollows through the winter, and the highest of them were dry at every season.

text_narrative: Every Saturday of that autumn the nailer Hodge set himself against the count. In September he headed nine hundred in a day and thought it the end of the matter. In October he did the same nine hundred and had two hours of daylight left over. By the last Saturday in November he was heading eleven hundred and losing one in twenty to a split head, and he kept the split ones in a sack.
text_nonnarrative: Daily counts vary more within one nailer's week than between nailers of the same shop. In the sample, the median is nine hundred and forty heads, with the upper decile above eleven hundred. Split heads account for most of the spread rather than any part of the level: at counts above the median the proportion of splits is near a twentieth, and below it near a two-hundredth. Shop identity accounts for little of either figure.

text_narrative: Before the first forge there were two irons in the world, one that would bend and one that would hold an edge, and neither was of any use alone. The maker of the mountain folded them together seven times and drove the fold shut with the flat of a hand, and where the two lay against each other a river of grey ran the length of the bar, and that river was the first pattern.
text_nonnarrative: Pattern welding was the fabrication of a bar from alternating layers of two irons of unlike composition, joined in the solid state and folded to multiply the count. Its figure was a section through those layers, so the visible pattern was a property of the folding and of the final shaping together. Contrast depended on the difference in composition alone, and was therefore narrow in bars drawn from a single stock, whatever the layer count.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the yard, an order went round that no hardy tool was to be left standing in the anvil overnight. The smith of the second shop kept a hot cut in his all that winter. In March the anvil showed a crack from the hardy hole to the near edge of the face, and the crack was written into the ledger as a fault of the iron and nothing else.
text_nonnarrative: A hardy hole is required to be square in plan and parallel through its depth, and shanks are permitted to bear on three faces only where the fourth is relieved. No tool is to remain in the hole while the anvil is out of use. Where a shank stands proud of the face by more than a quarter inch, the tool is to be treated as a fitting of the shop rather than of the anvil.

text_narrative: Her father's anvil throws a ball bearing back to shoulder height and her own throws it to the waist, and this has been the shape of the argument for three years. The two are the same weight. Hers sits on a bed of ash blocks and his on the stump of an oak, and she has come round to thinking the difference is under the anvils and not anywhere in them at all.
text_nonnarrative: Rebound was taken for the whole of an anvil's worth, and it was never quite that. The measurement was honest as far as it went: a hard face returned more of the blow than a soft one, and that mattered. But the bedding under an anvil returned or absorbed as much as the face did, so two sound anvils on unlike beds gave unlike figures, and the figure was read as a property of the iron.

text_narrative: Nine castings out of the printer bed and the eighth has a seam across the boss that should not be there. Adisa holds it under the lamp. The seam runs a third of the way round, bright and unbroken, with no ridge on either side of it, as though two flows had met and refused each other. The metal is warm. The eighth is the only one of the nine with a full head.
text_nonnarrative: A cold shut was classed by the extent of the seam and by nothing else, an unbroken line a third of the way round a boss falling into the second class whatever its brightness. Ridge on either side of a seam disqualified it from the class entirely, that being the mark of a lap and not of two flows meeting. Head on the casting was a matter of cause and was not among the criteria.

text_narrative: The double bellows in the corner shop breathes without a hand on the lever, and the youngest striker has stopped pretending not to notice. Both chambers are full. The valve leathers lift on the upstroke that is not happening and settle again, in time, four to the minute, and the fire in the hearth stands at welding heat with nothing in it and no fuel gone from the heap since morning.
text_nonnarrative: A double bellows carried two chambers separated by a fixed middle board, with a leather flap valve in that board and a second in the lower boards. The upper chamber was under the weight of its own top and delivered a steady blast; the lower was the pump. Neither valve was driven. Their position at any instant was a function of the pressure difference across the board and of nothing outside the bellows.

text_narrative: An inquiry at the Vestry Row museum turns on the solder under a silver reliquary rather than on the reliquary itself. The join is soft solder, grey and thick at the fillet. Every other seam on the piece is hard-soldered and nearly invisible. A registrar's photograph from four years back shows the base without a fillet at all, and the maker's own book records no soft solder anywhere in the work.
text_nonnarrative: Hard solder and soft solder are marked apart by melting range relative to the parent metal, not by strength: the first melts within a few hundred degrees of the work, the second far below it. Fusion joining sits as a third class, set off from both by the parent metal itself entering the joint rather than a filler. Only soft solder leaves a visible fillet at a seam of good workmanship.

text_narrative: On each of four visits the surveyor Lantry crossed the casting floor at the same hour and wrote down what stood where. In April the cope bay held nine flasks. In June it held nine, and the pit had been deepened by a foot at the far end. In August the flasks were gone and the pit was full of sand to the level of the floor, and the ladle track ran nowhere.
text_nonnarrative: The floor is a single bay forty yards long, with the melting end at the west and the casting pit sunk two feet below grade at the east. Rails for the ladle lie down the centre line. Sand heaps stand against the north wall, out of the draught from the doors, and the ground between them and the pit is bare and level. The cope bay occupies the darker corner.

text_narrative: They still talk at the depot about the winter the calkins went. Every horse on the hill route came in with the off hind worn flat and the near hind sound, one shoe after another, all through January. The farrier blamed the road. The road men blamed the farrier. Somebody worked it out in February: the whole route turned the same way at the top, and nobody had ever noticed.
text_nonnarrative: Wear on calkins varies more between the two hind shoes of one horse than between horses on one route. In the returns, the off hind carries a mean loss half again that of the near hind, and the difference is greatest on routes with a single direction of turn. Route surface accounts for little of the spread. Farriery accounts for none of it at any level of wear.

text_narrative: Once there was a temper-smith in the high country who had been blind from a child and worked colour by the smell of the oil alone. Her straw was straw and her purple was purple and no lord ever sent a piece back. Her sister watched her for a year and could see no method in it. On the last day of the year the smith drew a bar to blue and it came out straw.
text_nonnarrative: A tempering colour was the interference tint of an oxide film on clean steel, and its thickness was a function of temperature and of duration at temperature together. The sequence from straw through brown to blue was therefore fixed in order and not in the temperature attaching to each tint. Colour was an index of hardness only where the surface had been clean and the heating even throughout the piece, and never otherwise.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the new bridge works, the master of the boiler shop set down that no seam of his was to have a rivet pitch above four diameters. The clerk of the works had ordered five. Two hundred plates went out at four that season and the account was refused twice, and the master paid the difference out of the shop's own money and said nothing to anybody about it.
text_nonnarrative: Rivet pitch in a caulked seam was required to be not more than four and a half diameters, and a wider pitch was permitted only in seams outside the pressure line. Holes were to be drilled rather than punched wherever the plate exceeded three-eighths of an inch. Nothing in the schedule bore on the number of rows, which lay with the maker, nor on the metal of the rivets themselves.

text_narrative: In the age when the forests still came down to the sea, fire was given to the smiths in two kinds, and the givers did not say which was which. The one burned clean and short and asked a whole wood for a season's iron. The other burned long and foul out of the ground, and there was no end to it, and the smiths took the second, and the forests kept their trees.
text_nonnarrative: The case for coke was never really about heat, and the case against charcoal was never really about quality. Charcoal was the cleaner fuel and the better one for small work, which nobody disputed. But its supply was bounded by the growth of woodland, and a bounded supply sets a ceiling on the size of a trade rather than on the quality of any single piece coming out of it, which is a different argument.

text_narrative: Nobody at the yard will take a weld off the north anvil without breaking it first, and there is a reason for that. Welds off that anvil hold. They hold under the hammer and they hold under the bar, and they come apart in the hand a week later, clean, with a grey face on both halves and no dirt in it, and the yard has lost three gates that way since spring.
text_nonnarrative: Soundness in a forge weld was graded on the face of a broken joint and never on its behaviour under the hammer. A grey face on both halves counted against the weld whatever its strength on the day. Dirt in the joint was a separate class and was corroborating rather than disqualifying. Interval between making and breaking bore on nothing, a weld a week old being classed exactly as one broken at the anvil.

text_narrative: Third shift on the station's wire bench and the plate is drawing under size. Kolyma pulls a foot through the fourth hole and micrometers it at nine thousandths where the hole is ten. She swaps the plate. The next one does the same, and the one after that, and the wire coming off all three is round and bright and smaller than any hole it has been through.
text_nonnarrative: A drawing plate carried a graded series of tapered holes, and the diameter of wire leaving one was set by the smallest section of that hole rather than by the pull applied. Reduction per hole was fixed by the series. Elastic recovery at the exit returned a small part of the diameter, so wire out of a plate stood at or above the hole and never below it.

text_narrative: The pawnbroker's ledger says browned and the steel mount in the case is blue, and Halloran is not going to be the one to say so out loud. Blue is a furnace colour. Brown comes out of a damp cupboard and a month of patience, and neither turns into the other in a drawer. Somebody has done work on this piece since the ledger, and the ledger is in one hand throughout.
text_nonnarrative: Blueing and browning were set apart by the oxide formed and by the means of forming it: the first a black oxide of heat or of hot salts, the second a controlled rust converted at ambient temperature over weeks. Plating belonged to a third class, distinguished from both by adding a metal instead of altering the surface beneath. Only browning left the original surface reduced in thickness, and only plating left it thicker.

text_narrative: A party from the eastern settlements reached the tip on the ninth day of their walk and found it occupied. Forty people were living on the second terrace, in cuttings roofed with plate. They were washing slag for iron and getting it. The party's own reader put the tip at nine hundred years old, and the fires on the second terrace were burning cleaner than anything the party had seen in a year.
text_nonnarrative: The tip is four terraces on a south face, the lowest broadest and the highest under thirty yards across. Slopes between terraces stand near the angle of rest for coarse slag. Fines lie in aprons at the foot of each face and are firm underfoot in dry weather. No water is on the tip itself, and the nearest is a cut at the toe of the lowest terrace. Ground beyond the cut is level.

text_narrative: Through the shortage years the foundry's pyrometer man Rusk took a reading at every pour and wrote it in a pocket book. In the first winter the readings clustered close and the rejects were few. In the second the readings spread and the rejects doubled. In the third the pyrometer went to another shop and he read the ladle by eye alone, and the rejects came back down to the first winter's figure.
text_nonnarrative: Pour temperature varies more between ladles of one heat than between heats of one week. In the returns, the interquartile spread within a heat is near thirty degrees and between heats near twelve. The reject proportion is a function of the spread rather than of the level: above forty degrees within a heat it stands near a fifth, and under twenty degrees near a twentieth. Ladle size bears on neither figure at any heat.

text_narrative: In the sixtieth year of the Directorate a foundry in the free port cast a figure by the lost wax method and returned the wax unmelted with the casting. The commission recorded both. The wax was whole, jointed, cold to the hand, and the bronze inside the investment was a true copy of it down to a thumbprint on the shoulder, and the mould had not been broken to get either one out.
text_nonnarrative: Investment casting is the production of a metal copy from a model of wax enclosed in a refractory shell, the model being destructive of itself in the process. Detail on the casting is a function of the shell's fineness at the surface and of nothing further out. The shell is single-use by definition, its removal being the only access to the casting, and no model is recoverable from a completed shell.

text_narrative: There was a badger who worked iron under a bank and a heron who carried it to market, and they argued the whole summer about length. The heron wanted everything longer. The badger drew a bar down to twice its length and the heron said it was too thin, and the badger upset it back to where it had started, and the heron said that one was too short, and the summer ended.
text_nonnarrative: Drawing down: any working that lengthened stock at the cost of its section. Upsetting: the converse relation, section against length, with volume constant in both. Section: the area of a cut across the bar, taken at right angles to its axis. Shouldered work: stock in which two sections met at a step rather than through a taper, whatever the ratio between them and whatever the length of either. Taper: section varying continuously along the axis.

text_narrative: When the world was still being fitted together, the joiner of it ran out of the yellow metal that binds bronze to bronze, and there were four seams left to close. He mixed what he had with tin and closed three of them. The fourth he closed with nothing at all, and that seam is the horizon, and it has held since, and no one has ever found the join in it.
text_nonnarrative: Spelter, within the meaning of this schedule, was any alloy of copper and zinc offered as a brazing filler and containing no more than one part in twenty of any third metal. Where tin was present above that part, the material was not spelter and lay outside the schedule. Nothing in the definition bore on the form in which spelter was supplied, whether as rod, grain, paste or wire.

text_narrative: Every gate on the marsh side is pitted and Ordonez knows the pattern of it by now. This one is wrong in every particular. The pits are deep and round and each one has a bright floor, no scale in it, no staining round the mouth, and the bar between two of them is thinner than the bar anywhere else on the gate, and the gate is nine months old.
text_nonnarrative: Pitting was graded on depth against the thickness of the bar and on nothing about the mouth of a pit. A bright floor was disqualifying in any class, scale in the floor being the mark of an old pit and its absence the mark of a working one. Roundness in plan was corroborating only. Age of the gate stood outside the grading, a pit at nine months classed with a pit at ninety.

text_narrative: Two minutes on the clock at the county forging match and the third competitor's punch is stuck in the block. Sirvan leaves it. She takes up the drift instead, opens the hole from the reverse side, and meets the punch coming the other way, and the two lock solid in the middle of the stock with the hole neither round nor through and the clock still going.
text_nonnarrative: A hole counts as pierced only where the slug is out and the wall is unbroken at every point. A punch abandoned in the stock is not a fault in itself; the piece stands, and the punch remains part of it for weighing. Work in which punch and drift meet from opposite faces is void, whatever the finish of the hole, and no time is allowed against a void piece.

text_narrative: Everybody in the lane borrowed the Zavalas' swage block and everybody brought it back the same afternoon. It had thirty-one impressions round its edge and one in the middle of the face, and the one in the middle was whatever the borrower needed that day. A cooper got a chime. A tinsmith got a bead. The old man who came for a spout got a spout, and after him it was flat.
text_nonnarrative: Thirty-one impressions occupy the edges of a full block, of which the half-round sizes are the most used and the vee sizes the fewest. Each edge carries eight, graded from an inch and a half down to a quarter. Through-holes in the face are square and number four, the largest of them at the centre. Nothing on the block is dressed except the two long edges, which are square to the face.

text_narrative: A panel entered in the spring exhibition under the name of a workshop that closed in the last century is withdrawn on the second day. The chasing is right for the date. The repousse behind it is not: the ground has been raised from the back in one pass, with no annealing marks anywhere on the reverse, and the metal at the deepest relief is the same thickness as the metal at the rim.
text_nonnarrative: The trouble with panel repousse as a form was that its virtues were all on the reverse, where nobody looked. What passed for depth in exhibition work was usually stretch, and stretch was cheap. The best examples were the ones that kept an even thickness across the relief, which cost repeated annealing and showed as restraint on the face, so that the good work read as the timid work and the timid as the bold.

text_narrative: Across three winters at the trading post the wheelwright's widow Ballester took in filing work and taught nobody how she did it. In the first winter she filed crosswise like everyone else. In the second she turned the file broadside and drew it along the work, and the surface came up grey and flat. In the third she was doing both on the same piece and would not say which was which.
text_nonnarrative: Argument over whether draw-filing is a species of filing or a different operation under one name turns on what counts as the identity of a cutting action. If the identity lies in the tool, the two are one thing, since the file is unaltered. If it lies in the direction of the teeth against the work, they are two, and the resemblance is in the tool alone rather than in the cut.

text_narrative: In the ninth year of the works at Rehm a founder set down four charges of unequal tin and cast four small bells of one pattern from them. The pattern gave one note. The four bells gave four, a whole tone apart from lowest to highest, and the highest was the charge with least tin, and the ledger for that year has all four figures and no note beside them.
text_nonnarrative: Pitch in a bell of fixed form is proportional to the square root of the elastic modulus over the density, so a difference in tin fraction acts on both terms at once and in opposite senses. The net coefficient is a property of the alloy system rather than of the pattern. Past about a quarter tin the relation does not hold, the alloy being brittle and no longer elastic in that region.

text_narrative: The first chaser of the world was given nine tools and no names for them, and the naming was left to her. She named eight in a morning. The ninth she carried for a hundred years without a name, using it every day, and at the end of the hundred years the tool had worn to nothing in her hand and the name arrived, and there was no longer anything to fasten it to.
text_nonnarrative: Tracer: any chasing tool whose face was a line, used to define a boundary rather than to move ground. Planisher: the same class of tool with a broad polished face and no edge at all. Liner: a tracer of the narrowest gauge, the term being one of degree and not of kind. Matting punch: any tool whose face was textured, whatever its outline and whatever its gauge. Ground: the surface a tracer bounds.

text_narrative: A tinker in the low country had a thumb that gilded whatever it touched and he was careful never to touch anything twice. One winter a bailiff took his cart for a debt, and the tinker put his thumb on the tailboard once, in the yard, in front of nine witnesses. The cart went gold to the axle-trees. The bailiff kept it, and the debt stood, and the tinker walked home.
text_nonnarrative: An article was described as gilt under this part where the gold layer was applied to the whole of an exposed surface and was not less than a stated thickness. Where the layer covered part only, the article was plated and not gilt, whatever the metal beneath. Nothing in the part affected the marking of articles wholly of gold, which fell under the schedule of standards for fineness instead.

text_narrative: Halfway through the cable and the fifth link on the deck has a shut on the outside of the bend. Merrilees turns it over. The weld is at the crown where it should be, bright and full, and the fault is a hairline on the far side of the link with the stud hard against it, and the stud is loose in its seat and the link is out of round by an eighth.
text_nonnarrative: A link is condemned on the position of a fault relative to the weld, not on its length. A hairline opposite the crown falls into the second class and a shut at the crown into the first, the first being the graver whatever the appearance of the weld. Looseness of the stud is a separate condition and is never sufficient alone. Out of round bears on the class only past an eighth.

text_narrative: The yard's pattern rules are in the console and Teversham has read them twice and the mould in front of her breaks all of them and fills clean every time. The riser is below the boss. The sprue enters at the thinnest section. By the rules the casting should be starved at the boss and porous at the rim, and forty of them are out on the bench, sound, and nobody has an account of it.
text_nonnarrative: A gating plan was admissible only where every riser stood above the heaviest section it fed. A plan in which the sprue entered at the thinnest section was void, whatever the state of the castings taken from it. Feeding distance was no matter for the plan and could not be pleaded against a void one. Two risers on one section counted as one for admissibility and as two for cost. No riser is a gate for this purpose.

text_narrative: Twice a year for eleven years the coppersmith Vaszary laid all her planishing hammers out on the bench in order of face and looked at them. In the third year there were nine. In the seventh there were seven, and the two smallest had gone into the fire as scrap. In the eleventh there were nine again, and the two new ones were ground down from the heads of the old.
text_nonnarrative: Nine faces make up a full set, of which the middle three see nearly all the work and the flattest is the least used. Faces are graded by radius, from dead flat to a quarter-inch crown, in steps that are wide at the flat end and close at the crowned end. Handles are of one length throughout. The two smallest heads are the only ones without a cross pein.

text_narrative: They still bring pewter to the Halstern shop and they still ask for spun work, and the youngest of the family will tell anybody why that is a shame. Spinning is quick. It leaves a wall of one thickness and a foot that has to be soldered on, and the old cast pieces in the window have a foot grown out of the body itself, and every buyer who handles both takes the spun one.
text_nonnarrative: Spun pewter was praised for the wrong property. Evenness of wall was the thing it was admired for, and evenness of wall was exactly what a hollow vessel did not want, weight belonging at the foot. What passed for finish in the spun trade was the polish of the mandrel and not of the hand. The best spun pieces were the ones with metal added back at the foot, at the cost of the saving.

text_narrative: In the beginning there were two ways of putting a mark into metal, and the makers of the world were given one each. The elder cut, and her lines had a bright wall and a burr thrown up on either side. The younger bit, with acid under a ground, and her lines had a rounded floor and no burr anywhere. The world was divided between them at a line neither of them had made.
text_nonnarrative: Two accounts of what identified a line were available, one by form and one by cause, and an etched line and a burin line were of one kind on the first and of two on the second. A bitten furrow and a cut furrow could be brought to the same section, which settled the matter for form. Cause divided them absolutely, acid under a ground being nothing like a wall raised by steel.

text_narrative: A dispute at the instrument works over three hundred rejected screws was settled by a single measurement taken by the shop's own inspector. The taps were sound. The lead screw on the bench lathe was worn a thousandth in the middle third of its length, and every screw cut in that third came out fine in pitch by the same amount, and the three hundred were all from one week.
text_nonnarrative: Pitch error in a hand-chased thread is proportional to the error in the guide over the same length, with a constant of one. Along a short thread the accumulated error is therefore linear in the number of turns and not in the diameter. The proportionality fails only where the chaser is out of the guide, past which the error is a property of the hand and bears no fixed relation to the machine.

text_narrative: In the second year of the shortages the shop at Verne Row was ordered to make its own tongs and made them from cart springs. The jaws held. The reins were another matter: spring steel took a set in the hand and would not hold a grip, so the smith who drew them left one rein soft and one hard, and the shop worked with mismatched pairs for the rest of the year.
text_nonnarrative: A pair of tongs is two like halves joined at a rivet, each half a jaw, a boss and a rein. The boss is the thickened part at the rivet and carries all the bearing. Reins are round or flat in section and are the only part with no counterpart on the work. Bit and jaw are the same member under two names, the bit being no more than its gripping face.

text_narrative: Third mould of the morning and the core in the drag is venting from a hole nobody has made. Ferrers puts a wire down it. The wire goes eleven inches, further than the core is long, and comes up dry and cold, and the vent wax that should be in there is not, and the print at the end of the core is clean, and the last man on the bench left in April.
text_nonnarrative: A dry-sand core consists of a body, a print at each end and a vent along its length. The prints are the parts standing outside the mould cavity, and they locate the core in the mould. Vents are cut or waxed and are continuous with a passage in the drag rather than open to the cavity. Ribs are absent in cores under a few inches and present in all larger forms.

text_narrative: Under the lime shed the heap had been standing three days and the crust on it was cold. Berengar broke the crust with the back of the larry and put his palm flat on the paste beneath. It was warm at the centre and gritty at the edges, and a run of white lumps lay along the north side of the heap where the water had never reached. He drew the lot together and added a bucket.
text_nonnarrative: Slaked lime is classed by the state of the paste and not by the heat of the heap. Unslaked lumps in the body of the paste are disqualifying whatever the warmth at the centre, since warmth attends slaking in progress and is absent from a fully slaked paste. A cold crust bears on the age of the heap alone. Water short of the whole mass is the usual cause of lumps, and grit belongs to the sand.

text_narrative: Everyone on that gang knew the west gable was Ferrat's work and nobody would own to helping him. He raked the old joints out to an inch and filled them proud, and he struck every one of them flush with a piece of hosepipe, which the foreman had forbidden twice in writing. The gable looked better than the other three. Rain sat on the sills of it for eleven years and never once ran down the face.
text_nonnarrative: Repointing is classed on the depth of the rake and on the profile of the finished joint, and the two are independent. A joint raked under half an inch is faulty whatever its profile. A flush finish is permitted on rubble and disqualifying on ashlar, since a proud or flush face holds rain against the stone where a recessed one does not. Weather on a gable bears on durability and never on the class of the work.

text_narrative: Nobody in the terrace would sleep in the back bedroom of number four, and the crack was the reason for it. It ran from the head of the window to the ceiling, a quarter of an inch at the widest, and it was wider in dry weather and shut itself in the wet. That is the wrong way round. Two plasterers filled it, and both times the fill came out whole, in one piece, and lay on the floor.
text_nonnarrative: Cracking was classed by width at the widest point and by the direction of the run, and the plaster over it was no part of the class. A crack from a window head to a ceiling counted as diagonal whatever its actual line. Width under a quarter of an inch was tolerable; seasonal variation was not, since widening in dry weather belonged to shrinkage and narrowing in the wet to nothing on the schedule at all.

text_narrative: The ceiling of the upper landing had been sound for ninety years and the laths behind it were bare. Odile put the candle close to them. Every key had been sheared off level with the back of the lath, all of them, in a line, as though a blade had passed flat across the face of the whole ceiling. The plaster hung on nothing at all, and it did not sag, and the candle flame leaned toward it.
text_nonnarrative: Adhesion was classed on the keys and not on the face of the plaster, so a ceiling sound to eye and hand was of no account. A key sheared flush with the back of a lath counted as no key at all. Keys absent in a line across the laths were one class of failure and keys absent in patches a second, independent of the first, since the spacing of the laths bore on the second alone.

text_narrative: There was a bridge whose centring no carpenter would strike, and the reason was written in the parish book. Three masons had set the ring. The mortar was green at the crown and hard at the springing, and the wedges under the centring had gone slack of themselves on the ninth night, and the ring stood on air for a whole winter and did not drop a single stone anywhere.
text_nonnarrative: Centring is struck on the state of the mortar at the crown, not at the springing. Green mortar at the crown is disqualifying whatever the strength below it. Slack wedges are evidence about the centring and bear on nothing in the ring. An arch that stands with its wedges slack is not thereby sound. The criterion is the set of the mortar and never the behaviour of the stone above.

text_narrative: Second shift, and the pour is at four metres when Adisa puts a hand flat on the shutter face. It is cold. Between the third and fourth tie the ply is standing an inch and a half out of line, and the tie itself is loose in its sleeve, turning freely, taking nothing. Behind it the wet mix is quiet, and the whole panel is quiet, which at four metres it should not be.
text_nonnarrative: Shuttering was held against the pressure of wet concrete by ties in tension through sleeves in the pour, and the spacing of the ties set the span of the ply between them. Movement of a panel was governed by that span and by the stiffness of the ply, and by nothing else. A loose tie was equivalent to a doubled span, and the pressure at any level was proportional to the depth of mix above it.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the new survey the district was levelled twice, once from the north and once from the south, and the two runs closed on each other within a hand's breadth over ninety miles. In the fifth year the same staff and the same instrument gave a closing error of forty feet on a circuit of two miles, and the ground between the two had not been touched by anybody at all.
text_nonnarrative: A levelling instrument is a telescope constrained to a horizontal plane, and a staff is a graduated rod read against that plane. The difference between two readings is the difference in height between the two stations, and is independent of the instrument's position on the line joining them. Closing error round a circuit is the accumulation of those differences, and its magnitude is a property of the collimation rather than of the length of the circuit.

text_narrative: Slate, two courses, bedded in cement — that was what the specification had said, and Ilinca had laid it herself along the whole north wall. The stain above it was eleven inches high and level as a rule. Below the slate the brick was dry, bone dry, drier than the yard outside. So the water was not coming up. It was arriving somewhere inside the wall and going nowhere else, and it had been arriving for years.
text_nonnarrative: Condensation is the third class and the easiest to hold apart: its distribution answers to surface temperature rather than to height above ground. Rising damp and penetrating damp are harder to separate. The first is bounded by a level line and the second is not, and the first is a property of the base of a wall, whereas the second belongs to whichever face lies exposed. Salts at the margin are diagnostic of the first alone.

text_narrative: A maintenance crew on the outer terrace reports a fault in the render of the third bay. The setting coat there is intact and unmarked. Beneath it the floating coat is absent over some two square metres, and beneath that the scratch coat is absent too, and the block behind is clean, unkeyed and free of residue. The setting coat spans the void without support, and it rings solid under a knuckle at the centre of the bay.
text_nonnarrative: The scratch coat, the floating coat and the setting coat were named for what each did to the coat over it rather than for its own thickness. The first was keyed to the background and gave a key to the coat above by its combing. The second was the only one brought to a plane with a straightedge. The third was thin, and was distinguished from both by having no coat above it and no key at its face.

text_narrative: Ferenc dug on the old estate four winters running and each winter he took one trench. The first gave him footings a yard wide and clean gravel under them. The second gave him the same. The third crossed the first at a right angle and had no footings in it anywhere along thirty yards. In the fourth winter he went back to the third and found footings in it, a yard wide, clean gravel under them.
text_nonnarrative: The site was a shallow terrace of gravel over clay, some two feet lower at the south boundary than at the north. Trenches on it lay on two axes only, the longer of them parallel to the slope. Depths were between three and five feet, deepest at the southern end, where the clay stood highest. Spoil lay on the uphill side of every trench, and the ground between trenches was level to within a few inches.

text_narrative: When the fields were first divided, the walls were set out by a woman whose name the fell keeps and the valley does not. She walked the boundary once. Where her heel turned, a corner stood, and the stone of that corner was not the stone of the hillside, and the throughs of it ran the whole thickness of the wall, and no frost ever lifted one of them in all that time.
text_nonnarrative: Walls on that flank of the fell lay along the contour above eleven hundred feet and straight up it below. Enclosures were smaller near the valley floor and of some forty acres at the head. The stone was a thin flag, so wall sections were narrow at the top and the coping stood on edge. Throughstones were visible at two courses, and the intake wall was the one with a footing of larger blocks.

text_narrative: The party's mason takes the plumb of the tower on the second afternoon and gets nine inches out of true to the east. He takes it again from the north face and gets four inches to the east. Both readings are repeated with a heavier bob and both stand. The tower's own courses are level to within half an inch over sixty feet, which is the part he writes down twice.
text_nonnarrative: Departure from plumb was greater within a single wall, face to face, than across the walls of one building. The median in the sample was three inches in sixty feet, with a tenth of readings above nine inches and a tenth under half an inch. Instrument and observer accounted for little of the spread. Most of it sat with the choice of face, sunlit faces standing a mean two inches from shaded ones.

text_narrative: Every spring Delma buys boards off the same wagon and every spring she stacks them under the shed roof with laths between. The first year they cup. The second year she turns them weekly and they cup the other way. The third year she leaves them flat and weighted and they come out straight, and the wagon man tells her he changed his mill in the second year and not the third.
text_nonnarrative: Spread in moisture content was wider within a layer of a stack than from layer to layer. Median moisture in the sample ran to eighteen percent at the outer edges of a stack and twenty-four at the core. Season of purchase accounted for about a third of that spread, and board thickness for none of it. The mill of origin was recorded in fewer than one return in five.

text_narrative: Before there were quarries the makers of houses had only the ground under them, and the first wall of the world was earth trodden into a heap between two hurdles. It was raised in lifts of two feet and pared with a spade at the sides. The rain of a thousand years took nothing off it. What took it in the end was a gutter that a grandson set wrong, and that is why roofs overhang.
text_nonnarrative: Cob is a wall material of subsoil, water and a fibrous binder, placed wet in lifts and pared to a line rather than moulded in a box. Its strength is a matter of clay fraction and of compaction, not of any binder in the mix. Wall thickness is therefore large in proportion to height, and openings are few and narrow. Protection at the head and at the foot is the whole of its durability, the material being soluble.

text_narrative: A roofing gang at a chapel on the coast reported a defect in an apron flashing eleven weeks old. The lead was sound and unwelted. Water had reached the boarding beneath it along a length of three feet, and the boarding was wet on the upper side and dry underneath. The dressing over the tile was tight, the upstand was chased and wedged, and the fall of the roof was four inches in a yard.
text_nonnarrative: An apron flashing is a single sheet of milled lead dressed over the head of a slope and lapped into a joint above it, and it is a weathering rather than a seal. Its length between laps is limited by the thermal movement of the sheet, and that limit is narrow in soft lead. Fixing is at the upstand only; the lower edge is loose by design and depends on its own weight.

text_narrative: Late in the pour, and the vibrator is still on the far side of the raft when Nkem crouches at the edge shutter and looks along the top mat. Three bars in the second row are hard against the ply. There are no spacers under them for a good two yards, and the ones further along are lying on their sides, and the concrete is at bar level and coming on.
text_nonnarrative: Cover to the outermost bar was to be not less than forty millimetres in any direction, measured to the face of the shutter and not to the line of the mat. Spacers were required at intervals such that no bar lay against a shutter at any point. Spacers resting on their sides were not admissible as spacers. Cover in excess of the stated figure was permitted only where the schedule named a tolerance.

text_narrative: There was a gate whose keystone was cut by two masons who would not speak, and each of them dressed one bed of it. The stone went in true. On the side the elder had cut, the joint was a knife's width and dry; on the other it was a finger wide and packed with lead, and the arch carried a wall of sixty feet above it for four hundred years without a settlement in the ring.
text_nonnarrative: Beds of a keystone were required to be dressed to the same joint width on both sides, and packing of any kind was permitted in neither. The stone was to be seated dry on the two voussoirs adjoining. It was to bear on the whole of each bed and not on a part of it. Lead was admissible at the ring only where the schedule named it, and never at the crown, whatever the load standing above.

text_narrative: The record for the second year of the works gave the length of every needle in the north range and the load on it. Five bays were needled that year. Bay three took a needle of eleven feet where the drawing gave nine, and the pin under it was set eighteen inches short of the line, and the bay stood, and the mason who ordered it was paid off in the following spring.
text_nonnarrative: Needles were to be of a length giving a bearing of not less than two feet outside the wall on each side. They were to be pinned at both ends, no excavation beneath a needle being permitted with either end unpinned. Bearings were required to be on undisturbed ground. No more than one bay in three was permitted to stand open. A bay wider than the stated figure was to be pinned whatever its depth.

text_narrative: Over one summer Halvard was called to three barns in the same parish, and in each of them a tie beam had drawn off its post. At the first the pegs were sound and the tenon had split along the grain. At the second somebody had put a bolt through and the oak around it was black and soft. At the third the joint was dry, the peg was dry, and the shoulder stood a full inch clear.
text_nonnarrative: A peg is weaker than a bolt and that is the argument for it. Oak in tension against iron bears on the iron and on itself, and the damage sits at the hole, out of sight and beyond making good. A peg of the same timber is no stiffer than the frame around it, and its weakness is legible at the surface. The objection is that legible weakness is weakness, which is true and does not tell against the peg.

text_narrative: A wren who lived in a ridge told the sparrows that the spars were put there for her sake, and the sparrows believed it for nine years. The thatcher came in the tenth and took the ridge off whole. Under it the spars were bright and unbroken and had held nothing but straw, and the wren's nest was in the eaves course, where no spar had ever been driven and no thatcher had ever looked.
text_nonnarrative: Spars were held to be the weak element of a ridge, and a ridge was the element most often renewed, so the two facts were read as one fact. They were not one. A spar of split hazel outlasted the straw around it in most work, and the renewal of a ridge was a matter of the exposure of straw at the apex rather than of any weakness beneath. The reading was durable because it was convenient.

text_narrative: In the winter of the third year of the siege the works struck the soffit forms of the new magazine at four days instead of twenty-one, on an order that nobody in the office would put a name to. The concrete held. It held under a hundred tons of stone that spring, and the engineer who gave the order spent the rest of that war on trenching and on drainage at the far end of the line.
text_nonnarrative: Striking early was cheap, and the saving was never made by the party carrying the risk. That was the whole of the case against short periods, and it was an argument about who bore a cost rather than an argument about concrete. The reply, that a member sound at four days was sound, was true in itself and beside the point, a schedule being a rule for the general case and not a claim about one member.

text_narrative: There was a hearth in a farm on the moor that drew so well the neighbours would not sit at it. The gather above it was a foot narrower than any mason would cut, and the throat was set to one side. Smoke never once came into the room in sixty years, in any wind, and on the stillest nights the flame lay flat along the back of the grate and hummed.
text_nonnarrative: Gather: the tapering brickwork between a fireplace opening and the throat. Throat: the narrowest section of a flue, directly above the gather. Withe: the division of brickwork standing between two flues in one stack, of one half brick in thickness. Register: a plate closing part of the throat area, adjustable and no part of the structure. Flaunching: the mortar fillet at the head of a stack, weathered away from the pot.

text_narrative: Everybody in the house knows the front bedroom sash and everybody has a way of dealing with it. The cord is sound. The weight in the left box is four pounds heavier than the one in the right, so the sash goes up crooked and jams at the second pane. The joiner's grandson keeps a wedge on the sill for it, and the youngest child can open the thing and nobody else can.
text_nonnarrative: Pulley stile: the upright of a sash frame carrying the axle pulley at its head. Box: the cavity behind that stile, closed by a removable pocket piece. Weight: a cylinder of iron or lead of one half the sash's own weight, one to a side. Parting bead: the strip dividing the two sashes in their runs. Staff bead: the innermost bead, and the one held by pins rather than by housing.

text_narrative: Each Michaelmas the carpenter's widow lets a different man look at the frame in the long barn, and each man finds something different in it. The first counts the bays. The second reads the assembly marks and finds them running from both ends toward the middle, which is not the practice of the county. The third puts a rule on the scarfs and gets four lengths in one plate.
text_nonnarrative: Scarf: any lengthwise joint between two timbers making up a single member. Mortise: the housing cut to receive a tenon, and the female element in every instance. Assembly mark: an incised numeral common to two members of one frame and to no further pair. Jowl: the swelled head of a post at the plate. Sole plate: the lowest horizontal member, distinguished from a sill by carrying no wall.

text_narrative: Nine years into the tenancy the trustees ordered a schedule of dilapidations on the whole of the east wing, and the surveyor gave them four hundred and six items. Two of them were structural. The other four hundred and four were decorative, and the trustees pursued all four hundred and six, and the tenant paid for the two and left the wing standing empty for eleven more years and paid nothing further.
text_nonnarrative: In this part a want of repair meant any condition of the premises falling short of the standard set by the covenant, whether or not it was apparent at the date of the demise. Where a condition was attributable to the design of the premises, it was not a want of repair. Nothing in a schedule affected the liability of a party for damage of a kind expressly excepted by the covenant itself.

text_narrative: Halfway through the morning the frame is in and Yusra is holding the level against the hinge jamb. The head is out by three millimetres over the width of it. The reveal on the lock side is eleven millimetres deeper than the reveal on the hinge side, and the wall itself is true, and the opening was formed to the drawing, and the drawing has the two reveals equal to within a millimetre.
text_nonnarrative: An opening, in this schedule, means a void through the full thickness of a wall, whether or not a frame stands in it; and a reveal means the finished face of that void, between the frame and the outer plane of the wall. Where a reveal is unequal on the two sides of an opening, the lesser of them governs. Nothing in the definition of an opening bears on the fixing of a frame within it.

text_narrative: In the first age of the ring the floors were poured by hands that had no instrument but patience, and the law of that age was ninety days under wet cloth. One bay was left uncovered by an oversight nobody afterwards owned to. That bay was the only floor of the first age with no crack in it, and the makers of the second age poured every bay of theirs uncovered, and all of those crazed inside a year.
text_nonnarrative: A curing period means the interval for which the surface of a placed member is required to be kept from loss of water. It is reckoned from placing. The striking of a form is no part of the reckoning. Where the schedule states a period in days, a day means twenty-four hours at or above the stated temperature, and no other day counts. Nothing in a period so reckoned bears on the striking figures given elsewhere in the schedule.

text_narrative: The county surveyor's office recorded a fault in the roof of a market hall in the spring of that year. One truss in eleven had a diagonal missing from the panel next the ridge, and the hall had carried snow for forty winters. The absent member was not broken and not cut. The mortise for it was there in the rafter and there in the strut, and the peg holes were unbored.
text_nonnarrative: A pin-jointed frame is a truss only where its members number twice its joints less three; a frame with fewer members is a mechanism and is not a truss whatever the load on it. A frame with more is admissible but is not determinate, and its member forces are not fixed by the geometry of the frame alone. An empty mortise is no member, and a panel lacking its diagonal is no panel at all.

text_narrative: The fabric roll for the abbey works named the four men who raised the west range in a bond the master mason had not authorised. Every fifth course was a heading course instead of every fourth. The perpends ran true from plinth to eaves on the whole of a hundred-foot face, and the range outlasted the two beside it by three centuries, and no course of it was ever taken down.
text_nonnarrative: A bond is admissible only where no perpend in one course stands over a perpend in the course below it. A course in which two such perpends coincide is faulty from that point onward. Broken bond at a stopped end is permitted. It is not a fault of the same kind. A closer is no header. It may not be reckoned toward the heading pattern of a course.

text_narrative: Sixteen risers, and the sixteenth was the one that had been wrong for a hundred years. Anselma had the rule on it: seven and a quarter inches, where every other riser in the flight was seven and an eighth. An eighth of an inch. Nobody in the house had ever caught a toe on it, and the whole family went up that stair sideways, and none of them knew the reason.
text_nonnarrative: A flight is admissible only where every rise in it equals every other rise; a single rise out of agreement with the rest makes the whole flight irregular, whatever the difference. Two rises in agreement with each other and not with the flight are not thereby a second flight. A landing interrupting a run is a division between flights and is itself neither a rise nor a going.

text_narrative: The slaters on that coast would not use the biggest size on any roof within sight of the sea, and they had a name for it that nobody would translate. It held water in the lap. They took the second size instead and holed it high, an inch and a half from the head, and roofs done that way went eighty years where roofs done the other way went thirty.
text_nonnarrative: Six sizes are in common supply, of which the second and third account for most work. Each is sold in one thickness, the larger sizes being the thicker. Holing is centre-punched from the back at a fixed distance from the head, and that distance is a property of the size rather than of the pitch. The smallest size has no head hole at all and is nailed at its centre.

text_narrative: Three panes out of the six, and all three on the street side. The putty on those three is soft enough to take a thumbprint and the putty on the other three is eleven years hard, and the same hand bedded the lot on the same afternoon. Somebody has been at the street side with a knife and oil, and no glass is missing, and nothing in the room has been touched.
text_nonnarrative: Four grades were kept, of which the second was the general glazing grade and the fourth a bedding compound rather than a putty. Each was sold in the same weight of tin, the coarser grades being the darker. The first grade was linseed-bound and hard at the surface only, to a depth of a few thirty-seconds. The third was for metal and had no oil in it that a knife would raise.

text_narrative: There was a village where the vane on the church stood always to the north-east and the vane on the mill turned as it pleased. The people took their weather from the mill. A smith came through and trued the church vane on its spindle, and from that day it turned as freely as the other, and nobody in the village would trust either of the two vanes again, in any weather.
text_nonnarrative: The common fault of the modern finial is that it is a silhouette and nothing besides, drawn to be read against sky from one direction and blank from the other three. What passes for revival work is usually a stock casting on a stock spindle. The best examples of the form are the ones carrying a real function in the fabric, a lead cap or a fixing for a rod. Ornament in those is second.

text_narrative: A district officer reports an unrecorded pargework panel on the gable of a cottage in the fourth parish. The panel is eleven feet by four and the lime of it is original. Its pattern is a lattice of forty-nine cells, and in each cell there is a different device, and no device in the lattice appears twice in the parish, the county or the surviving pattern books of the trade.
text_nonnarrative: Pargework is judged by the plane it keeps rather than by the incident in it, which is why so much of it disappoints in a photograph and satisfies on a wall. Repetition is not the vice critics of the form take it for; a lattice of identical cells is stronger under raking light than a lattice of forty-nine inventions. The strongest panels are the ones with the least to look at.

text_narrative: The great nave stood open to the sky for two generations, and in that country the thrust of a vault was a living thing with a name of its own, and buttresses were built to hold it as a man holds a dog. Each pier took a share. The share of the fourth pier was double and the pier was no larger, and the masons of that age said the stone above it had agreed to lean the other way.
text_nonnarrative: Whether thrust was a force in the wall or only a direction taken by the weight standing in it was no matter of measurement. The two accounts gave the same buttress at the same size. On the first, a buttress was an addition to the fabric. On the second, it was a restriction on what the fabric could do. The difference was real and bore on repair, since only the second made the relief of load a remedy.

text_narrative: Long before the deep builders had a name for it, a vault was raised over water, and the ribs of it were cut from a single tree that nobody in that country could name. The web between them was thin as a shell. The ribs bore nothing, and the web bore nothing, and the whole of it hung on the memory of the tree, and the water beneath never once ran dry in four thousand years.
text_nonnarrative: Two claims about a rib were commonly run together: that it was a member carrying its share of the web, and that it was a division of the web into panels of workable size. Neither of the two entailed the other. A rib decorative in the first sense could be indispensable in the second, and a vault whose webs stood with one rib gone was evidence about the first claim only and about nothing further.

text_narrative: Nine and a half inches, and the span is fifteen feet three, and Marisol has the figures in her head from the schedule she wrote out herself. The floor should be soft. It is not soft. It is dead flat and dead quiet under the heaviest thing in the room, and the joists in the void below are nine and a half inches deep and one of them is not there.
text_nonnarrative: Deflection under a uniform load was proportional to the fourth power of the span. It was inversely proportional to the cube of the depth. The constant was a property of the timber alone. A joist of nine and a half inches at fifteen feet stood at about two and a half times the deflection of the same joist at twelve. Beyond a span-to-depth ratio of some twenty the elastic relation was of little use.

text_narrative: Nobody on the street can account for the gutter at number nineteen and the plumber has stopped trying. It runs uphill. Water put in at the stop end goes the length of forty feet and out at the outlet, which stands a clear two inches higher, and it does that in a dry week and in a wet one, and the brackets have not shifted in thirty years by the width of a nail.
text_nonnarrative: Discharge in an open gutter varied as the square root of the gradient and as the five-thirds power of the depth of flow, so a doubling of fall bought about two-fifths again in capacity and a doubling of section a good deal more. Fall was therefore the cheaper variable up to a point and no further. Below a gradient of one in six hundred the relation held in theory and not in a fouled gutter.

text_narrative: On each of four watches the shift carpenter climbs the same frame and finds the same thing wrong in a different place. On the first watch a purlin is short of its cleat by a finger.
