On the second the cleat is short of the purlin. On the third both are true and the rafter above them is out of plane, and on the fourth watch nothing is out at all and the frame hums.
text_nonnarrative: Principal rafters are the heavier members and stand at the bay centres, carrying the purlins between them. A common rafter is a member from eaves to ridge and lies perpendicular to every purlin it crosses. Cleats are small blocks spiked to the face of a principal, and a purlin bears on its cleat rather than in a housing of its own. Collars are absent in the shallowest pitches and doubled in the steepest ones.

text_narrative: Four lights, and the drawing in the file gives five. Osian has the file open on the sill and the sill is original, and the mortises in it are five, evenly spaced, and one of them is filled with a plug of the same stone and the same weathering. The fourth mullion is not missing from the window. It has never been in the window at all.
text_nonnarrative: The jambs and the sill are the outer members of a stone window and are worked in one piece with the wall wherever the coursing allows. Mullions are the intermediate uprights, housed top and bottom and never built in. A transom is the horizontal counterpart, and is absent in single-light openings. Cusping belongs to the head and to the tracery above a transom, and is no part of any mullion.

text_narrative: Half past four in the morning, and the furnace had been at temperature since the feast. Silvestre turned the blowpipe in the glory hole, gathered, and came out with too much on the end of it, a pear where a plum was wanted. He rolled it along the bench rail, blew once into the pipe, and the neck sagged clear away from the shoulder before he could gather over it a second time.
text_nonnarrative: Parison: the mass of glass on the pipe intermediate between first inflation and shaping at the bench. Gather: the same mass as taken from the pot, without inflation of any kind. Overgather: a gather heavier than the pattern allows, a fault of weight rather than of form. Neck: the drawn section of glass between the parison and the pipe. Sag: reduction of section at the neck under the load hanging below it.

text_narrative: The marver plate on the third bench is out of true by the thickness of a coin, and no one at the bottle works will own to having shifted it. Kolarov measures it twice, with a straightedge and with a card. The plate is iron, four feet by two, bedded in ash, and the near corner stands proud of the rail. Every parison rolled across it this morning leaves the bench with one flat side.
text_nonnarrative: A marver was a flat iron slab bedded level with the bench rail, and its function was the removal of heat from the outer skin of a parison while the form was made round. Contact was over the whole face of the slab or over none of it. Trueness of the slab therefore set the evenness of chilling, and a corner standing above the plane of the rest took heat from one side only.

text_narrative: Nobody at the works would buy a stem glass off Dorotea's bench, and it was nothing to do with the stems. She finished a punty scar better than anyone in the room, ground it flat and polished it until a thumb could not find it. The trouble was she ground into the foot. Half a millimetre off the underside of every foot she touched, and the glasses rocked on a level table for the rest of their lives.
text_nonnarrative: Punty scars are graded on residual height above the plane of the foot, never on width and never on polish. A scar ground flush is sound whatever its diameter. Loss of glass from the underside of the foot is a separate and disqualifying class, since the foot, not the scar, is what holds a stem glass level on a table. Polish bears on the grade of finish and never on the grade of the foot.

text_narrative: Twenty-two years on the lehr and Miroslava had never once trusted the far end of the belt. The near end was honest. Anyone could read the near end. It was the last nine feet, out past the third damper, where the ware came off warm on one side and cool on the other, and nobody would say why, and the book said the belt ran even, and the book was signed by a man who never walked it.
text_nonnarrative: An annealing lehr is a tunnel with a moving belt through it and a series of dampers along its roof, and the temperature at any station on the belt is a function of the damper settings upstream of that station and of belt speed. Cross-belt uniformity is a separate property, fixed by the width of the flue rather than by its length. A mean temperature at a station carries no information about difference across the width of the belt.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the new glasshouse the cabinet of presentation flasks was opened for the spring inventory. Of forty flasks, nine were clouded through the wall, and two wept a fine damp that stood in beads on the shoulder. The clerk entered all eleven as sound, on the ground that no surface was cracked. The master entered nine as spoiled and two as beyond keeping, and both entries stood in the book for a century.
text_nonnarrative: Crizzling is classed on the state of the surface and not on the integrity of the wall, so uncracked flasks are not thereby sound. Clouding through the wall is one class, and weeping, meaning free damp standing in beads on the shoulder, is a second and graver class. A crack is neither, and forms no part of the grade. Beyond keeping is the class of any flask whose surface is wet at ordinary humidity.

text_narrative: Forty crates of sheet glass came back to the Brankstone works on a wet Tuesday, refused by the buyer of a hotel front. The refusal named cord. Of the twelve sheets drawn out for the record, eleven carried seed only, small and evenly scattered, and the twelfth carried a single wave of cord the full height of the sheet, and that twelfth sheet was the one set in the window above the entrance.
text_nonnarrative: Seed and cord fall into separate grades, and a sheet takes the worse of the two rather than a count of either. Seed, being small and scattered, is admitted in any number below the density at which it reads as haze. Cord is disqualifying at a single wave where the wave runs the height of the sheet, since cord distorts what is seen through the window and seed does not.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the window duty the assessors came twice to the borough of Larnhoe, once in April and once at the end of harvest. At the first visit they counted the bullseye panes in the almshouse and let them pass as waste. At the second a different assessor counted the same panes as glazing, and the almshouse owed on nineteen lights it had owed nothing on in the spring, and the warden paid.
text_nonnarrative: Waste glass, within the meaning of this part, is the central boss of a crown table together with any pane cut from that boss, whether or not the pane is set in a light. A light is not chargeable by reason only of containing such a pane. Where a light holds both waste glass and glass cut from the outer rings, the whole of that light is chargeable. Nothing here affects the count of lights in a frontage.

text_narrative: Every third week that autumn Isadora walked the flattening stone at a works on the plains, and every third week something different was wrong with it. In September the stone was cold at the near edge and the sheets came off it bowed. In October a chip in the middle put a crease down forty sheets. In November nothing was wrong with the stone at all, the sheets came off bowed, and the man laying them had changed.
text_nonnarrative: Cylinder glass is a sheet made by splitting a blown cylinder along its length and opening it flat on a heated stone. Flatness in the product is a property of the stone and of the temperature of the glass admitted to it, both of which are common to the whole width. Bow is therefore general across a run rather than local to one sheet, and a crease is the mark of a defect in the stone itself.

text_narrative: The back of the glass takes the silver evenly along its whole length, which is not what the workshop expects of a plate this old. Teodolinda holds the lamp close. Under the new film there is an older film, thin as breath, and it carries the shape of a room — a doorway, a table, the corner of a chair — none of which stands in the workshop behind her. She tilts the plate and the room tilts with it.
text_nonnarrative: Resilvering was destructive of the evidence of a mirror's history and was nonetheless the only means of keeping the mirror a mirror. The argument for stripping rested on the reflective surface, which was the object's whole function. The argument against rested on the backing, which carried the marks of its making and of every repair. Those marks were real evidence. They were also evidence of a plate unable to reflect, and a stripped plate was not the lesser object.

text_narrative: There was a chapel in the wood whose east light held ninety-nine quarries of glass and a hundredth space that would hold none. Three glaziers tried it. The first cut a quarry to the gap and it fell out before the cement was dry; the second leaded a plain diamond in and it clouded within a week; the third set nothing there at all, and the light kept that empty diamond for four hundred years.
text_nonnarrative: Each quarry in a leaded light was a diamond of glass held on all four edges by the flange of an H-sectioned came, the cames being soldered to one another at every junction. Saddle bars lay across the back of the panel and were tied to the cames with copper wire at intervals. The perimeter came was of heavier section than the interior ones, and cement between flange and glass was absent only in the coarsest work.

text_narrative: The station's glazing shop logs a wheel that cuts deeper the slower it runs, which is the reverse of every other wheel in the inventory. Ochieng puts it on the bench rig at a tenth of standard speed. The score goes eleven microns into a plate rated for four. At full speed the same wheel leaves no mark on the same plate, and the wheel comes off the rig cold, and the plate under it is warm.
text_nonnarrative: Depth of score varied with the load on the wheel and with the included angle of its edge, and was independent of traverse speed over the working band. The constant of proportionality was a property of the glass rather than of the wheel. Beyond a load at which the edge deformed, depth no longer varied with load at all, and below a certain angle the relation held for the first few metres of a wheel's life only.

text_narrative: Four winters running, Benedek's aunt sent him a copper wheel at midwinter and never the one he had asked for. The first was a broad flat wheel for polishing, which he had asked for and used. The second was stone. The third was a wheel so small he could not chuck it in the spindle he owned. The fourth was a spindle, and by then the small wheel had lain two years in a drawer and gone green.
text_nonnarrative: Thirty-odd wheels made a working set, of which perhaps eight were in use in any month. The commonest were flat-edged and between a quarter inch and two inches across. Mounting was on a tapered spindle nose. Two or three were stone rather than copper. These were for cutting rather than for the grey matt finish. The smallest were under a tenth of an inch and were the likeliest to be absent from an old set, being the easiest to mislay.

text_narrative: Anselma knows what a second firing does to a white and this white is not doing it. It should sink into the surface and go dull. It stands up off the glass instead, a raised line she can feel with a fingernail, and it has taken a colour she never mixed, a blue that darkens toward the middle of every stroke as though the stroke had been drawn twice, the second time by a steadier hand.
text_nonnarrative: Enamelled glass was the most forgiving of the decorated wares and the weaker for it. What passed for drawing on it was usually a raised line over an unconsidered ground, and the fault was one of temperature: fired short, the enamel stood proud and read as paint on a window rather than as part of the window. Its better examples were those in which the white lay level with the glass, so that the drawing belonged to the vessel.

text_narrative: Before there were flowers in the world there was a glassmaker at the first furnace who set coloured rods in a ring and gathered clear metal over them. Two of her daughters took the ends and walked away from each other along the bank of the river until the mass between them was a thread nine miles long. Every flower since has been a slice of that thread, and the ring at the heart of each is her ring.
text_nonnarrative: A millefiori cane is a composite rod in which a pattern in section holds along the whole length, the pattern being laid out at full size and reduced by drawing rather than composed at its final scale. Reduction is in cross-section alone; the order and the relative area of the elements are invariant under it. Length is inversely proportional to the square of the diameter, and a slice from any point carries the figure of any other.

text_narrative: Everyone on that street bought beads from the woman at the corner house, and everyone knew she wound them three at a time on one mandrel. The middle bead was always the good one. The outer two came off her lamp a little flat on the inner face, and she sold all three at the same price, and nobody argued, because the middle bead of hers was rounder than anything the shops in town had on a card.
text_nonnarrative: Seven sizes make the ordinary trade card, of which the third and the fourth account for most of what is strung. Each is a wound bead, meaning glass laid on a mandrel and turned to a round. The hole is on the full axis. The two outer positions on a three-bead mandrel are flat on the inner face. The middle position is round on both faces. Colours number eight in the smaller sizes and fourteen in the largest.

text_narrative: Third round at the county pottery fair and the clay on Hasan's wheel is off centre by a finger's width, which he has known since the first pull. He can true it or he can go on. The board beside him holds two cylinders already, both to height, both inside the gauge. He goes on. The wall thins on the near side at twelve inches and the whole pot leans out of the gauge with the timer at forty.
text_nonnarrative: An attempt counts as legal only where the cylinder stands inside the gauge at the call of the timer and is raised from a single ball. Two cylinders on one board are a single entry, and the lower of the two fixes the height of that entry. A leaning wall is no fault in itself. A wall outside the gauge is outside it whatever the lean. Clay added beyond the original ball voids the attempt, and a void attempt does not stand.

text_narrative: The first vessels in the highlands were not thrown but built, and the building of them fell to the mountain's youngest daughter, who had one hand of stone and one of wood. With the wood she beat the wall from outside. With the stone she held it from within. Nine coils she laid for the belly and three for the neck, and where the two hands met the wall went thin and shone, and every pot since shows that line.
text_nonnarrative: Built ware falls into a base, a belly and a neck, the base being a disc or a spiral coil and the belly a series of coils laid on its rim. Each coil stands on the one below and is thinned between an anvil held inside the wall and a paddle worked outside it. The neck is the uppermost coils, of smaller diameter and of the same section. A foot is absent in the earliest built forms.

text_narrative: They still talked in that valley about the dish Ferenc trailed for his own wedding, and not kindly. He put a lattice on it in white slip, forty lines each way, and every line was the same width from rim to rim. It took him a day. The old woman who had taught him looked at it a long while and said it was a fine tiled floor, and gave him a jug of hers with three lines on it.
text_nonnarrative: Trailed slipware was at its worst where the trailing was most even. What passed for control in the tradition was largely the absence of it: the line was broader where the pot lay longest under the horn and narrower elsewhere, and the pattern was legible on account of that inequality. A lattice of uniform width read as tile rather than as pottery. The best of the dishes were those whose lines were unequal from one end to the other.

text_narrative: The slip is dry enough and Ondine's tool is sharp enough and the line she is cutting is not the line she is cutting. She keeps her wrist where it belongs. Under the point the white peels back off the red in the shape of a hare, then a second hare, then a border of hares she has never drawn in her life, and her hand goes where it is taken, and the vessel turns under it.
text_nonnarrative: Sgraffito was the least generous of the incised decorations, in that nothing cut away was recoverable. What passed for spontaneity in it was commonly the opposite: a design worked out on paper and transferred, the slip allowing neither hesitation nor correction. Its finest examples were those in which the ground showed through in unequal widths, the tool being held at a constant angle rather than a constant depth. Evenness of line was the mark of a copy.

text_narrative: Every dry month Nkemdi walks the old road for shards, and every dry month the same argument runs in the settlement. In the fourth month she brings back a rim with a surface like a wet stone and no glaze on it anywhere. In the fifth she brings a whole cup of the same. In the sixth she brings the pit itself, or the news of the pit, a bank of red clay fine enough to hold a thumbprint.
text_nonnarrative: Burnish was the poor relation of glaze in every account of the craft, and the ranking was an artefact of what endured in the ground rather than of what the two surfaces did. A body sealed by burnish alone needed no glass over it at all. The case for glaze rested on impermeability, which burnished sigillata gave at lower temperature and without a second firing. That the case was pressed regardless said more about kilns than about surfaces.

text_narrative: In the second year of the Compact the pottery at Hedern was allowed one firing a month and no more, and the books show how it was managed. In March the biscuit went in alone. In April the glost went in alone. In May both went in together, glazed ware on the upper shelves and raw on the lower, and the whole setting came out with a grey bloom on it that nobody at Hedern had seen.
text_nonnarrative: The higher of the two firings was the earlier, and the two stood apart in respect of the body rather than of temperature. Biscuit was the condition of a body permanent in form and porous throughout. Glost was the condition of the same body under a glass surface, its porosity unaltered beneath. Single firing was a third case, marked off from both by the absence of any porous interval, and not by its economy of fuel.

text_narrative: There was a magpie that lived in the roof of a bottle kiln and stole one wad from every saggar in the setting. The placers never caught her. They set the saggars in bungs of nine, wadded them level, and closed the wicket, and every firing came out with one bung leaning and a black feather in the ash beneath it. In the end they left a wad on the roof for her and the bungs stood straight.
text_nonnarrative: Wads are required to be of the same clay as the saggar. Thickness is to be sufficient to close the joint against flame. A bung is permitted to nine saggars in height, and to no more than that where the floor is unbedded. Each saggar is to bear on three wads and never on two. A saggar out of plumb by more than its own wall thickness is not to be set, whatever the state of the wads above it.

text_narrative: The kiln is cool enough to open and the first plate off the top shelf has the glaze standing back from the rim in a clean crescent, bare clay showing under it. Petra sets it down and takes the next. The next has pinholes, a hundred of them, fine as a needle and evenly over the whole face. The third has both, the crawl at the rim and the pinholes in the well, and all three came from one setting.
text_nonnarrative: Crawl and pinholing were classed apart, crawl being bare clay where glaze had no hold, pinholing being fine perforation in glaze otherwise continuous. Crawl at the rim was a fault of the surface of the clay. Pinholes in the well were a fault of temperature in the setting. Neither crawl nor pinholing was graded on the count of marks. A plate with both belonged to the worse class rather than in a class of its own, and one setting carried both.

text_narrative: When the sky was still being decided, the potter of the eastern kiln fired nine jars and stopped the mouth with green wood, and the smoke had nowhere to go but into the glass. Three jars came out the colour of shallow water and three the colour of deep, and the last three had no colour at all. Those three she gave to the sky, and the sky has been every colour since except the one it was given.
text_nonnarrative: Celadon colour admitted two accounts, and they were not one account under a pair of names. On the first, colour was a property of the glaze, atmosphere being merely the means of its realisation. On the second, colour was a property of the firing, the glaze being a medium indifferent to hue. If the first held, jars of one glaze in one kiln were necessarily of one colour, and difference between such jars was the standing objection to it.

text_narrative: A glaze laboratory at a technical institute recorded an anomaly in its white standards in the winter of the ninth intake. Tin oxide had been weighed at four, six, eight and ten parts in the hundred, and the eight-part tile was whiter than the ten. The weighings were repeated by a second hand on the same balance with the same result, and the ten-part tile came out of the kiln with a faint grey in it.
text_nonnarrative: Opacity is a function of tin oxide content and not a proportional one: the difference in whiteness between four and six parts in the hundred is several times the difference between eight and ten. Above roughly ten parts the relation is flat, the added oxide being in excess of what the melt takes up. The constant relating content to opacity is a property of the glaze base and of thickness on the ware rather than of the oxide.

text_narrative: Nothing in the lustre chamber is where Serafim left it, and the door has been latched shut since the reduction. The dish on the top prop is right. It is the wrong right — a copper red so exact that he can see the shelf through it, and the shelf is not behind the dish, it is under it, and the film on the surface is thinner than the dust that ought to be lying on the film.
text_nonnarrative: Lustre invites a pair of descriptions, and whether they are rival or merely differently pitched is not settled by looking. Under the first, lustre is a colour and belongs with the pigments. Under the second, it is a film of metal some tens of atoms thick, and colour in it is an effect of thickness alone. If the second description is correct, a lustre has no colour of its own, and two names for one property are one too many.

text_narrative: Nobody in the lower town will take a lead glaze off the yard at the bridge, and the reason goes back three generations. The old potter there works alkaline and only alkaline. His turquoise crazes the moment it cools and everyone knows it and everyone buys it anyway, because the blue off a lead pot in that town has always come out the colour of a bruise, and nobody can say whether it is the clay or the water.
text_nonnarrative: Alkaline and lead fluxes stood apart in respect of colour rather than of melting point. Copper in an alkaline glaze was turquoise. The same copper under lead was green. Fit was the second distinction: alkaline glazes were the higher in expansion and so the more liable to craze on any body, whatever the water or the clay beneath. Boron was a third flux aligned with neither, marked off from both by its indifference to the colouring oxides.

text_narrative: In the third season of the orbital works the shelf inventory was entered as usual, and one entry did not agree with the rest. Shelf nine had been washed with alumina and kaolin at the opening of the season, as all of them were. At the season's end the wash on shelf nine stood four millimetres thick, nothing had been laid on it since the first firing, and the record of its washing showed one coat.
text_nonnarrative: Wash: a refractory coating on the upper face of a shelf, lying between the shelf and anything set upon it. Bat wash: the same coating where the shelf is a bat in a tunnel setting. Coat: one application of wash, of the order of a tenth of a millimetre in the dry state. Build-up: wash thickness in excess of the sum of the coats recorded. Shelling: wash detached from the shelf in flakes, of no bearing on thickness.

text_narrative: Three firings into the season and the field kiln has bent a different cone every time. On the first, the eight goes over and the nine stands. On the second, the eight and the nine both go and the ten leans a little. On the third, the eight stands upright at the end of a longer soak than either of the others, and the pyrometer in the wall reads the same on all three afternoons.
text_nonnarrative: Bending in a cone is a function of temperature and of time at temperature together, in a relation nearer to a product than to a sum. Equal end temperatures therefore correspond to unequal bends wherever the soak is unequal. A pyrometer indicates one of the two variables only, so its reading is not sufficient to fix a bend. Below a threshold rate of climb the relation is of little use, the cone being sensitive to duration alone.

text_narrative: There was a potter's wife who could hear a dunt three rooms away and always knew which pot it was in. One winter she heard nine and found only eight. The ninth pot stood on the shelf without a mark on it and no crack anywhere in the wall, and it gave a true ring, and it held water for a year, and in the winter following it lay in two pieces along a line no eye had found.
text_nonnarrative: A dunt is classed by the line it follows and never by what it sounds like. A crack through the wall on a straight line is one class whatever its length. A crack turning with the throwing rings is a second, and the second is disqualifying in a pot meant to hold water. Ring under a blow bears on presence and not on class. A pot with no visible mark for a year falls in no class at all.

text_narrative: A dealer in the arcade lists nine plates from one workshop, all of a size, all with the same turned foot ring. Eight of them sit flat. The ninth rocks, and the rock is not in the plate but in the ring: the ring is oval, by two millimetres on the long axis, and it is oval in the direction of the light from the window, whichever wall of the arcade the plate is carried to.
text_nonnarrative: Below the well of a plate stands the foot ring, a raised annulus turned from the same clay and concentric with the rim. The ring bears the whole weight of the plate on its lower edge, which lies in one plane in true ware. Width of the ring is a fraction of the diameter of the well. In the smallest forms the ring is absent and the plate rests on the underside of the well itself.

text_narrative: The mould shop was down to one bag of plaster and Ludmila had six insulator patterns waiting on the bench. She mixed thin. The first two moulds came off the pattern with a surface like chalk and drank the slip so fast that the wall was at thickness before she had the last corner filled, and the sixth mould, mixed from the bottom of the bag, took no water out of the slip at all.
text_nonnarrative: Moulds were required to be of gypsum plaster mixed at a stated ratio of water to powder, and no other ratio was permitted for casting work. Absorbency was to be uniform across the whole face of a mould. A mould was to be dry to constant weight and was not to be in service above a stated moisture content. Powder recovered from the foot of a bag was not permitted for any mould intended for production.

text_narrative: Anyone on the flatware line will tell a newcomer to watch the third jigger and not the fourth. The fourth is the one with the worn template, and everyone knows it. The third is the one that runs sweet all morning and then puts a lip on every plate off it for an hour after the break, and the man on it swears he does nothing different, and the fitters have had the head off four times.
text_nonnarrative: Wall thickness varied more between plates from one jigger than between jiggers on a line. Across the sample, 62 percent of plates lay within a tenth of a millimetre of the median for their line, the remainder distributed unevenly toward the thicker side. Template wear accounted for a small part of the spread and play in the machine head for most of it. Position in the shift was uncorrelated with thickness at every station but one.

text_narrative: Four times a year the works at Chelby sends a case of encaustic tiles to a pavement contractor, and four times a year the contractor sends some of them back. In the spring case it is the reds, short on the long side. In the summer case it is the reds again. In the autumn case every colour is short and the case is kept. In the winter case the reds are long, and no die at Chelby has changed.
text_nonnarrative: Finished dimensions varied with the colour of the body more than with the die a tile came from. In the returns examined, the median shortfall on the long side was under half a millimetre, and the red bodies accounted for most of the spread in both directions. Position in the year bore on the mean and not on the ranking of the colours. Acceptance by contractors was uncorrelated with the measured shortfall in three cases out of four.

text_narrative: The first floor laid on the new world was a court of tesserae nine hundred paces across, and the woman who cut them was the last of the ship's glassworkers. She cut with a hammer and a hardie and no rule. Every tessera she set was a little out of square, and the court read true from the gallery above it, and those who came after her cut by rule, and no court of theirs read true.
text_nonnarrative: The court is an irregular quadrilateral of some nine hundred paces on its longest side, level to within a hand over that distance. A gallery stands along the northern edge at a height of four storeys, and the whole surface is in view from it. Tesserae across the field are of two sizes, the smaller toward the centre. The pavement is dry at all seasons, the ground beneath it being made ground over rubble.

text_narrative: There was a brickfield in the marsh that made a nogging tile no other field could copy, and the men who dug there would not say what they mixed with the clay. The tiles were the colour of a plum and rang like a plate. A gentleman built a whole gable of them on the high road. Ivy would not grow on that gable, and no swallow nested under it, and in wet weather the wall was warm.
text_nonnarrative: The lower ground holds three clay pits in a line, the deepest of them at the marsh edge and the shallowest against the road. Drying hacks stand between the pits and the kiln, in eight rows on made ground a foot above the water table. The kiln itself sits on the only rise of ground in the field. Standing water is general in the pits from October onward and absent from the hacks in every season.

text_narrative: In the age when stone was still soft, the makers of the white ware asked the moon for a body that would hold the light, and the moon gave them a stone and a rule: thin enough and no thinner. The first bowl they turned to that rule shone through and held soup. The second they turned finer, and it shone through and held nothing, and the third finer still, and the light went round it and not through.
text_nonnarrative: Whether translucency belonged to a body or to a wall was no idle distinction, since the two answers were claims about different subjects entirely. Held as a property of the body, translucency was present in a thick wall and merely unobserved. Held as a property of the wall, it had no existence below a thickness. On the second account translucency was a relation and not a quality, and no whiteness was intrinsic to the body at all.

text_narrative: In the eighth year of the northern concession the pattern books of the blue-and-white works were bound and numbered, and the eighth book was the one nobody would use. Its forty-one patterns were drawn in the usual four strengths of cobalt. Under glaze the weakest bled a hand's width and the strongest not at all, which was the reverse of every other book on the shelf, and one hand had drawn them all.
text_nonnarrative: The ordinary palette held four strengths of cobalt, of which the second was the commonest in production. Each was a measured dilution of one oxide, from a wash near grey to a near black in the pot. The weakest carried the most flux and were the widest in bleed under glaze. Patterns drawn in more than two strengths on a single vessel were uncommon, and none of the four was proof against bleed at a rim.

text_narrative: Sixteen tons of cullet in the yard and Aurelio could account for eleven. The other five had come in over the wall, and he knew whose wall, and he knew that a batch made up with foreign cullet would take the colour of whatever had been in it, and that nobody upstairs would read a colour in a melt as an accusation. The melt was due at six. He weighed the eleven tons and stood there.
text_nonnarrative: Cullet, within the meaning of this part, was broken glass returned to a batch, whether from the works' own production or from elsewhere. Foreign cullet was cullet whose origin stood unrecorded in the batch book. A batch holding foreign cullet in any proportion was not thereby irregular. A batch whose composition was unrecorded was irregular whatever its cullet. Nothing in this part affected the weights required to be entered in the book on delivery.

text_narrative: There was a village with one kiln to nine potters and a stick with nine notches for the claiming of shelves. The youngest potter cut a tenth notch. Nobody could say whose it was, so the kiln stood cold through a whole autumn while they argued it, and in the end the tenth notch was given to the kiln itself, and one shelf in every firing after that went out empty and warm.
text_nonnarrative: A claim to a shelf was good only where the notch answering to it was single and the claimant's mark stood beside that notch. Two marks against one notch made a claim void, and a void claim was not answerable by a second claim in the same firing. An unclaimed shelf was not a shelf held by the kiln; it was a position outside the claiming, and nothing set upon it lay within any potter's account.

text_narrative: Half a mile up the fell the ewes had bunched against a wall, and Perrin sent the young bitch out on the right hand. She ran wide, too wide, and swung behind the bunch a good thirty yards further out than the ground wanted. The ewes lifted clean. At the top she flattened and came on slow, and one ewe broke toward the gate, and the bitch took the flank late, and the whole bunch shifted six yards.
text_nonnarrative: An outrun is graded on the shape of the run and not on its speed. Width is a fault only where the ground does not want it; thirty yards wide on open fell counts as correct and the same width in a walled field does not. A ewe out of the bunch bears on the lift, never on the flank. Late flanking at the top is one fault; a bitch that runs narrow is another, and the two are separate.

text_narrative: Nobody on the high grazing whistles the way old Marden does, and the young hands make a joke of it. Two notes where anyone else uses four, and the dogs read them at half a mile. The trick, so the saying goes, is that he pitches the second note under the wind instead of over it. Whether that holds or not, his dogs turn on the rise while the rest are still casting about below the wall.
text_nonnarrative: Carrying distance in a working whistle was a function of pitch and of the wind gradient, and not of loudness. The two-note code was the simplest form: one note for direction, one for degree, with the interval between them doing the work. A wider interval was harder to hear at the far end of a valley. Without a settled interval the direction note and the degree note were not separable at all, and the dogs had nothing to read.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the new tillage, the yoke-maker at Ardhen was set to cut bows for eleven pairs before the spring ploughing. Nine pairs were matched in height and gave no trouble. The tenth pair had one beast a hand taller than the other, and the bow cut for the shorter rode up on his neck. The yoke was hung again with the beam bored off centre, and the pair worked out the season.
text_nonnarrative: A neck yoke had three parts of consequence: the beam, the bows, and the pins that held them. Each bow was a bent rod set into two holes in the beam, one bow to a beast, with the pins above the beam and the load below it. The beam was the only part common to both animals. Ornament on the beam ends was absent in working forms and present in ceremonial ones, whatever their size.

text_narrative: The near fore had been shod four times that year and it was still landing toe first. Kessa set it on the tripod and looked down the pastern. Too much heel, or not enough, it was hard to say which, and the wall was flared out on the outside quarter where the horse had been loading it. Rasping the flare would make the balance look right and be wrong. She took the heel down instead.
text_nonnarrative: Balance was a matter of the flight of the foot and not of the look of the wall. A hoof that landed toe first was out of balance whatever the height of the heel; a flared quarter was a separate class of fault and had no bearing on the landing. Wear on the shoe told against the one and never against the other. The horse and not the pastern was the unit of grading.

text_narrative: A gelding entered under the name Ninefold was withdrawn from the third class at the county meeting after an inspection at the collecting ring. The horse had shown a head nod at the trot on the hard strip and none on the turn. Stewards recorded the fault as a two on the six-point card. The rider, one of four from the northern club, took the animal home unloaded and did not appeal.
text_nonnarrative: Lameness is graded on the head nod at the trot and on nothing else in the horse's way of going. A fault shown on the hard strip and not on the turn is a two on the six-point card, whatever the class entered. Soundness at the walk is no part of the grading. The animal and not the rider bears the record, and withdrawal at the ring is a separate matter from the grade.

text_narrative: Three times that winter the grey mare Ombril refused the hill road. The first time the carter blamed the ice and doubled the load behind her. The second time she stood at the foot and would not lean into the collar, and the dog spoke up for her and was told to be quiet. The third time the carter lifted the collar off and found the hair worn away in two bands across her shoulders.
text_nonnarrative: A collar is required to bear on the shoulders and never on the windpipe, with two fingers of clearance at the throat. Draught from a collar that rides high is permitted only on level ground. Where the hair under a collar is worn in bands, the fit is to be altered and the pad is to be replaced. Nothing about the load bears on the requirement, which holds in every harness of any pattern.

text_narrative: The column halts on the third switchback and the loads come off two mules of the seven. A bar of salt has shifted on the near side of the second animal and the sawbuck sits crooked against the withers. The packer restacks both sides and takes a stone off the light side. Nothing is lost over the edge. The delay runs to forty minutes and the column reaches the saddle before the light goes.
text_nonnarrative: Tolerated side-to-side difference on a pack saddle was inverse to the gradient: on the flat a mule would carry a difference of some pounds, and on a steep pitch almost none. Load height above the withers told in the same direction, the righting moment being smaller by the square of that height. Beyond about a third of the animal's weight the relation did not hold, the limit being the animal and not the balance.

text_narrative: There was a loft keeper on the marsh road who kept one bird she never flew. The others she sent out at first light and they were home by noon, but this one sat in the end box. Her neighbours said the bird had no wing for it. In the year the fog stood for nine days and no bird came back, that one flew out and brought the rest in behind her.
text_nonnarrative: Homing capacity in a loft bird is not a property of the bird alone but of the bird and one particular loft together. A homer is any pigeon whose return is reliable from a distance greater than its natural range of flight, the loft being the sole reference point. Its range is a matter of settling in the first months. Birds without a settled loft have no homing character at all.

text_narrative: Cold comes up through the boards at the north end of the shed and the chicks pile there anyway, three deep against the wall. Ilva lifts the hover an inch and moves the lamp a hand's breadth toward the corner. The pile loosens. Within the hour the birds have spread into a ring, thickest at the rim and thin under the lamp itself, which is the pattern she wants. The far end stays cold.
text_nonnarrative: Losses in the first week varied more between sheds than within a single brood. The median across the recorded sheds was under three in a hundred, though a fifth of them ran to twice that. Floor temperature at the rim of the hover accounted for most of the spread; stocking density accounted for little of it. Keepers reporting a settled ring of chicks reported the lower figures, and the sample was small.

text_narrative: Before the hills had names the goats of the first flock ate upward, and what they could reach they took. The line they left ran level around every wood, as straight as water finds. The oldest of them, a dun nanny with one horn, stood on the shoulders of the others to eat higher, and the line above her head was the line that stood on the far slopes ever after, level and unbroken.
text_nonnarrative: A browse line is usually read as a sign of hunger, and that reading is too simple. Its height is set by the reach of the tallest animals in a flock, not by the number of animals or the poverty of the ground; a well-fed flock of tall goats marks a wood as sharply as a starved one. Density does bear on how fast the line hardens. It has no bearing on where the line sits.

text_narrative: Four times the warrener at Skell went out to the sandy piece with a spade, and four times the pattern of holes was different. On the first visit there were eleven mouths in a rough ring. On the second, nine, and the ring was tighter by a yard. On the third the ring had a gap on the north side. On the fourth there were eleven again, and the turf over them had never been cut.
text_nonnarrative: The sandy piece lay on the seaward side of a low bank, drier than the ground either way from it. Burrow mouths were thickest along the crest and sparse in the hollow. Below two feet the sand was damp and the runs were shallow there for that reason. The nearest cover was a line of thorn some forty yards off, and between the thorn and the bank the turf was bare and close-bitten throughout.

text_narrative: Out at the line camp they still talk about the way Cutler works a bank. Nets on every hole he can find, and then he sits on his heels and waits, and the hands who come for sport get bored inside ten minutes. But he does not lose a ferret down a stopped hole, which is more than the rest of them can say, and he does not dig either.
text_nonnarrative: A hole under water was not counted as a hole, and a bank with such a hole was not netted at all. Any burrow with an unnetted mouth was an open bank, and ferrets were not entered on an open bank. Digging was no part of the working and could not stand in for a net. A ferret below ground beyond the hour ended the bank, whatever the state of the nets.

text_narrative: In the eleventh season of the mulberry grant, the rearing house at Vellum Cross held forty trays. The worms of the third moult were fed at four hours through the night of the equinox, and the leaf ran short an hour before dawn. Two trays were given elm instead. Those two spun late and their cocoons were counted apart from the rest in the return made to the guild that autumn.
text_nonnarrative: Five grades of leaf are held in a rearing house, of which the second is the commonest in use. The first is the youngest shoot, chopped fine, for worms under the second moult. The third and fourth are whole leaf, the fourth with the stalk in. The fifth is elm or lettuce, kept only against a shortage, and never more than a night's worth is on the shelf at once.

text_narrative: The water at the low end has gone the colour of weak tea again, and Sarnia knows what that means before she has the lantern over it. Nothing wrong with the stock. The stock is fine, thriving, more than thriving. It is the count that troubles her. Eleven hundred went in at the thaw and the pond is carrying nearer two thousand now, and nothing has been added, and nothing feeds them but the pond.
text_nonnarrative: Under the pond orders, a stocked water meant any standing water held for the increase of leeches, whether banked or natural. Where the water was fed by a running stream, the orders relating to standing water did not apply. A keeper of a stocked water was the person in whose occupation the bank stood, and no separate licence was needed. Nothing in the orders affected rights of common in the fen beyond the bank.

text_narrative: When the drowned kings held the low country, every hall kept a stew pond below its wall, and the largest of them was at Harrowmere, four acres of still water. The carp of that pond were said to have been put in by the first of the line and never taken out. In the year the sluice failed the water ran off in a night and the bed showed nothing but weed.
text_nonnarrative: Two feet of water covered the shallow end and better than six the deep, with the sluice at the deepest corner. Reed stood in a band along the eastern margin and nowhere else. The bed was clay under a hand's depth of silt, and firm enough to walk on at the margins. Willow on the southern bank shaded a quarter of the surface, and that quarter was the coolest in high summer.

text_narrative: A raft on the outer line parted from two of its four moorings during the spring tides and drifted a quarter mile inshore before it grounded on soft ground. Forty ropes hung from it, all of them seeded the previous autumn. The crew that recovered the raft found the lower two metres of every rope stripped clean and the upper part untouched. The raft was towed out and remoored on six blocks.
text_nonnarrative: Weight, not current, set the working depth of a seeded rope. Each rope hung free from the raft beam with a small clump weight at the foot, and the spacing of the pegs along it fixed how much of the crop the rope could hold. Below a certain depth the ropes were within reach of bottom feeders and the pegs made no difference there. The raft itself bore the whole load through its four moorings.

text_narrative: Off the head the swell was long and slow and the boat lay to it easily while Doret hauled the eighth pot of the string. The pot came up light. Its funnel had pulled half out of the lath frame on one side, and the mouth stood open wider than a hand. She unshipped the ring, worked the funnel back through, and lashed it at four points instead of two before the pot went over again.
text_nonnarrative: No part of a creel was under more strain than the funnel, and none was less rigid. The body was a lath frame bent over two bows, netted on all faces but the base, which was boarded and weighted. Two funnels were set in the sides, each a cone of net held by a ring at the inner end. The parlour, a second chamber behind a third funnel, was absent in the older single-chamber creels.

text_narrative: Twice a year for nine years the warden of the sand spit worked the same three nets. In the earliest seasons the catch was mostly young birds and the rings went on quickly. In the middle years a bird from another coast turned up in the second net, ringed and unreadable, and was let go with a second ring. In the last season the nets stood empty on both visits.
text_nonnarrative: Recovery rates for small ringed birds sit below one in fifty, and the figure is lower for young birds than for adults. Most of the difference between coastal stations is a matter of net hours rather than of the birds present. Wardens report more variation within a single season than across a decade at one station. The sample of long-distance recoveries is thin enough that the median distance means little.

text_narrative: No keeper of that park would mend the paling on the eastern side, and there was a reason. The deer went out through the gap every autumn and came back thinner by the spring, and never once did a hound follow them through it. The year the lord had the gap closed with new oak, the deer stood in the open and would not feed, and by the spring the herd was half its number.
text_nonnarrative: A leap was permitted at one point in every furlong of paling and nowhere nearer a gate than twenty yards. The pale itself was required to stand six feet above the outer ditch, cleft oak and not sawn. Where a park bordered common ground, a double ditch was to be dug and the inner one kept dry. Repair was the charge of the holder of the park and of no one below him.

text_narrative: In the twelfth season of the Marbury pack, the huntsman entered nine couple of young hounds and struck four out of the book by midwinter. Two of the four were from the same dam, a bitch whose stock had always run wide. The book for that season carries a line against her name in a later hand. Her one remaining daughter bred the litter from which the pack's best nose descended.
text_nonnarrative: Three kinds of entry stand in a hound book, and only one of them is a pedigree proper. A pedigree entry names both parents and admits no alteration. A record entry names the dam alone and stays open to correction, which is what separates it from the first. The third kind, a note against a name, belongs to the pack and not to the hound, and shows no descent at all.

text_narrative: Every granary on that street kept a cat, and the one at the corner mill kept three, and still the mill lost more grain than any of them. The story the carters told was that the corner cat did its work in the wrong place. It sat all night on the sacks by the door, where nothing ran, and the mice worked the far bins under the wheel where no cat ever sat.
text_nonnarrative: A mousing cat was rated by where it sat and not by what it took. Sacks by the door counted for nothing, since nothing ran there; the bins under the wheel were the whole of the class. Grain lost in a granary told against the mill and never against the cat. Three cats in the wrong place were worth less than one in the right, and the count of mice was no part of it.

text_narrative: The column for the fourth cow did not add up, and Brann went back three weeks looking for the place where it stopped adding up. Nothing wrong with the animal. Nothing wrong with the arithmetic either, as far as could be seen. Which left the possibility that somebody had been writing down what the cow ought to give rather than what she gave, and that was worse than a bad cow.
text_nonnarrative: Between-animal variation in a yield ledger is smaller than most keepers suppose, and within-animal variation across a season is larger. Roughly a fifth of the recorded spread in a herd of thirty belongs to the day of recording rather than to the animals. Ledgers kept by one hand show less scatter than those kept by several, which is itself a finding about ledgers. The median entry is a poor summary of any cow.

text_narrative: A consignment of six hundred eggs is held at the packing station after candling on the morning line. Eleven show a blood spot against the lamp and are set aside. Forty more show an air cell above the permitted depth and go to the second grade. The station manager records the lot as mixed and releases it at the lower price the same afternoon, and the grader signs the sheet and initials the margin.
text_nonnarrative: Grade under candling was fixed by the air cell and by the spot, and by nothing about the shell. An air cell above the permitted depth put an egg into the second grade whatever its weight; a blood spot put it out of grade altogether. The proportion of either in a consignment set the class of the lot, so that eleven spots in six hundred made the lot mixed and not the eggs sound.

text_narrative: Halfway down the mob Teller finds the ewe that has been standing apart all morning. The wool over the tail is dark and lifting away from the skin in a patch the size of a hand. She cuts the patch out wide of the edge, down to clean fleece on all sides, and dresses what is under it. The ewe goes into the small pen and the mob moves on without her.
text_nonnarrative: Strike: any patch of fleece lifting from the skin with the wool discoloured at the base. Crutching: the removal of wool from the tail and hind parts, whether or not a strike is present. Wide edge: the margin of sound fleece taken with a struck patch, conventionally two inches. Susceptible mob: a mob in which the proportion of long tail wool is above the district figure for the month.

text_narrative: After the roads closed, the herds of the dry plain were held in common and marked in nine ways, one for each of the valleys that still had water. The mark of the deepest valley was a notch in the upper edge of the near ear, and it was the oldest of the nine. In the drought year a herd came down off the ridge bearing all nine marks, and no valley claimed it.
text_nonnarrative: An earmark is not a brand and the two are separate in law. A brand means a mark burnt into the hide in a registered form and place; an earmark means a cut of settled shape in either ear. Where a beast bears marks of two holders, ownership follows the brand and the earmark is evidence only. Nothing in this part touches beasts held in common, which are outside the register altogether.

text_narrative: In the second decade after the eastern grants, the keeper of the northern book refused eleven entries in one sitting, all of them from the same coastal district. His grounds were entered in the margin: no witness to the covering. The district petitioned the board twice and was refused twice, and the eleven horses were bred from all the same, off the book, and their get went south under other names.
text_nonnarrative: Closed books were defended on the ground that they preserved a type, and there was something in it. What they preserved, though, was a record rather than a type: the animals outside the book were not different animals, only unwitnessed ones. Breeders who worked off the book bred to the same standard and kept their own notes. The book had its use, but that use was administrative and not zoological.

text_narrative: Each spring Halder takes the same road north and stops at the same four stances. The first is a walled acre below the pass, wet at one corner. At the second he waters short because the burn is low by the time the herds are through. The third has no water at all and is used only in a wet year. At the fourth he pays the toll and counts the beasts out.
text_nonnarrative: Nothing but heather covered the mile above the pass, and the road there was two cart widths of bare peat between banks. A stance lay on the western side at the halfway point, walled on three sides with the fourth open to the road. The ground within it stood lower toward the south-west corner, which was boggy in any weather. Shelter was on the lee side of the wall alone.

text_narrative: There is a man at the yard who will tell anyone that the bedding is where the trouble starts, and he is not wrong, though he has his own reasons for saying it. Wheat straw one week, barley the next, whatever comes cheap off the back of a lorry at eleven at night. The dogs cough by the week's end. Nobody writes any of it down, which is the point.
text_nonnarrative: Only three beddings are in common use in a working kennel, and shavings are not among them. Wheat straw is the standard, long in the stem and slow to break down, and it is the warmest of the three. Barley straw is shorter and dustier, cheaper by a third, and unsuited to young stock. Shredded paper is the last, cold underfoot and used mainly in the whelping boxes.

text_narrative: There was a caravan master in the salt country who would not let a pad be made of anything but reed. The other masters used felt, and their beasts came in sore at the third well. His did not. When he was old he was asked the reason and said only that reed lets the wind through and felt holds the heat against the hump, and that the beasts knew it before he did.
text_nonnarrative: Pressure under a pack saddle is a function of the bearing area and of the stiffness of the pad beneath it, and the two work against each other. A thick pad spreads the load and traps heat; a thin one sheds heat and concentrates the load along the bars. Reed sits between the two because its channels hold the bars clear of the skin. Without those channels the material does nothing a felt pad does not.

text_narrative: On the chalk a mill stood where the water failed every summer, and a donkey walked the gin from midsummer to the rains. The miller's daughter counted the rounds one year and found the beast made the same number each day whatever the load, which she thought a wonder. The truth was simpler and sadder: the gin was geared so that the sacks came slower, not the donkey.
text_nonnarrative: Work done at a horse gin is the product of the pull at the trace and the distance walked, and the gearing has no part in it. A beast walking a circle of thirty feet covers the same ground in a day as one walking a circle of sixty at half the rounds. Gearing bears on the speed at the shaft and never on the product.

text_narrative: Something is wrong with the count and Ostler knows it before the last sheaf comes off the rick. Nineteen last year in the same yard, and the yard has stood untouched since. Eleven tonight, and the dog working as hard as ever, and no holes in the stack floor. Which leaves the granary wall, or the drain, or somebody moving them, and none of the three is a comfortable thought.
text_nonnarrative: What passes for a good ratting dog in most yards is a fast one, which is the least useful thing to breed for. Speed at the stack is showy and adds nothing where the cover is down; steadiness at a single hole is what tells. The better strains are the ones bred for patience and marked down for it by anyone watching. The reputation of the practice is worse than the practice.

text_narrative: The pipe curves away from the pool under its hoops of netting and the light at the far end is the wrong colour, greenish, as it always is by the fourth screen. Vessa walks the screens with the little dog at heel and shows it and hides it, shows it and hides it. The birds come up the pipe after the dog. They do this every time and no one at the decoy can say why.
text_nonnarrative: A pipe of a single bend was not a decoy, whatever its length. A decoy was a pool with two or more curved pipes leading off it, each hooped over with netting and screened along the outer side, the curve being what kept the far end out of sight from the pool. Its capacity was a matter of the number of pipes and of the wind, since only a pipe with the wind behind it was in use.

text_narrative: In the first age of the oak wood the swine were counted as part of the wood and not as beasts belonging to anyone. They came under the branches at the mast fall and went out again at the turn of the cold, and the wood was reckoned rich or poor by how many it could keep. The year the great oak stood barren, the swine stayed under it all winter and were not counted at all.
text_nonnarrative: The dispute whether pannage names a right in the wood or a right in the swine is not settled by the word itself. If the right is in the wood, it attaches to the holding, and the number of swine is a measure of the wood. If the right is in the swine, the wood is only their pasture, and a count of animals is the whole of it. The two readings part company where the mast is poor.

text_narrative: Three shifts running, Corin walks the terrace beds under the dome lights and finds the same thing. Bed four is full and heavy. Bed five has the shells thin at the lip, the way they go when the grit runs out. Bed six is worse. On the fourth shift he moves the grit line up a bed and by the shift after that the lips are hardening again in five, though six stays thin.
text_nonnarrative: Shell quality in a farmed snail was limited by calcium and by nothing else that a keeper controlled. A snail garden was any enclosed bed of damp soil stocked at a density above the wild one, with a lime source at the surface and a cover against light. Its yield was set by that density and by the length of the active period. Beds without a lime source held stock of no market value.

text_narrative: In the third year of the blockade the cactus terraces above the town were the only trade left, and the guild kept the count. Nine hundredweight of dried scale went out by the mountain road that season, half what the terraces had given before the road was cut. Two of the seven terraces were lost to frost in the same winter. The guild recorded the loss against weather and not against the war.
text_nonnarrative: Wild scale and cultivated scale are not two species but two conditions of one, and the line between them is a matter of husbandry rather than of form. The cultivated kind is larger, slower, and unable to hold to a pad in wind, and that inability is the practical mark of the difference. A third grade, the mixed gathering off unattended pads, belongs to neither and is classed by weight alone.

text_narrative: Two hours out and the line is still wrong. Anyone at the depot will say a gangline is a gangline, and Rask has believed it herself for four seasons. But the swing pair are pulling across and not along, and the tugline on the near side is slack at every stride, and the whole team is working half again as hard as it needs to for the same ground on a level trail.
text_nonnarrative: The best gangline work was the least visible, and that was the trouble with the whole literature of driving. Writers on the subject dwelt on the leaders, who did little of the pulling, and passed over the tugline lengths, which did most of it. The received account of harnessing was in fact a set of habits nobody had written down. The better practitioners were the ones least interested in the leaders.

text_narrative: The old wether at the head of that flock had opinions about the race, and the young ones listened. Twice a year the whole flock went through it, and twice a year the old wether went last and came out sound. He told them the trick was to keep to the dry side of the trough and let the crowding sheep take the wet. Nobody believed him until the wet spring.
text_nonnarrative: Scald is not an early stage of footrot but a separate condition, and the two are told apart by where the damage sits. Scald is confined to the skin between the claws; footrot undermines the horn of the wall and the sole. Interdigital growths are a third thing again, neither infectious nor answerable to a foot bath, and they belong with the conformation faults rather than with either of the first two.

text_narrative: There was a ewe in the high fold who took every lamb that was offered her and never asked whose it was. The shepherds brought her four in one season, three of them in borrowed coats and one with no coat at all, and she took that one too. The other ewes in the fold would have none of it and said she brought the count into disrepute, and she went on taking them.
text_nonnarrative: A lamb on two ewes is not a legal position and cannot stand at the count, whatever the state of either ewe. A ewe with one lamb of her own is open to a foster; a ewe with two is closed. Marking is not a claim and cannot be answered by a counter-mark. Where a coat is used, the coat holds no standing of its own and the fold book governs.

text_narrative: A herd of forty goats aboard the ring station is combed out of sequence this cycle after the fibre store reports a shortfall. The animals are taken in groups of eight to the low-spin deck, where the loose undercoat lifts more readily. Two of the older does yield nothing and are returned uncombed. The station log records the whole gathering at eleven kilos against a standing figure of nineteen.
text_nonnarrative: Undercoat: the fine layer beneath the guard hair, and the only part of the fleece of any value. Guard hair: the coarse outer layer, which is a contaminant in the sorted product. Yield: the mass of undercoat off one animal in one gathering, stated dry. Shortfall: any gathering below the standing figure for the herd, whatever its cause. Cycle: the interval at which a herd is combed, set by the moult.

text_narrative: Long before the walls of the inner yard were raised, geese kept the ground, and it was said that no thief had ever crossed it unheard. The birds were counted as watchmen in the old reckoning and were fed from the same store. When the walls went up the geese were put outside them, and the yard within was quiet, and the quiet was held afterwards to have been the beginning of the trouble there.
text_nonnarrative: Two accounts of a guard animal were available, and they parted over what was owed to it rather than over what it did. On the first view, a goose that gave the alarm held a place in the household and a claim on the store, and the claim did not depend on any alarm being given. On the second, it was a thing kept, and its keeping was a cost. Neither view was decided by the noise.

text_narrative: Before light the ridge hut was furred white on its windward side, and Anselm went round it with a lamp to see which kind had come. Hoar crystals stood off the guy wires in feathers, dry and separate, and he brushed one wire clean with a glove. On the lee corner the coating was milky and welded to the boards, and it would not brush. He wrote both down and marked the wind side wrong.
text_nonnarrative: Neither density nor thickness settles the class of a frost deposit: crystal habit and the side of the wire on which it sits are the whole of it. Feathered hoar, dry and brushable, counts as one class whatever its depth. Milky rime hard against the boards is a second, and windward position is disqualifying for hoar however fine the crystals. Wind speed along the ridge bears on the cause and never on the class.

text_narrative: A hailfall on the eastern grazings on the second of June left stones large enough for the district officer to collect a dozen from a single roof gutter. The officer split four of them on a bench with a warmed knife and photographed the cut faces. Each showed alternating bands, clear and opaque, and the largest carried eleven. The find was entered in the parish record and the stones were kept in a chest of ice.
text_nonnarrative: Bands in a hailstone alternate clear and opaque, and the count of them is a function of the depth of the cloud and of the strength of its updraught. The opaque layers are the porous ones; the clear are dense and heavier for their thickness. Diameter is independent of band count, since a stone of eleven thin bands and one of four thick bands are of a size. Bands are legible only on a cut face.

text_narrative: Halfway along the crest Ivrea stops, because the snow underfoot has gone hollow in a way that is not the wind's doing. There is a line out there, she thinks, a hair of shadow running parallel to the drop, and it was not there in the morning. She backs off two paces and looks along the surface. The line is there. It is a fracture, and it is behind her heels.
text_nonnarrative: Two fractures in a cornice were distinguished by the position of the surface of separation and not by its depth. A crown fracture lay back on the crest, well behind the lip, with the whole slab inboard of it. A lip fracture sat at the overhang alone. Settlement cracking was neither: a hollow sound underfoot with no line of shadow, and no discontinuity anywhere in the depth of the slab.

text_narrative: In the fourth winter of the new road the slope above the seventh milestone discharged twice. The first release stopped short of the culvert. The second overran it by ninety paces and buried the pole line to the crossheads, and the road master ordered the markers reset in the spring. Two carters wintering at the hut below were not found until the thaw. The survey of the following year moved the line uphill by a furlong.
text_nonnarrative: Markers on a runout are required to stand at the far limit of the longest release on record and not at the mean of several. A pole line is permitted inside that limit only where the poles are frangible at the base. Shelter is to be sited outside the limit altogether, on ground beyond every recorded reach, and a road within the zone is to carry a warning board at each of its ends.

text_narrative: In the second season of the northern survey the party crossed the lower field on the eleventh of March. Four bridges held. The fifth gave under the second man of the rope, who went in to the chest and was drawn out on a shortened line, and the sledge was abandoned where it stood. The party lay that night on the dirty ice below the belt. On the twelfth the crossing was made by the outer margin.
text_nonnarrative: The field lies in three belts between the icefall and the flat. The upper belt is the narrowest, its crevasses transverse and close-spaced, and the bridges there are thin. The middle belt is wider, and its openings sit oblique to the line of travel. Below that, the ice is dirty and nearly whole, with a single marginal gap along the rock wall. The safest ground of the three is the outer edge of the lowest belt.

text_narrative: Before the valleys had names, the ice at the shoulder of the world stood in towers, and the towers were the teeth of a thing that slept under the mountain. In the first age one tooth leaned out above the col and hung there through nine winters. In the tenth it let go. The sleeper turned once in the dark of its bed and did not wake, and the col was shut for a generation.
text_nonnarrative: An ice tower was best understood as a consequence of the bed beneath it and not of the cold above. Where the floor of a glacier stood in steps, the surface answered in blocks, and the blocks were only what the fracture pattern allowed. That the towers were the most conspicuous feature of the ice did not make them the governing one, though they did govern which lines of passage were open.

text_narrative: Three summers running, the horse-breaker Cobb took the short way over the shale above the dry creek, and three summers running the shale took a horse's footing out from under it. The first year the mare went down to her hocks and came out sound. The second year the slide carried thirty feet of the path away. The third year Cobb walked, leading, and the shale ran anyway, and he stood in it to the knee.
text_nonnarrative: Thirty-four degrees is the usual ceiling for dry angular waste, and the figure is a property of the grains rather than of the slope. Coarse fragments hold a degree or two above fine ones. Height bears on nothing: a bank of ten feet and a bank of three hundred stand at one angle. Beyond the ceiling no stable configuration is available, and the relation between angle and grain size fails. Moisture alters the figure by less than a degree.

text_narrative: There was a shepherd who would not walk beneath the crowning block of the high tor, and the parish thought little of it until the winter the block came down. It fell in the night and split along an old joint, and the halves lay apart like a loaf. Under it, in the sand of the socket, the parish found a shepherd's crook of a pattern nobody had cut for two hundred years.
text_nonnarrative: Corestone: a rounded mass of sound rock standing where the jointed rock about it was weaker. Grus: the gritty waste of that jointed rock, in place and undisturbed. Tor: a group of corestones in position, one upon another. Clitter: the same material below the group, out of position and downslope. Basin: a hollow in the upper face of a corestone, without outlet. Socket: the seating of a block, defined by its bearing surface.

text_narrative: The pasture at Vellum Farm lost eleven yards of its western corner in the small hours of a Tuesday, and the hole that replaced it was forty feet deep, with clean walls and a sharp rim. A gate, two rolls of wire and a water trough went down with the turf. The farm dogs would not go within a chain of the edge. No sound had been heard at the house.
text_nonnarrative: A hollow of this kind is classed by the state of its walls and not by its contents. Clean walls and a sharp rim put it in the collapse class whatever the depth. Sides of sloping turf make it a subsidence hollow however deep. Loss of a gate or a trough bears on the value of the pasture and never on the class, and quiet at the farm is no criterion at all.

text_narrative: Under the lip of the terrace the water comes over in a sheet and turns the moss to stone, and the woman who keeps the orchard hangs things in it. A ladle. A child's shoe. A pair of spectacles on a wire. After a season each comes out white and heavier and not quite the shape it went in as. She hangs the spectacles back up, because they are not finished.
text_nonnarrative: Tufa was a porous freshwater limestone deposited where hard water stood in contact with air at a fall or a seep. Its texture was a cast of whatever it enveloped, so moss, leaves and cloth were all legible in the finished rock. Rate of accumulation depended on temperature and on the loss of carbon dioxide from the film. Its strength was therefore low, and its bulk high for the weight of stone in it.

text_narrative: Nobody in the upper township digs a well, and the reason is the band of clay. The water walks sideways along the top of it and comes out in a row of seeps under the beech line, and every house in the row is set on a seep. Old Marrec keeps the middle one clear with a paddle twice a year, and says the others have gone slovenly about theirs.
text_nonnarrative: Under this part a spring line means the horizontal band at which water is held up by an impermeable stratum, and not any single issue of water within it. Where a dwelling stands on such a band, the right of access to the issue nearest it is appurtenant to the dwelling. Nothing in this section affects a well sunk below the stratum, which is outside the definition altogether.

text_narrative: Over the four years she held the gauge round, Ferran read the standpipe at the mill four times a winter. The first winter it stood a hand above the collar. The second it stood two. The third year it topped the collar and ran out over the yard, and the miller cut a channel for it. The fourth winter she found the pipe dry and the collar rusted, and recorded nothing.
text_nonnarrative: Head varies more between valleys than within them, and the spread inside one valley is mostly a matter of elevation. The median standing level in the surveyed bores is a little under two feet above the collar. A quarter of bores stand in overflow at the winter maximum and none in late summer. Figures reported by millers make up most of the older record and run systematically higher than the instrumented ones.

text_narrative: The commissioners of the Vale walked the three benches above the water in the ninth year of the Protectorate and set a boundary stone on each. The lowest stone was carried off by flood in the same decade. The middle stone stood until the roads came. The highest was found in the last survey, upside down in a hedge bank, with the Protectorate arms still legible on the buried face.
text_nonnarrative: A flight of terraces was a set of benches, each with a flat tread and a steeper riser below it. The tread was underlain by gravel of the old channel; the riser was cut in whatever the valley side was made of. Paired benches sat at one height on both banks. Unpaired ones were absent from one side entirely, and the lowest bench was commonly the widest of the flight.

text_narrative: The deeds say the boundary is the river, and Halla is standing in what the deeds call the river, on dry grass, holding a rake. The water is over there now, a quarter mile off, behind the willows. Her neighbour's cattle are on this side of the old bend and therefore, by the deeds, on her land. Or she is on his. She cannot make the sentence come out the same way twice.
text_nonnarrative: A boundary held to the old channel wherever that channel was traceable on the ground, and to the live water only where it was not. A bend severed by the river was no change of boundary and could not be pleaded as one. A boundary lying under standing water at every stage was void, and the bank line was taken in its place. Silt on the bank was not evidence of either.

text_narrative: There was a heron who claimed every bar in the braided reach and could not hold them, for the water remade the bars each spring and his marks meant nothing to the new ones. One year the river left him a bar of grey shingle, wide as a barn floor and empty of fish. He stood on it all summer out of pride, and grew thin, and told the other birds it was the best of them.
text_nonnarrative: Four bar forms were recognised in the reach, of which the longitudinal was the commonest. It was lens-shaped in plan, coarse at the upstream end and fine at the tail. The transverse bar was squarer, with a steep front face. Point bars were confined to the few curved sections. Diagonal bars were the rarest, set across the flow at an angle and drowned at all but the lowest stages. None of the four was permanent in position.

text_narrative: When the mountain gods were still owed tribute, the debt was paid in stone. Each spring the torrent brought a lobe of it down to the plain and spread it in a tongue below the gorge mouth, and the tongue was measured by the priests of the low country. In the year the tribute doubled, the tongue reached the wells, and the low country stopped asking for rain.
text_nonnarrative: Whether a fan was one landform or a sequence of them turned on what was allowed to count as a part. Taken as a body of debris with a single apex, it was one thing. Taken as a set of lobes, each with its own limit, it was many, and the apex was merely what they shared. Nothing in the deposit itself settled which of the two descriptions was correct.

text_narrative: Every time the road party came back through the yellow bluffs, Sennen cut a fresh notch at the foot of the standing column and stepped away to look at it.
