The first year the notch was at knee height. The second year the column had a new crack down its road face and the notch lay buried in fallen dust. The third year there was no column, and Sennen cut into the bank behind where it had been.
text_nonnarrative: A column of this silt is classed by the geometry of its face and not by how much dust lies at its foot. A vertical face is the sound condition, whatever the height. Any crack parallel to the face is disqualifying, and one on the road side counts double, since undercutting at the bank governs the failure. Notches cut for measurement bear on the record of the bluff and never on the class of the column.

text_narrative: Out past the last of the rovers the dune stands at its full height, and Oyelaran walks the crest of it with the sampler dragging behind. Sand goes over the lip in slow tongues under a thin gravity, each tongue taking a minute to arrive at the base. He stops to watch one. The seismometer in his pack registers nothing at all, which is the finding, and he writes it down at the top of the slope.
text_nonnarrative: Most accounts of slipface movement failed on one point: they treated grain flow as a single happening rather than as a condition of the surface. What passed for observation in them was usually a set of times taken at the crest, with nothing said of the base. The better accounts were the ones that gave both angles and left the drama out. Vividness in this literature was almost always a substitute for measurement of the angle.

text_narrative: The pilots on that coast never gave the outer stack a name, and there was a reason for it. Old hands said a stack with a name got trusted, and the arch behind that one was down to a span of four feet at the top. They took their bearings off the headland instead. The arch fell in the winter of the great easterly, and what was left stood a cable off the cliff and looked like nothing on the chart.
text_nonnarrative: A stack is what remains of a headland where the arch that held it to the land is absent. Its stability is a function of the bedding attitude and of the width of the wave-cut platform at its foot. Where the beds dip seaward the column is inherently the weaker. Without a platform the base bears the full force of the water, and the two properties are not independent of each other. Height above water is no part of either.

text_narrative: The insurance man walks the base of the cliff at low water with a rule in his hand and finds the notch running clean under the property line for a hundred and forty feet. Above it the turf hangs over on nothing. The house at the top is empty and has been since the sale. He measures at four points, photographs the overhang, and puts the rule away without writing anything down.
text_nonnarrative: Three notch forms were kept apart in the older descriptions of a cliff base. A wave notch was cut at the level of the water and was deepest at its inner angle. A solution notch had the same profile but sat on soluble rock and was independent of wave energy. A spring notch was the odd one, sited wherever the face was wet from a seep, at any height and in any rock.

text_narrative: In the second spring of the siege the hill above the north battery moved, not quickly, and the toe of it came out across the sap in nine days. The gunners shifted two pieces and left the third. By the end of that month the lobe stood twelve feet over the parapet and the sap was closed. Neither side worked the ground again, and the third piece was never recovered.
text_nonnarrative: Toe: the downslope end of a slipped mass, standing above the undisturbed ground beyond it. Scarp: the bare face at the head, where the mass was formerly continuous with the hill. Lobe: a single tongue of the mass, bounded by its own flanks. Flank: either lateral margin, commonly sheared. Bulge: any convexity of the surface in advance of the toe, whether or not the surface there was broken.

text_narrative: When the mountains still spoke, one of them said the same word for eleven days and the word came down as grey meal on the plain. It lay a hand deep. The year after, the mountain said a shorter word and the meal was finer and paler. Seven times it spoke in that generation, and the plain kept the count in seven layers, and the people read them from a cut bank.
text_nonnarrative: The cut bank above the ford showed seven grey layers in a face of about four feet. The lowest was the coarsest and the thickest, a hand deep at the northern end and thinner southward. Over it lay three fine pale bands, none more than a finger. The uppermost layer was the palest and sat directly under the turf, with no soil between the two. The face itself was vertical for its whole height.

text_narrative: From the rim of the collapse Dessa can see how thin the roof is, thinner than the chart allows, which means the chart is old or the chart is wrong. Two metres, perhaps. The rover sits forty metres back on ground that reads the same on the survey as the ground under her boots. She does not walk back the way she came. She goes out sideways, toward the rock.
text_nonnarrative: Vehicles were required to stand on ground of known thickness and never within two spans of a skylight rim. Foot traffic was permitted across a roof only where the span was under six metres and the cover above four. Loads over a tonne were to bear on the flanks and not on the crown. Charts of more than one season were to be held advisory and no warrant for either.

text_narrative: A king wanted a stair of white stone that no mason had cut, and his steward found him one at the head of a hot valley, where the ground built its own steps a hair a year. The king sat on the seventh step and waited for the eighth. He waited eleven years. The stair rose two fingers in that time, and the king had the steward's name struck from the roll.
text_nonnarrative: Sinter was the pale siliceous crust of a hot spring, set apart from lime deposits by its material and not by its form. It occupied rimmed pools whose lips stood a little above the water in each. Its rate of accretion was slow, of the order of a millimetre in a year, and depended on the silica load of the water and on the temperature at the surface of each pool.

text_narrative: A mason once took a commission for a sea wall church and chose the honey-coloured stone because it cut sweetly under the chisel. Within a lifetime the west face was pocked like a sponge, cell inside cell, and the north face was sound. His grandson was called to make it good, looked at the two faces, and refused the work. He said the wall had chosen its own weather and would keep on choosing.
text_nonnarrative: A wall stone is classed as fretted on the form of its cavities and not on how deep they go. Cell inside cell puts it in the fretted class whatever the face. Sound stone with a powdered surface is a separate condition. Aspect and weather bear on the cause and never on the class, so a west face and a north face of one sea wall may be graded apart on a day.

text_narrative: A survey flight over the northern flats returns eleven hundred frames of patterned ground, and the analyst on the crew counts sides on the first two hundred by hand before the machine is allowed near them. Her count and the machine's part company at the eighth frame. She marks it and goes on. By the two hundredth the two counts differ by a third, and the whole discrepancy sits in the five-sided cells.
text_nonnarrative: Mean polygon diameter stood in proportion to the depth of the thawed layer, with a constant peculiar to the substrate. Six sides was the modal count, and the arithmetic mean lay a little under six. Trough width bore no fixed relation to diameter. Past a diameter of forty metres the proportionality failed, and the larger nets were of another order, with secondary cells inside the primary ones. Trough depth was proportional to trough width throughout.

text_narrative: No party in the north would camp on a round hill, and the story behind it was always the same. A crew had pitched on a low dome out of the wind, and in the night the floor of the tent had gone soft and then gone altogether, and the camp had finished in a bowl of cold water. Whether it happened or not, the rule held, and the parties pitched on the flat.
text_nonnarrative: A mound of this kind is better treated as a body of ice with a skin of soil than as a hill with ice in it, because everything about its shape follows from the core. Its height is the thickness of the ice; its summit cracks are the surface answering to the form beneath. That the soil cover is what a party actually stands on does not make the cover the thing itself.

text_narrative: Below the shoulder path the valley is a lake of white with the church tower standing out of it, and Ceridwen knows the tower is three miles off and has known that since childhood. The bell sounds. It sounds close, the way it does when the lid is on, and the second stroke arrives from behind her, from the bare hillside where there is no tower and never was one. She keeps walking upward.
text_nonnarrative: The layer had three parts. Beneath was the cold pool, filling the valley to a level top and taking its plan from the contour. Over that stood the lid itself, a shallow band of warm air a few tens of metres thick. Above the lid the free atmosphere was unaffected. The upper margin of the pool was sharp; the lower had no margin at all, being the ground. Lid thickness was independent of pool depth.

text_narrative: Four winters in the house under the ridge taught Ilse to read the door. On the first warm night she opened every window and the linen dried indoors by morning. On the second she left the shutters loose and lost a pane. The third winter she kept a wedge in the frame and the door held. The fourth she stopped minding it, which was the year the roof went.
text_nonnarrative: Temperature at the foot of a lee slope varies more from valley to valley than from year to year, and the spread inside one valley is small. The median difference reported at the settlements is eight degrees across twelve hours. Households at the mouth account for most of the extreme returns. Humidity is the least consistent part of the record, since few of the returns are instrumented at all.

text_narrative: Two miles to leeward a grey rope hangs from the cloud base to the water and the mate has the glass on it. The ring of spray at its foot is the part that matters, he says to nobody, and the ring is holding. The master orders the course altered eight points and the topsail handed. The rope leans, thickens, and stands still, and the ship passes it at something like a mile.
text_nonnarrative: A funnel over water means, in this schedule, a visible condensation column between a cloud base and the surface, whether or not it is in contact with either. Where a ring of disturbed water lies below it, the column is a spout for all reporting requirements. Nothing in this schedule affects a column over land, which falls under the preceding item and carries a definition of its own. Duration is no part of the meaning here.

text_narrative: They still do not fell the spiral tree at the top of the long field, and the reason is what lies under it. The scar goes from the crown to the root in a slow turn, one full turn and a little more, and the bark on either side of it is sound. Twice the parish has marked the trunk for the saw. Twice the chalk is gone by morning, and the tree keeps its turn.
text_nonnarrative: A tree is standing timber only where the trunk is entire; a trunk with a groove to the heartwood is not, whatever its height. A single spiral scar does not put a tree outside the class. Two crossing scars do, and the position is then not arguable. A mark made on a trunk is no part of its condition and cannot be answered by removing the mark. A tree outside the class is nonetheless timber for every other rule.

text_narrative: A bargeman counted three suns over the frozen reach one morning and took it for a sign that the year would be threefold. He sold his barge, bought three of everything, and told the towpath what was coming. The three suns hung an hour and left one. By spring he was hauling for another man, and the towpath called him Threefold for the rest of his days.
text_nonnarrative: Old chronicles of sky signs were poor sources on halo phenomena, and poor in a consistent direction. What passed for a record in them was a count of suns and an omen, with no note of angular distance from the true sun and none of the colour order. The best of them were the ones that gave the distance and left the omen unstated.

text_narrative: On the ninetieth day out the floe closed against the shore lead and threw up a ridge across the whole of the depot line. The sail stood eleven feet and the keel was sounded at forty. Two sledges were brought over it in a day and a half. The rubble at the flanks was loose and took a man to the waist twice. The depot was shifted half a mile east.
text_nonnarrative: A ridge is classed on the height of its sail and on nothing beneath the water, since the keel is not measurable from sledges. Rubble loose at the flanks is a separate matter, bearing on the crossing and never on the class. A ridge across a depot line and one across open floe fall into the same class, the position being no part of the grading at all.

text_narrative: After the last of the cities went quiet, the wind took the plain for itself and wrote on it in one direction only. The old people of the shelters called the carved forms the wind's alphabet and held that the reading of it was lost with the towers. A runner crossed the plain in the tenth winter and came back saying the letters all pointed home, which was the last useful thing anybody said of them.
text_nonnarrative: Five kinds of wind-carved snow are common on an open plain. The commonest is a low ridge a hand high, cut away at the windward end and tapered to leeward. Next in frequency are shallow blade forms, sharp-edged and no wider than a boot. Pits are the third kind, round and steep-sided. Whaleback forms are broad and smooth. Crescents are rare and sit only where the surface is soft. All five lie aligned to a single wind.

text_narrative: The district engineer's office recorded the front of the lobe at eleven metres from the road margin in the spring survey and at nine metres in the autumn one. A second party was sent out to look at the mark and found the peg upright but tilted forward at the head. The office entered both figures without comment. A note in the margin observed that the boundary named in the lease was the front itself.
text_nonnarrative: Nothing in the composition of such a body settles whether it counts as ice or as rock, since it is plainly both. If the criterion is what bears the load, it is ice, and the debris is a coat. If the criterion is what an instrument stands on, it is rock. The two answers are not rivals but replies to different questions asked under one word. Neither is available as a settlement of the other.

text_narrative: The ledge had been under the second gate when Ruvan started on the leat, and it was above the second gate now, which meant the water had taken eight feet of rock in nineteen years. Nobody had asked him to keep the figure. He kept it because the leat had to draw from above the ledge and one day it would not, and on that day somebody would want to know when.
text_nonnarrative: An abrupt step in the bed of a watercourse, separating a reach of one gradient from a reach of another, is a knickpoint within this article. Where the step lies upstream of a lawful intake, the intake is unaffected by any change in its position. Where it lies downstream, the entitlement of the holder is measured from the step as found at the date of grant and from no subsequent position.

text_narrative: The shelf comes across the lake in a single grey step with clear air beneath it, and the man on the jetty does not go in. He watches the underside instead, which is turning over on itself like something breathing. The gulls are down already. When the edge passes above the jetty the cold drops through his coat and the water goes white, and he is standing there yet, watching the wrong way, upward.
text_nonnarrative: Craft on the lake were required to be off the water on the appearance of a step-edged cloud with clear air below it, and not merely on a freshening of wind. Moorings were permitted on the lee shore only. A jetty was to be clear to the landward gate, and any structure of more than one storey was to stand back from the head of the jetty by its own height.

text_narrative: Each evening the shepherd counts the steps on the facing slope, because the count is not the same twice. Monday it is nineteen. Wednesday it is nineteen. On the Friday there are twenty, and the new one is at the bottom, below the wall, on ground that has been flat since the wall was built. He counts again at first light. There are twenty, and the wall leans outward.
text_nonnarrative: Terracette: one of a set of small steps on a grassy slope, of the order of a foot in height. Tread: the near-level upper surface of a step, commonly the width of a boot. Riser: the steeper face below the tread, often bare where the turf is torn. Lobe: a terracette whose front is convex in plan. Front: the downslope limit of any of these, whether or not the turf is intact.

text_narrative: During the age of the second sun the stones of the waste were given a skin so that the world could be written on. Every boulder took a dark rind of its own making, thin as a breath, and any scratch through it stood out pale for a thousand years. The first scribes cut their whole law into one field of them. The law stayed legible in patches long after the readers were gone.
text_nonnarrative: Dark rind on a desert boulder was better read as an accumulation from outside than as an alteration of the rock beneath it, because its composition had little to do with the stone it lay on. Manganese and clay out of dust made up the bulk of it. That the rind followed the surface exactly gave the contrary impression, but conformity of that sort was what any thin coating would show.

text_narrative: Guides on that side of the range will not cross the upper snowfield in the afternoon, and it is not the softness they mind. The hollows there run a foot deep and hold shadow all day, and a party crossing them in the low sun sees a second party going the other way, hollow for hollow, keeping step. Nobody has ever met one. The guides go round by the rock, which costs an hour.
text_nonnarrative: Ground of this sort counted as broken, and a party on broken ground was not held to the ordinary rate. A crossing in the low sun was no legal crossing at all, whatever the state of the surface. Depth of hollow was no ground of exception. A party held back by the rule was not thereby a party in difficulty, and no report was owed. The rule bound guides and independent parties alike.

text_narrative: In the fourteenth year of the wood account, the eastern cant came round for cutting and the reeve found it short by four stools. Two had been grubbed for a cart track and two were dead under bramble. He cut the cant regardless, bound the poles in fifties, and set a mark of tarred rope on the stump nearest the ride so the next rotation would start from a known corner rather than from the hedge.
text_nonnarrative: No cant is to be cut twice inside the fixed term, and the term is fifteen years on the eastern soils and twelve on the western. Stools grubbed for a track are to be counted against the cant and not against the wood at large. Poles are permitted in bundles of fifty, no larger. A mark of tarred rope on the corner stump is required wherever a cant abuts a ride rather than a hedge.

text_narrative: There was a willow at the ford that had been headed so often the crown of it was a fist of old wood the width of a barrel. The tale went that a woman of the valley cut her share from it every eighth winter and left a coin in the split each time. One winter she came late and found the head bare, and the coins of forty years lay in the mud below.
text_nonnarrative: A pollard head was the swollen mass of old wood at the top of a bole cut repeatedly above the reach of stock. Its width was a rough index of the number of cuttings it had borne, though not of their spacing. Regrowth was confined to the outer rim of the head and never to the centre, which was dead wood in all but the youngest examples, and often hollow at the core.

text_narrative: Before the forest had names for its own kinds, the first tree was cut across by a wind that did not stop at bark. What the wind found inside was two woods in one: an outer ring still wet and moving, and a dark column at the middle that had given up moving long before. The tree stood a hundred years after the cut, and every tree since has carried that same division in it.
text_nonnarrative: Sapwood is the outer sleeve of a stem, bounded outside by cambium and inside by heartwood. The boundary between the two is a surface, not a layer, and in some kinds it is invisible in fresh section. Heartwood occupies the column at the centre and is absent in young stems and in a few kinds at all ages. Rays cross both zones without interruption, and are the only tissue common to both in the mature stem.

text_narrative: A dispute over the age of a boundary oak goes to the county surveyor in the second week of the month. Two cores are taken at right angles from the same trunk at chest height. One gives a hundred and forty rings, the other a hundred and sixty-two. The surveyor finds no rot and no double sheath, and reports that the pith lies eleven inches off the geometric centre of the trunk.
text_nonnarrative: Ring width in a given year was inversely related to the number of stems competing on the same rooting area, and the relation held only above a threshold of about eight stems to the square rod. Radial counts differed between two cores from one trunk in proportion to the eccentricity of the pith. A displacement of one inch corresponded, on the older stems, to a discrepancy of two rings in ten.

text_narrative: Marika kept the seed room at the nursery for nine seasons. In the first she found a lot of parsnip four years old and sowed it thick out of stubbornness; a quarter came up. In the fourth she threw out a whole bin of onion after a chit count of eleven in a hundred. In the seventh she pulled a paper of leek from behind a beam, undated, and it came up like grass.
text_nonnarrative: A seed lot is graded on its chit count alone, and never on the age written on the paper. Undated stock is not disqualified in a nursery; it is simply counted. Fifty is the floor for parsnip and leek, seventy for onion, and a lot at forty-nine in a hundred is out of class whatever the vigour of the seedlings. Thickness of sowing bears on the crop and not on the grade.

text_narrative: The chill room on the outer ring holds four hundred trays and one technician on the night shift. Sabbe walks the aisle with a lamp and finds tray sixty-one lifted half an inch off its rail. Something inside has swelled. She takes the lid off and the sand is standing in ridges, and every ridge has a white hook at the top of it, three weeks ahead of the schedule on the door.
text_nonnarrative: Moisture and cold were separate requirements in a stratification tray, and the tray was built so that neither could be adjusted without the other holding. Sand was the medium in the standard pattern, held between two perforated plates. Chill time was a function of the mean temperature at the lower plate and of the depth of the charge above it. Without free water in the sand the temperature was of no effect at all.

text_narrative: Half the sheets in the third cabinet were mounted with the label at the wrong corner, and the assistant keeper knew whose hand it was without turning them over. Forty years of it. Nobody had ever said a word, because the man had also written the only usable key to the sedges in the county. She squared the sheet under her palm and thought that the strap across the rhizome was in the right place.
text_nonnarrative: Three grades of mounting paper were in use in the cabinets, of which the middle weight was the commonest by far. Straps were of gummed linen in two widths, the broader kept for rhizomes and the narrower for stems. Each sheet bore a label at the lower right corner, a fragment packet at the lower left, and a stamp of accession above the packet. Card mounts were held only for the fleshier fungi.

text_narrative: Everyone on that terrace had a story about the ferns Orlan raised in the dark room under the stair. What is certain is that he sowed the dust off a frond onto a pan of brick and covered it with glass. Six weeks later the pan was green with flat scales the size of a thumbnail, and he swore that on the ninth week they had begun to turn to face the door.
text_nonnarrative: A prothallus is the free-living gametophyte generation of a fern, a flat green scale seldom broader than a thumbnail and one cell thick over most of its area. Its underside bears the organs of both kinds and a fringe of rhizoids in place of roots. Dependence on a film of surface water is therefore absolute, which is why the generation is confined to shaded and constantly damp surfaces such as brick.

text_narrative: Rain has not reached the churchyard wall for a fortnight and the cushions on the coping are still swollen. A boy sent to fetch the ladder puts his hand flat on one of them and it is warm. He takes the hand away, waits, puts it back. Warm again, and warmer at the north end of the wall than at the south, which is where the sun has been all afternoon.
text_nonnarrative: Cushions of moss sit along the coping in a broken line, thickest on the northern face and absent for the last few yards at the western end. The wall is two courses of limestone over rubble, and the mortar between the upper courses stands proud of the stone. Depth of the cushions at the crown is under two inches. The southern face is bare above the string course and green below it.

text_narrative: The second survey party reached the head of the inlet nine days behind the first and found the marked trees unreadable. Every trunk on the seaward slope had been scoured to white wood by wind-driven grit in the interval. The party recorded the loss, moved the line half a mile inland, and cut fresh reference notches at breast height on twelve alders, tagging each with a numbered strip of lead.
text_nonnarrative: Cover varies more between the seaward and landward faces of one trunk than between trunks a mile apart. Crustose forms account for most of the total on exposed bark; foliose forms are largely confined to the landward quarter and to the lower six feet. Height above ground is a weak predictor by itself. Among recorders, disagreement is greatest in the band where the two growth forms overlap.

text_narrative: The frame arrives flat, in nine pieces, with a diagram that assumes a yew already four feet across. Hers is two. Still, the thing can be set over the plant now and grown into over the years, which is what the diagram means by establishment, and it is not as though anyone visits the side garden. She wires the neck to the shoulders and steps back. It looks like a birdcage with a shrub in it.
text_nonnarrative: What passed for skill in framed topiary was mostly patience with a pair of shears, since the frame did the shaping and the clipper only kept the growth off it. The form was at its worst in the geometric figures, where the wire showed through the surface for years and the finished cone was flatter than a freehand one. Its best examples were the ones in which the frame had been removed and the fault left visible.

text_narrative: Each spring the under-gardener walks the south wall and takes down whatever the frost has spoiled. In the first year he loses the lowest tier of the pear and ties in a shoot from the stem below it. In the third he finds the second tier standing nine inches above the first instead of fifteen, and leaves it. In the sixth the top tier has no shoot at all on the western arm.
text_nonnarrative: A trained pear was faulted on the spacing of its tiers and on the symmetry of its arms. Fifteen inches was the nominal interval; a tier at nine was a defect of the tree and not of the wall. A missing shoot on the western arm counted the same as one missing on the eastern. Frost was admitted as a cause and never as a class, and a bare top tier was disqualifying at any age.

text_narrative: Nobody on the allotment asks Bevan about the cordons any more, and the reason is that he answers. Anyone who wants to know why the leader is stopped at the wire gets it from the beginning, from the difference between a spur and a shoot, and he is still going when the light fails. The cordons themselves are the best on the site. That is the trouble with it.
text_nonnarrative: A shoot is not a spur and cannot be shortened as one; the distinction rests on the age of the wood and not on its length. Cutting to a bud pointing inward is admissible on a cordon only where the leader is stopped at the wire. A branch arising below the graft has no standing on the tree. Two leaders on one cordon is a position with no legal continuation.

text_narrative: There was a hedge-witch in the northern march who owed a debt to a hazel and paid it in the old way. She bent a living branch down, pegged it with a fork of blackthorn, and heaped earth over the bend. In the second year the branch had roots and she cut it free of the mother. The debt, she said, was doubled and not paid, and she went on pegging until the wood was hers to the ridge.
text_nonnarrative: Stooling is the third of the layering methods and the only one in which the parent is cut back rather than bent. Simple layering is distinguished from it by the retention of an upright parent and by the pegging of a single shoot. Air layering belongs with neither, since the rooting medium is held above ground and no part of the plant is buried. Depth of cover separates the two ground methods more reliably than season does.

text_narrative: The propagation bench in the lower dome had been running unattended since the second crew left. Idris found the trays in order, the mist heads firing on time, and callus on nine cuttings in ten. On the tenth tray the callus had gone on forming past the cut and closed over the whole of the stem, a white collar an inch thick, with no roots anywhere on it and the leaves still green.
text_nonnarrative: Callus and root are independent products of the same wound tissue, and a bench that favours one does not favour the other. Water loss through the leaf sets the limit on how long a cutting is viable, and the mist interval is a function of that loss and of the vapour deficit above the bench. Bottom heat acts on the cut surface only. Without a wound there is no tissue for either product to arise in.

text_narrative: A consignment of budding knives reached the field nursery in the third autumn of the emergency, forty-eight of them, all ground on the wrong side. The blades were flat on the face and bevelled on the back, which is the reverse of the pattern in use. Nine were reground on the depot wheel and the rest were issued as they came. Under none of the forty-eight did the bark lift cleanly on a wet stock.
text_nonnarrative: A budding knife was condemned on the geometry of its blade and not on the state of its edge. Bevel on the back with a flat face was the one admissible pattern; the reverse was a fault of manufacture and could not be excused by a well ground edge. Rust anywhere on the blade bore on the price and never on the class. Whether the bark lifted cleanly was a property of the season, not of the knife.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the Directorate nurseries, the register of understocks was reduced from nine classes to three by order, and the two most vigorous were struck out entirely. Growers in the eastern districts held back stools of the lost classes in ditches and hedge bottoms. The register recorded a shortfall of eleven thousand trees that autumn, and named no cause. The following spring the three surviving classes were themselves renumbered.
text_nonnarrative: Dwarfing stocks were separated from the semi-dwarfing not by the height of the finished tree but by whether the tree stood without support. Vigorous stocks made a third class, marked off from both by the absence of any bearing in the first six years. Seedling stocks were outside the scheme altogether, being a population and not a clone, and were graded on uniformity rather than on vigour at all.

text_narrative: Nine lights to shift before the frost came in, and the head of section had gone home at four with a note about the ventilation schedule. Typical. The note said the lights were to be closed at a two-inch gap and no less, which was correct for October and wrong for a night like this one. Halldis closed them flat and wrote nothing in the book, and slept badly.
text_nonnarrative: Lights on a frame are to be ventilated at the back edge and never at the front. A gap of two inches is required whenever the air outside stands above forty degrees, and a closed light is permitted below that figure only where the frame is matted. Entry in the frame book is required for every closing made out of the daily order, with the reading that occasioned it.

text_narrative: They still talk in the parish about the hotbed the smith made the year the fair was moved. Four feet of stable dung and a foot of loam on top, and he had cucumbers on the table a month before the manor did. What nobody mentions is the second bed, made the same way from the same yard, which went cold in a week and grew nothing but a crop of ink-caps.
text_nonnarrative: Peak temperature in a fermenting bed was roughly proportional to the cube of its linear dimension, so that a bed of four feet held heat some eight times as long as one of two. The constant was a property of the material rather than of the season. Beyond about six feet the relation failed, since the interior was anaerobic and the yield of heat per unit of dung was much lower.

text_narrative: The glasses came with the house, forty of them, and Ruta used them as they were meant to be. Under the first she raised lettuce in February. Under the ninth, set over bare ground by mistake, she found a print of a hand on the inside of the glass. She set it over bare ground again the next night, and again in the week after, and the print came back each time, smaller.
text_nonnarrative: Bell glass: the older pattern, blown in one piece with a knob at the crown, and standing without support. Handlight: a square glazed frame of the same purpose, made in four panes and a lid. Continuous cloche: a run of glasses in a rigid frame, open at both ends of the run and closed by a pane set on edge. Bare cloching: the same equipment over ground with no crop under it.

text_narrative: The shed behind the reservoir still has its bins, six of them, labelled in a hand nobody alive can read. Teilo turns over the third with a trowel and finds it dry to the bottom and full of grit. The fourth is loam, or was, and holds together in a ball when he squeezes it. He mixes the two by eye at three to one, fills nine pots, and sets them along the sill where the glass is thickest.
text_nonnarrative: Four mixtures were held in the standard series, of which the seed compost was the leanest and the potting compost of the third size the richest. Loam made up two parts of the seed mixture and seven of the heaviest potting mixture. Grit was constant at one part throughout. Leaf mould appeared in the two intermediate mixtures only, and lime in none of the four. Each was named for its use and not for its content.

text_narrative: Two years, the book says, and the book has never had to make a heap in a garden nine feet wide. The wire cage takes the whole of the corner where the rhubarb wants to be. Still, the leaves have to go somewhere, and burning them is out of the question with washing out next door on a dry day. Kestrel forks the top layer down and decides not to turn the rest until the frost has been at it.
text_nonnarrative: Leaf mould is worth less as a food than as a structure, and the complaint that a heap gives nothing back to the soil mistakes the second for the first. Its value lies in what it does to the pore space of a heavy soil, which no dressing of fertiliser reproduces. Turning the heap is said to halve the time. It does, and the mould is coarser for it, so the saving is a real one only where the coarseness is no objection.

text_narrative: In the fourth season of the avenue planting, a gale off the estuary loosened sixty of the young limes at the collar. The contractor had staked to two-thirds of the stem height throughout, against the schedule, which called for one-third. Sixty holes were found open at the base, each the width of a fist, and water standing in them. The trees were refirmed and the stakes cut down in the following month.
text_nonnarrative: Wind rock means, in this schedule, any opening at the collar wide enough to admit water, whether or not the stem is displaced. Where a stake stands above one-third of the stem height, the tree is deemed unstaked for the purpose of a claim. Nothing in this clause affects the liability of a contractor for the stake itself. A tree refirmed within the season is not a defective tree.

text_narrative: When the wasps were still owed a debt by the oaks, each wasp was given a room and the oak was made to build it. The grub lay at the centre in a hard cell, and around the cell the oak laid nine layers of its own flesh, and around those a rind. The wasps forgot the debt in time. The oaks did not, and they built the rooms thicker every age, and left no door.
text_nonnarrative: At the middle of a mature gall stood the larval chamber, a cavity lined with a hard shell of a single layer. Outside the shell lay a zone of nutritive tissue, thin and pale, and outside that the bulk of the gall in soft parenchyma. The rind was the outermost part and bore the tannins. An exit canal was absent in the unemerged gall and present as a clean bore in the rest.

text_narrative: Over one summer the foreman of the walled garden lost three crops to the same bloom and named none of them. In June it was the apple at the west end, grey on the young shoots only. In July the gooseberries went, fruit and all, under a felt that rubbed off on a thumb. In August it took the marrow leaves from the edge inward, and the fruit under them swelled as usual and tasted of nothing.
text_nonnarrative: An outbreak is classed by the tissue it occupies and never by the crop. Bloom on young shoots is one class; bloom on the fruit is a second, and the two are held apart even where both are on one apple. Grey felt that rubs off under a thumb is diagnostic of neither. Leaves taken from the edge inward count with the shoots, and loss of flavour in a marrow is no part of the grading at all.

text_narrative: Anyone who parks under the limes on the square knows what comes down in July, and there is an argument about it that has run for twenty years. Half the street calls it sap and half calls it rain off the leaves. The old woman at the corner house says it is neither, that the trees are paying something back, and she leaves a saucer out under the worst branch every night of the month.
text_nonnarrative: Whether honeydew counted as an excretion or as a food was less a matter of chemistry than of which end of the relation was taken as primary. Treated as waste, it belonged to the aphid and its presence on the leaf below was incidental. Treated as payment, it belonged to the ant, and the aphid was a herd. Neither account explained the sooty mould, which was a third party to a bargain it had no share in making.

text_narrative: A surveyor's report on the old bonded warehouse is filed in the morning and withdrawn the same afternoon. The report finds the south gable sound under nine inches of ivy and recommends nothing. The withdrawal notice gives no reason. What the file does contain, on a loose sheet, is a photograph of the gable with the ivy stripped from a strip a yard wide, and mortar missing to the depth of a finger.
text_nonnarrative: Ivy on masonry was blamed for damage it was seldom the author of, and the blame rested on a confusion between adhesion and penetration. The rootlets held to a surface by a secretion and penetrated nothing that was not open. Sound mortar was therefore in no danger from them. That said, a wall under ivy could not be inspected, and the cover was worth more to a bad wall than to a good one.

text_narrative: There were two sisters in a village under the downs who were left a sack of bulbs and no instruction. The elder planted hers at a hand's depth and had one flower from each for nine years. The younger planted hers shallow, a thumb under the grass, and had a great many flowers the first year and none at all the fourth, and a mat of small white bulbs under the turf instead.
text_nonnarrative: Offset production per parent bulb is higher the shallower the planting, and the increase is closer to inverse-square than to linear over the usual range. Flower size runs the other way against the same variable. The two relations cross at about three times the height of the bulb, which is the depth at which neither yield is at its maximum and both are near it. Below six inches the relation is unreliable.

text_narrative: In the third year after the enclosure award, the cutting of the common meadow was set back a fortnight by the vestry and the dispute went to the quarter sessions. Two tenants had cut on the old date and carried the hay before the notice was read out. The court held the notice good and the hay theirs, and ordered the date entered in the parish book, where it stood for sixty years unaltered.
text_nonnarrative: Meadow, in this article, meant land shut for hay and not land grazed in the same season, whatever its herbage. A cutting date entered in the parish book bound every tenant with a share in the ground, and a share was defined by the doles and not by the acreage. Where a date coincided with a day of rest, the day following was the date. Nothing in the article touched the aftermath.

text_narrative: A parish walk to count the hedges was completed in one day in the second week of the month, with eleven walkers on six miles of boundary. The count on the lane hedges ran between four and seven woody kinds in a thirty-yard stretch. On the field boundary behind the pumping station the same stretch gave eleven, and the walkers went over it twice before entering the figure.
text_nonnarrative: Counts on adjacent stretches of one boundary differ by as much as counts on boundaries in different parishes. The mean over lane hedges is five woody kinds to the thirty-yard stretch, with most of the spread accounted for by the presence or absence of a single climber. Observer variance is small on the woody kinds and large on the ground flora, which is why the ground flora is excluded.

text_narrative: Halfway up the ridge the tape runs out before it meets itself and Odger has to mark the bark with chalk and start again from the mark. The trunk leans across the slope, so breast height on the upper side is two feet below breast height on the lower. He takes both, writes both down, and adds a note about the burr at four feet that the tape has had to ride over.
text_nonnarrative: A girth was rejected on the position of the tape and not on the manner of reading it. On a slope, breast height was taken on the upper side alone; a figure read on the lower side was out of class however carefully the tape was held. A burr under the tape was disqualifying whatever its size, and chalk on the bark bore on the record and never on the girth itself.

text_narrative: In the age when trees could still be persuaded, the makers went out with knives and taught two woods to be one. A long slope was cut on each, and a tongue raised in the face of each slope, and the tongues were slid past one another until neither could be drawn out. What the makers could not teach was the joining itself. That the trees did in the dark under the wax.
text_nonnarrative: Each half of the union bears a sloping face and a single tongue cut back into that face at about a third of its length from the upper end. The tongues are reciprocal, one raised toward the tip and the other toward the base, and interlock without any fastening. Cambium is continuous across the joint only along the two long edges. A third tongue is absent in every form of the union.

text_narrative: Nobody in that orchard would ring a tree after the middle of the month, and the reason given was never the sap. The story was about a grower two valleys over who took a half-inch band off a pear in the wrong week and hung the strip of bark on a nail in his shed. The tree bore heavily for one season. The strip, they said, was still green on the nail nine years later.
text_nonnarrative: A complete ring was not a permitted position on any stem carrying the whole of a tree, and a band wider than half an inch was not permitted anywhere. Bark taken from a branch ringed in the same year had no standing. A tree bearing on spurs alone was outside the rule entirely, since the position it forbade could not arise on such a tree. Grafted stems counted as one stem throughout.

text_narrative: Nine hundred feet of ridge and the vent gear answers on eight hundred of it. The rest is the western span, where the rack has been off its pinion since before the handover and nobody has costed the repair. Vaska stands under it with the lamp. Hot air has to go somewhere, and it is going out through the broken pane at the gable, which is why the span nearest the door is the coldest in the house.
text_nonnarrative: The house lay on an east-west axis with a single ridge some nine hundred feet long. Ventilators sat in a continuous run along the southern pitch and in short banks of three along the northern. Below the ridge the roof was of nine-inch panes in a lead frame, and the western gable was blind. The floor stood four feet under the outside ground at the eastern end and level with it at the western end.

text_narrative: In the seventh year of the new planting, the sward between the rows was let to a grazier for the first time and the arrangement lasted one season. Sheep took the bark off nineteen trees below the guards. The account for that year records the loss, the cost of nineteen new guards, and a scythe bought in the autumn. The sward was mown by hand for the eleven years following.
text_nonnarrative: Five kinds of ground cover are found under standard trees, of which close-mown grass is by far the commonest and bare tilth the rarest. Herbal leys hold a middle place, being sown to three species in the ordinary mixture and to nine in the richer. Guards are of two patterns, wire spiral and slatted timber, the second being the only one proof against sheep. Nothing in the list is proof against rabbits.

text_narrative: There was a basketmaker on the flats who would cut no rod that had been left three winters, and the other makers laughed at her for it. Her baskets went to market and came back empty; theirs came back full. In the year the water stood late over the beds, only the young rods were fit to cut, and every maker on the flats worked from her stools and paid her in salt.
text_nonnarrative: Rod quality was habitually judged by colour, which was the least reliable of the indications available and the easiest to fake by steaming. Uniformity of taper mattered more and was harder to see. The trade held that a bed declined after its twentieth year, a claim that rested on no comparison worth the name, since the beds that lasted were the ones cut hardest and the two causes were never told apart.

text_narrative: The first planting on the open ground was made of two peoples, and only one was meant to stay. The quick trees went in between the slow ones and grew over them and kept the wind off their heads for thirty years. Then the axes came for the quick trees, as had been agreed before either was sown. The slow trees have never spoken of it, and they stand in rows to this day.
text_nonnarrative: Calling a nurse row part of the crop or part of the site is not a quibble, since the two answers make different things into failures. On the first account, a nurse that outlives its term is a crop tree in the wrong place. On the second, it is a condition that has failed to lapse, and no tree. What hangs on the choice is whether the belt can be said to have a single age.

text_narrative: Every spring the bed by the gate gives Anka the same argument in a different form. In the first year it is one shoot from below the knuckle, seven feet of it, with nine leaflets to a leaf instead of five. In the third it is four shoots and the named rose down to a stub. In the fifth the bed is all briar and she has stopped calling it the rose bed.
text_nonnarrative: Knuckle: the swelling at the base of a budded rose, where the named wood meets the stock. Sucker: any shoot arising below that swelling, whatever its vigour. Briar: the stock itself, considered as a plant in its own right rather than as a base. Reversion: the condition of a bed in which the briar holds the ground and the named wood does not. Blind wood: a shoot of either kind that bears no flower.

text_narrative: Long before the towers, the keepers of the small trees held that a tree in a tray was a promise and not a possession. Each spring they lifted the tree out, cut a third of the root away, and set it back in the same earth. The tree owed them nothing for it. What it owed, they said, was owed to the tray, which had agreed to be small so that the tree need not.
text_nonnarrative: Most writing on the tray trees was writing about age, and it mistook the sign for the thing: a trunk thickened by fifty years of confinement looked old, and a trunk thickened by feeding looked older still. The honest work in the tradition was in the roots, where nothing showed and no credit was to be had. Its best practitioners were the ones whose trees looked unremarkable in the third decade and plain in the fifth.

text_narrative: A finch and a miller once fell out over a heap of chaff, and the dispute was put to the sieve. Three screens were set in a frame, coarse over fine, and the heap was worked through all three. The miller took what stayed on the top screen and the finch took what fell through the bottom. Neither had thought about the middle, and the middle was where the seed was.
text_nonnarrative: Purity of a lot and cleanness of a lot diverge under any definition of either. Purity is a ratio within the seed itself and takes no notice of what else is in the bag; cleanness is a statement about everything that is not seed. A screen acts on size, so it can raise the second without touching the first. Only a difference in density distinguishes a full seed from an empty one.

text_narrative: Half past four in the meridian room, and the bubble in the striding level will not settle. Ilva lifts the level off the pivots, reverses it end for end, and sets it back down. The bubble stands two divisions out the other way. She notes both readings on the slate, wipes the pivots with a linen pad, and tries the reversal again. The same two divisions, the same side. The error belongs to the pivots, not to the level.
text_nonnarrative: Pivot wear and level error were separate classes of fault, and reversal was the only thing that distinguished them. A bubble standing the same number of divisions to the same side after reversal counted against the pivots. Divisions reading out the opposite way belonged to the striding level itself. Neither class was settled by the slate readings alone, and cleanliness of the pivots bore on the cause of a discrepancy, never on its class, whatever its size.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the survey the south mark was found to be no longer visible from the transit room, a poplar having thickened across the line. The committee ordered a second pillar cut into the chalk of the far ridge, three hundred yards east of the first. Masons set the stone in November and painted the sighting slot white. The old mark was left standing, unpainted, and struck from the register that winter.
text_nonnarrative: The two marks stood on a ridge of chalk that lay open to the south of the observatory grounds. Between them the ground was low and damp, under poplar and thorn for most of its width. The nearer pillar was the shorter of the two and sat in shallow soil; the far one was bedded in rock. From the transit room the line to either was clear only above the tops of the trees.

text_narrative: There was a mate on the coasting run who would not touch the index screw, and the hands made a joke of it. He took his sights with the error in and subtracted it after, the same three minutes on the arc every morning of the passage. When the glass fogged off the cape he found the error at four and a half, and he kept subtracting three, and the noon position walked west for two days.
text_nonnarrative: An index error is classed by whether it is constant on the arc, not by the size of the reading. Three minutes off the arc and three minutes on it fall in one class. A shift of half a minute between one sight and another is a second class, with the mirror, the glass or a knock to the screw as the usual cause. Subtraction after the sight bears on the position, never on the class.

text_narrative: Before the roof-glass was known, the star-takers of the low country read the sky in a shallow trough of dark oil, and the trough gave back a second sky, inverted and colder. The old telling held that the drowned kept that lower sky and would not be counted twice. A star seen once above and once in the oil was one star; a star seen only in the oil belonged to the dead and was struck from the night's reckoning.
text_nonnarrative: The commonest of the three bowls is the plain oil trough, with a glass-roofed bowl for wind and a spirit bowl for hard frost making up the set. Each is a hand across at the rim and has a lip of unpolished horn. The glass roof is a separate piece in two leaves, and the horn lip is absent from the spirit bowl. Nothing in the set is graduated, since the reflected sky itself supplies the angle of the star.

text_narrative: The rate is the only thing the depot has to offer, and Halden turns the page back to check it again. Eleven seconds slow a day for the first fortnight, then nine, then eleven. Not a drift, not a trend, nothing that would let a curve be drawn through it. The box has sat in the same cold shed the whole while. Something in the balance, then, or in the way the winding falls at a different hour each morning.
text_nonnarrative: Daily rates varied more between chronometers of one maker than between makers. The median rate on the depot books was eleven seconds slow, with a spread of four seconds either way across the winter. Temperature in the shed accounted for most of that spread, and the hour of winding for a little of the rest. Boxes stored on the floor were no worse rated than those on the shelf, though a third of the observers held otherwise.

text_narrative: The first catalogue of the tower was cut into nine copper plates, and the star-wardens held that the plates were true for one reign and no longer. Sky-drift, they called it: the slow westward creep of every place in the heavens, a hand's breadth in a long life. Each new warden reduced the old plates to the year of the crowning, and the ninth plate, being the one the drift touched least, was left uncut for three reigns together.
text_nonnarrative: Reduction to a common year was less a courtesy to the reader than a condition of the catalogue being a catalogue at all. Positions given for different years were not comparable, and a list of incomparable positions was a heap of separate observations under one binding. The objection that reduction imported an error of its own was sound as far as it went, and beside the point, since an error of known size was preferable to quantities that did not belong together.

text_narrative: A speculum of twenty inches cracked across the face at a shop on the canal road, in the course of the third figuring. The lap had been cut into squares an inch on the side and left to cold-flow overnight under the glass. Warmth from a stove set too near the bench softened the pitch on one edge only. Pressure went to the far side of the disc, and the glass parted along a scratch left by the coarse emery.
text_nonnarrative: Under the tool lay a coat of pitch a quarter-inch deep, and under the pitch a plaster backing keyed to the iron. The facets were square, an inch on the side, with channels between them of a knife's width. Facet size stood in no relation to the diameter of the tool, though the channels did. On the smallest laps the plaster backing was absent, the pitch being poured straight onto the bare iron and faced there with a warm plate.

text_narrative: Long before glass was drawn fine enough, the makers of eyepieces took their lines from one spider only, a pale weaver that spun in the roof-beams of the meridian houses and nowhere else. A single thread of it would cross a field of view and cast no shadow. The weavers were owed warmth in return, and a house that let its roof go cold found the lines in every glass slack and doubled by the spring.
text_nonnarrative: An eyepiece reticle is a frame of fine lines set at the focus of the objective, so that the lines and the image are in view together. Its usefulness depends on the lines being narrower than the smallest detail the glass will show. Spider silk is thin enough and elastic under changes of damp; drawn glass and etched metal are thicker and stiffer. Tension across the frame is therefore fixed at the making and is not adjustable.

text_narrative: The screw is worn at the middle of its travel and Devi works around it, taking every measure in the first ten turns and running the carriage back the long way. Outside the pressure hull the double star sits steady, no air to trouble it. She sets the fixed wire on the brighter component, brings the movable one across, and reads the drum. Eight hundred and four. The same to the tenth of a division, four times running.
text_nonnarrative: Screw error was largest at the middle of the travel on most instruments and smallest within the first few turns. Across the shop books, measures taken in one direction of run differed from measures taken in the other by about a tenth of a division. The spread between observers was wider than the spread between screws. A quarter of the drums showed no periodic error worth a correction table, and the rest were of one pattern.

text_narrative: Five nights out of six the disc is boiling and Ravn writes down a two, and the two means nothing except that the air was bad. Tonight the limb holds hard and sharp for whole seconds together. A four, surely, maybe a five. But the star at the zenith is quiet and the one low down is dancing, and the scale has no room for both. The number goes in the column for the zenith, as always.
text_nonnarrative: Seeing was graded on the steadiness of the limb and not on the brightness of the disc. A disc boiling through whole seconds counted as a two whatever its altitude, and a limb holding hard and sharp counted as a four or a five. Altitude bore on the cause of bad air and never on the grade. Two stars of unequal steadiness in one field were a defect of the scale, not two grades.

text_narrative: Nobody at the hill station would send a first-year up to the shutter, and the reason was the north gale. The slit ran from the ring to the crown, and the two leaves rode on a chain that had been spliced twice. A student called Oskar took it on himself one January to free a jammed leaf with a boathook. The leaf came down the last eight feet on its own and folded the boathook against the rail.
text_nonnarrative: Two hands are required at the shutter whenever the leaves are off their catches, and one of the two is to be a rated observer. Ascent to the crown ring is permitted only in winds under fifteen knots. A spliced chain is to be replaced rather than shortened, and no splice is permitted above the upper sheave. Hooks and gaffs are not to bear on any leaf, and the hauling line alone is to take the load.

text_narrative: The worm is out on the bench and Bettan has the wheel turned face up under the lamp. Twelve teeth in one arc of it are bright where the rest are grey. She runs a thumbnail across them and feels the ridge. The old grease had gone to varnish on that arc, and the drive has been climbing the same twelve teeth for a year, once a night, always at the same hour angle.
text_nonnarrative: A sidereal drive is a worm bearing on a wheel at the polar axis, with the rate set by the ratio between them and by the speed of the governor. Wear depends on the load at the tooth and on the state of the grease, not on the number of hours run. Without a counterweight on the tube, the load is unequal on the two sides of the meridian, and so are the rates.

text_narrative: The clock in the transit room keeps two rates, and everyone on the staff has a version of why. The zinc and steel rods are the right lengths, the bob hangs true, and from May to September the thing is faultless. In the cold half of the year it gains a second a night and always on the nights the room is left dark. Nobody sits with it now to see whether the gaining stops when a lamp is lit.
text_nonnarrative: Going rate depends on the square root of the effective length, so a change of one part in a million in length is worth half a part in a million of rate. Steel has an expansion near eleven parts in a million for each degree of temperature, zinc nearly thirty. Compensation is therefore a matter of the ratio between the two column lengths and not of their absolute size. Beyond a few degrees the linear relation is approximate only.

text_narrative: There was a dial-cutter in the hill country who would set no stone until he had asked the wall what it faced. Walls lied, he said, and masons lied worse. He would hang a plumb line at noon on three days well apart and take the shadow of the line on the stone. A wall that gave him the same angle three times got its dial. One farm waited eleven years for a dial and never got one.
text_nonnarrative: Substyle: the line on a dial face from which hour lines are counted, lying under the edge of the gnomon. Declination: the angle between the wall and the true east-west line, positive to the west. Reclination: the same quantity taken in the vertical plane, for a face that is not upright. Difference of longitude in arc: any part of the hour line spacing owed to the site rather than to the aspect of the wall.

text_narrative: Nineteen points, and the twentieth had been filed off by somebody before the instrument ever came to the shop. Marya set the rete back on the pin and let it swing. The gap was on the winter side, low, where a bright star ought to have sat. Somebody had wanted that star gone, or had broken the point and tidied the stump. Either way the plate under it was for a latitude two hundred miles south of the shop.
text_nonnarrative: Above the plate lay the rete, a pierced disc turning on a central pin, and above that a single rule of brass. The star points were tongues cut from the body of the rete itself and bent inward, each ending at the place of one star. An ecliptic circle stood open in the middle of the disc, joined to the rim at two places only. Small retes had no rule and no graduation on the ecliptic.

text_narrative: A brass-caster of the marsh towns was asked for a sphere with every ring divided, and he asked in return for a year and the loan of a straight-edge that had come out of the sea. The straight-edge would only mark true when the tide was making. So the caster worked six hours in twelve, and at the end of the year the solstitial ring was divided and the rest were blank, and the sphere was accepted as it stood.
text_nonnarrative: Six rings made a full sphere, of which three at most were graduated on the smaller instruments: the meridian, the equinoctial and the solstitial colure. Each was a flat band of brass, the outermost the widest, with the divisions cut on the inner face where the sight lay. The horizon ring was wooden on the cheaper spheres and bore a calendar scale in place of degrees. Nothing under a foot across had a movable ecliptic or a fitted hour circle.

text_narrative: Three times now the bob has hung off the true. The first time Ovin blames the draught and shuts the port. The second time the air is dead still and the cord leans a finger's width toward the north wall, and stays there through a whole altitude. The third time it leans the same width and the same way while the quadrant itself is lying flat on the floor, which is not a thing a plumb line does.
text_nonnarrative: A hanging fault and a graduation fault were told apart by their distribution over the arc and not by their size. The one was constant across a single side and absent from the other; the second was proportional to the reading and present on both. A third kind, seated in the pivot of the sight rule, resembled the one at small angles and the second at large, and took its name from neither of them.

text_narrative: Four stations in a day, and at each one Halvard levels the board, orients on the last ray, and draws. At the second station the far cairn will not come into the sights at all, being under cloud, so he draws the ray to the shoulder of the ridge instead and marks it doubtful. At the third the two rays cross a quarter-inch apart. At the fourth they cross clean, and the doubtful ray is the one that misses.
text_nonnarrative: Closing error on a three-ray fix is inversely proportional to the sine of the angle between the weakest pair, so a fix from rays within twenty degrees of each other is worth little. The triangle of error varies as the square of the distance from the nearest station. Orientation error contributes a term of its own, independent of that distance. Under about five degrees of intersection the relation between error and angle is no guide at all.

text_narrative: A boundary chained across the flat north of the crossing comes out eleven links long against the record of forty years ago. The two chainmen work downhill in the morning and uphill after noon, taking offsets to the fence line with a ten-foot rod. Sag in the chain accounts for most of the excess, according to the county man on the ground. The remainder sits in three offsets taken across a gully that no longer holds water.
text_nonnarrative: Chained lengths were in excess more often than in deficit, and the excess was larger downhill than uphill in about three cases in four. Across the district books the median discrepancy on a mile of flat ground was seven links, with the spread wider on rough ground than on smooth. Offsets accounted for less of the total than the chain itself. A quarter of the parties recorded no temperature, and their returns were the widest scattered.

text_narrative: Every second Sunday that spring the instrument came out onto the yard table, and Nilla learned the screws by feel. The first Sunday she chased the bubble around the plate for an hour. The second she had it in two minutes and lost it again reversing the alidade. By the fourth she could set the plate level, turn it through a half circle, and find the bubble where it had been left, and her aunt stopped watching.
text_nonnarrative: A tribrach means the three-screw base by which an instrument stands on its head, together with the plate against which the screws bear. Where a plate is levelled in two positions at right angles and holds in both, the instrument is level within the meaning of this part. A bubble out by less than one division on reversal does not affect the levelling. Nothing in this section applies to bases of four screws or to a base without a plate.

text_narrative: Six setups along the cutting and the staff man was new. On the first he held the staff plumb and the reading was clean. On the third he let the top lean back toward the instrument, and the middle wire read low by four thousandths of a foot. On the fifth the staff foot sat on a loose stone. Only at the sixth did the sum of the three wires come out equal to twice the middle.
text_nonnarrative: A staff reading is rejected on the arithmetic of the three wires and not on the look of the staff. Where the top and bottom wires do not sum to twice the middle, the reading is out however steady the staff appears. A staff leaning back from plumb is one class of fault; a foot bedded on a loose stone is a second, and settlement under the foot, not the instrument, is the cause of the second.

text_narrative: Forty-one marks were cut that season between the coast road and the head of the valley, the district having been ordered to cut its own. Eleven went into church plinths, the rest into bridge abutments and gate piers. The bracket at the ninth mark was cut two inches above the horizontal bar by a mason working from a bad sketch, and the whole of the northern line was carried on it for three years.
text_nonnarrative: A bench mark meant a horizontal bar cut into masonry, with a bracket beneath it, the upper edge of the bar being the surface to which heights referred. Where a bracket stood elsewhere than under the bar, the mark was of no effect for levelling and was recorded as defective. Nothing in the schedule of defective marks affected the heights of lines run from them, which held until re-levelled from a sound mark.

text_narrative: There was a needle-maker in the iron hills who swore that the north the needle sought was a person and not a place, and that the person walked. His grandfather's needles pointed one way, his father's a finger's width off it, and his own another finger further. He kept a slate on the shop wall with a mark for each generation, and the marks made a line, and he told the guild the line would bend back inside three lifetimes.
text_nonnarrative: Declination was the angle at a place between the direction of a freely suspended needle and the true meridian, counted east or west of it. Its value was a property of the place and of the date together, and never of the needle. Annual change at a given station was small and of one sign for long periods, with a slow reversal of sign over centuries. Charts of equal declination were of use only with the year of compilation stated.

text_narrative: A pedlar left a dip circle at a farm in payment for a night's lodging, and the farm kept it in the dairy. The needle stood at seventy degrees the first winter and at seventy the second. In the third winter it stood at eighty-one, and the dairy went sour, and every needle brought into the room afterwards read eighty-one too. The pedlar was looked for on the coast road and was not found.
text_nonnarrative: Freedom about a horizontal axis is what sets a dip needle apart from a compass needle, and the absence of a counterpoise sets it apart from a balance needle. The one is free in the vertical plane and reads inclination; the other is free in the horizontal and reads direction. A third kind is a hybrid, weighted to stand level at a single latitude, and is a compass elsewhere and a dip needle nowhere.

text_narrative: A barometer taken from a locked room on the harbour front reads three-tenths of an inch low against the station standard and has read low since the room was sealed. The case is sound and the glass unbroken. A jeweller called in to open it finds the capsule stack sound but the hairspring bearing on the wrong side of its stop, which is a fault of assembly and not of age. No maker's plate is fitted.
text_nonnarrative: An aneroid and a mercury barometer are distinguished by what supplies the restoring force rather than by what is measured. In the one it is the elasticity of an evacuated metal capsule and of its spring; in the other, the weight of a column of liquid. A third instrument, the altimeter, is an aneroid with the scale cut in feet, and is unlike the barometer proper in nothing but what the pointer is read against.

text_narrative: The wick dried out four times that August, and each time Ansen found it dry at the same hour. On the first occasion the reservoir was empty and the explanation was easy. On the second and third the reservoir was full and the muslin was stiff as paper an inch above the water. On the fourth he sat in the screen doorway from four to five and watched the muslin whiten from the bulb downward.
text_nonnarrative: A wet-bulb thermometer was an ordinary thermometer with its bulb wrapped in muslin, the muslin fed from a reservoir by a wick of the same material. Its reading depended on the rate of evaporation from the cloth and so on the dryness of the air passing over it. Continuity of the wick was essential, since a dry length anywhere in it rendered the reading that of a dry bulb. Ventilation was therefore specified rather than left to chance.

text_narrative: The birds held the funnels to be small wells set out for them, in the first years of measured rain, and drank, and the tallies came up short in every dry season. The council of gauges was called by the swifts, who alone had no use for standing water. It was agreed that a rim should be knife-edged and set five feet up, too narrow to perch on and too high to wade to.
text_nonnarrative: The gauge enclosure lay on flat ground east of the barn, inside a fence of four posts. The funnel stood at five feet, its rim level with the top rail and clear of the fence by a yard on every side. Ground under the enclosure was gravel, drier than the grass beyond it. The nearest tree was thirty yards to the north and taller than the funnel by four times its height.

text_narrative: A cup anemometer on the water tower at the eastern settlement runs slow by a fifth against the hand instrument and has done since the winter. Two of the three cups are original; the third is a cut tin can of about the right size but heavier. The spindle turns freely by hand. Grit in the lower bearing is the reason given by the two people who look after the tower, though the salvage crew blames the odd cup.
text_nonnarrative: A cup anemometer was graded by whether the error was constant with speed or not. A reading slow by a fixed fraction at all speeds belonged to the bearing, grit in it being the usual cause, and made up one class. An odd cup, heavier than the other two, was a second class, since its effect on the spindle was largest at low speeds, irrespective of the height of the tower. Freedom of the spindle by hand bore on neither.

text_narrative: When the ground was young it spoke without record, and the first of the drum-keepers blacked a cylinder in lamp smoke so that the speech would leave a scratch. A weight was hung that the earth could not persuade to move, and a stylus was set against the black from the weight's own arm. The ground shook and the drum turned under it, and what the weight refused to do became a white line on the black.
text_nonnarrative: A drum recorder is a smoked cylinder on a screw, with a stylus bearing on it from a mass suspended so as to have a long free period. Its sensitivity is a matter of that period and of the ratio of the lever arms, not of the mass itself. Without damping, the trace is a train of free oscillations at the instrument's own period, and ground motion of any other period is unreadable in it.

text_narrative: Nobody on the quay trusts the readings out of the north well, and the reason goes back further than the current keeper. The well is sunk beside the lock wall and takes its water through a two-inch pipe that somebody widened once and never entered in the book. On a running ebb the float in it sits four inches above the harbour, every time, and the trace comes out smooth as a drawn line.
text_nonnarrative: The well was a brick shaft eight feet across, sunk in the quay a little inshore of the lock wall, with the gauge house over it. Its inlet pipe lay below the level of the lowest tide and ran out under the coping to the harbour. Inside, the float sat on the water with the counterweight hanging clear of the brickwork. The chart table stood at the landward end, where the floor was driest.

text_narrative: In the fishing towns it was held that the sea gave back an hour of every sun, and that the hour was owed. A man on the beach saw the disc sitting whole on the water when by the tables it was already under. His neighbours saw the same and thought nothing of it. He alone kept a book of the borrowed minutes, and by the time it was full he could not be got to look at a sunset.
text_nonnarrative: Debate over whether the disc seen on the horizon is the sun or an image of it depends on what is meant by seeing a thing at a distance through a medium. If every sight through air is an image, the distinction is idle, since nothing is ever seen otherwise. If it is not, the horizon case belongs with the mirage and not with ordinary sight, and the boundary between the two is one of degree and not of kind, fixed by convention.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the republic the great orrery of the assembly hall was taken down for recutting, the outermost wheel having lost four teeth in a single season. The clerk of works recorded that the wheel had been cut in a soft alloy on the excuse of cost, and that the fault dated from the second administration. A brass replacement was fitted in the spring and the outer body ran nine days behind until the index was reset.
text_nonnarrative: Motion in an orrery is taken from one input shaft and divided among the bodies by trains of spur wheels, each train fixed at the making. Period ratios are properties of the tooth counts alone and independent of the rate of the shaft. Backlash in a train is a function of the number of meshes in it, so the outer bodies stand furthest from their true places. Without a brake the outer arms hang where they were last set.

text_narrative: Two mirrors, and the second one was the problem, as the second one always was. Teu had the first driven off the station clock and it held the field without a tremor. The second, the flat that threw the beam down the tunnel, sat on a mount stiffened for a gravity the station had not had since the spin was cut. Every correction at the first mirror asked for a correction at the second, and the second answered late.
text_nonnarrative: Most published designs for two-mirror feeds are honest about the drive and silent about the second mount, though the limit sits there rather than in the drive. What passes for a stiffness specification in the literature is usually a static figure with no period attached to it. The better designs are the ones that treat the pair as one structure and quote a settling behaviour for the whole, rather than a tolerance for each mirror alone.

text_narrative: The line came out barred, and it came out barred on every plate from that instrument and no other. Ottiline took the slit apart on a sheet of paper under the window. One jaw was clean along its whole length. The other had a bloom of something white in the middle third, a deposit no thicker than a breath, and it stood exactly where the bars fell on the plates. She scraped a little onto a slip of glass.
text_nonnarrative: Jaw: either of the two straight edges between which the slit is formed, one fixed and one adjustable.
