Bilateral opening: an arrangement in which the two jaws stand equally displaced from a fixed centre line, so that the middle of the slit is independent of the width. Bar: any interruption of a spectral line along its length, taking its position from an obstruction on a jaw. Ghost: a false line owed to the grating rather than to the slit.

text_narrative: The oval is cut for this latitude and no other, which is the whole point of the thing, and Rethe knows the shape of it as well as the shape of the window. Tonight the oval is wrong. Not turned, not slipped on the rivet — wrong in its curve, flatter at the south end than a horizon for this place can be. The card is the card, and the rivet has not been touched. Somewhere the latitude has been changed.
text_nonnarrative: The horizon opening was the one part of a planisphere that could not be made general, and this was a limitation of the form rather than of any maker. A single card served all dates and all hours because the motion of the sky was uniform; it could not serve all places, because the horizon was not a circle concentric with the pole. Makers who offered one card for a band of latitudes conceded the point in the price.

text_narrative: There is a nocturnal in the guild hall that nobody will read after the turn of the year, and the older members will tell anyone why. The pointer is set to the date and the guard stars are brought under the arm, and the hour reads true from midsummer to the solstice. After the solstice it reads true as well, but it reads the hour of the following night, and the guild has a rule about acting on it.
text_nonnarrative: A reading was valid only if the date index stood on a graduation and not between two. A setting in which the guard stars stood outside the sweep of the arm was void, and no hour was assigned to it. Reversal of the instrument was not a setting and could not be answered by a reading of the hour. Where two readings of one night disagreed by more than a quarter hour, neither stood, and the night counted as unread.

text_narrative: In the third winter of the siege the sector in the north bastion was still worked nightly, the garrison having nothing else to do with the instrument. The plumb line hung in a well of still air four floors deep, and the observers recorded a wandering of the zenith of two seconds over the season. The engineer attributed the whole of it to the settling of the bastion under its own guns, and closed the register in March.
text_nonnarrative: A wandering zenith and a settling instrument are, on one account, the same fact under two descriptions, since the zenith is defined by the plumb line and the plumb line hangs from the building. On another account they are distinct, for the local vertical is a property of the ground and the masses near it, and a tilt of the mounting is no change in the vertical. The choice decides whether the record is a datum or an artefact.

text_narrative: Four hundred graduated circles left the eastern works that year from a single engine, and the trade took a season to notice that all four hundred shared one error. The master wheel of the engine had been divided by hand in the old shop and carried a periodic defect of six seconds in every sixtieth of its circumference. Every circle off it repeated the defect, and the pattern of the repetition was the same on all of them.
text_nonnarrative: Graduation of a circle over eight inches is to be done by engine and not by hand, and a circle divided by hand is permitted only as a pattern. The master wheel is required to be examined for periodic error before any run and after any recutting of its teeth. Divisions finer than ten minutes of arc are not permitted on brass. Numbering is to stand outside the graduated band and never across it, in figures of one height.

text_narrative: The autumn meeting of the finders' league went to a competitor from the coast club on a margin of eleven seconds. Objects were called out by catalogue number and the circles alone were allowed for pointing, with the finder covered. The winner lost the third object entirely, having set the hour circle before the declination, and made the time back on the last two by reading both circles from one side of the pier.
text_nonnarrative: A pointing counts only if both circles are read with the eye on the same side of the pier as the reading index. An object found with the finder uncovered is not a pointing and does not count against the competitor. A position in which the tube meets the pier before the object is reachable is dead, and the object is withdrawn. Corrections to a circle between objects are not permitted, whatever the cause of the error.

text_narrative: The card came out of the holder with two burns on it, one clean and one furred at the edges, and Hedda laid it on the kitchen table beside the week's others. The furred burn ran from ten to noon. Outside, the sphere sat in its cradle on the shed roof with a film of pollen on the underside, yellow enough to see from the step. Nobody had cleaned the glass since the lime came into flower.
text_nonnarrative: The instrument's reputation for fairness was owed to the absence of a clock in it, though that same absence was why its records resisted comparison. What passed for an hour of sunshine on one card was a burn of a width fixed by the card stock and by the damp of the morning, neither of which was recorded. The stations whose returns held up best were those that kept to one card supplier and said so in the register.

text_narrative: Rain on the workshop roof and the light going, and Verity had the soundpost setter through the f-hole for the fourth time that afternoon. The post went in a hair behind the bridge foot and stood. She tapped the belly with a knuckle and got a dull answer. Out it came again. On the fifth setting the post stood a shade tighter and the top note came up thin, so she left it and cleaned the tool.
text_nonnarrative: Placement of a soundpost is graded on its distance behind the bridge foot and not on the force of its fit. A post a hair off that distance counts as badly set whatever the belly sounds like. Tool marks inside the f-hole bear on the workmanship and never on the setting. Tightness is disqualifying only where the belly is under visible strain, and the note itself is no criterion at all, whatever its colour.

text_narrative: There was a cello in the loft room at the almshouse that nobody would play twice. It sounded well enough up to the F sharp on the top string, and at that one note it howled and shook the ribs against the player's chest. The warden had two instrument makers look at it. Both said the same thing and neither would take it away, and it stayed in the loft with the wolf still in it.
text_nonnarrative: A wolf is classed by the note at which it sounds and by nothing else about the cello. The same howl at a second string counts as a second wolf, since the class follows the note. Sympathy in the ribs is a symptom and never a criterion, whatever the player reports about the chest. An instrument sound at the F sharp and rough above it falls outside the class altogether, however loud the roughness.

text_narrative: A ring of twelve handbells goes back to the founders in the third week of the season. Six of them are flat at the hum and two are wide at the nominal. The guild's tuner takes the smallest bell first, thins the inner lip on the lathe, and brings the hum within a cent. The ninth bell will not come in at all. Its nominal moves and its hum moves with it, and the ring goes back short.
text_nonnarrative: Tuning of handbells was judged at the hum and the nominal together, and a bell true at one and false at the other counted as untuned. Thinning at the inner lip was no part of the class, since the class attended to the intervals and not to the metal. A ring was sound only where every bell in it lay inside a cent. One bell wide of that put the whole ring out of class.

text_narrative: Three winters running, the cane cutter at the marsh edge worked the same beds. The first winter he took only two-year growth and split every stalk at the node, and the reeds held their scrape into spring. The second winter the frost came late and he cut green cane out of impatience. Half of it warped in the drying loft. The third winter he cut nothing at all and sold last year's bundles at twice the price.
text_nonnarrative: Cane was classed by the age of the growth and by the position of the cut, never by the season of cutting. Two-year stalks cut at the node were of the first class whatever the weather of that winter. Green cane was disqualified outright, and no amount of drying in a loft made it otherwise. Warp bore on the price of a bundle and had no bearing at all on the class of the reeds.

text_narrative: The lathe had been quiet for six days and the grooves on the last cymbal were wrong, Kestrel thought, though she could not say how. Even spacing, even depth, a clean spiral from bell to edge. She turned it under the lamp. The spiral ran the wrong way round, against the direction the tool could travel, and it had been like that since the blank came off the hammer bench, and no hand had touched it.
text_nonnarrative: Lathing is graded on the spacing and the depth of the grooves, and on their direction only where the direction is inconsistent within one cymbal. A spiral running from bell to edge and a spiral running the other way are of one class. Hammer marks under the grooves are a matter for the blank and never for the lathe. Wrongness a hand can feel and an instrument cannot is outside the grading altogether.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the guild house at the ford, the old bass bars were taken out of nine instruments and new ones sprung in. Two of the nine split at the treble end within the month. The bar in a tenth instrument, left as it stood, outlasted all of them. The record of that year notes the spring given to each bar in barleycorns and gives no reason for the two failures.
text_nonnarrative: Spring in a bass bar was the difference between the curve of the bar and the curve of the belly it was glued along. The load taken at the treble end was a function of that difference and of the arching under the bridge foot. Without the bar, belly and string tension stood in no fixed relation to each other, and the bar alone set that relation, at rest and under the full pull.

text_narrative: The instrument recovered from the drift hull had no maker's mark and eleven valves. Survey crews measured its leadpipe at forty-one points along the bore. The taper reversed twice, narrowing to the second valve and widening again before the slide, which no shop on the station would cut. A pressure trace run on the fourth day showed the standing wave sitting where the second narrowing began. The hull yielded nothing else of the kind.
text_nonnarrative: A leadpipe is the length of tubing between the mouthpiece receiver and the first valve, and its taper is what distinguishes it from the tubing beyond. Bore diameter at any point along it is a function of distance from the receiver alone. Where the taper is monotonic, the standing wave and the valve positions are independent; where it reverses, the two are bound together and neither is free of the other in that stretch.

text_narrative: There was a maker in the forest villages who cut purfling channels for the little people and was paid in shavings that turned to silver by morning. The bargain held while the channel stayed a hair inside the edge. One autumn he cut wide, to save a night's work, and the shavings stayed shavings. The channels he cut after that were narrow enough, but nothing came of them, and the silver never returned.
text_nonnarrative: Painted purfling is the third class, and the one that removes nothing: a line drawn on the plate where the other two are set into it. True purfling is distinguished by the channel, cut to depth before the strips go in. Scratched purfling has a channel too, but a shallow one that takes no strip. Width at the edge separates none of the three, since all three are cut narrow.

text_narrative: Out on the cattle route the freight drummers all knew which shop had lapped a head by the sound of it in the cold. Sennet's shop glued the skin to the flesh hoop and the heads went dead the first frost past the pass. The old widow at the crossing tucked and pinned hers, no glue anywhere, and those heads came through two winters of hauling with the crown still true and the lap unopened.
text_nonnarrative: Neither glued nor tucked heads were the older kind; pegged heads were, and they held the skin against the shell without a hoop at all. Glued lapping bound the skin to the flesh hoop and could not be undone. Tucked lapping folded the skin over the hoop and under itself, and was distinguished from the glued sort by what it kept removable rather than by any difference in the crown or the tone.

text_narrative: Halfway down the undercroft the sexton stops and claps once, the way the guidebooks say to. The return comes back doubled, one report and then a second a beat behind it, from the far wall and from somewhere much nearer. He claps again at the stair and gets one. He claps at the same flagstone and gets two. Nothing stands between that flagstone and the wall but forty feet of cold air.
text_nonnarrative: The undercroft lay eighty feet by thirty under the north range, with a barrel vault of dressed stone and a floor of flagstones worn hollow at the centre. Two stairs stood at the east end, one blocked. The far wall was blank ashlar without recess or door. Nothing in the space was soft, and the driest corner was the one furthest from the stair, where the vault stood within a foot of the floor.

text_narrative: Before the towers had bells in them, the makers of the first sky hung their instrument from the pole star and ran the wires down through nine floors of cloud. The keys were at the bottom, in the dark, where no one could hear what they struck. One of the makers cut a wire to listen and the note it carried was never heard again in any tower after.
text_nonnarrative: Nine floors stood between the keyboard chamber and the bell frame. The chamber itself was low, with the clavier at its centre and the transmission wires rising in two banks behind it. Each wire was slack in its guides and lay clear of the stair well. Above the seventh floor the frame timbers were closer set, and the space between wire and timber was narrowest there.

text_narrative: For four seasons the copying room at the exchange gave Ilse the wind parts and nobody else. She did the second oboe in a morning and the horns by lunch. One spring she asked for strings and was given the harp, which has one line and forty pages of rests. She counted the rests twice and found the engraver had dropped a bar in the middle of a long silence, where nobody would ever hear it.
text_nonnarrative: Copyists vary more within a room than between rooms, and the spread is widest on parts with long rests. The median error rate on wind parts is under one in a thousand bars; on harp and percussion parts it is roughly four times that. Most of the difference is accounted for by rest counting rather than by pitch. Experience shortens the tail without moving the median much, though it narrows the spread within a room.

text_narrative: The survey party reaches the upper hamlets in the second week and finds the whistling still in use across the gorge. A herder on the north slope calls a phrase four times and a woman on the south slope answers it with a longer one. The party's recorder catches both. Neither speaker will repeat a phrase for the machine on its own, and the recording ends when the wind turns and the answers stop coming.
text_nonnarrative: Whistled speech was commoner among herders than among the settled households of the same hamlets, and the gap was wider on the steeper slopes. Roughly three in five adults on the north side could hold a whistled exchange; on the valley floor the proportion was under one in ten. Distance accounted for most of the variation, though the median exchange was short everywhere, and vocabulary was narrower than in speech by a wide margin.

text_narrative: A glassmaker's daughter in the river town ground her bowls a shade thinner than the trade allowed, and the instrument she built of them could be heard through walls. The neighbours complained and the magistrate came with a rule and a scale. Every bowl was within the trade's thickness. He measured again in the yard, where the sound did not carry, and every bowl was thinner than the rule allowed, and thicker again indoors.
text_nonnarrative: Bowls of a glass armonica were nested rather than ranked side by side, which was what set the instrument apart from tuned glasses in a frame. Pitch depended on the diameter of a bowl and on its thickness together, so no bowl was ground to size without reference to its neighbours. Compass was therefore narrow, and fixed once by the widest bowl the spindle would carry and by the smallest a hand could reach.

text_narrative: When the clay of the second world was still soft, the shaping powers made vessels with holes in them and found that a hole anywhere served as well as a hole in the proper place. The lesser makers who came after did not believe it. They bored their holes in rows, as on a pipe, and the vessels answered in the same scale as before, and the rows meant nothing.
text_nonnarrative: A vessel flute is a closed chamber sounded at a lip or fipple, and it is characterised by the fact that its pitch is a function of total open area rather than of hole position. Placement is therefore free, and spacing is a matter of the hand. Overblowing is not available to it, so its compass is one octave or less, fixed by the volume enclosed and by nothing else.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the concert trust the two harps in the small hall were taken apart on the same afternoon. Eleven of the fourteen pedal rods in the older instrument were found bent at the same height above the base, and the twelfth was cracked through. The trust's minute for that quarter records the finding, the cost of the rods, and a note that no player had reported anything amiss.
text_nonnarrative: Rods in the pedal box are required to be of drawn steel of one gauge throughout, without joint or braze along the run. Brass is permitted only in the linkage at the head. No rod is to bear against the column between its guides, and clearance of an eighth of an inch at every guide is to be maintained whatever the pedal position. Slack in the springs is not permitted at any setting.

text_narrative: The garrison band loses its mutes in the second week of the withdrawal and the bandmaster has forty made from ration tin. Each one is rolled on a broom handle and corked with three strips of felt cut from a greatcoat. Twelve of them are too tight and will not seat. The rest sit well enough, and the band plays the evening call with tin in the bells and nobody remarks on the tone.
text_nonnarrative: Mutes on issue were required to be of tinned plate, seamed and not soldered, with three corks set at equal spacing round the body. Cork of less than a quarter inch was permitted only on the smaller bells. No mute was to seat deeper than its own shoulder, and each was to be free of the bell under a light pull. Felt in place of cork was permitted nowhere on issue patterns.

text_narrative: Nobody at the ministry works would say where the mica came from now, and Halloran had stopped asking. Sheets that thin, split that clean, and every crate stamped with the same district that had been under water for six years. He held one up to the window. It passed light like the old stock and rang under a fingernail like the old stock, and he set it in the soundbox without a word in the book.
text_nonnarrative: Diaphragms for a soundbox are to be split mica of four thousandths, free of cloud within the sprung ring and unpierced anywhere. Glass is permitted for shop patterns and for nothing on sale. The bearing of the stylus bar is required to fall on the centre within a thirty-second of an inch. Gaskets are to be rubber at both faces, and shellac at either face is not permitted on any pattern in the current list.

text_narrative: The frets on the dead man's guitar are not where frets go, and that is the whole of what Devrim has. Eighteen of them, unevenly spaced, the ninth almost touching the eighth. A bad job, the shop said. But the file marks are patient and the inlay is exact, and whoever set them was working to a rule of some kind. Devrim measures the gaps again and writes the numbers down in a column.
text_nonnarrative: Equal spacing of frets was never the ideal that irregular spacing failed to reach; it was a different ambition. A fixed ratio at every fret bought freedom of key at the cost of a slightly sour third in all of them. Irregular schemes bought a pure third in a few keys and paid for it everywhere else. That the pure schemes sounded better in their own keys was true, and beside the point.

text_narrative: In the sixth season of the hall on the market street, the instrument was voiced twice. The first voicing in autumn took the top two octaves down by needling, and the reports of that winter called the tone woolly. The second voicing in spring took nothing off and lacquered the striking point instead. Attendance in the following season was recorded as unchanged, and the voicer's fee appeared twice under the same heading in the accounts.
text_nonnarrative: Hardness in a hammer is not a property of the felt but of the felt under compression, which is why the same head is soft at a whisper and hard at a shout. Voicing that treats it as one number has to choose a dynamic. Needling at the shoulder rather than the crown answers the objection in part. It does not answer it, since the crown is where the string meets the felt.

text_narrative: A crane who lived by the smithy claimed she could hear a gong's pitch before the hammering began, in the flat disc, and the smith's apprentice bet her a fish on it. She named the note. The smith hammered the disc for nine days and it came out a whole tone above what she had named. She ate the fish anyway and said the bronze had changed its mind, not she.
text_nonnarrative: Hammering a gong was never a way of tuning it, whatever the trade said of itself. The pitch of a disc under any one blow was a function of every blow before it, and of nothing a smith could fix in advance. The craft lay in stopping, not in aiming. A smith who claimed to hammer to a note was describing an outcome and calling it a method.

text_narrative: Every player on the square knew the gut seller by the smell of the cart and by the way he sized a string against his thumb and never a gauge. He was right more often than the men with brass rules. One year a lutenist brought a false top string back and the seller measured it in front of everyone, thumb and eye, and made him a new one from the same hank, and that one held.
text_nonnarrative: False: of a string, uneven in diameter along its length, so that no two stops give the same interval. Hank: the coil in which gut is sold, of thirty strands cut to one length. Gauge: the diameter of a strand at its thickest, named in sixtieths. True: of a string, within a sixtieth of one diameter throughout. Top: the thinnest string on an instrument, and the one most often found false in a hank.

text_narrative: Three times that month the rehair man in the basement shop gets the same bow across his bench. The first time the hair is cut short at the frog and he says nothing. The second time it is cut again, cleanly, on the same side. The third time the owner does not come in person and the bow arrives in a case that is not the bow's case, with a cake of rosin in it that nobody in the trade sells.
text_nonnarrative: Ribbon: the flat band of hair between frog and head, of even width and no crossings. Camber: the curve set in a stick by heat, measured at the middle under no tension. Cake: rosin in its poured form, graded dark or light by the season of the tapping. Slip: any part of a ribbon loose at one end while the rest held. Wedge: the block that pinned a ribbon into its mortise, and the commonest thing lost in a rehair.

text_narrative: In the age when the winds still had names, each of them was given a string in the window of the world and told to sound only its own. The north wind took two and the others said nothing. For a long while the chord held, six strings and one silence where the seventh should have been, and no wind since has been able to find the string that was never strung.
text_nonnarrative: Common stringing: an arrangement in which every string on a wind harp is tuned to one pitch. Aliquot: any partial sounded above that pitch, and the only source of melody in the instrument. Threshold: the least air speed at which any partial is available. Sill draught: air across the box rather than along it, under which no partial above the third is available. Silence: the state of the harp below threshold, whatever the tuning.

text_narrative: In the twelfth year of the workshop by the canal, forty-one instruments were returned with slipping pins and the plank of every one was found to be of a single board. The house changed to five laminations that autumn. Of the instruments made after the change, three came back in the following decade, and all three had been kept in unheated rooms through two winters, which the house recorded against each.
text_nonnarrative: A wrest plank meant, under this article, the laminated member into which the tuning pins were driven, and no other part of the frame however pinned. Where a plank was of fewer than three laminations, the article did not apply to it and the pin holes were governed by the general rule. Nothing in this article affected the seating of the bridge or the liability of the maker for it.

text_narrative: Under the shop lamp the comb has ninety-six teeth and Wren counts them twice, because the ledger says ninety-five. The extra tooth sits between the forty-first and the forty-second, filed as neatly as the rest, tuned to no interval in the scale. She turns the barrel by hand. Every pin passes the extra tooth without touching it, and the tooth sounds anyway, once, at the end of the tune.
text_nonnarrative: Comb meant, in this schedule, the toothed steel plate as a whole and not any tooth of it taken singly. A tooth silent under every pin on the barrel counted as part of the comb notwithstanding. Where the tooth count differed from the declared count, the declaration and not the comb was in default. Nothing in this schedule bore on the barrel, the pins, or the governor.

text_narrative: In the first days of the recording world, sound was a thing with a shape, and the makers built horns to catch it as one catches rain. The widest horn caught the least. A maker of the second generation cut hers to the taper of a sea shell and caught a voice that had not been made yet, and the wax held it, and no one would say whose it was.
text_nonnarrative: Horn means, in this part, the collecting cone alone, from the mouth to the throat coupling, and excludes the coupling itself. Where a horn is of two or more sections, each section is a horn for the measurement provisions and for no other. Nothing in this part is to be read as fixing the taper. A horn of no measurable flare is not a horn within this definition.

text_narrative: At four contests running, the tuner from the coast finished last on time and first on the unisons. At the first she left a single beat in the middle octave and the panel would not pass it. At the second she left none and ran twelve minutes over. At the third she was given a piano with two cracked bridges. At the fourth she tuned in silence, hearing nothing anyone else could hear, and won outright.
text_nonnarrative: A unison stands as clean only where no beat is audible at the bench through a full four seconds. One beat in four seconds is a fault of the unison and not of the octave above it. A string damped out of the way is not a unison and is not open to correction. Where two strings of a trio are clean and the third is not, the trio is unclean entire, whatever the state of its neighbours.

text_narrative: The shop on the yard road had a man who cut snare beds by eye and would not use the jig, and for eleven years no drum of his ever buzzed. When he went, the shop kept his last shell on a shelf and cut every bed to match it with calipers. Half of those buzzed. The foreman said the beds were identical to the thousandth and never worked out what else the man had been doing.
text_nonnarrative: A head seated on a shell with no bed at all was in play and was not a fault. A bed deeper at one side than the other put the drum out of play whatever the head sat like. Snare contact at two points was the least that counted as contact; at one point the drum was out. Buzz off a neighbouring drum lay outside the rules entirely and was answerable by nobody in the shop.

text_narrative: There was a wheel player at the winter fairs whose cotton never wanted rosin, and the other players said she had wound it from a cloud. She would let anyone look. The cotton was cotton. But her drone never scratched and never dropped, through six hours of playing and a change of weather, and when she stopped coming to the fairs the cotton in her wheel was found unwound and lying loose in the box.
text_nonnarrative: Cotton on a string was permitted at any thickness, and a string bare of it was still a legal string. A drone that scratched was not thereby out of the piece; scratch counted against the wheel and not against the player. Where the wheel ran untrue, no position of the cotton put it right and the instrument was out of the round. Rosin on the wheel face was allowed nowhere in the fair rules.

text_narrative: In the second year of the sound archive, two hundred cylinders were taken in from the county collectors and shelved by donor rather than by subject. Nine of them were blank. Four had been recorded over twice, the older groove still legible under the newer in raking light. The archivist of that year listed all four as duplicates and the error stood in the catalogue for a decade.
text_nonnarrative: Four standards are in circulation, of which the two-minute is much the commonest. Each is a hollow cylinder of brown wax, three inches across at the mouth and open at both ends, with the groove cut in a spiral of a hundred turns to the inch. The four-minute pattern is the same body at twice the turn count. Blanks are the same again, without the groove.

text_narrative: The fork in the cold locker reads three cents flat and that is exactly right, Anselm tells himself, that is the whole of the correction table. The fork in the warm bay reads three cents flat as well. Same alloy, same batch, sixty degrees between them. He puts a third fork in the airlock and waits out the cycle. Three cents flat, and the table on the wall is now a piece of paper.
text_nonnarrative: Six patterns made up the standard set, of which the middle two were in daily use. Each was of hardened steel, forked at the head with tines of square section, and stamped at the stem with its nominal pitch and the temperature that pitch belonged to. The heaviest pattern carried a foot for a resonator box. The lightest was the only one without a stamp of any kind on either face.

text_narrative: The kitchen is warm and the instrument is not, and Fen has the jack rail off and eleven jacks on a cloth in front of the stove. The tongue of the fourth one will not swing. She works the axle with a pin. It swings, sticks, swings. Her sister comes through for the kettle and does not ask, and the tongue sticks again in the same place, at the same quarter of its travel.
text_nonnarrative: What the revival gets wrong about jacks is the tongue, not the plectrum, though the plectrum takes all the blame in print. A tongue hung on too fine an axle is quiet and unreliable, and makers who hang theirs coarse are called crude for it. The best modern jacks are the ones that give up on delicacy at the axle and keep it where it can be heard in the room.

text_narrative: The first roses were not carved but grown, in the days when the belly of a lute was living wood and the maker only asked. Each rose was a different tree's answer. When the wood stopped answering, the makers took knives to it and cut the old patterns from memory, and the memory was already thin, and every rose since has been a copy of a copy of a thing that was once alive.
text_nonnarrative: Interlace in the late roses was praised for its depth and was the least interesting thing about it. What passed for invention in the pattern books was almost always a denser grid, and density was cheap. The roses worth looking at were the shallow ones, cut in three planes at most, where the eye had somewhere to stop. Fashion held otherwise for a century and was wrong about it the whole time.

text_narrative: Sixty seconds, Marat counts, and the clap is still coming back off the far end of the concourse. Nothing in the building is soft any more, that is all it is. No seats, no bodies, no coats. But sixty seconds is not a room, it is a canyon, and he has been sleeping in it for a month without noticing that every word he does not say stays in the air behind him.
text_nonnarrative: The issue whether reverberation is a property of a space or of a sound in it turns on what is being individuated. On one account the decay time belongs to the enclosure, and any sound merely reveals it. On the other, decay is a feature of an event and the enclosure is one condition among several. Both accounts agree on the number and disagree on what the number is a number of.

text_narrative: Every watch for nine watches, Odile tunes the same three strings on the station's only instrument and every watch they are flat again by the same amount. She tries a longer settle. She tries pulling them past pitch and letting them fall back. On the ninth watch she stops tuning them and plays anyway, and the flatness is gone, and the strings are where she left them two watches before.
text_nonnarrative: Drift and detuning were not the same concept, though the same measurement served for both. A string that settled slowly was in one state throughout, on the view that a state is what persists under a single cause. On the competing view each moment of a slow settle was a distinct state, and tune was instantaneous, so no string was ever in it. The dispute was about persistence and not about strings.

text_narrative: The brass shop at the river gate draws forty bells this season and eleven of them split at the flare. The master sets the mandrel back a hand's breadth and draws twelve more. Two split. He sets it back again and the metal wrinkles instead of splitting, which is worse, and the apprentices are put to annealing every third pass through the winter with no explanation given.
text_nonnarrative: Thinning at the flare goes as the square of the ratio between mouth diameter and mandrel diameter, and not as the difference between them. The constant belongs to the alloy and to the temper it is drawn at. Below a ratio of about one and a half the relation holds closely; above that, wrinkling sets the limit instead and the square law says nothing useful.

text_narrative: They still tell it on the hill farms that the piper at the crossroads tunes his drones to the hill and not to the chanter. Anyone can hear it. The bass drone sits a shade under where it should and the hill sits a shade over, and between the two of them there is a beat that a walker on the road can feel in the chest before hearing it, and the piper never touches the slide.
text_nonnarrative: Beat rate between a drone and a chanter note is the difference of the two frequencies and is independent of how loud either is. A drone two cents low against a low A gives about a beat every two seconds. Doubling the interval doubles the rate, so the relation is linear and not proportional to pitch. At rates above about twenty a second the beat is beyond counting and roughness is the better description.

text_narrative: The bridge on the bench has been fitted to an arching that is not this instrument's. Ivo lays it on the belly and light shows under the treble foot on both sides. He tries it on the second violin from the same case and it beds down flat, all the way across, with no daylight anywhere. Two instruments, one bridge, and the case has been locked since the spring.
text_nonnarrative: Two feet, a waist pierced by a heart and two kidneys, and a top edge curved to the fingerboard: these were the parts of a bridge, and the feet were the only ones fitted to a particular instrument. The waist stood free of the belly at every point. Kidneys were absent in the plainer patterns, and the heart was absent in none of them, however plain the rest.

text_narrative: There was a piano in the schoolhouse at the fen that kept its crown for sixty years in a damp room, which no piano does. The tuner who came after the school closed found the ribs sound and the belly still bellied. He also found that the ribs had been cut from coffin boards, which the parish record confirmed, and nobody after him would take the instrument away.
text_nonnarrative: Ribs run across the grain of a soundboard and stand proud of its underside, and the crown is the curve they hold it in. The bridge sits on the other face, crossing the ribs at an angle and notched where it meets each one. Cut-off bars stand at the two short sides. In the smaller instruments the bars are absent and the ribs are shorter at both ends.

text_narrative: Half an hour before the bell for none, Ilvet took the barrel of the goose feather across her knee and set the knife where the quill was hardest. The first cut ran too shallow and the slit closed on itself. She pared the shoulders back, opened the slit against the thumbnail, and cut the nib square. On the trial stroke the ink came away clean at the hairline and flooded at the thick.
text_nonnarrative: Shoulder length is no part of how a cut quill is classed. What counts is the angle of the nib against the slit and whether the slit runs true to the barrel's spine. A slit that closes under pressure is one class of fault, flooding at the thick a second, and neither bears on the hairline. Goose and swan differ in hardness, and hardness sets the tolerance rather than the class.

text_narrative: The page is warm where it should not be, and Hesper knows before she turns it what the warmth means. Iron gall has eaten through the descenders again, letter by letter, and the holes are the shape of a hand that has been dead a hundred years. She holds the leaf to the window. Light comes through where the ink lay thickest. Somebody is still writing on the other side of it, she thinks, and sets the leaf down.
text_nonnarrative: Corrosion in an iron gall ink was a function of two quantities held in the same fluid: free acid and unbound iron. Neither was harmful to a sheet on its own. The gum arabic was the suspending medium, and its proportion governed how far the ink stood proud of the surface rather than lying within it. Where the sheet bore an alum size, the acid had a second host and the descenders were no more at risk than the hairlines.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the copying house at Vaudre, the master ruler was replaced and the frames with him. The new frames were strung with waxed linen instead of gut, thirty-two lines to the opening, and the first quire off them was rejected by the corrector. The lines had printed too faint to follow. A second stringing at heavier tension was ordered before the feast, and the quire was ruled again on the same skins.
text_nonnarrative: Two uprights and a pair of cross-bars made the body of a ruling frame, with the cords strung between the bars and not between the uprights. Wedges at the foot held the tension. The bars were slotted at fixed intervals, so that line spacing was a property of the frame and not of the hand. Smaller frames had no wedges at all, the cords being knotted directly, and in those the spacing was fixed for good.

text_narrative: There was a limepit outside the village that nobody would draw from twice in a season, and the parchmenters knew why. Skins left in it came out white as milk and thin as breath, and they took ink like nothing else in the county. But they went on stretching after the frame was off them. A book made from that pit grew a finger's width a year, and after forty years the boards would not close on it.
text_nonnarrative: Alum-tawed skin is the odd member of the three, since the tawing is reversible in water and the other two are not. Limed parchment and oak-tanned leather stand apart on what the process takes out: the limepit strips hair and fat and leaves the fibre network open, while tanning fills it. Thickness is no ground of division. A thin tawed skin and a thin limed skin are unlike in every property that bears on stretching.

text_narrative: A conservation unit aboard the orbital repository reports that the reconstructed gathering fails at its fourth opening. The scanner logs hair side against flesh side at two of the eight junctions, which the rule of the house forbids. Technicians on the second shift pull the quire, unpick the sewing, and reverse the middle bifolium. The reassembled gathering passes on the next pass, and the unit files the fault against the sorting stage rather than the sewer.
text_nonnarrative: Flesh side: the face of a leaf that lay inward on the animal, smoother and paler, and readier to take a fine hand. Hair side: the outer face, marked with follicle pattern and greyer under raking light. Junction: any opening at which two facing pages are of unlike side. Rule of the house: the requirement that every opening in a gathering be flesh to flesh or hair to hair, from which the sorting of bifolia follows.

text_narrative: Three times that winter the collator at the deposit library found a quire out of order, and three times it was the same binder's work. In November it was a duodecimo with the fourth and fifth gatherings transposed. In January a folio came through with one gathering inverted, the catchwords reading backward down the fold. In March she found a volume whose third gathering belonged to another title, and she set all three aside together.
text_nonnarrative: A gathering inverted within its own fold was not out of order, since order was a relation between gatherings and never within one. Only the sequence of signatures could put a volume wrong. A gathering belonging to another title was outside the question of order entirely and was treated as a foreign body. Where two gatherings bore the same signature, neither position was defensible, and the register rather than the fold was decisive.

text_narrative: Before there were books there were only leaves in heaps, and the first binder went down to the rope-walk of the world and asked for five cords. She was given three. With three she sewed the leaves and the spine stood round, and the swell of the sewing lifted the fore-edge so that the heap became a block. The two cords withheld were kept for the last book, which has not been sewn and lies still at the world's foot.
text_nonnarrative: Raised-cord sewing is the older of the two structures in which thread passes round a support rather than through it. The support is a cord of hemp or linen laid across the spine, and the thread encircles it at every station. Swell in the spine is proportional to thread thickness and to the number of stations. Because each cord takes the pull of the whole gathering, the slips at the ends of the cords are the attachment for the boards.

text_narrative: There was a binder in the mountain hold who would not sew a headband over a core of rolled paper, and the reason was old. Her grandmother had used cane, and the cane had been cut on the wrong side of the water. Every book so finished sang a thin note at the head when the boards were opened. The hold kept them in a room with the door barred, and the binder used gut cord after that.
text_nonnarrative: At the head of a sewn book the headband stood on three parts: a core, a covering of silk or thread wound over it, and a set of tie-downs passing into the gatherings. The core was cane, rolled paper or leather, and its diameter fixed the height of the whole. Tie-downs were absent in decorative work, where the band was stuck to the spine and bore no load. Beading was a property of the winding alone.

text_narrative: The bench is too low for the work and Corin does not stop to change it. He threads the frayed slip through the first channel in the oak, brings it up through the second hole, and hammers it flat into the bevel. The board rocks. He turns it over, finds the slip has doubled on itself in the channel, and picks the whole run out with an awl. The second attempt lies flush and the board sits still.
text_nonnarrative: Lacing through the board was permitted in oak and in beech, and in no other wood. Channels were to be cut on the outer face and never on the inner, so that the slip lay below the level of the leather. Three stations were required for a folio and two for anything smaller. A slip doubled in its channel counted as unlaced, and a board pegged rather than laced was permitted only in temporary covers.

text_narrative: Every binder in the lower street had a panel stamp, and only old Wenna's would strike clean on damp calf. The others blamed the leather. Wenna said nothing and went on selling impressions at twice the price, and when she left the trade the stamp went to her apprentice, who could not get a clean strike out of it either. It turned out she had been warming the brass on the glue pot before every panel.
text_nonnarrative: Depth of bite is what collectors praise in blind-stamped panel work, and it is the least interesting thing about it. A deep impression on soft calf is easy and tells nothing of the cutter. The panels worth attention are those whose ground stays flat while the fine lines hold, since that combination is a matter of even pressure across an uneven skin. Most surviving examples fail at the corners, where the pressure is always least.

text_narrative: Four in the morning and the glaire has gone tacky in the pot, which means the panel will not take. Doran breathes on the leather anyway. Too cold, too dry, the shop unheated since the landlord changed the locks. He lays the leaf, sets the hot tool, and rocks it once. The gold lifts away with the tool and leaves a bruise. Somebody wants this spine lettered by noon and somebody is going to be disappointed.
text_nonnarrative: Adhesion of gold leaf to a glaired surface was inverse to the age of the glaire, and roughly so, doubling in poorness for each day past the second. Tool temperature acted as a threshold rather than as a proportion: below the point at which the albumen set, nothing held, and above it the excess showed as scorch. The two variables were independent, so a hot tool could not compensate for stale glaire at any temperature.

text_narrative: A marbler in the river quarter produced four sheets in one afternoon that would not dry. The colours held their comb pattern but continued to move, slowly, in the manner of oil on water, for eleven days. Buyers were found for three. The fourth was bound into a ledger of accounts, where the marbling went on turning under the pastedown and was reported by two later owners as a fault in the paper.
text_nonnarrative: Six patterns make up the standard stock of a marbling shop, of which the stone is the plainest and the shell the dearest. Between them lie the comb patterns proper: nonpareil, at a quarter-inch tooth; curl, in which the comb is drawn twice at right angles; and peacock, the same as curl with a second gathering rake. Each is a state of the same bath, and none requires a colour the others lack.

text_narrative: Whenever the almoner fans the edge of the third volume, the painting underneath shows a different room. On Monday it is a stairwell with the door open. On Thursday the same stairwell with the door shut and something on the landing. She has stopped fanning it in company. Tonight she holds the block at the angle that works and finds the landing empty and the stair gone, and she closes the book square so the gilt returns.
text_nonnarrative: Either a fore-edge painting was a property of the book or it was a property of a particular flexure of the book, and the two accounts had different consequences. On the first, the painting existed while the edge was square and was merely hidden; on the second it existed only under fan, and squareness was not concealment but absence. Nothing in the gilding decided between them, since gilt was applied to the square edge in both accounts.

text_narrative: In the fourth year after the paper duty was abolished, the mill at Corrow altered its watermark wire from a crowned pot to an uncrowned one, and the change was entered in the mill book on a Tuesday. Eight reams of the old mark remained in the drying loft. These were sold as seconds to a stationer in the port, who used them for shipping bills, and both marks appeared in the same bound volume of accounts.
text_nonnarrative: A tranchefile wire sewn to the mould counts as a countermark and not as a watermark, however placed. Under this part a watermark means a design in wire attached to the laid surface such that its impression is visible by transmitted light and absent by reflected light. Where a mould bears two designs, the larger is the watermark and the smaller the countermark. Nothing in this part affects the dating of paper by mould twin.

text_narrative: The vatman had two moulds at his elbow and picked up the wrong one, which he knew from the weight before the deckle was even on. Wove was heavier by an ounce and hung differently in the shake. He set it down, took the laid mould, and dipped. The couching went badly all the same: the sheet came off the felt with a chain line doubled where the wire had lifted clear of the rib beneath.
text_nonnarrative: What separated the two mould surfaces was not the wire but its support. In the laid mould, closely set wires ran across ribs and were tied to them by chain wires, so the impression held a fine grain and a coarse periodic one. The wove surface was a woven cloth of equal wires with no ribs beneath, and its impression was uniform. Antique laid was a third class, marked by rib shadows readable across a full sheet.

text_narrative: In the age when paper was new the makers asked the water for a straight edge and the water refused, and the refusal is why every hand-made sheet thins toward its border. The first maker built a frame to hold the pulp back. The water went under the frame regardless, thinning as it went, and left the four ragged margins the frame was meant to prevent. Machines were promised later, and they cut what they could not make.
text_nonnarrative: Nothing about a deckle edge is decorative in origin, and treating it as ornament inverts the case. The feathered border is the residue of pulp escaping under the deckle frame, which is to say a tolerance rather than a feature. Collectors who prize untrimmed sheets are therefore prizing an imperfection. That the imperfection is also a reliable index of hand manufacture is true and worth something, but it argues for the edge as evidence, not as beauty.

text_narrative: The kitchen is the only room warm enough and that is the trouble, Meret thinks, laying the damp sheets between blotters on the table. Too warm at one end, too cold by the window. She weighs the pile with the flat iron and goes to bed. In the morning the outer sheets are flat and the middle ones have dried into shallow waves running with the grain, and the whole stack has to be damped again.
text_nonnarrative: Cockling was commoner in gelatine-sized stock than in internally sized stock, though the gap was smaller than binders supposed: fourteen percent of sheets against nine. Variation within a single ream exceeded variation between mills. The median amplitude was under two millimetres, and most of the spread lay in the outer sheets of a stack rather than in the sizing. Humidity gradient across the drying room accounted for the largest share of the remainder.

text_narrative: A punchcutter in the hill country struck her matrices in copper that had come out of a bell, and every letter cast from them rang faintly when the forme was locked. The founder would not sell the fount. He kept it in a chest of sand, where the ringing could not be heard, and he justified the matrices himself, filing the depth even and the drive square, so that at least the ringing came out level.
text_nonnarrative: A struck matrix is judged on the evenness of its drive and on nothing else that the eye can reach. Depth out of true by more than a hair is disqualifying whatever the quality of the punch. Copper of any origin is admissible, since alloy bears on the casting and never on the class. A letter that rings in the forme is a fault in the fount and not in the matrices from which it came.

text_narrative: A dispute at the foundry in the cathedral quarter is settled this week over the depth of a counter. The cutter for the small pica has sunk the bowl of the lowercase a by a third more than the specimen requires, and the founder refuses the punch. Two arbiters from the stationers take smoke proofs of both. The deeper counter prints identically at text size, and the punch is accepted, with the specimen amended rather than the letter.
text_nonnarrative: Every punch had a face, a shank and a shoulder, and the three were of one piece of steel. The letter stood in relief on the face, with the enclosed white areas, or counters, sunk below it. Counter depth was not uniform across a fount: closed letters were sunk deeper than open ones. The shoulder was the sloped transition to the shank, and in the smallest sizes it was almost absent, the face standing nearly flush.

text_narrative: Nobody at the composing contest will stand next to Aldo, and it is not superstition. He sets faster than anyone in the hall and he sets kerned sorts as though they were ordinary, which means the overhangs snap off against the stick and land on the neighbouring case. Two of his f-ligatures go every heat. The judges count broken sorts against the shop and not against the man, so the shop pays and Aldo keeps winning.
text_nonnarrative: Fit is the part of type design that reviewers of specimens least often discuss, and the part that decides how a page reads. Kerning pairs are a repair, not a virtue; a fount needing many of them has been drawn without regard for its own sidebearings. The founts that hold up are those whose lowercase sits evenly at three sizes without adjustment. Praise for an elegant italic usually rests on a roman that carries it.

text_narrative: Four jobs came through the small shop that month and the stick was wrong for three of them. For the handbill the measure was set at twenty ems and the last line of every paragraph ran a nick short. For the ticket work the knee slipped under pressure and gave a ragged edge. For the pamphlet the screw would not hold at all. Only the final job, a plain card, needed no measure and came out square.
text_nonnarrative: A composing stick holds three surfaces at right angles: a fixed head, a fixed back, and a movable knee. The knee slides along the back and is clamped by a screw bearing on a serrated bed, so the measure is quantised to the pitch of the serrations rather than continuous. Rigidity under the pressure of a full line depends on the clamp alone. Without the serrated bed the knee and the measure are not independent.

text_narrative: Half the forme is on the stone and the other half is missing, which is the first thing the overseer notices. The chase is there, the furniture is there, the quoins are driven tight against nothing on the near side. Vesna runs a thumb along the empty channel. Somebody has lifted eight lines of standing type out of a locked forme without slackening a single quoin, and the ink on the stone beside it is still wet.
text_nonnarrative: Furniture bearing directly on type rather than on a reglet leaves the forme illegal however tight the quoins. A forme in which any quoin sits at its full extension is unlocked by definition, since no correction remains available to it. Loose lines at the foot are not a fault of lockup and cannot be answered by driving the quoins harder. Only a forme that lifts clear of the stone when raised at one corner is legal to move.

text_narrative: In the second winter of the siege the press in the undercroft went over to octavo, since paper came in half-sheets only. The imposition scheme was rewritten twice in one week. The first attempt put pages two and fifteen on the same side of the sheet and produced a run of four hundred with the third gathering reading backward. The second held, and the run stood as the whole of that month's printing.
text_nonnarrative: Pages to a sheet doubled with each fold, so an octavo held eight leaves and sixteen pages to the side pair. Bulk at the fold followed the same power, and beyond four folds the swell at the spine exceeded the thickness of the flat stack by a measurable fraction. The relation failed for thin papers, where compressibility was the dominant term and the count of folds mattered less than the substance of the sheet.

text_narrative: Six weeks out and the ship's log was a bound blank book with the signatures printed at the foot of every eighth leaf, which the purser had never once thought about. Now he did. The sequence ran A, B, C and then jumped to E. He counted the leaves twice against the fold. Eight leaves were gone from the middle of the book and the entries either side of the gap were in his own hand.
text_nonnarrative: Signature: a letter or figure at the foot of the first leaf of a gathering, marking its place in the sequence. Direction line: the same line, considered as the position rather than as the mark it holds, and empty in unsigned work. Volume signature: an added letter distinguishing one volume from another under a single title. Skipped letter: any letter of the alphabet omitted by convention, three of which are absent from every full sequence.

text_narrative: The correction of a civic almanac was suspended for a week last spring after the reader and the compositor were found to be using different marginal conventions. The reader marked a transposition with a hooked stroke; the compositor read the hook as a deletion and lifted forty sorts. Two formes were pulled apart before the discrepancy was traced. The house afterwards fixed one set of marks to a board above the stone and the almanac went to press.
text_nonnarrative: Marginal marks were classed by what they instructed and never by the shape drawn. A hooked stroke counted as a transposition wherever the house convention said so, and as a deletion wherever it did not, the mark itself being neutral between the two. Position in the margin bore on the line affected and not on the class. A correction lacking any mark in the text was void, however clear the marginal note, since the compositor had no anchor for it.

text_narrative: After the last mill fell silent the printers of the low country went back to damping, and a saying grew up about the first sheet. It was said the water remembered every hand that had touched the fibre and gave the impression back deeper for each one. The presses in the drowned towns pulled sheets so black they could not be read. Nobody dampened above four hours after that, and the rule outlived the reason for it.
text_nonnarrative: The damping room lies below the press floor, on the north side, where the wall is thickest and the light is poorest. Two stone troughs stand against the long wall with a plank between them at waist height. Above the troughs the racks hold the damped reams under boards and weights, four reams to a rack. The floor is two inches lower at the drain end. Air from the stair is the only air in the room.

text_narrative: Three times on the long transit the archivist opens the same volume and finds the offset worse. At the first opening the facing page carries a ghost of the plate, legible in reverse. At the second the ghost has a ghost of its own two leaves further in. At the third she stops counting and interleaves the whole block with tissue, though in null gravity the leaves will not lie and the tissue drifts from the gutter.
text_nonnarrative: Setoff was the transfer of wet ink from a printed surface to the leaf laid against it, and was distinguished from offset only by the age of the impression. Its extent depended on three quantities: the tack of the vehicle, the absorbency of the stock, and the pressure of the stack. Slip-sheeting was the standard remedy, being the interleaving of waste at the press rather than at the bindery. Heavy plates were the usual source.

text_narrative: Everyone in the terrace knew which books had come out of the house at the end of the row, because they all had the same brown stain a hand's width up from the foot. The cellar there took water twice a year. The owner dried them on the range and the drying made it worse, and by the time they reached the second-hand stall the spots had spread into a band across every gutter.
text_nonnarrative: Reports from the trade put foxing three times commoner in machine-made stock than in earlier handmade sheets, with wide disagreement over cause. Tide lines were far less common and much more strongly clustered: a single damp store accounted for most of any dealer's holdings. Neither condition was evenly distributed within a volume. The median affected leaf lay in the outer third, and the endpapers carried a share out of all proportion to their number.

text_narrative: There was a keeper of a hill library who gave every book a mark of three parts, and the third part was a number nobody else could read. When she was gone the marks stayed on the spines and the shelves stayed in her order, which nothing in the catalogue explained. A reader who wanted a book had to guess. The library grew famous for what could be found in it by accident and for nothing else.
text_nonnarrative: A shelfmark struck through remains a shelfmark for provenance, and its removal is not permitted. Under this article a shelfmark means any notation fixing the location of an item within a sequence, whether or not that sequence is subject-ordered, and whether or not the item is present. Where an item bears two marks, the later is operative and the earlier is treated as a former location. Nothing here makes a mark a description of contents.

text_narrative: In the ninth year of the county repository the accession register was closed at entry four thousand and a new series begun, the old volume having filled to the last ruled line. The final entry recorded a bundle of estate papers with no donor named. A marginal note in a second hand added the word doubtful. The new register opened with the same bundle re-entered under a fresh number, and both entries stood.
text_nonnarrative: An entry is to carry a number, a date of receipt, a source and an extent, in that order across the opening. Numbers are required to run unbroken; a number withdrawn is to be left standing with a line through the body of the entry. Sources are permitted to be given as unknown, but not to be left blank. Extents are to be stated in linear measure for bundles and in leaves for single items.

text_narrative: In the third year of the union of the two record offices, the joint finding aid was abandoned at the series level and never carried below it. The larger office had described to the item; the smaller had described to the box. A committee sat for eleven months. Its report proposed a scheme of five levels, of which only the top two were ever completed, and the boxes of the smaller office remained unlisted.
text_nonnarrative: Levels of description were either divisions of a real object or conveniences of the describer, and archival theory had never settled which. Treated as real, a series had boundaries independent of any list, and a wrong level was an error about the world. Treated as convenient, level was a function of how much description was affordable, and no arrangement could be wrong, only coarse. The practice of both offices assumed the first and defended the second.

text_narrative: Two hands, or one hand tired, and the difference matters more than anyone else in the room understands. Sabin sets the leaf flat under the lamp. The ascenders in the upper half are clubbed; in the lower half they taper. Same ink, same ruling, same slope. A scribe grows tired in the shoulder, not in the pen angle, she thinks, and the pen angle has shifted four degrees between the two halves of the page.
text_nonnarrative: A change of hand was established on pen angle and on ascender treatment, and on no other feature of the page. Slope was excluded, since slope varied within a single stint. Clubbed and tapered ascenders were distinct classes whatever the ink, and identity of ink bore on the occasion of writing and never on the identity of the scribe. Fatigue was admitted as a cause but was no ground for assigning two halves to one hand.

text_narrative: When the first scribes were given more to write than there were hours, a bargain was struck with the letters themselves: every letter might stand for two, provided a stroke was set above it to mark the debt. The strokes multiplied. In the last age of the copying houses a single page carried more marks than letters, and the readers who could unfold them were fewer each generation, and the debt was never called in.
text_nonnarrative: Abbreviation in manuscript was a saving of parchment before it was a saving of labour, and the usual account has these the wrong way round. A suspension stroke saved perhaps three letters; the skin saved by a page of them was worth more than the hour it cost the scribe. That the system also served speed was true of the practised hand only, and the practised hand was a consequence of the saving, not its motive.

text_narrative: At each depot the survey party impresses the same seal into wax and each impression comes out worse than the last. At the first depot the legend is crisp all round. At the second a burr on the counterseal drags a line across the field. At the third the wax is too cold and the device fills unevenly. Nen files the burr flat on the fourth night and the fifth impression is clean but a quarter shallower than the first.
text_nonnarrative: An impression was classed on the legend and on the field, which were graded apart. A burr dragging across the field was disqualifying however crisp the legend, since the field was where forgery showed. Depth was no criterion at all: a shallow clean impression and a deep one counted alike. Wax too cold to fill the device was a fault of the sealing and never of the matrix, and the counterseal was graded on the same terms.

text_narrative: Half the psalters that came out of the workshop on the bridge went out with the initials never filled, and the reason was always the same: the rubricator worked by the quire and the binder worked by the book. Guide letters sat in the blank squares in a hand nobody was meant to see. Buyers complained for a season and then stopped, and within ten years the empty squares were taken for a style.
text_nonnarrative: Initial spaces in a plain service book run to four sizes, counted in ruled lines: two-line, three-line, five-line and the full page. Two-line spaces are the commonest and take a plain red letter with no infill. Three-line and five-line spaces carry a red letter with penwork in a second colour, blue in most houses and green in a few. The full page is reserved to the opening of a division and is rare in small books.

text_narrative: A magpie in the abbey orchard learned which books had clasps of brass and which had clasps of horn, and took only the brass. The librarian moved the brass-clasped books to a high shelf. The magpie waited a winter and took the bosses off the lower boards instead, one to a book, so that every volume in the case sat crooked on the shelf and none of them would close flat.
text_nonnarrative: Metal furniture on a covered board falls into three kinds. Bosses are the largest and stand at the corners and centre, five to a board where the full set is present. Clasps are of two parts, a hinged strap on one board and a catch-plate on the other, and are the only kind that bears a load. Cornerpieces are the smallest and the least regular, absent altogether from books under octavo.

text_narrative: A settlement on the ash plain restarts ink production this month, using soot swept from the vents rather than burnt oil. The first grinding runs four hours on a stone quern and yields a mixture that separates in the pot overnight. A second grinding with more gum holds, but the black is grey under lamp light. The settlement trades the grey ink anyway and the record keepers to the east accept it at half weight.
text_nonnarrative: Along the seaward wall of the ink house the soot bins stood in a row, deepest at the end nearest the flue. The grinding floor was a single slab, worn hollow at its centre by a hand's depth. Between the slab and the bins the gum store was a dry recess with no window. The roof over the whole was low, and the smoke line on the plaster ran level a foot below the beams.

text_narrative: The pastedown lifts in one piece, which never happens, and under it is a leaf of an older book. Tova reads three lines and stops. The leaf describes the room she is sitting in, the lamp, the angle of the window, the lifted pastedown. She turns the board over to look for a second leaf. The board is bare oak on the other side and the first leaf, when she looks back, is blank.
text_nonnarrative: Scholarship on binder's waste tends to treat every recovered fragment as a witness of equal standing, and that is where it goes wrong. Most waste is waste because it was spoiled, so the surviving text is a bad text twice over. The fragments worth argument are those whose discard can be dated from the binding around them. Cataloguers who record the fragment and not the binding throw away the only evidence that made it useful.

text_narrative: There was a copyist whose last quire was left unfinished, and the book he left behind kept its catchwords. At the foot of the last written leaf stood a word that appeared nowhere after it. Whoever bound the volume set blank quires behind that leaf, and each morning the topmost blank carried the promised word at its head and a new catchword at its foot, and the book was never finished and never stopped.
text_nonnarrative: One catchword to a quire was the ordinary rate, so the count of catchwords in a volume stood to the count of leaves as one to the leaves in a gathering. Where the rate was one to a leaf, the ratio approached unity and the mark lost its diagnostic value. Density above that was not observed. Below one in twelve the marks were too sparse to carry the sequence, and the relation ceased to be useful.

text_narrative: On the long ships the menders were given a rule older than the ships: what is added must be visible to the eye that looks for it and invisible to the eye that does not. They spun tissue from the same stock as the leaves and dyed it a shade light. Ten generations on, the shade had faded to a match, and no mender could say which fibres were original and which were repair.
text_nonnarrative: Reversibility and detectability are often run together in conservation doctrine, though they answer to different demands. A repair may be perfectly reversible and wholly undetectable, in which case the object misleads while remaining recoverable. It may equally be detectable and permanent, which preserves the truth of the object at the cost of its integrity. Whether an infill is part of the leaf or an addition to it is settled by neither property alone.

text_narrative: Late in the afternoon the tower room went dim enough for the aperture to bite, and Verrick widened it a half turn with the brass collar. The image of the courtyard swam on the table, brighter and softer at once. He stopped the collar back a quarter and the cart wheels outside came good and hard again. A cloud crossed and the whole table went to grey, and he sat down to wait it out.
text_nonnarrative: An image on the table is graded on hardness and never on brightness, so a dim courtyard counts for nothing against it. Aperture is the sole term that bears on the class: a collar open past a half turn is soft whatever the light. Cloud is a cause and not a fault. Cart wheels at the edge of the field are outside the graded area, and the brass itself is no part of the matter.

text_narrative: Nobody in the shop pours a plate standing up except Halloran, and the corner always tells on him. He tips the collodion to the far edge, brings it back along the short side, and drains off the near corner into the bottle. The film sets thick down one margin. Everyone else sits to it and turns the glass twice, and the coating comes even to within a hair of the clip.
text_nonnarrative: A plate was faulted on the evenness of its coating and on nothing else. Thickness down one margin was the whole of the fault; the drained corner was a matter of waste and never of grade. Standing to the pour bore on neither, nor did the number of turns given the glass. Collodion short of the clip counted against the plate, whatever the state of the film along the far edge.

text_narrative: The gloss is wrong and Ferrick knows it before the print is out of the bath. Too flat, too even — albumen that thin never holds a sheen. And there, in the shadow under the chair, a second sheen where nothing in the room could put one. Someone has been at the coating tray again. He lifts the sheet to the window and the shape under the chair stays exactly where it is.
text_nonnarrative: Gloss was graded on the shadows and never on the lights, so a flat sheen in the highlights disqualified nothing. Albumen too thin was a defect of the coating and not of the print, and the bath was indifferent to both. A sheet with two sheens in one shadow was outside the grade altogether, since the tray was held to give one surface and one only, whatever the state of the room.

text_narrative: The plate shop on Veren Station released a corrected sheet at the end of the third shift after a ruling error left the whole run coarse. Screens rated at one hundred and fifty lines had been cut at ninety. The fault reached print before anyone counted the dots. Two thousand sheets went to the recycler. The shop supervisor attributed the error to a mislabelled screen drawer and ordered every drawer re-marked.
text_nonnarrative: Coarseness is a fault of the screen and not of the plate, and a run is classed by the ruling actually cut rather than by the rating on the drawer. A sheet at ninety lines is coarse whatever its dots are like. Mislabelling bears on the cause and not on the class. Discovery at the shop and discovery in the finished run are two distinct classes of one error.

text_narrative: Three plates that winter, and the youngest engraver rocked each one differently. The first she took in eight directions and the ground came up even but shallow. The second she carried to sixteen and wore the burr off the rocker before the last pass. The third she left at twelve and scraped the highlights out of it in a single evening, and that was the plate the shop kept.
text_nonnarrative: A rocked ground was judged on its depth and on its evenness, and the two were graded apart. Eight directions counted as a light ground whatever the pressure; sixteen counted as a full one. Wear on the burr of the rocker was a charge against the tool and not against the plate. Highlights scraped in one evening bore on the labour and never on the class of the ground.

text_narrative: In the second year of the hall's endowment the lantern threw a hot spot no cleaning would shift. The warden ordered the front condenser reversed, and the spot moved to the lower left. In the third year a second lens of shorter radius was fitted behind the first, and the field came up flat to the corners. The old lens went into the cupboard with the broken slides and stayed there.
text_nonnarrative: Two condensers in series stand between the illuminant and the slide, the shorter radius nearest the slide. Evenness of the field at the corners is a function of that spacing and of the distance to the illuminant, and of nothing else in the stack. A hot spot is the signature of an image of the source in the plane of the slide rather than a defect of the lens surfaces.

text_narrative: Before the first glass was ground, light came whole into the world and no eye could take it apart. The maker of the second dawn cut a slit in the shutter of the sky and set a wedge of clear stone behind it. What passed through lay out along the wall in a band, red at the low end and violet at the high, and the maker named each colour once and left them so.
text_nonnarrative: A wedge of clear stone stood behind a narrow slit, its faces at a fixed angle to each other. The width of the band on the far wall was a function of that angle and of the material, and its purity a function of the slit alone. Wide slits gave overlapping bands. Red lay nearest the undeviated line and violet furthest from it, the two ends being properties of the stone and not of the light.

text_narrative: The shutter curtain hangs slack in the low gravity and Osric will not close the housing until it sits flat. He winds the tension on, notch by notch, and the slit narrows to a finger's width. Outside the port the tender is turning and the light off its hull moves across the bench. He fires the shutter once against his palm and feels the curtain drag at the end of its travel.
text_nonnarrative: Exposure in a focal plane housing was set by the width of a travelling slit and not by the speed of the curtain across the frame. Tension on the roller governed that speed; the two adjustments were independent. Drag at the end of the travel meant a wider slit on one side of the frame, so uneven density across the image was a property of the mechanism rather than of the light.

text_narrative: There was a dyer's daughter who printed the shapes of ferns on cloth and washed them in the stream at the foot of the garden. The blue held. When a hard winter came she washed in still water from the butt instead, and the ferns bled at every edge until the cloth was one flat colour. The old women told her the stream had wanted paying, and she carried a coin down to it in spring.
text_nonnarrative: Bleeding at the edge and a general loss of blue are two faults, and only the first is a fault of the washing itself. Bleeding is a matter of unreduced salt remaining in the cloth; loss of blue is a matter of water too weak in acid for the ferns to hold. A third case, in which the whole ground is flat and the shapes are even in tone with it, belongs to neither class.

text_narrative: A collector in the eastern counties reports that four prints from one album now carry a blue metallic sheen along their upper edges, and that the other eleven do not. The four sat in the same corner of the same box. A conservator engaged by the collector finds no difference in paper stock or in mount. The album's binder cannot be traced and the shop that supplied the board no longer trades under that name.
text_nonnarrative: Mirroring at the edge of a sheet and mirroring across its whole face were held to be separate faults.
