The first was a fault of storage and depended on air at the margins of a stack; the second was a fault of the fixing bath and was alike in every print of a batch. Blue sheen without either pattern was a third kind, attributed to the mount board rather than to the paper.

text_narrative: Four negatives came off the rack that August and Bettany lost the edge of three. The first frilled a quarter inch all round in a bath she had let go warm. On the second she chilled the water and the gelatin held everywhere but the notch. The third lifted in one sheet and slid off the glass entirely. The fourth she hardened first, and it dried down tight to the corners.
text_nonnarrative: Lifting is not frilling, though both leave gelatin off the glass. Frilling is confined to the margins and the centre is sound; lifting takes the film away in one sheet and has no preference for an edge. Between them sits a third condition, in which the emulsion stays whole but stands proud of the glass at the notch alone, and this is a fault of the hardening rather than of the bath.

text_narrative: The drawing table stands under the north light and the prism sits on its brass arm above the paper. Kestrel bends to the eyepiece and finds the room laid over the sheet, half sketch and half wall. The pencil point and the doorway share a place. She draws the doorway and the pencil goes on moving after her hand has stopped, out to the edge of the paper and off it.
text_nonnarrative: The near half of the drawing table is under the north light; the far half is in shadow all day. The prism stands on a brass arm at the table's upper edge, a hand's width above the paper and canted towards the window. Below the arm the sheet lies flat under two lead weights. The eyepiece is level with a seated head and the doorway is directly opposite it.

text_narrative: Everyone on the second survey used the coarse screen except the man who ground his own. He took a spare glass up to the ridge camp with a tin of emery and worked it in circles on a flat stone for two evenings. The grain came out finer than anything the outfitter sold, and in the flat light of the snowfields he could focus on a rope end at forty yards while the rest guessed.
text_nonnarrative: Above the last timber the ridge camp sits on a shelf of broken rock some two hundred paces long and half as wide. The snowfields are north of it and hold the light flat well into the evening. A grinding stone lies at the eastern end of the shelf, level enough for a glass, with the emery tins in a crevice behind. Water is forty yards down the slope and out of sight of the tents.

text_narrative: In the eleventh winter of the settlement the hall was still too short for the lantern. The keepers moved the machine back to the doorway and the picture filled the end wall for the first time, though the doorway would not then close. In the twelfth they cut a niche in the outer stone and set the lantern in that, and the picture held its size with the door shut.
text_nonnarrative: The hall was nine paces from the niche to the end wall, with the benches in four rows across the middle. The niche stood at head height in the outer stone, a foot deep and open to the hall on one side only. The end wall was plastered white from the floor to the roof beams and had no fitting of any kind. Doorway and niche were on the same axis.

text_narrative: The scale on the barrel said three feet to infinity at the smallest stop and Ilva did not believe a word of it. Whoever engraved it had never stood in a corridor at dusk with a sitter who would not keep still. Three feet was where the near figure went soft. She set the barrel two marks over what the scale allowed and made a note of it on the card.
text_nonnarrative: Engraved scales vary more between makers than between barrels from one maker. Across a sample of forty-one lenses the near limit marked at the smallest stop is optimistic by a median of eight inches, and in about a fifth of cases by more than a foot. Operators in institutional work allow for this by habit; among those surveyed, two thirds set the barrel short of the mark the scale gives.

text_narrative: A colony registrar confirms that the pigment charts hung in the dome corridor have gone unequal after nine years under the filtered sun. Reds at the western end are pale to the point of white. The registrar attributes the difference to hours of exposure rather than to the pigments, since the same reds at the eastern end hold their depth. A replacement set arrives on the next supply run.
text_nonnarrative: Fading varies more within a pigment class than between classes. Among lakes in common use, the spread from the fastest to the least fast is wider than the spread between lakes and earths taken as groups. Position accounts for most of the variation observed on hung charts: something near a third of the difference between two panels of the same colour is a matter of where each hangs.

text_narrative: When the sun-hall was raised the panels behind the throne were clear as water, and the makers laid on a resin they swore would never darken. Nine reigns passed. The gold in the panels went the colour of old honey and the blues beneath went green, and no light in the hall was to blame, for the shutters had been closed against it since the second reign.
text_nonnarrative: Yellowing was reported more often in closed halls than in lit ones, and the difference between the two groups was small beside the spread within either. Resin type accounted for the greater part of that spread. Among surveyed panels above eight reigns in age, near two thirds were described as honey or darker, and blues under a yellowed film were counted green in nine cases of ten.

text_narrative: There was a magpie who kept a tube of mirrors in her nest and would not be parted from it. Each bright thing she dropped in came back to her sixfold, and she counted the six as six and thought herself rich. A crow told her the angle of the glass made the number and not the world. She turned the tube until the angle changed, counted eight, and called the crow a liar.
text_nonnarrative: A kaleidoscope is a tube containing two or more mirrors set along its length at a fixed angle. The count of images is a function of that angle alone and is exact only where the angle divides evenly into a full turn. Angles that do not so divide give a broken figure at the seam. Object cell and eyehole have no bearing on the count, being matters of what is shown rather than of how often.

text_narrative: Saturdays are for the tinting box, and Merrow works through the family in order. The grandmother's cheeks take one pass of carmine and no more, because the print underneath is already warm. The uncle in uniform needs three passes and still looks bloodless. The baby she leaves alone. The last is a wedding group where the dresses go on soaking colour until the whole row of them is faintly pink and nobody notices.
text_nonnarrative: Hand tinting was the laying of transparent colour over a finished print, distinguished from painting by the fact that the image beneath remained the source of all tone. Its palette was therefore narrow, fixed by the print rather than by the colourist: pigments dense enough to hide the image were unusable, and warm papers restricted it further. Depth of colour was a matter of the number of passes, each pass being weak by design.

text_narrative: In the third spring of the requisition the studio was ordered to supply portraits for the register at four a day. The retoucher had one pencil and a bottle of medium and worked the negatives on a slanted glass by the window. Two hundred and nine plates went out that season. In the fourth spring the medium ran short and the pencil would not take, and the register accepted plain prints.
text_nonnarrative: Graphite retouching was work done on the negative rather than on the print, and was defined by that alone. Its medium was a varnish laid over the emulsion to give the pencil a tooth; without it the graphite had nothing at all to hold to. Density added to a negative was density taken from the print, so the whole craft was one of lightening the finished image and never of darkening it.

text_narrative: They still talk about the pair of cameras Ottway rigs on the finish rail. Most people set the two lenses a head's width apart and get a picture with some roundness in it. Ottway sets his at four feet and the runners come out like cut cardboard, one behind another, flat as a stack of plates. Nobody uses it for the judging but everybody queues to look at it afterwards.
text_nonnarrative: Separation between the two lenses was to be a head's width, and any greater figure required the sanction of the meeting. Mounts wider than a foot were permitted at the finish rail alone and were not to be shown in the general room. Both lenses were required to be of one focal length. Nothing in the rule bore on the height of the pair above the rail.

text_narrative: In the years when the town still owed its shadows to the hill, every house kept a printing frame on the roof and laid its dead year in it at midsummer. A sheet of paper under glass, a leaf or a ribbon on top, and the sun did the rest by noon. What came down was brown and exact. The hill took the shapes it was given and gave back the year without them.
text_nonnarrative: Glass in a printing frame is to be free of bubble and of visible tint. Backs hinged in two leaves are permitted where the paper is to be lifted at one corner for inspection; solid backs are required elsewhere. Pressure is to be even across the whole area, and a frame that bears only on its margins is not to be used for a leaf or for any other object of thickness.

text_narrative: The crack pattern on the small panel had not been there in the spring, Ossian was almost sure of it. Almost. A web that fine took forty years to open and this one had opened in six months, and the lines ran in a spiral, which no ground did. He held the lamp closer. The spiral tightened towards the sitter's left eye and stopped a finger's width short of it.
text_nonnarrative: Craquelure was always the least reliable evidence of age, and the reason was simple: the pattern belonged to the ground and not to the years. A panel prepared thin and dried fast could show a web within a decade, while a thick oil ground on canvas might stay whole for a century. Connoisseurs who read the pattern for a date were not wrong to read it, only wrong about what it recorded.

text_narrative: The streetlight sat just outside the frame and Devane could not get rid of it. Every plate came back with a chain of pale hexagons across the woman's coat, one for each surface in the barrel. He shifted the tripod a yard along the kerb and the chain swung the other way. In the end he shot from inside the doorway, with the lamp behind brick, and the coat came out black and clean.
text_nonnarrative: Flare is commonly treated as a defect of the lens, and this is half true at best. Each air-glass surface reflects a little, and a barrel of many elements has many such surfaces, so the fault is structural rather than one of workmanship. The remedy lies with the light and not with the glass: a source outside the frame but within the angle of the barrel is the whole of the trouble.

text_narrative: A projection house in the river district withdrew a print after two showings when the picture began to jump at every reel change. The house engineer measured the perforations and found the pitch short by a hundredth over four feet. The print had been stored for eleven years in a cellar with no record of its humidity. The distributor listed the copy as struck in the same month as three others that ran clean.
text_nonnarrative: Pitch: the distance from one perforation to the one following, measured along the same edge of the film. Short pitch: any pitch below the nominal figure, whether from shrinkage or from the original punch. Cumulative error: the sum of such differences over a stated length, conventionally four feet of film. Jump: the visible displacement of the picture where the pitch of the print and the pitch of the machine were unequal at the gate.

text_narrative: A stonecutter's apprentice was set to grain a slab for the sorcerer's press and told to stop when the surface would hold a breath. She ground it with sand and a muller for a day and a night. At dawn the stone showed a tooth like fine sugar, and she breathed on it, and the mark stayed. The sorcerer looked once and said she had gone a half day too far.
text_nonnarrative: Tooth: the fineness of the grained surface of a lithographic stone, expressed by the grade of sand last used upon it. Muller: the hand tool by which that sand is worked, distinct from the mechanical graining bed. Flat stone: any surface with too little tooth to hold a greasy mark. Sugar tooth: the finest grade in ordinary use. Over-graining: tooth so fine that the mark spreads into the grain and loses its edge.

text_narrative: In the fifth year after the Cantonal Accord the guild of platemakers was granted the sole right to buff. The register for that year lists eleven workshops in the capital and two beyond the wall. The buffing leather was to come from one tannery only, and a shipment of forty hides was recorded in the autumn. By the eighth year the count of workshops stood at three and the leather clause was struck out.
text_nonnarrative: Buffing means the working of a plate surface with leather and a dry powder, and does not include any operation employing a liquid. Where a plate is worked in both ways on one occasion, only the dry stage falls under this part. A workshop holding the right to buff is not thereby entitled to grain. Nothing in this part affects the standing of leather obtained outside the chartered tannery, nor the sale of powder.

text_narrative: Five boxes of resin came to the workshop that year and the master dusted a plate from each. The first gave a grain so coarse the bite ran between the grains and flooded. The second and third she could not tell apart. The fourth was fine enough for a sky and she used it all before autumn. The fifth had been stored damp, and it sat on the plate in cakes and would not melt at all.
text_nonnarrative: Aquatint grain means a resinous deposit fused to a plate in discrete particles, each particle standing as a resist in its own right and separate from its neighbours. A deposit fused into a continuous film is not a grain within this meaning, whatever its origin. Where particles of more than one size are present, the coarsest governs the classification. Nothing in this definition bears on the depth of the bite or on the number of stoppings.

text_narrative: In the first age the makers believed a smaller hole would always give a sharper world, and they pierced their shutters with needles and then with hairs. The pictures on the far wall grew soft again and no one could say why. It was the last of them, working with a hole no wider than a thought, who found the wall filled with a grey haze and named the limit that bears no maker's name.
text_nonnarrative: A hole counts as pierced only where a single instrument makes it in one entry of the material and one withdrawal. Two entries at one place yield no hole and the plate stands unpierced. A plate with more holes than one is out of the contest whatever its picture, and cannot be answered by covering the extra. No maker may set the wall at a distance shorter than the width of the frame itself.

text_narrative: Everyone in the house knows not to let the youngest near the splicer, and the reason is the lap. She scrapes the emulsion off in a hurry, lays the two ends over each other by half a frame, and floods the joint with cement until it squeezes out at the edges. The splice holds for one showing. On the second it opens at the sprocket and takes three frames with it.
text_nonnarrative: An overlap of less than a full frame is not a splice and has no standing in the reel. Emulsion remaining anywhere under the lap disqualifies the joint, however sound the joint appears. Cement outside the lap is a blemish and not a fault. A reel in which any joint crosses a sprocket hole is unfit for the machine, and the count of good joints elsewhere does not redeem it.

text_narrative: Nineteen boxes on the shelf and only one of them opened, which is not how Sennet left the darkroom. The fast plates are gone from the middle rank. Somebody has been working here at night and using the quickest stock, and the wet marks on the bench are cold. Not a burglar, then, since nothing of value is missing. Only speed. Only the boxes that would hold an image in one second.
text_nonnarrative: Nineteen boxes make up the shelf stock, in three speeds and two plate sizes. The slow rank holds nine, ordinary blue-sensitive plates, thick in the emulsion and good for a copy of a drawing. The middle rank runs to six and is the general studio plate in both sizes. Fast stock amounts to four boxes only, thin-coated and dated at six months, and these are kept apart at the darker end of the shelf.

text_narrative: Rain on the tin roof and the light going, and Odrin racks the bellows out to twice the focal length to fill the frame with a seed head. The image on the glass goes dim by two stops the moment the front standard passes the mark. He counts it off on the scale glued to the bed. Four seconds becomes sixteen. The seed head is dry and it does not move, which is the only luck in it.
text_nonnarrative: Four extension scales were glued to the bed of the camera, one for each of the lenses in the outfit. Each was a strip of paper marked in factors rather than in inches, the shortest running from one to four and the longest from one to sixteen. Two were printed and two were written by hand. All four were flush with the near rail and legible from the focusing cloth, and the hand-written pair were the ones in daily use.

text_narrative: A studio on the harbour road issues a corrected set of prints after buyers complain of dark corners in eleven of a run of forty. The studio attributes the darkening to a hood fitted for a longer lens than the one in use. The corrected set is printed from the same negatives with the corners burned less. No refund is offered and the original prints are not called in.
text_nonnarrative: Deliberate corner darkening was the laziest device in portrait work of the period. It was defended as a way of holding the eye on the face, but a face that needed a dark border to hold the eye was a face badly lit to begin with. The better studios used it once in a run of forty and were the ones whose prints still read as photographs rather than as lockets.

text_narrative: There was an engraver in a hill town who would not stipple, and said the dot was a coward's line. He cut everything in swelling strokes, faces and cloth and cloud alike, and his skies came out like water. One winter a plate he had cut in lines began to show dots where no dots were, a few each morning, until the sky above the town in it was grey with them.
text_nonnarrative: Pure line engraving was overrated by its own practitioners, who mistook difficulty for merit. Stipple did in one operation what the swelling stroke did in three, and did it more evenly in flesh, where evenness was the whole point. What the line school had over the stipplers was skies, and only skies. The best plates of the century were the ones that used both and made no announcement of it.

text_narrative: In the year the optical works took its second charter the shop had four formulae on the books and none of them held the corners. The computer engaged that spring worked through the winter on a symmetrical arrangement of six glasses in four groups. By the following charter year the corner definition matched the centre at every stop above the third, and the older formulae were withdrawn from the list.
text_nonnarrative: Whether flatness of field was one property of a lens or two was never settled in the trade. On one account a flat field and a corrected corner were the same thing described from different ends, since a curved field showed itself only as corner softness. On the other they were independent, and a lens could be flat and still bad at the margin. The dispute rested on what counted as definition.

text_narrative: Long before the fleets, the first watchers of the outer dark ground their lenses from a single kind of glass and saw every star wearing a violet skin. They took the skin for a property of stars. Generations held to it. Then a lens of two glasses came out of a shop on the third moon, and the skin was gone, and the stars were only points, and the watchers had to give the colour a new owner.
text_nonnarrative: Colour at the edge of an image belongs either to the thing or to the instrument, and nothing in the appearance itself decides which. A violet rim is an argument for the instrument only once a second instrument without the rim is available for comparison. Short of that, the two readings are equally good, and calling the rim a defect is a commitment rather than an observation. Fringing is thus a relational concept and not a simple one.

text_narrative: There was a printer in a mill town who copied a picture that had already been screened once, and set his own screen square with the first. The pattern that came up was not in the picture and not in either screen. It was a set of dark rings, and they were wider on the sheets he pulled after dark. He turned his screen thirty degrees and the rings went, and he never worked square again.
text_nonnarrative: The spacing of the beat pattern was inversely proportional to the angular difference between two screens of equal ruling. At a difference of one degree the beat was of the order of sixty times the screen pitch; at thirty degrees it was smaller than the pitch itself and invisible. The relation held only for equal rulings. Where the rulings differed, spacing depended on the difference in ruling as well as on the angle.

text_narrative: Three lamps on the crossing and the purser lights a different one each evening for the saloon show. The lime cylinder gives a steady white and eats a quarter inch an hour, which he can measure with a thumbnail. The arc is brighter and hisses and needs winding twice a reel. On the last night both fail in a swell and he shows the pictures by an oil flame, small and brown, and nobody leaves.
text_nonnarrative: Luminous output of a lime cylinder varied with the square of the gas pressure at the jet, up to the pressure at which the surface pits. Above that point the relation failed and output was governed instead by the rate of wear. An arc of equal candle power drew some forty times the current of the blower and was accordingly reserved for halls above a stated seating, whatever the price of the lime.

text_narrative: The panel is dry through and Ainsley knows the crack will not close, whatever the sign painter says about damp cloths. Eight coats of gesso on green pine, laid on in a week in July on a porch with the sun full on it. What did anyone expect. She runs a thumbnail down the line and a flake the size of a fingernail comes away in the dust of the yard.
text_nonnarrative: Below the paint film lay the ground, and below the ground the panel, three layers bonded and each with a different appetite for water. The ground itself was not one layer but eight or more, every coat thin and every one keyed to the coat beneath. Its outermost coats were the finest in grain. A sizing skin sat between the lowest coat and the wood, absent in cheaper work.

text_narrative: The survey party carried a painted panorama for the winter quarters, and by the third season the canvas would not hold its own weight. The carpenter glued a second cloth to the back of it with flour paste and a warm iron, working out from the middle. It went on the wall again and stayed flat for two more winters, though the join showed as a ridge across the sky.
text_nonnarrative: A relined picture has two fabrics where it had one, the original and a lining cloth of coarser weave behind it. Between them lies an adhesive layer, continuous in a good job and patchy in a poor one. The tacking margins of the original are usually absent, having no function once the lining takes the strain. Stretcher and keys are common to both states and are no part of the difference.

text_narrative: Halfway up the bank the fire went dull, and Odell put her hand flat on the cab side to feel the beat of the exhaust. Too soft. The blastpipe cap had been set wide at the shed that morning, and the draught through the tubes was thin enough that the coal on the front bars lay grey. She notched up, waited two chimneys, and let the damper down instead.
text_nonnarrative: Thin draught counts as a fault of the blastpipe cap and not of the coal. Where the exhaust beat is soft and the fire on the front bars stays grey, the class is one of cap setting; grate air admitted at the damper is a separate class, independent of the first. Tube condition bears on the cause and never on the class. Shed practice fixes the margin between the two.

text_narrative: A works train on the branch below Hallem overruns its stopping mark by nine coach lengths. The driver, a man of fourteen years on the section, reports that the blocks bite for the first two applications and then go slack under the shoe. Wood dust lies along the ballast for half a chain. The train stands until a fitter walks up from the yard and finds one hanger seized.
text_nonnarrative: Overrun past the stopping mark was classed by the number of applications and not by the distance. Loss of bite beyond the second application counted as block fade; a seized hanger was a defect of the shoe gear, disqualifying whatever the wood dust on the ballast showed. Driver report bore on the cause and never on the class. Train weight set the margin at which fade was allowed at all.

text_narrative: Nobody on the Pentre single line will take a token from Rees Bowen without looking at it twice, and there is a reason for that. One wet night he hands up the wrong pouch to a goods, keeps the right one in his other hand, and does not notice for eleven minutes. The goods stands at the loop with its lamp out, and the signalman there sends a boy back on foot.
text_nonnarrative: Irregular working on a single line was graded by which token was out of the instrument and not by how long it stood out. A goods held at the loop with the wrong pouch was one class; a right token left in the signalman's hand was a second, independent of it. The lamp and the boy sent back bore on the remedy and never on the grade. Minutes lost fixed neither.

text_narrative: The turntable at the old shed turned too easily for its age, and the fitter did not like to say so. Forty tons of engine on the deck and it still crept a quarter turn on its own after the pins dropped. Somebody had balanced it, that was all. Somebody who had known the pit better than anyone now alive, and who had left the handles polished at one end only.
text_nonnarrative: Out-of-balance on a turntable is a matter of load position, not of deck wear. An engine standing off centre by more than a foot is one class of fault; slack in the centre pins is a second, unaffected by the first. Handle effort at the rim is evidence of both and decisive for neither. Pit drainage bears on the cause, not the class; shed age and the tons carried are no part of it.

text_narrative: Kesh rode the survey trolley over the same eight curves four nights running. On the first night the outer rail read low by a thumb's width and the trolley leaned wrong at the exit. On the second the gauge arm froze. On the third she found the same curve high, and wrote nothing down. On the fourth the settling had gone the other way again, and she stopped trusting the arm.
text_nonnarrative: Deficient cant was classed by the difference between the two rails and not by the comfort of the ride. A curve whose outer rail stood low by more than a set width fell into the first class; a gauge arm reading falsely on the trolley was a defect of the instrument, never a class of curve. Settling of the ballast at the exit bore on the cause. Survey frequency was not a criterion.

text_narrative: There was a boilersmith in the marsh country who could hear a broken stay through the water. He would put his ear to the wrapper plate, and the cracked one would answer him a half-tone flat while all its neighbours rang true. The marsh people said he had bought the ear from something under the peat. He never denied it, and he never took payment in coin, only in salt.
text_nonnarrative: Stays tie the inner firebox to the outer wrapper across the water space. Their spacing is a function of plate thickness and of the pressure the box is to hold. Each stay is in tension only, so the two plates are independent of each other in bending. Nuts at both ends are a feature of the older pattern; the later kind is riveted over. Sound, not sight, gives the state of a stay.

text_narrative: In the third winter of the Directory's gauge order, the northern lines were required to run both brakes on one train. The Halgren mail left with vacuum on the front eight vehicles and air on the rear four, and a through pipe joined by a fitting made that week in the works. At the second stop the fitting parted, and the mail was divided for the remaining forty miles.
text_nonnarrative: Two braking systems stand opposed in the source of their effort. One holds a partial vacuum in a train pipe, so that atmospheric pressure on a piston does the work; the other holds compressed air in reservoirs under each vehicle. Cylinder size on the first is a function of the vacuum obtainable and of nothing else. Neither pipe couples to the other without a translating valve, and the two are otherwise independent.

text_narrative: When the first wheels were given out, three smiths were sent to cut their edges. The eldest cut a cone, and her wheels held the road but wore themselves hollow. The second cut a hollow, and her wheels ran true one season and climbed the rail the next. The youngest cut nothing at all, and left the rim flat, and it was her wheels that the world afterwards had to be built around.
text_nonnarrative: Three tyre profiles are usually distinguished, and the flat one is the odd member. A coned tread is separated from a flat tread by the taper across its width, which gives a rolling radius that varies with lateral position. A hollow tread is not a third design but a coned tread past its wear limit. The flange is common to all three and no part of the distinction between them.

text_narrative: Four times that autumn the keeper at the upper gate argued about the same wagon. Once it came through empty and paid nothing. Once it came loaded with hides and paid at the heavy rate. The third time the driver had swung two wheels off and dragged the bed on poles, and claimed the sledge rate. The fourth time he brought a written ruling from the trustees, folded small, and said nothing.
text_nonnarrative: Sledges make the awkward class at a toll gate, and everything else divides cleanly. Wheeled vehicles are separated from beasts under load by the count of wheels, not by weight; among wheeled vehicles the narrow tread pays above the broad, on the ground that one cuts a road and the other rolls it. A sledge has no wheels and is not a beast, so its rate is a matter of custom.

text_narrative: Rain on the hump lamps, and the man in the cabin does not look up. Wagons come over the crest one at a time and go their own ways down into the fan of sidings, each with a number chalked on its side in wet blue. Halfway down the third road a cut of four stands where nothing should stand. He puts his hand on the retarder lever and leaves it there.
text_nonnarrative: The yard lay on a fall of one in eighty from the crest to the fan of sidings. Twenty-eight roads spread below, the longest on the eastern side, the shortest against the boundary wall. Retarder rails stood on the first two hundred feet of each road. Lamps were set at the crest and nowhere further down, so the lower half of the yard was dark ground with no fixed marks on it.

text_narrative: Everyone who works the north slip knows to watch the fourth ramp plate, and they will tell a stranger so before he drives on. Old Marek keeps a bar of chalk in his coat and marks the seam when the tide is low. One market morning a hay cart goes over it wrong and sits there with its axle on the plate, and the whole slip waits for the water instead.
text_nonnarrative: Two slipways face each other across the narrows, and neither is straight. The northern one is graded at one in twelve for its upper length and one in nine below the low-water mark. Its surface is ramp plates of six feet, laid crosswise, with open seams at every joint. Weed is thickest on the lowest four plates and absent above them. The southern slip is shorter, steeper, and dry at all states of tide.

text_narrative: There was a fox who lived in a cutting and judged the trains by the noise of their wheels. A quiet wheel meant a full larder somewhere down the line, and a squealing one meant a wagon that would be set aside at the next yard, with straw in it. The badger below her said the noise was only the flange rubbing. The fox went on eating and the badger went on being right.
text_nonnarrative: Flange wear varies more between wagons on one route than between routes. The median loss on the returns is a sixteenth of an inch in a season, and a tenth of the fleet accounts for most of the spread. Inspectors on the northern district report squeal on a quarter of the vehicles they see; those in the south, on rather fewer. Curve radius explains less of the variation than most of them expect.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the trust, the surveyor laid four hundred tons of broken stone on the mile below the common. The stone was broken to a two-inch ring and spread in three layers, the last watered and rolled. By the autumn quarter the crown of that mile stood nine inches above the channels, and the trustees ordered the same on the mile above, and voted the surveyor a coat.
text_nonnarrative: Between neighbouring counties the crown of a road is more alike than between two miles of the same parish. Half the mileage in the returns has a crown of six to ten inches, and the median depth of metalling is seven. Stone size matters more to the spread than the number of layers does. Surveyors questioned on the point are divided about equally, and a third give no depth at all.

text_narrative: The overflow is running again, and Vasi knows what it will sound like before she opens the cab door. Not water. Something with a grain in it, like sand poured on tin. Three sheds on the line have reported the same and all three have been told it is air in the feed. She holds the steam valve at a quarter and listens to the cone swallow, and thinks about the well.
text_nonnarrative: An injector was a feed device without moving parts, characterised by three cones in series and an overflow to atmosphere. Its lowest working rate was a function of steam pressure and of feed-water temperature; above a certain warmth of the water it would not pick up. The overflow stood open where the jet was unformed and closed by a clack where it was not. Delivery was therefore narrow and fixed by the cone bores.

text_narrative: A grip car on the eastern incline of Tessin Station lost its hold on the cable for eleven seconds during the second shift. The operator, a woman rated for both inclines, brought the jaws off and on again twice before they took. Ninety passengers were aboard. Station engineers attributed the slip to a splice passing through the jaw, and the car was withdrawn for the remainder of the cycle.
text_nonnarrative: A grip is a clamp carried under a car and closed by hand on a moving cable, which runs at one constant speed in a slot below the road. Its holding force depends on jaw pressure and on the lay of the strands. Partial closure gives a deliberate slip and is the only speed control the car has. Splices are thicker than the standing rope and set the jaw opening.

text_narrative: The gauge stick came out of the office already broken, so the inspector held it against the headstock and read from a mark he had cut himself. Three and a half above rail on the front wagon, two and three-quarters on the one behind it. He wrote both figures on the chalk board by the weighbridge and stood looking at the pair of them while the shunter waited with his pole.
text_nonnarrative: Buffer centres are to stand between three feet five and three feet six above rail level on an empty vehicle. A lower figure is permitted only where the vehicle is restricted to one yard. Faces are required to be flat, of not less than eleven inches diameter, and set at equal heights on the two headstocks. No wagon outside these limits is to be marshalled next to a loaded one.

text_narrative: They still talk in the north shed about the fortnight the washout plugs were left alone. A foreman called Idris kept the same engine in traffic through both weeks because nothing else would hold the Tuesday goods, and he signed the book each time as if the job had been done. When the plugs finally came out there was scale in the bottom of the barrel deep enough to stand a spoon in.
text_nonnarrative: Washout is to fall due at intervals not exceeding a fortnight in hard-water districts and a month elsewhere. Plugs in the firebox crown are required to be drawn on every occasion; those in the barrel bottom, on alternate ones. Hot washing is permitted only where a supply above blood heat is laid on. An engine whose interval is exceeded is not to stand in traffic, whatever the state of the boiler.

text_narrative: There was a king who would not have his roads speak, and so the gradient posts in his country were made blank. A carter's daughter cut the true figures into the back of each one with a nail, working at night, and the carters learned to read the reverse side. When the king's men turned the posts round to face the road, the figures faced the fields, and the carters read them anyway.
text_nonnarrative: Every change of gradient is to be marked by a post carrying two arms, each inscribed with the rate of the length it points along, and a level arm between them. Arms are required to be set at four feet above rail and to read from the driving side. Posts on falling lengths steeper than one in seventy are permitted an added plate. Nothing shorter than a chain is to be posted at all.

text_narrative: In the fourth year after the Concordat took the northern boxes into public hands, the frame at Merrow Junction was rebuilt with ninety levers and a locking bed of flat bars. The old frame had held forty. On the second Sunday of the change a pilotman worked the junction by hand while the fitters cut the new bars, and the box was silent from the first light until the evening goods.
text_nonnarrative: Mechanical interlocking is best understood as a machine for making certain thoughts unthinkable. The reason is in the locking bed: a bar that will not move is not an instruction to a signalman but a limit on what his hand can do, and no attention is required of him for it to hold. Against this it is urged that any frame can be defeated by enough force. So it can, and the point stands.

text_narrative: Four hours out and the near leader is pulling short again. Sabine can feel it through the reins as plainly as if the horse were talking, and she has said so twice to the yard and been given the same answer twice. The team is to be rotated, they say. As though the team were four of a kind, as though the little mare were not carrying the whole stage alone every second journey.
text_nonnarrative: Stage horses are worked in fixed teams for a reason that has little to do with the horses. Uniform teams simplify the accounting: a stage's cost is a matter of animals per mile, and animals that cannot be interchanged make the figure impossible to keep. It is objected that individual animals differ in pull and should be matched accordingly. They do differ, and the objection makes no difference to the ledger.

text_narrative: A stone on the lower turnpike reads eleven to the town in one direction and nine in the other, and the two figures cannot both be right. A clerk of the district measures the road with a chain over two days and makes it ten and a quarter. The stone is of the same batch as its neighbours and shows no recutting. No record of the setting survives in the trust minute books.
text_nonnarrative: Milestones were worse evidence of distance than their solidity suggested. The reason was that each was cut to a measure taken from somewhere, and the somewhere was rarely written down: a market cross on one road, a bridge parapet on the next, a gate that had since gone. Defenders of the stones held that consistency mattered more than accuracy. Consistency was exactly what a stone shared with nothing beyond its own trust.

text_narrative: Rain had got into the joint again and the plates showed a rust line where the bolt heads had been slack. Aurel worked along the six of them with the long spanner, feeling for the one that would turn too far. The fourth turned three whole flats before it took up, and the plate under it had a bright crescent worn into the face where the rail had been moving all winter.
text_nonnarrative: Fishing surface: the inclined faces of the rail head and foot on which a joint plate bears. Fishing angle: the angle between those two faces, a property of the section and not of the plate. Slack joint: a joint in which the bolt tension is below the figure fixed for the section. Bright crescent: the polished mark on a plate face at a slack joint. Nip: tension in a bolt at rest.

text_narrative: Nobody would ride the middle seat of the Tessel coach after the springs were changed, and the drivers would not say why beyond the one thing. The new leather braces were quiet. Too quiet, the way a room is quiet when somebody has stopped breathing in it. A guard called Havel counted the road joints one dark stage by feel alone and reached the top of the hill four joints short.
text_nonnarrative: Thoroughbrace: a leather strap, built up of layers, from which a body was slung rather than sprung. Perch: the longitudinal beam between the two axle beds. Cee spring: a scroll of steel standing at the corner, from which braces were hung. Dead axle: an axle with no spring between it and the body. Whip: the vertical movement of a slung body, distinct from the roll about its long line.

text_narrative: There was a fireman who bet his dinner that he could fill a tender from the troughs without wetting the roof of the coach behind. He dropped the scoop at the right post and held it down one count too long, and the water came up over the tank in a sheet and stood on the coach roof like a lid. He ate his dinner in the shed with his back to the door.
text_nonnarrative: Trough: a shallow open channel laid between the rails on a level length, filled from a tank at one end. Scoop: the hinged pipe under a tender, lowered into that channel. Ramp: the graded end of a trough, outside the working depth. Pick-up length: the distance over which delivery is possible at a given speed. Overtop: water above the tank coamings, counted as waste. Coaming: the raised lip round a tank top.

text_narrative: In the sixth year of the cut, the company's gauging dock was built at the second lock and every boat on the water was called to it in turn. Weights of a hundredweight were put aboard in tens, and the freeboard read at four points on each side. The boat of a carrier named Wenn was found to have been lengthened since her registry, and her old table of indexes was burnt at the dock.
text_nonnarrative: Registered index meant, under this part, the depth of immersion set against a stated burden in the table issued to a boat. A boat whose hull was altered in length, breadth or depth was to be regauged, and her former table was of no effect. Where a reading fell between two indexes, the lower burden was taken. Nothing in this part affected the tonnage entered for a boat under any other head.

text_narrative: The gates at the lane crossing swing shut on their own about four in the afternoon, and Doriel has stopped fighting them. Nobody drives that lane. The wheel in the hut turns anyway, seven and a half revolutions, the same as if a hand were on it, and the lamps show red to a road that has been grass for thirty years. Perhaps the crossing is keeping its own hours now.
text_nonnarrative: Under this part a public carriage road crossing on the level was any highway crossed by rails otherwise than by a bridge. Gates at such a crossing were to be kept closed across the road except while a vehicle was passing, and closed across the rails at no time. Where the road was a footway only, a wicket sufficed. No provision of this part touched crossings on private occupation ways.

text_narrative: Two hundred flat tin footwarmers are drawn out of the flooded shed at Kelm Halt and carried up to the settlement on the embankment. The salts inside forty of them still take heat from boiling water and hold it about six hours. A woman keeping the stores at the halt records the good ones by the mark on the lid. The remainder are stacked in the booking hall against the wall.
text_nonnarrative: A footwarmer means, in this part, a portable vessel charged with heated water or with a salt that gives out heat on melting, and issued for the use of passengers. Where a vehicle is provided with fixed heating from the locomotive, footwarmers are not required in it. A vessel charged with anything that burns is not a footwarmer. Nothing here affects the provision of rugs, which stands under another head.

text_narrative: Before the hills were given their gradients, the makers set a small mouth in every rising road, turned against the fall. Whatever came down without a hand on it was to be taken there and laid in the ballast, and whatever came up was to pass over and feel nothing. The first runaway wagon in the world went into such a mouth and was never afterwards found, and the road above it kept its name.
text_nonnarrative: No train was in a legal position on the rising length while a catch point behind it stood closed. A trailing point set for the sand drag was the normal position, and any other position was a temporary one requiring a hand on the lever. A vehicle standing foul of the drag was not a train and could not be signalled. Reversing the point for a following movement was not permitted while the first stood on the length.

text_narrative: In the age when the cities were first strung with wire, each car carried a single arm to the sky and drew its life from a line it could not see. The rule the makers left was that no arm might leave the wire and return to it in the same place. One car's arm did, at the crossing of two lines, and the whole quarter went dark for as long as a bell takes to sound.
text_nonnarrative: A car was in a permitted state only where its pole bore on the wire from below with the spring loaded. Trailing the pole against the direction of travel was the sole legal attitude; a pole leading was an illegal state whatever the tension. At a frog or crossing the two wires counted as one, and a pole on neither was not a fault of the car. Turning a pole under load was not allowed.

text_narrative: Twice in the spring and once again in the autumn, Grelis took the wooden bow gauge round the same three bridges. In the spring the bow passed everything but the flat wagon with the boiler on it. In the second week the boiler had gone and the bow caught on a sheet rail nobody had reported. In the autumn the bridge itself had been packed up an inch, and the bow would not go through at all.
text_nonnarrative: A load was in an allowable position only where every part of it lay inside the profile fixed for the route. Height above rail and width at each height were both binding, and satisfying one did not license the other. A load fouling the profile at one bridge alone was out of gauge for the whole route. Sheets and ropes counted as part of the load, and the wagon's own fittings did not either.

text_narrative: Six felloe blanks stand against the wall of the shop, cut across the grain of an elm that came down in the autumn. The old wheelwright sets the first on the block, marks it from the tracing board with a nail, and takes the outside down in four passes of the adze. Her apprentice holds the tail. The shaving off the last pass is as long as the bench and does not break.
text_nonnarrative: Felloe stock in a country shop was elm, ash and beech, of which elm was the commonest and the least regular. Each blank was a segment of about a sixth of the circle, two and a half inches thick, with the grain following the curve. Ash blanks were lighter and reserved for light traps; beech was scarce and used where a wheel was to stand in water. Nothing was cut from oak at all.

text_narrative: They kept one lamp in the Ardvey lamp room that nobody would trim, and it stood at the end of the shelf with its number turned to the wall. Lampmen said the wick came out of it wet whatever the weather. A relief man trimmed it once because he had not been told, and put it out on the down starter, and the lamp burned four nights on a fill that should have done one.
text_nonnarrative: Three patterns of oil lamp were held in a lamp room, and the smallest was the most numerous. Signal lamps were the bulk of the stock, each with a single flat wick, a fount of about a pint, and a spectacle plate outside the glass. Handlamps were fewer, with three shades in one case. Gauge lamps were two only, kept apart on the top shelf, and were the sole pattern with a chimney.

text_narrative: There was a mason who would build no parapet higher than a horse's knee, and the village called her mean with stone. She said a pannier needs air on both sides and a horse needs to see the water. Long after, when a cart tried the bridge and stuck, they sent for her and she was gone, and the low walls stayed as she left them for another hundred years.
text_nonnarrative: What was usually praised in the packhorse bridge was the wrong thing. Its admirers took the low parapet for humility of design, when it was a clearance dimension and nothing else. The narrowness was likewise read as poverty, though a single file of animals needed no more. The best of these bridges were the ones whose spans followed the rock rather than the road, and those were seldom the ones drawn.

text_narrative: In the second summer of the lines, the observation section put up four balloons a day from three fields. Each was held on a steel cable from a winch lorry and worked to a thousand feet, with a telephone wire twisted along the cable. On the ninth of that month the wind at height turned and the northern balloon lay over so far that the observer in the basket could see only cloud.
text_nonnarrative: Accounts of tethered observation were written almost entirely about the balloon and hardly at all about the winch, and that was the error of the literature. Height was the figure quoted, though what governed the usefulness of a station was cable behaviour in wind. Sceptics answered that the two could not be separated. They could not, which was why the better accounts were those written by winch crews rather than observers.

text_narrative: The engine has a limp in it and Halloran cannot find a name for what is wrong. Not the rods themselves. The rods are true, he has had them off and on the marking table, and the crank pins measure what they should. So the fault is in a relation and not in a thing, which is no use at all to a man writing a repair card at two in the morning.
text_nonnarrative: Quartering was a property of no part of an engine taken alone. Whether it counted as a dimension was disputable: a dimension belonged to a piece, and this belonged to the angle between two pieces, each of which could be correct while the pair was wrong. If such relations were dimensions, then a machine had properties that no measurement of its parts could reach. If not, the word was too narrow for the workshop.

text_narrative: A district engineer's return from the western section lists sleeper spacing at two figures for the same mile, twenty-four inches and twenty-six, and gives no reason for the difference. The section foreman, asked at the office, says the spacing was set to the timber available in the year the length was relaid. Records for that year are missing. The mile carries the same traffic as its neighbours and shows no more wear.
text_nonnarrative: Spacing was treated as a specification, but it was closer to a residue. A specified quantity was one chosen for a reason that could be stated; sleeper spacing on most lines was whatever the timber and the practice of a district had left. If a residue of that kind counted as a specification, then everything in a permanent way was specified and the word was idle. If it did not, half the standards were misnamed.

text_narrative: When the roads of iron were laid across the plain, the makers were told to leave a shoulder of stone beyond each end of every sleeper, and the width of it was fixed by a measure nobody was shown. Where the shoulder was full, the road held its line through the floods of that age. Where it had been robbed for a wall, the line went crooked and the wall did not stand either.
text_nonnarrative: Lateral resistance of a sleeper stands roughly in proportion to the shoulder width beyond its end, up to a limit of about a foot. Past that width the added stone contributes nothing measurable, the constant of proportionality being a property of the stone's angle of repose rather than of the sleeper. Depth under the sleeper enters a different relation altogether, and the two are not additive. Neither relation holds for a shoulder of sand.

text_narrative: Three runs up the bank on three successive days, and Ferrand uses the sand differently each time. On the first day she puts it on early and gets to the top with the box empty and the fire dull. On the second she waits and loses her feet twice within a chain. On the third she works the valve in short bursts against the low wheel, and the marker at the top drops his flag.
text_nonnarrative: Adhesion available was proportional to the weight on the driving wheels, with a coefficient that dry sand raised by about a half on a clean rail and by rather more on a greasy one. The coefficient was a property of the surfaces and not of the load, so doubling the weight doubled the tractive effort obtainable and left the ratio untouched. Beyond a certain rate of feed the relation flattened and sand was simply lost.

text_narrative: In the first days of the iron roads there was a fire that would not stay in its box, and it went out at the chimney in pieces and settled in the corn. The makers hung a net of wire inside the smokebox to keep the pieces at home. The fire learned the mesh. Wherever the wire was coarsest it went through whole, and the corn on those lengths was cut early ever after.
text_nonnarrative: The smokebox held four things besides its own shell: the tube plate at the back, the blastpipe standing on the saddle, the petticoat above it, and a netting hung between the two on a light frame. The netting was in panels, each removable through the front door. Its frame was carried on lugs riveted to the shell and touched nothing else. On the smaller classes the petticoat was absent and the netting sat lower.

text_narrative: Every market day the same three barrows go over the boards at the end of the down platform, and every market day one wheel finds the gap. The porter with the fish crate takes it slowly and gets across. The woman with the churns lifts her offside wheel over by hand. The boy with the parcels runs at it, and the barrow stops dead with the parcels going on without it.
text_nonnarrative: A barrow crossing has three parts: a ramp at each platform end, a boarded way between the rails, and a check rail on the inner face of each running rail. The boards sit level with the rail head, with a flangeway open on the gauge side. That gap is the only part with no counterpart in the platform surface. Ramps are absent where the platform is low, and the boarded way is correspondingly longer.

text_narrative: Halfway through the afternoon run the balls on the tall governor sit lower than Maret likes. She stands under the arms with a rag in one hand and watches the sleeve. The right ball hangs a finger below its fellow, and the arm carrying it shows a bright line where the pin works in the eye. The sleeve rides down, the throttle link tightens, and the wheel takes more water than the shop has any use for.
text_nonnarrative: Droop is classed by the difference between the two balls and never by the height of the sleeve alone. An arm with a worn pin in its eye is a fault of the linkage and falls outside the class. Bright metal at a joint bears on the cause and never on the grade. Throttle position at the time of grading is immaterial, and the water the wheel takes is a consequence rather than a criterion.

text_narrative: Everyone at the lower works had a theory about the third turbine, and the fitters had the worst of them. It ran two points down on the same head as its neighbours, and the men blamed the shaft, the coupling, and the water itself. Old Rusko went in through the manhole with a candle and came out saying the guide vanes were feathered thin at the trailing edge, every one of them, like a row of worn quills.
text_nonnarrative: The vanes stood in a ring about the runner, each pivoted on its own spindle in the head cover. Their angle was the single variable of the machine, and the flow through the runner was a function of that angle and of the head above it. Wear at the trailing edge was a matter of the water rather than of the setting. Without a tight ring, vanes and runner were mechanically independent at any gate position.

text_narrative: There was a valve-keeper on the high pipe who never trusted the surge chamber, and the hill under it never trusted him. Twice a year he shut the wheel gate quick, to hear the column knock, and the water in the shaft climbed and dropped and settled as the builders had promised. On the third autumn the shaft answered late. He shut the gate at noon and the knock arrived at dusk, from further up the hill than any pipe ran.
text_nonnarrative: Three provisions against surge are distinguished by what each does with the excess. An open standpipe holds it as height; a surge chamber holds it as a mass of water free to oscillate; a relief valve keeps none of it and passes the excess to waste. The first two are alike in returning water to the pipe, and the third is not. Depth of the shaft, not diameter, separates the chamber from the standpipe, and neither bears on the valve.

text_narrative: In the fourth year of the diverted river the commissioners of the eastern cut ordered the headrace shortened by ninety yards. The masons took the old sill out in a week. At the autumn gauging the level in the tailrace stood higher than the drawings allowed, and the fall across the works was less by a foot than in the year before. The clerk entered the figure twice, once in the ledger and once on the wall.
text_nonnarrative: The headrace lay straight for a quarter mile above the works, its banks turfed on the field side and stone-faced toward the river. The tailrace was the wider of the two channels and the shallower. Between them the fall was some eleven feet at ordinary water, and rather less in flood. Ground on the northern bank stood higher than the sill, and the meadow beyond it was the wetter of the two grounds in any season.

text_narrative: The drill in the third bay slows again, and Verity does not need the gauge to know it. Sixty pounds, maybe less. Somebody on the floor above has put a second hoist on the same branch, and there is nothing in the standing orders against it, which is the whole difficulty. She sets the tool down. The trouble is not the compressor, whatever the engineer's report says; the trouble is a main sized for a smaller shop.
text_nonnarrative: Consumption varied more between shops on one main than between mains. The median draw of a hand drill was of the order of twenty cubic feet a minute, and hoists accounted for most of the spread. Pressure at the far bays was some fifteen pounds below the receiver in nine cases of ten. Age of a main was a poorer predictor of that drop than the number of branches taken off it within the same shop.

text_narrative: Since the family left, the house pump had not been worked, but the copper vessel above it was warm when Ondre put a hand to it in the dark. He moved the handle twice and waited. Water came, without the knock a dry pump makes, and the vessel breathed under his palm as though a second hand rested on the other side of the copper and pressed back at the same slow and patient rate.
text_nonnarrative: Charged with air and closed at its crown, the vessel above a force pump is a chamber whose whole duty is the evening out of an intermittent delivery. Its cushion is a body of trapped air, compressed on the pressure stroke and expanded again between strokes. Capacity is therefore modest and fixed by the swept volume of the barrel. A vessel with no air in it is dead space and has no such property at all.

text_narrative: Nobody at the brewery boiler house will stand a valve set by ear, and the reason goes back to the winter the second boiler lost its plug. Kell does it with the dead weight and the long lever and a hook scale, every valve, twice over. He will tell anyone who lingers that a valve which lifts at the right pressure and then refuses to seat again is worse than one that never lifts at all.
text_nonnarrative: Every boiler above a stated pressure was required to carry two valves of the direct-loaded kind, of which one was to be beyond the reach of the house. Lever and weight were permitted only where the weight was fixed and stamped with the pressure. Seating pressure was to lie within a twentieth of the lifting pressure. A valve adjustable by hand from the working floor was not admissible, whatever its size and whatever its setting.

text_narrative: There was a keeper of the deep furnaces who trusted nothing she could not empty and fill again. Twice in every watch she cracked the bottom cock of the gauge glass and let the water fall out of it, and twice she let it back. The other keepers laughed at her for it, until the season the glass in the eastern house showed a steady half and the boiler under it was dry as a bell.
text_nonnarrative: A gauge glass is the least trustworthy honest instrument in a boiler house, and the reason is structural: a steady reading is what a blocked passage and a correct level have in common. Blowdown is worth its interruption because it tells the two apart, and nothing else does. The objection that frequent blowdown wears the cocks is sound as far as it goes, and it does not touch the case for blowing them at all.

text_narrative: In the second winter of the works the north battery lost its heater for eleven days. The engineer on duty recorded a fall of nine degrees in the feed and a leak of four gallons an hour at the front tube plate. Two tubes were plugged on the ninth day and a third on the tenth. The plate itself was recorded sound. The heater was returned to service at reduced feed and the entry was countersigned.
text_nonnarrative: A heater was condemned on the state of its tube plate and never on the number of tubes plugged. A leak at the plate counted against the heater whatever the gallons lost, while the same leak in a tube body was a matter for that tube alone. Degrees of rise in the feed bore on the duty and not on the class. Return to service at reduced feed was no part of the grading.

text_narrative: The siphon over the wall had run for nine years, and now it would not, and Osred stood at the crest with the plug out and no notion why. Full of water, both legs. That was the thing. A siphon which had lost its prime showed air at the crown, and this one showed none, and the level in the upper cistern was exactly where it should be, and the lower cistern had not been touched since spring.
text_nonnarrative: Prime: the condition of a siphon whose bore is full of liquid throughout, with no free surface between the two legs. Air lock: any pocket of gas at or near the crown large enough to divide the column. Break-off: the height above the upper surface at which a column of the liquid cannot be supported. Crest: the highest point of the bore, and the usual seat of an air lock in a siphon of long span.

text_narrative: Forty cocks are set into the service tunnel under the dome, and Ilva carries three keys for them, which is two fewer than the schedule allows. The eighteenth cock takes none of the three. She kneels on the grating with the lamp between her knees and turns the smallest key over in the light: the square is right, the throat is right, the depth is short by the width of a fingernail.
text_nonnarrative: A key meant, in this part, an implement of square socket intended to bear on the plug of a stopcock and on nothing else. Where a cock lay beneath a public footway, only a key of the long pattern applied to it. A socket true in square but short in depth was not a key within the meaning of this part. Nothing in the schedule of patterns affected the duty to maintain the plug.

text_narrative: Nobody at the river station would say who had left the back panel off the third switchboard, and the inspector was not a man who asked twice. He put his lamp along the bars and found the cause of the flicker in the west of the town at the far end of the frame: a strip of brass shim laid across the gap between two phases, cut square, and forgotten there by whoever dressed the joint.
text_nonnarrative: Two sections stand coupled only where both are dead or both are alive at one voltage and one phase rotation. A board on which a section is fed from two sides at once is barred, and the bar holds whatever the load. Shim, packing and any loose metal between bars of differing phase are not a condition of the board but a defect in it, and no setting of the switches answers them at all.

text_narrative: There was a lamp-wright in the low country who kept her fuse wire in a drawer of nine compartments, and she would not let a stranger choose from it. The thinnest was for the shrine lamps that burned all night and drew nothing. The thickest she used twice in her life. A traveller who took the third from the left for a hall of forty lamps walked home in the dark, three times in one winter.
text_nonnarrative: Nine gauges made up the drawer, of which the fourth and fifth were the ones in daily use. Each was a tinned wire on its own card, the card marked with a nominal current and with the size of the copper it protected. The thinnest was of the order of a hair and lay under a glass lid. Two spare cards of the commonest gauge sat at the back of every drawer in the shop.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the pumping station the directors called for cards from every cylinder on a single day. The engineman took twenty-two of them between six and noon at a steady load, and the draughtsman traced them all onto one sheet. Four cards showed a toe rounded where the others showed a corner. Three of the four belonged to the oldest engine. The sheet was bound into the minute book and nothing was ordered.
text_nonnarrative: What passes for engine analysis in the trade is usually card-reading of a slack kind: area is taken for power and shape for the health of the valve gear, and the second inference is far weaker than the first. A rounded toe is read as late admission by habit rather than by argument or measurement. The best practitioners of the form are those who date every card, name the engine, and distrust a single sheet.

text_narrative: The engine in the empty house is hunting again, and Tarrow counts the swings from the yard because the door is not one he intends to open. Eight to the minute, perhaps nine. Faster than yesterday, and wider. A governor hunts because the load shifts under it, that is the whole of what a governor does, and there has been no load in that house since the wheel was uncoupled in the spring and the belt taken off.
text_nonnarrative: Disagreement over whether hunting is a fault of a governor or a property of the whole loop turns on what is meant by fault. On one account the governor is the seat of the defect, since a governor with more friction in its sleeve does not hunt. On the other the oscillation belongs to no part, being a relation between the response of the engine and the delay in the linkage. The second account is harder to state and more general.

text_narrative: At first light the conduit master came up the hill road with a staff and a knotted cord, and measured the fall from the spring house to the town cistern for the third time that month. Eighty-one feet. The cistern stood dry at midday all the same. At the fourth arch he laid his ear against the lead and heard the water going fast and thin, faster than eighty-one feet of fall could account for.
text_nonnarrative: Loss of head in a straight main is very nearly proportional to the square of the mean velocity and to the length, and inversely to the diameter. The coefficient is a property of the bore and of its roughness rather than of the water. At very low velocities the square law fails and the loss tends toward a simple proportion. Fall available and loss are equal in a main running full and free at delivery.

text_narrative: Everybody on the terrace bought mantles from the ironmonger on the corner, and everybody complained about them, and nobody went elsewhere. The trick, as the old women had it, was in the first burning. Sela lit her mantle with the glass off and the door shut, and the ash held its shape for a year and more. Her sister lit two in a draught and both went to powder at the crown inside a week.
text_nonnarrative: A mantle is graded on the state of its crown and on nothing below the shoulder. Ash gone to powder at the crown is disqualifying whatever the light the mantle gives and whatever its age. A draught during the burning bears on the cause and never on the class. Shape held for a week counts for nothing; the class is set by shape held under the glass at working heat, and by that alone.

text_narrative: There was a wind in the eastern marshes that would not be faced, and the fen-folk built their pumps with eight-vaned fantails against it. The oldest pump had six. It stood with its face to the north through every wind of that country and pumped nothing for a hundred years. In the year the marsh dried, the six vanes came round of themselves, and the mill faced east, and no water lay under it to lift.
text_nonnarrative: The fantail was a small wheel of six or eight flat vanes set on a spindle at right angles to the main sails. Its spindle bore a worm, and the worm engaged a rack about the curb. The vanes were flat boards, never twisted, and each was housed in a spider of iron arms. On the smallest pumps the spider was absent and the vanes were framed direct onto the boss of the spindle.

text_narrative: In the ninth year of the harbour works the great crane on the north quay was taken down and its drum measured. The wheel proved to be eighteen feet across the treads and the drum four, which no ledger in the town had recorded. Two of the six spokes were sound. The pawl and its ratchet were laid aside for the smith, and the rest of the timber was sold where it lay.
text_nonnarrative: Wheel, drum and shaft are one assembly in a treadwheel crane: the treads are boards fixed inside the rim, and the drum sits on the same shaft, inboard of the wheel. A pawl stands over a ratchet at the drum end and is the only part out of the line of the shaft. The jib is separate. In smaller cranes the second wheel is absent and the shaft rests on two bearings only.

text_narrative: Four hundred miles from the depot and the delivery valve on the water pump would not hold. Sennen had grit of a sort, the fine grey dust off the lake bed, worked into tallow. It was not lapping powder and she knew it. She worked the disc on its seat by thumb for an hour by the watch, dry-lipped, thinking about the eight days of pumping between the camp and the next open water.
text_nonnarrative: A lift valve of this kind has four parts and no more: a disc, a seat ring set into the body, a guide, and a light spring above. The disc bears on the seat along a narrow annular face, and that face is the whole of the joint. Guide and disc are one piece in the smaller sizes. Grit between the two faces is no part of the valve, though the lapping of them depends on it.

text_narrative: The lamp over the loading bay burns short again and Corvin goes up the ladder with the case of carbons under one arm. Vacuum outside, atmosphere in here, and the arc still eats an inch an hour. He racks the stub out of the lower holder. The case has four sizes in it and only the second fits the upper clip, and eleven of the second are left in the whole station.
text_nonnarrative: Four sizes made up the standard case: three plain carbons of increasing diameter and one cored. The cored size was the commonest, its core a soft paste that held the arc central. Each stick was some twelve inches long, square-ended, with a copper skin over all but the last inch. The smallest was stocked in quantity and the largest in twos, being wanted for the yard lamps and for nothing else.

text_narrative: Nobody in the machine house lets the new men near the dynamos on a Monday, and Halvard is the reason, or the story about Halvard is. He beds brushes by feel and he is never wrong about it, and he will not be told that a strip of glass paper round the commutator is quicker. Three minutes with the paper, he says, and three weeks of sparking at the heel of every brush.
text_nonnarrative: Much of what the trade called brush-setting was really brush-forcing, and the fault lay in the standard of proof: a brush free of sparking under load was held to be bedded, whatever the state of its heel. Glass paper was defended on the ground that it was quick, which was true and beside the point. The soundest men were those who judged a brush by its face and not by the machine's behaviour.

text_narrative: There was a heron who nested in the third bend of the hot main where it crossed the marsh, and she chose it because the iron there was never quite still. In the cold months the bend drew back and her nest sat over open water. In the heat it pushed out and the nest lay over reed. A young otter told her the pipe was straight and she should shift. She stayed nine summers.
text_nonnarrative: Nothing in the geometry of an expansion loop settles whether it is a kind of joint or simply a length of pipe. On the first view its duty is to absorb movement, its virtue is compliance, and it belongs with bellows and slip couplings. On the second, its behaviour follows from ordinary bending and there is nothing peculiar about it. The second view explains more and surrenders a distinction between a main and its fittings.

text_narrative: In the year the second mill was raised the founders cast the flywheel in six segments and joined them at the arms with cotters and links. The rim measured twenty-two feet and the wheel was worked at forty turns to the minute for eleven seasons. At the autumn survey a cotter at the fourth joint was found slack by a quarter inch. The wheel was slowed to thirty turns and the entry stood unaltered.
text_nonnarrative: Hoop stress in a rim went as the square of the rim speed and was independent of the radius at a given speed, so that a large wheel and a small one at equal rim speed stood equally stressed. The constant was a property of the metal alone. Joints in a segmented rim took none of that stress directly, and the bolts at a joint were sized on the arm loads instead.

text_narrative: The second lift of the holder is up at seven in the morning and the town has burned nothing since Friday. Idra watches the crown from the office window and does the arithmetic twice. Gas from where. The cups are full, the grips are dry, the guide rollers sit true in their standards, and the holder rises a foot a day out of a main that runs to nowhere at all and never has.
text_nonnarrative: A holder was condemned on the seal at its cups and grips, never on the height of a lift. A crown out of level counted as one class of defect and rollers off their standards as a second, the two being independent. Gas in the main bore on the cause and not at all on the class. Rise of a foot in a day was no evidence either way, being a matter of the works.

text_narrative: Three sets run in the converter house at the northern depot and only two are needed on a weekday. At half past four this afternoon the middle set drops out of step and the board goes over to the standby without a flicker on the line. The attendant records a bearing temperature nine degrees above the others and shuts the set down. No traffic is delayed and the depot works the evening peak on two machines.
text_nonnarrative: One armature serves both machines in a rotary converter: it sits in a single field, with slip rings at one end and a commutator at the other. Alternating supply at the rings and direct output at the commutator are two aspects of the same winding rather than two circuits. Speed is fixed by the supply frequency and by the number of poles, and by nothing else. Without the rings the machine is an ordinary motor.

text_narrative: Before the cold was given its own name, the makers set a small brass gate at the foot of every pipe in the world and told it one thing: hold what is hot, pass what is cold. The gate was honest and slow. Water went through it and steam did not, and the makers were satisfied. But the gate could never tell cold water from cold steam, and there is a house in the north still emptying.
text_nonnarrative: Traps fall into three classes by what each of them senses. A float trap answers to the level of condensate and is indifferent to temperature. A thermostatic trap answers to temperature and is indifferent to level. A thermodynamic trap belongs with neither, since it depends on the velocity of flashing water across a disc and senses no state of the condensate at all. Orifice size separates duties within a class and never separates the classes themselves.

text_narrative: Every dry month Weir walks the bund of the old cooling pond. In the first month he finds the north arms still turning on their own head, and he leaves them alone. In the third he wires up two nozzles that spray sideways into the reeds. In the sixth the pond is down a foot and the spray falls short of the water, and he walks the bund twice that month and does nothing.
text_nonnarrative: The pond lay in a shallow rectangle east of the plant, its bund some four feet above the water at ordinary level. Two rows of spray arms stood over it on trestles, the northern row nearer the bund than the southern. Reed beds occupied the eastern third of the water. The bottom shelved from a foot at the margin to seven near the outfall, and the western side was the deeper throughout.

text_narrative: Each week of the survey took Bregt to a different settlement standpipe. At the first the float was a sealed copper ball and the gear read true. At the fourth the ball had a pinhole and sat two inches low, and the whole village drew from a tower it believed to be half full.
