At the ninth there was no float at all, only a boy on the ladder with a chalk mark.
text_nonnarrative: Error in the indicated level varied more between towers of one pattern than between patterns. The median discrepancy was some two inches, and floats with any breach in them accounted for most of the spread. Attendants at the larger towers reported the gear as trustworthy in nine cases of ten, and the sample of smaller towers was too thin to bear a figure at all, whatever the pattern of the gear.

text_narrative: A ram at the foot of the hospital garden was found still beating on the morning of the third, eleven days after the drive pipe above it had been cut for the new road. The gardener reported the beat as regular, at some sixty to the minute. The delivery tank was full and the overflow running. No connection to the upper spring could be traced by the two men sent out, and the beat continued.
text_nonnarrative: Among pumps that use no outside power, the hydraulic ram is the one that works on the momentum of its own supply. A long drive pipe, a waste valve at its foot and a delivery valve into an air vessel are the whole of it. Delivery height is a large multiple of the fall, and the delivered fraction correspondingly small. Beat rate depends on the length of the drive pipe and on the waste valve setting.

text_narrative: In the first age of the deep engines the smiths packed every gland with rope of hemp and tallow, and the water they held back was not water. Each box took nine turns of it, cut on the skew, with the joints of the turns set a third of a circle apart. The last smith to pack a gland in the old way went down to the sixth level with a coil on her shoulder.
text_nonnarrative: Packing was to be of square section, cut on the skew, and laid in rings of one turn each with the joints staggered by a third of a circle. Six turns were required in a box of ordinary depth and nine where the pressure stood above a stated figure. Hemp was permitted only below a stated temperature. A gland drawn hard enough to prevent all leakage was not acceptable on any shaft in motion.

text_narrative: The pacing machine at the winter track runs off a flat belt, and Nolwenn dresses it before each meeting. On the first night she uses too much and the belt grips hard and the rider behind it complains of a jerk out of the banking. On the third she uses none and loses four seconds to slip in the last mile. On the fifth she splits the difference and nobody says anything.
text_nonnarrative: Slip in a flat belt was a safeguard and not a loss, and the trade was slow to say so. A belt incapable of slipping transmitted every shock in the load straight into the shafting, and the shafting had no other relief. The objection was that slip wasted power, and it did waste power, at some two parts in a hundred. That cost bought a margin no other part of the drive supplied.

text_narrative: Three times on the southern passage the vacuum in the main condenser fell away, and each time Odhran was sent below to find it. The first time it was the air pump, out of stroke on one side. The second it was a joint at the gland of the exhaust, whistling faintly. The third time the gauge showed twenty-four inches and every joint was tight, and the sea outside was warmer than the chart allowed.
text_nonnarrative: Vacuum is classed by the seat of a loss and not by its depth. An air pump out of stroke is one class; a leaking joint at a gland or in the exhaust is a second, and the two are graded apart however alike the gauge reads. Sea temperature bears on the cause and never on the class, since warm water is no defect in a condenser. Inches of vacuum fix degree within a class.

text_narrative: Twice at the change of shift the ring main on the third habitat level knocks, and the duty engineer logs it as a slam at the outfall valve. Pressure at the far gauge touches nine hundred and returns. No pipe is displaced and no joint shows wet. A second knock at the same hour the following day is logged with a note that the valve is now closing in eleven seconds instead of two.
text_nonnarrative: Slam: the shock in a main proper to too-rapid closure of a valve, reckoned as a rise above the working pressure. Column separation: the condition of a water column parted from itself at a high point, with a void between the parts. Rejoinder: the second and usually larger shock, peculiar to a separated column. Surge: any pressure change of the same family slow enough to be measured in seconds rather than in fractions.

text_narrative: When the sky was first strung, the makers gave each pole three cups of glass, one under the other, so that the rain of the world would find no road down the wood. The rain accepted this. In the country of long mists it sent no rain at all and laid its water on the glass from beneath, and the poles there were given a fourth cup, turned upward, and they stand taller in the west.
text_nonnarrative: An insulator meant, in this part, a body of glass or glazed clay interposed between a conductor and its support, having not fewer than two sheds. A shed meant any downward skirt whose under surface stood clear of the body. Where a line lay in a district of salt air, three sheds were required and a fourth was permitted. Nothing in this part affected the sizing of the pin or of the crossarm.

text_narrative: Sera keeps six substations alive along the coast road and each one teaches her something about horn gaps. At the first the horns are set wide and the arrester has never once flashed over. At the third they are set close and it flashes in clear weather. At the fifth somebody before her filed the points to needles. At the sixth there are no horns, only two lengths of fence wire.
text_nonnarrative: A gap is admissible only where its setting lies below the withstand of the apparatus behind it and above the crest of the working voltage. A station in which the earth resistance exceeds the stated figure counts as unprotected, whatever the gap. Filed or pointed horns are not a setting and cannot be answered by any adjustment. Two arresters on one line at differing settings are barred as a position.

text_narrative: The city was given its water pressure by seven towers, and each tower held a weight, and each weight was said to be the patience of the district beneath it. The tower in the glass quarter held the smallest, and its cranes were the quickest in the port. The tower over the salt flats held two hundred tons and shifted a hand's breadth in a year, and that district never hurried at anything.
text_nonnarrative: Three patterns of accumulator are found in a works of any size. The smallest is a plain ram in an open frame, loaded with cast weights on a crosshead, and it is the commonest. The middle pattern is the weighted tower proper, a ram in a case filled with slag or gravel. The largest is a differential accumulator with two rams of unequal diameter, rare and kept for high pressures alone.

text_narrative: The lighting plant behind the freight office at the cattle stop was reported dead on the morning of the eleventh, four months after the last train of the season. An electrician up from the junction found thirty cells standing at less than a volt and the positive plates white to the edge. The shed was dry and the connections clean. The plant had been left charged and unattended, which the company book allowed.
text_nonnarrative: Much of the battery practice of the period rested on a false comfort: a plant standing idle was thought to be a plant at rest, when idleness was the one condition under which sulphation was certain. Company books that allowed months of standing without charge were the visible form of the error. What was called neglect in the tender was usually compliance. The best houses treated a full cell as a thing needing work.

text_narrative: The first shaft was a single length of iron laid along the roof of the world, and it turned everything. When it wore, the smiths cut it and set a hanger at the cut, and it was two shafts that turned as one. They cut it again and again, until the roof was a hundred lengths in a hundred bearings, and nobody in the shops below could say where one shaft ended.
text_nonnarrative: Counting the shafts in a mill is not a matter of counting the couplings. On one criterion a line of shafting is a single object, because it has one angular velocity throughout and no part of it is free of the rest. On another it is many, since each length has its own bearings, its own deflection and its own history. Neither criterion is idle, and the disagreement is about objects rather than words.

text_narrative: At ten minutes to three the night chart from the river substation shows a second peak, as high as the evening one and half an hour wide. The district it feeds is four streets of shuttered warehouses and a bonded store. Nothing on the schedule accounts for it. The recorder is checked against the station meters and agrees with them to within a hundred units, and the same peak is on last night's chart.
text_nonnarrative: Peak demand stood in rough proportion to the number of consumers, while the diversity factor diminished with it, so that the sum of the individual maxima always lay well above the maximum of the sum. Load factor was the ratio of the mean to the peak over a day and rarely exceeded a third on a lighting supply. Beyond a certain size of district the diversity factor was near enough constant.

text_narrative: The steward's clerk has the roll open on the trestle and cannot make the entries balance. Fourteen tenants presented, thirteen fines entered, and the margin of the membrane carries a fifteenth name in a different ink. Outside, the tenants stand in the yard with their strips of parchment. He turns the membrane over, finds the missing fine written on the back in the same different ink, and sets down a cross beside it.
text_nonnarrative: A defective roll was distinguished by where the entry stood, not by whose hand set it there. An entry in the margin of a membrane counted as good where the same ink ran through the body; a fine written on the back of a membrane was of a second class, admitted only on the clerk's oath. The count of tenants presented bore on the remedy and never on the class. Parchment quality bore on neither.

text_narrative: They talk in the vestry still about the year the overseers questioned a woman named Alys Prendle for three sittings and could not settle where she belonged. She had been hired at one place by the year, married in a second, and had rented at eight pounds in a third. Every answer she gave was true and every answer moved her parish. In the end the clerk wrote down all three and left it.
text_nonnarrative: Settlement is determined by the last head that applies and not by the number of heads a person can show. Being hired for a year in one parish, being married in a second and having rented above ten pounds in a third are independent grounds, of which the latest governs. Answers given at three sittings weigh no more than answers given at one. The entry of the overseers bears on proof, never on the ground.

text_narrative: There was a harbour clerk who would sign no bill of health he had not read aloud, and a ship came in one autumn with a clean bill in a language nobody at the office knew. The clerk read it aloud all the same, syllable by syllable, and the words made a shape in the room that the lamps went round. He signed it, and the ship lay in the roads forty days anyway.
text_nonnarrative: A bill of health is graded clean, touched or foul, and the grade attaches to the harbour of issue rather than to the ship. An untranslated bill is not foul; it falls outside the grades and is held unclassed for want of an office copy in a known language. The clerk's signature bears on admissibility and not on the grade. Forty days in the roads follow from the grade alone, whatever the cargo.

text_narrative: In the second year after the incumbent's death, a schedule of dilapidations was drawn on the parsonage house and its outbuildings. Twenty-two items were listed, of which nine touched the barn roof alone. The valuers put the whole at eleven pounds four shillings and set the figure against the estate. The successor refused the barn items on the ground that the roof had been thatched with reed against a covenant naming straw.
text_nonnarrative: Dilapidation is classed by whether an item restores or improves, and not by the sum a valuer sets against it. Want of repair to a parsonage roof is one class; departure from a covenant, as thatch of reed where straw is named, is a second, independent of the first. Outbuildings fall under the same classes as the house. The total in pounds and shillings bears on the charge to an estate, never on the class.

text_narrative: The stamp in the inspector's box is not the stamp that left the county office, and Ferrers knows it without knowing how. Same crown, same letter, same worn place at the rim. But the impression it leaves on lead comes up shallow on one side, the way the old inspector's always did, and the old inspector has been three years in the ground. She stamps a second weight and looks at that too.
text_nonnarrative: Verification depended on the impression and not on the instrument that made it. A shallow impression in the lead of a weight was one class of defect, curable by restamping; a crown or county letter differing from the pattern held at the office was a second, and no impression of that kind counted at all. Wear at the rim of a stamp bore on the cause. The inspector's own book bore on neither class.

text_narrative: A registry of the county surveyor's office was rebuilt during the spring recess and the pigeonholes recut to a smaller size. Eleven thousand bundles were moved in nine days by four clerks working from a written plan. Two hundred and six bundles were afterwards found in holes not answering to their marks, all of them in the range nearest the door, and the plan for that range was never produced.
text_nonnarrative: A pigeonhole registry is carried on two independent orders. Bundles sit in holes by a running number, and the subject index is a separate sequence of slips referring to that number. Retrieval time is a function of the index alone and of the depth of a hole, not of the size of the collection. Without the slips the holes are unsearchable, and without the holes the slips point nowhere.

text_narrative: When the first archive was raised, the keepers were given no names for its rooms and no numbers for its shelves, and everything in it was found by memory alone. The last keeper wrote a mark on one bundle before she went, three letters and a figure, and the mark held. After her the rooms took letters and the shelves took figures, and nothing in the archive was ever again found by remembering.
text_nonnarrative: A shelf mark is a composite of three fields: room, press and position, each independent of the others in what it can be changed to. Its stability rests on the building and not on the contents, so a bundle keeps its mark while it keeps its place. Reshelving breaks the third field only. Any mark whose room letter is absent stands in no fixed relation to the rest of the sequence.

text_narrative: Three market days in a row the tallyman's counterfoils come back short. On the first day the book is one leaf light and the stub for it is missing too, which is possible. On the second the stub is there and the leaf gone, which is not. On the third he sits with both halves of the book open on his knees at the gate and lets the queue wait behind him.
text_nonnarrative: A counterfoil book is two records on one sheet of paper, divided by a perforation and numbered alike on both sides of it. The strength of the arrangement lies in that shared number, which is printed before issue and cannot be altered on one half alone. A missing leaf is detectable from its stub; a missing stub is detectable from nothing inside the book. Loose leaves are outside the system altogether.

text_narrative: The rod passed from the widow's hand to the steward's and then to her son's, and the whole business took less time than the walk from the church. Nobody in the hall said the word sale. The steward entered a surrender and an admittance on two lines of the roll, took the fine in coin from a purse the son had ready, and gave the rod back to the bailiff to keep.
text_nonnarrative: Three tenures are distinguished here, and the middle one is neither of the others. Freehold is held of nobody and passes by deed. Copyhold is held of a manor and passes by surrender and admittance entered on a roll, the rod and the fine belonging to the form and not to the substance. Leasehold is a term of years, distinguished from both by having an end fixed at its beginning.

text_narrative: Everybody in the hundred knows the jury list for the upper division is wrong, and nobody will say which way. Forty-one names where there were fifty-three the year before. The high constable's returns are all in the same hand, including the two parishes that sent nothing that year. A clerk who asks about it at the sessions house is told the books for that division are out for binding.
text_nonnarrative: Two lists were kept and only one of them was public. The general list held every man qualified by property in a division, and was open at the parish chest. The panel was drawn from it for a given sitting and was not open at all, being distinguished from the general list by having a date. A third paper, the constable's return, was the material of the first and belonged to neither.

text_narrative: There was a chancellor's daughter who was given the counterseal to keep and told never to press it alone. For a year she carried it on a cord and pressed nothing. In the second year she pressed it into cold wax, and the wax took the small device on the back and none of the great one on the front, and the sheet was worth a manor to whoever held it.
text_nonnarrative: A counterseal is not a lesser seal but a second impression on the reverse of the same wax, and the pair is one authentication in two parts. The great seal stands alone on writs of the highest kind, where no counterseal is used. A signet is a third thing, distinguished from both by being personal to a holder and by leaving no impression on the reverse at all.

text_narrative: In the fifth year of the Commutation, the surveyors of the western division finished a map of nine hundred and four numbered parcels and lodged three copies, one of them in a chest that would not lock. The apportionment was read in the church over two days. Four occupiers found their names against parcels on the wrong side of the brook, and the brook itself was drawn a chain out of place.
text_nonnarrative: The parish lies in two unequal parts on either side of a brook, and the larger part is the wetter. Numbered parcels run from the church outward, so that the low ground carries the lowest numbers. Three lanes cross the brook, of which the middle one is metalled. The glebe is a single block on the eastern rise, and the common is above it, unnumbered and undivided on the map.

text_narrative: The bounds had been walked every seventh year since anyone could remember, and Ottilie had walked six of them. This one went wrong at the third mark. Not moved. The stone was where it had always been, and the ash beside it was where it had always been, but the two of them had changed places about the path, and nobody else in the line of forty seemed to notice.
text_nonnarrative: Eleven marks stand on the boundary, and no two of them are of one kind. Four are stones, three are trees, two are the corners of walls, and the remaining pair are holes in the ground. The line between the fifth and sixth marks is under water at every season. On the northern side the boundary is also the road; elsewhere it is a hedge with the ditch on the outer face.

text_narrative: The land office at Vesk Terrace issues a renumbering of the second district and eleven hundred holdings change their designations in one afternoon. Two adjoining plots receive the same number, 2-441, one on the register and one on the map. The holder of the lower plot lodges a query the same day. The office replies that the map governs, and the map is the copy that has not yet been corrected.
text_nonnarrative: The district lay in four quarters about a central square, and the numbering had its origin at the north-west corner of each. Odd numbers ran along the inner faces of the blocks, even numbers along the outer. Holdings on the square itself bore no quarter prefix and were the only ones so distinguished. The two streets running out to the west were numbered from the far end inward, against the rule everywhere else.

text_narrative: In the age when houses were counted by their fires, the counters went out with tallies of hazel and were told to write down smoke. A house with two fires was written twice and a house with none was not written at all. So the poor went out of the record like breath off a window, and the counters came back with a country smaller than the one they had walked.
text_nonnarrative: Hearth numbers vary more between neighbouring parishes than between one region and another. Half the houses in the returns are entered with a single hearth, and the exempt are a fifth of the whole in some places and none at all in others. Two-thirds of the spread is accounted for by how the exempt are treated rather than by any difference in building. Enumerators disagree most about outbuildings with a chimney.

text_narrative: Three times in five years the assessor came to the same house on the hill road and three times the number of windows was different. On the first visit he counted nineteen. On the second, fourteen, seven of them newly bricked and the mortar still pale. On the third he counted fourteen again and then walked round to the yard side, where a scullery had grown a window since the spring.
text_nonnarrative: Window counts differ more between two assessments of one house than between houses of a like size. A third of the dwellings in the schedules stand at the threshold figure exactly, which is more than chance would put there. Bricked openings account for most of the movement downward; additions at the rear, for nearly all of the movement up. Assessors in the same district return figures a fifth apart on average.

text_narrative: Candle end, and the rate book is still open at the letter M. The assistant overseer works down the column with a wet thumb, entering the sums the vestry set in April, and the column will not come to the total at the foot. Eleven shillings out. He goes back to the top, finds a house entered twice under two spellings of one name, and rules one of them through.
text_nonnarrative: Rateable values within one parish are spread more widely than the rents they stand on. The median assessment in the books is a fifth of a rack rent, and the highest tenth of properties carries above half the sum levied. Duplicate entries under variant spellings are commoner in the earlier books than in the later, and account for a small part of the difference between a book's total and its column sums.

text_narrative: In the old parish they will tell of the banns that were called three times to an empty church, because the couple named in them had never asked. The clerk swore he had the entry in his own hand and could not say who set it there. Both persons named came from villages a day apart and had never met. They met at the third calling and the thing went forward.
text_nonnarrative: Banns are a public notice of an intended marriage, characterised by publication three times over, on separate weeks, in the parishes of both parties. Their effect is negative: they create no obligation and only remove one impediment, that of secrecy. Publication in the wrong parish is of no effect, and the period of validity is short and fixed, running three months from the last calling. A licence is the alternative instrument.

text_narrative: There was a heron who kept a notary's office at the ford and would protest anything brought to him, for a fish. A vole brought a bill that nobody had refused, and the heron protested it all the same, and drew the instrument up with his own long hand. The vole's bill was afterwards worth less than the fish. The heron said the paper was correct, and it was.
text_nonnarrative: A protest is an instrument recording that a bill has been presented and not honoured, characterised by being made by a public officer rather than by a party. Its force is evidential, and depends on the presentment it records; a protest of a bill never refused proves nothing but its regularity. The form is narrow and fixed by the office, and the wording of the noting is not at the drawer's choice.

text_narrative: In the ninth year of the transit office, endorsements were required on every leaf of a passage book rather than on the last, and the books grew to forty leaves. A traveller of the outer stations arrived with thirty-one endorsements and one leaf missing at the fold. The clerk of the day entered a note of the gap, stamped the following leaf twice, and let the passage stand on the strength of the note.
text_nonnarrative: An endorsement is a mark added to a document complete in itself, characterised by standing outside the text it qualifies. Its authority is derivative: it can restrict a passage or extend it in time, and can do nothing where the underlying instrument is void. Continuity of leaves is therefore essential to the whole, since an endorsement proves only what it touches. A note of a missing leaf is itself an endorsement of the lowest order.

text_narrative: The rough minutes are in pencil on both sides of a folded sheet and the fair copy is due at noon. Twelve resolutions, and the eleventh has a word crossed through that might be adjourned and might be adopted. Halbin has been clerk for nine years and has never asked the chairman anything. He writes adjourned, in a round hand, and leaves the rough sheet in the book where anyone can find it.
text_nonnarrative: Minutes were to be engrossed in a bound book with ruled margins, in one hand throughout a meeting, and were not to be written on both sides of a loose sheet for the fair copy. Erasure was forbidden; a word struck through was required to remain legible, with the substitution above it. Rough notes were permitted to be destroyed only where the engrossment was signed. No resolution was to stand unnumbered.

text_narrative: A stock of unstamped paper was found in the flooded offices of the old revenue house and carried to the market at Ilder Cross. Nine reams were legible and dry. The market keeper ruled that any sheet bearing the old impression counted as stamped in the market's own registers, and that plain sheets did not. Two traders produced sheets with the impression drawn on in ink, and both sheets were refused.
text_nonnarrative: Instruments are to be written on sheets bearing an impressed stamp of the value fixed for the class, and the impression is required to be struck in advance of any writing on the sheet. A drawn or printed imitation is permitted for no purpose. Where a sheet is damaged, an office copy on a fresh stamp is to be substituted. Nothing written across an impression is to be read as part of the instrument.

text_narrative: When the first poll was taken in the valley towns, the names were written down in the order the voices came, and the book was left open on a table in the square for as long as the season lasted. Whoever read it aloud found the order changed. Not the names, but the order. The clerks held that a book read too often begins to arrange itself, and stopped leaving it open.
text_nonnarrative: Poll books are read as records of opinion, and they are better read as records of order. What they fix is the sequence in which men came forward, which is a fact about a town's arrangement of itself, not about anyone's mind. It is fair to object that the votes are also there on the page. So they are, and they are the part a later reader can least often use.

text_narrative: Four times this year the district clerk has renamed the same lane. In March it is Back Row, because that is what the rate book has. In June it is Chapel Walk, because the chapel trustees ask. In August it is Back Row again, on a petition of nine householders. In November he leaves the plate off the wall altogether and writes both names in the register, one above the other.
text_nonnarrative: Street names are worth less as description than as a record of who was asking. A name that describes, like the back of something, dates from a time when a district had one centre; a name that commemorates dates from a time when it had a committee. It is said that either kind will serve for finding a house. Either will, which is why the choice between them is never about finding.

text_narrative: The register had been rebound and the gutter took the last letter of every line on the left-hand page. Verrin held it under the lamp at an angle and read what he could. Four entries in a hand that leaned backward, all in one week of one year, and none of them in the index at the front. The rest of the volume leaned the other way and was indexed to the leaf.
text_nonnarrative: Secretary hand: the ordinary book hand of the older registers, upright and heavily abbreviated. Current hand: the later cursive, distinguished by the joining of every letter in a word. Gutter loss: text that was carried into the fold of a rebound volume and was thereafter illegible. Interleaf: a sheet that was added at binding and bore no original entry. Reversed leaning: any hand sloping backward, a mark of one writer.

text_narrative: Anyone in the office will tell a new clerk about the deed with the third interlineation, and they tell it the same way every time. Two words above the line in the habendum, initialled twice in the margin by the same two hands. The engrossing clerk who wrote them has been dead a long while and the family still holds the land. Nobody has ever needed to argue about the words themselves.
text_nonnarrative: Engrossment: the fair copy of an instrument, written for execution and not for revision. Interlineation: any words inserted above a line of an engrossment, which were required to be initialled in the margin. Rasure: a place where the surface of the parchment had been scraped, distinguished from an ordinary blot by its thinness. Habendum: the clause that limited the estate granted. Vacat: a marginal note that a passage was void.

text_narrative: There was a clerk of the rolls who could not write his own name and had held the office nine years by memory alone. Every man who subscribed the roll before him did so twice, once on the parchment and once aloud, and the clerk kept the second copy in his head. When the roll was lost in a wet spring he recited four hundred names in order to a boy with a pen.
text_nonnarrative: Subscription meant, in that part, the writing of a name on the roll itself and not on any schedule annexed to it. Where a subscriber was unable to write, a mark made in the presence of the officer was of the same effect. A roll wanting the officer's own subscription at the foot was of no effect, whatever it otherwise contained. No provision of that part touched oaths taken outside a roll.

text_narrative: In the seventh year of the register, memorials of eleven thousand deeds were enrolled in the county office and the index to them was left a year behind. A purchaser of land in the northern division found two memorials of the same deed, entered on different days by different hands, with the parcels described differently in each. The registrar enrolled a third memorial reciting both, and the matter rested there.
text_nonnarrative: A memorial was, under that head, a summary of a deed subscribed by a party and enrolled, and was not the deed. Where two memorials of one deed stood on the register, neither displaced the other and both were notice. A memorial was required to name the parcels; one that did not was notice of nothing. Enrolment gave priority by date of entry and by no other measure.

text_narrative: Forty-one beasts on the moor and the stint is thirty-eight, and Maren cannot make the three extra belong to anybody. She counts them again from the gate. The same forty-one, and the three at the back are the ones whose colour will not hold in the mind afterwards. Somebody's, then. She writes thirty-eight in the herd book, as every reeve before her has done, and closes it. The moor keeps its own count.
text_nonnarrative: A beast is lawfully on the common only where its owner holds a stint and the stint is not full. Two commoners may not make up one stint between them; a half stint is a holding and not a share. Beasts of a kind not named in the stint are outside it, whatever their number, and no count of them is a count of the stint. Levancy and couchancy bind independently of number.

text_narrative: A carrier of the eastern district applies for a licence in two names, his own and that of a partnership dissolved in the spring, and the clerk of licences declines both applications on one sheet. The carrier's waggon and horses are the same in each. A second application in the partnership name alone is entered on the following day and stands, on the ground that the partnership's registration has not been struck out.
text_nonnarrative: An application was in order only where one person or one firm was named in it, and a licence held in one name did not cover a vehicle worked in another. Two applications on one sheet were a single application and were refused together. A firm whose registration stood undeleted was a person for this purpose, whatever its condition otherwise. Refusal was not a decision on the vehicle and did not touch it.

text_narrative: In the first years of the wardships, the makers of the law required that everything belonging to a child be written down while the child was small, so that nothing could be added or taken. One inventory came back with a line for a thing the clerks could not name, between the beds and the linen, and it was left on the roll unpriced for the whole of that minority.
text_nonnarrative: A ward's inventory ran to five heads, of which the household stuff was always the longest. Beds and their furniture stood at the top, priced by the tester; linen came under the second head, by the pair; brass and pewter under the third, by weight; the stock on the ground under the fourth, valued by the head. Debts owing were listed at the foot and never valued.

text_narrative: Twice the incumbent tried to make the terrier agree with the ground, and twice he gave it up. In the first summer he walked the four closes with the old paper and found a fifth close in it that nobody could point to. In the second he found the fifth close, under furze, and no mention in the paper of the pond that was plainly there. He wrote both facts at the foot.
text_nonnarrative: A terrier held four kinds of thing and no more. The glebe land itself stood first, close by close, with the acreage of each and the names of the abutters. The house and its outbuildings were described by bay and by the material of the walls. The moveable goods of the church were counted by number. Rights in kind, such as timber or turf, were named without measure, and rents were not entered.

text_narrative: The appraisers have finished the upstairs rooms and are sitting on the stairs with the list between them. Forty-two items, and the sum at the foot is under twenty pounds. Everything in the house is old and nothing in it is worth anything, which is the third house of this kind on the street this year. The younger appraiser turns back to the first page and looks at the entry for the writing desk.
text_nonnarrative: Probate valuations were the least useful of the household records, and their defenders never met the reason. What passed for a price in them was a figure at which nobody had offered anything; the appraisers had no buyer and no instruction but to be low. Comparison between two such lists was therefore comparison of two habits. The best of them were the ones that described an object well and priced it badly.

text_narrative: Everyone in the village had a version of what the commissioners did with the north field in the second year of the war, and none of the versions agreed with the award. The award said forty acres to the depot and an exchange of twenty-two elsewhere. The old men said sixty and nothing back. A woman who had kept the tally of the hay crop said the award was right and nobody believed her.
text_nonnarrative: Awards were read for their maps and dismissed for their prose, which was the wrong way round. The schedules of exchange were the substance: a plain table of who lost what and took what instead, in a form that admitted no rhetoric. Critics held that such tables told nothing of how the thing was felt. They told nothing of it, and were the only part that could be checked against a field.

text_narrative: There was a master who bound an apprentice for a term of seven years and would not say when the term had begun. The indenture was in two parts, and the boy's half gave no date where the master's half had one. Every quarter day the boy asked, and every quarter day the master counted on his fingers and said not yet. The boy grew old in the shop, waiting to be free.
text_nonnarrative: The puzzle whether an indenture was one instrument or two was not idle. Both parts were engrossed together and severed, so that each was the whole in form and the half in fact; if the parts disagreed, there was no third document to appeal to. Treating the pair as one thing left the disagreement unexplained. Treating them as two left the term of an apprenticeship a matter of which half a reader held.

text_narrative: In the twelfth year of the Assembly's charter, admissions to the freedom of the city were made by three roads at once, and the register kept them in one column. Forty-one came by service, twenty by patrimony, and nine by redemption at a fee set that year. One man came by two roads on the same day, service and patrimony both, and was entered twice with a line drawn between the entries.
text_nonnarrative: Freedom of a city was either a status or a bundle of permissions, and the two accounts pulled apart at the double entry. If it was a status, a man could not hold it twice and one of the two entries was surplus. If it was a bundle, he could, and the register was right to record both roads by which the bundle was got. Neither account made the fee intelligible.

text_narrative: The tallies had come in short again and Wenceslas had counted them three times before the light went. Ninety-one sticks for a hundred and four holdings. Somebody was paying in coin and taking no stick, which was allowed, or somebody was taking two sticks for one payment, which was not, and there was no way to tell the two apart from a heap of hazel on a table by lamplight.
text_nonnarrative: The count of tallies stood in no fixed proportion to the sum received, since a payment in coin left no stick and a stick could be split. Error in the total varied as the square root of the number of holdings where the notches were cut by one hand, and faster than that where they were cut by several. Beyond about two hundred holdings the tally ceased to be a measure of anything.

text_narrative: A manifest lodged at the outport of Grennick lists ninety casks inward and the tide surveyor finds ninety-one in the shed. The extra cask carries the same mark as the fortieth and the same weight to the ounce. Both are opened in the presence of two officers and both hold the same quantity of the same oil. The surveyor enters ninety-one in the book and rules the total twice.
text_nonnarrative: Discrepancy between a manifest and a landing was proportional to the number of packages and not to their value, the constant being a property of the marking practice at the port of lading. Duty, being reckoned on weight, moved with the gross and not with the count, so that the two errors were of different orders. Beyond a certain size of cargo the relation broke down and the count governed nothing.

text_narrative: When the first charters were granted, each was made of four parts that had to travel together: the words, the seal, the cord that joined them, and a bag of the town's own earth sewn to the foot. A town that lost the bag kept its market and lost its name for it. The words alone were held to be worth nothing at all, and were copied freely by anyone who could write.
text_nonnarrative: A charter of market had three parts standing in a fixed relation. The text was a single membrane, written on one side, with a turn-up at the foot. The seal hung from a cord or a tag passed through that turn-up and was no part of the text. Warranty clauses stood at the end of the text and were absent in the shorter forms, where the witness list took their place.

text_narrative: Three times in one voyage the mate has to go up to the bond office with the same bundle of papers. The first time the warrant is right and the landing account is not. The second time both are right and the officer's counterpart is out of the book. The third time he takes all three halves at once, and the clerk keeps the middle one and gives back two.
text_nonnarrative: A bonded entry was a set of three documents of unequal size. The entry proper was a folio sheet, ruled in six columns, of which the last was left blank at lodging. The warrant was a quarter of that size and bore the marks and numbers only. The officer's counterpart was bound into a book and could not be separated from it. A fourth paper, the delivery order, was absent in warehousing entries.

text_narrative: The milling bench stood under the north window, where the light was flattest. Odila set the blank in the collar and worked the handle down until the ridges bit. The third turn came harder than the two before it, and a burr lifted along one quarter of the rim. She turned the piece over, found the collar had shifted a hair, and set the blank aside on the rejected tray.
text_nonnarrative: A milled edge is classed by the ridges themselves, not by the face of the blank. A burr along the rim counts as a collar fault; unevenness in ridge depth around one quarter of the circumference counts as a bench fault, and the two are graded apart. Neither bears on the weight. The setting of the collar, not the turn count at the handle, is what fixes the class.

text_narrative: Nobody at the sorting house would hand a doubtful spoon to old Verrin without first hearing what he had to say about the light. He rubbed the piece on the black stone, laid his needles beside the streak, and stood back a full minute. That morning the streak read paler than the needle he trusted, so he rubbed again lower down, and the second mark came out paler still.
text_nonnarrative: Comparison of a streak against a needle was a matter of colour alone, never of the breadth of the mark. A streak paler than the lowest needle placed the piece in the doubtful class; one darker than the highest was outside the scale and unclassed. The stone bore on neither heading. Light at the bench, not the pressure of the hand, was what set the margin between adjacent classes.

text_narrative: A pledge ticket numbered out of sequence turns up in the second drawer of the shop on Kesland Row. The broker, Anwen Falk, cannot account for it. The counterfoil is missing, the pledge itself is a plain brass rule, and the sum entered is twice what the rule would fetch. A constable takes the ticket away in a paper sleeve and returns the following afternoon with two more of the same run.
text_nonnarrative: An irregular ticket was classed by its number and its counterfoil, and not by the pledge it named. A ticket out of sequence within a run counted as one irregularity; a missing counterfoil counted as another, and the sum entered bore on neither class. Whether the pledge was worth the sum was a separate matter, handled under the redemption tables. The broker's hand on the ticket was never the ground of a class.

text_narrative: Nothing in the hall was worth the reserve set on it, and the auctioneer of the Thornguild knew it before the first lot came up. Let them bid. The bronze horn was chipped at the mouth; the reserve stood at nine marks and no hand went past six. He brought the hammer down anyway, called it sold to the guild's own account, and turned to the next lot without meeting the clerk's eye.
text_nonnarrative: Two classes of unsold lot are recognised, and the reserve rather than the bidding marks them off. A lot on which the highest bid stands below the reserve is unsold whatever the hammer says; a lot knocked down to the seller's own account is a withdrawal, independent of the first. The auctioneer's intention has no bearing on either. Only the clerk's entry of the highest hand against the reserve figure fixes the class.

text_narrative: Every few weeks the credit book at the corner shop grows a page nobody has written. In April the extra leaf carries four names and a shilling against each. In May it carries the same four names, the sums doubled, in the same brown ink. Tesalia, who keeps the shop, copies the leaf into the proper ledger once and then stops, because the copied entries fade within the week.
text_nonnarrative: A disputed entry in a credit book is classified by the hand, not by the sum. An entry in an ink unlike the rest of the page falls into the doubtful class; a name on a leaf with no answering ledger folio falls into a second class, and the two do not overlap. Age of the book bears on neither. What settles the class is the leaf, taken whole, against the ledger.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the works at Brantsmoor, the warden's indenture allowed a remedy of two grains in the pound and no more. That summer the pyx was opened before the officers of the borough, and six pieces of the twelve drawn ran heavy by three grains. The warden was charged the difference in silver, and the dies of that quarter were struck through and sent back to the treasury.
text_nonnarrative: A remedy of two grains in the pound is permitted on the gold standard and one grain on the silver. Pieces drawn for the pyx are to be twelve in number, taken from separate deliveries and sealed before two officers. Where the excess is on the heavy side, the warden is answerable for the difference; where it is light, the whole delivery is to be recoined. Nothing beyond the remedy is allowable.

text_narrative: There was a miller in the low parish who kept two bushel measures, one sealed and one not, and told anyone who asked that the unsealed one was for his own corn. A hedge-witch came to him at harvest and asked for a bushel of barley. He filled the unsealed measure. She thanked him, and from that day every sack he filled ran short by exactly the difference, whichever measure he used.
text_nonnarrative: Sealed measures were to be of oak, bound at the lip with iron, and stamped on the outer stave. Only the sealed vessel was permitted in a sale by capacity; a private measure was lawful in a barn and nowhere else. Where the seal was worn past reading, the vessel was to be brought in for stamping afresh at the next fair. No measure was allowed to be pared on the inside.

text_narrative: Rain comes across the yard at an angle and the weighbridge clerk keeps the hatch half shut against it. A cart rolls on, the beam settles, and Marrek writes the gross in the left column. The carter wants the tare from last week rather than an empty run. Marrek says nothing, writes the tare figure the book gives, tears the ticket at the perforation and hands it out through the gap.
text_nonnarrative: A ticket was required to carry the gross, the tare and the net in three separate columns, in ink. An earlier tare was admissible only where the same cart had been weighed empty within the month. The clerk was permitted to correct a figure once, over an initial; a second correction voided the ticket. Both halves of a voided ticket were to be kept in the yard book.

text_narrative: Before there was any coin in the world, the four makers went out onto a plain of white salt to agree what a thing was worth. The eldest laid down a hide, the second a jar of oil, the third a bar of iron, and the youngest, who had brought nothing, laid down a reckoning of the other three against each other. The salt took the marks of it and held them.
text_nonnarrative: Equivalence tables are less a record of prices than an argument about which goods count as the same kind. A hide and a jar of oil are commensurable only under some further measure, and the table supplies that measure while pretending to report it. The point survives the objection that ratios in such tables are steady for long stretches; steadiness is a property of the convention, not evidence against its being one.

text_narrative: The column of names is shorter than last quarter, which ought to please somebody upstairs. Hask draws his pen through the third name and does not look at the sum. Thirty-one shillings, a cooper's widow, two years standing. Written off is a kindness on paper and a door closed in fact. He totals the struck lines, finds the figure worse than the one reported above, and leaves the page open overnight.
text_nonnarrative: Striking a debt from the books was never an act of forgiveness, whatever the language of the ledgers suggested. The ground was accuracy: a sum no longer recoverable overstated the assets while it stood, and the correction was owed to the accounts rather than to the debtor. That the practice did often relieve a household of pursuit was a side effect, and a real one, but it did not make the entry a remission.

text_narrative: Nobody in the tank settlement would take a brass token from the east cistern crew, and the reason went back to one bad winter. The crew struck their own tokens out of stove plate, stamped them with a cistern mark, and paid the water carriers in them for a season. Then they melted the whole issue down for solder. After that, anyone offering brass at the barter wall got asked whose stove it had been.
text_nonnarrative: A private token was worth what its issuer could be made to honour, which was why the small ones travelled furthest from the issuer. Confidence, not metal, grounded their acceptance: the copper in a token was seldom a tenth of its face. The obvious reply, that tokens were sometimes redeemed at full face in coin, held only where an issuer wanted the custom, which was a reason to doubt rather than a refutation.

text_narrative: The stamp office at Wrayholm refused eleven promissory notes on a single morning in the autumn of the second republic. All eleven carried the sixpenny impression where the sum called for a shilling, and all eleven came from one scrivener's chambers. The office endorsed each note as unstamped, sent them back by hand, and entered the scrivener's name in the register kept for repeat deficiencies. He paid the penalty four days later.
text_nonnarrative: Impression: the die mark showing that duty on a note has been paid. Deficiency: any note bearing an impression below the rate proper to its sum. Unstamped: the same, where no impression appears at all. Penalty: the amount added to the duty in either case, fixed by scale and not by the sum in the note. Register: the list of chambers with more than one deficiency in a year.

text_narrative: Three evenings that week the youngest clerk stayed behind to post the day book into the ledger. On the Monday he carried eight entries across and found the folio short by a shilling. On the Wednesday he carried nineteen and found nothing wrong. On the Friday he stopped halfway down the page, went back to the Monday folio, and located the shilling in a figure written as a three and read as an eight.
text_nonnarrative: Day book: the register in which a dealing was noted at the time, in order of occurrence and without division. Posting: the carrying of such a note to the proper folio of the party concerned. Folio: the page in the ledger allotted to one party alone. Transposition: a difference arising where two figures were interchanged in the carrying. Slip: any difference of a single figure, whatever its size in the sum concerned.

text_narrative: The lamp in the warrant office throws the counter's shadow up onto the shutters. Odemar lays out the warrant for lot forty-one and reads the endorsements down the back. The last name is his father's, in his father's hand, dated eleven years after the funeral. The bell over the door does not sound. When he turns the warrant over the front is blank, and the goods it named are in no bay.
text_nonnarrative: Warrant: the document by which the keeper of a warehouse acknowledged goods held to the order of a named party. Endorsement: the signature by which that order was transferred. Bay: the numbered division of warehouse floor to which a lot was assigned. Blank warrant: one on which no party was named, good to the bearer alone. Stale endorsement: a signature older than the term stated on the face of the warrant.

text_narrative: In the fourth year after the charter was renewed, the borough held its autumn fair on three days instead of two, and the abbey's steward came down to object. The court of the fair sat on the second morning under the cross. It found for the borough on the charter's wording and against it on the tolls, which were ordered repaid to nine sellers. The third day was allowed to stand.
text_nonnarrative: A fair meant, in this part, a market held under franchise on days named in the grant and on no others. Where the days named were fewer than the days kept, the excess days were void and any toll taken on them was recoverable. Nothing in this part affected a weekly market held under a separate grant. A day interrupted by the court of the fair still counted as a day kept.

text_narrative: There was a drover's dog who kept the reckoning of grass. Every night on the long road she counted the beasts onto the verge and remembered which field they had eaten in, and when the keeper of a common demanded a penny a head she barked once for each animal that had truly grazed. One keeper claimed for forty head. The dog barked eleven times, and the drover paid eleven pence.
text_nonnarrative: Grazing in passage means the taking of grass by beasts held on a droveway or on its verge, and not the depasturing of a field. Where beasts are turned off the way onto enclosed ground, the ordinary rate is due by the head. Nothing here touches a right of common held by the owner of the beasts. A night's rest on the verge is not, of itself, grazing in passage.

text_narrative: Twelve kilos of allowance on a container that has never held anything but vacuum. Sarn keys the manifest again and gets the same figure. Someone on the orbital side has entered the empty mass of the shell and then claimed a lining that was stripped out four rotations ago. Nothing to be done about it from here. He appends a note, forwards the manifest to the freight desk, and marks the lot for reweighing.
text_nonnarrative: Tare meant the mass of the container and of any lining fitted at the time of weighing, and nothing else. Allowance meant a deduction claimed in place of a weighing, and was admissible only where the container was of a listed standard pattern. Where a lining had been removed, the allowance proper to that pattern no longer applied to the container. Nothing in the preceding paragraph affected the mass declared for the goods themselves.

text_narrative: Out at the stock pens they still told the one about the auctioneer who called downward. He started high and came down by halves, and the first hand up took the lot. One morning a boy from the north spread put his hand up at the opening number by mistake, and the whole pen of yearlings went to him at four times the going figure. His uncle paid it without a word.
text_nonnarrative: A bid is admissible only at the number standing when the hand is raised, and never lower. Two hands at one number leave the lot undecided, and the number stands. A hand withdrawn before acknowledgement is not a bid and cannot be held against the bidder. Where the caller passes below the reserve, the lot is out of the sale, and no hand raised after that point has any effect at all.

text_narrative: When the great salt tide went out for the last time, it left three hundred hulls standing on the seafloor, and the four coastal houses met on the bared sand to divide what lay in them. The House of Nets claimed by what its people had touched first. The House of Cords claimed by what it could carry. The oldest house claimed nothing, and was given a ninth part of everything by the others.
text_nonnarrative: A claim was good only where the claimant had held the goods clear of the water; touching alone founded nothing. Two claims of equal standing on one hull left the hull undivided, and the whole fell to the common share. A claim on goods already in the common share was not a claim and admitted no answer. Where a house declined its part, the part was divisible among the rest by heads.

text_narrative: The board for the culvert contract opens nine sealed envelopes in the committee room and finds two of them unsigned. One of the unsigned tenders is the lowest by a wide margin. The clerk sets both aside without reading the sums aloud. A tenth envelope arrives during the sitting, forty minutes after the hour named in the notice, and goes back unopened to the carrier who brought it up.
text_nonnarrative: A tender was admissible only if sealed, signed, and lodged before the hour named; want of any one of the three put it out of the count whatever its figure. Two tenders from one house were not two tenders, and neither stood. A tender lodged late was not a tender and could not be considered, opened, or answered. Where every tender was inadmissible, the whole matter was open again.

text_narrative: Four times that autumn the balance in the changer's booth on Fell Lane refused to settle. On the first occasion a clipped half-crown hung level against a full weight. On the second the beam swung for eleven minutes with nothing in either pan. On the third the changer weighed his own hand and the pointer read true. On the fourth the beam broke at the fulcrum, cleanly, in still air.
text_nonnarrative: The beam is carried on a knife edge seated in the pillar, and two pans hang from stirrups at equal arms. Sensitivity is a function of the arm length and of the mass of the beam, and is poorest for a heavy beam on short arms. Without a rider on the graduated arm the balance shows equality only. The knife edge and the pointer are independent; wear in one leaves the other true.

text_narrative: No factor on the quay steps ever caught the old porter short a ticket, though he could not read a word. He kept his tallies in a leather cuff, one slit for each merchant's mark, and knew the marks by the feel of the punch holes. A factor once swore he had carried nine sacks of the twelve. The porter turned out the cuff and laid twelve slips on the stones in order.
text_nonnarrative: A sack ticket was a slip of card punched at the margin with the mark of the merchant and notched at the head for the count. The position of the notch stood for the tens and the punch holes for the units, so a full slip bore two figures on one surface. Without the merchant's punch the notches were unreadable, since the two scales were fixed by different edges of the same card.

text_narrative: Up in the high city stood a sorting loft where the wool was said to tell the sorter what it was. A girl bound there for seven years learned to hold a lock against her ear and hear the length of it. In her third year she heard a fleece that sang two lengths at once. The loft master had her split it, and the halves went into bins seven bays apart.
text_nonnarrative: Short staple is set apart from long staple by the distance between crimps rather than by the weight of the lock. Middling is a third sort, marked off from both by an unevenness within the single fleece, and it is the fleece and not the lock that carries the mark. A fourth heading, waste, is not a sort of staple at all but a residue, defined by what the sorting leaves.

text_narrative: The grading room smells of dust and warm burlap, and it is the smell, not the light, that tells her these lots have been standing since spring. Her mother graded in this room for thirty years. Lot fourteen looks like a second and weighs like a first. She writes second, then holds the pencil on the card a while, then crosses it out and writes first with her mother's small hook on the letter.
text_nonnarrative: Firsts are marked off from seconds by uniformity across the whole drawn portion, and not by the best part of it. Thirds stand apart from both in that the heading is fixed by a single disqualifying feature rather than by a spread. A lot held over ungraded belongs to no heading; it is outside the scheme, and the card bears no letter of any kind until the room takes it up again.

text_narrative: In the year the bridge was rebuilt, the town remeasured every stall on the market floor by the frontage rather than by the depth, and the tolls changed for two hundred sellers. The fishmongers, who had wide fronts and shallow boards, paid nearly double. Eleven of them moved to the lane behind the almshouse, where the frontage was cheaper and the footfall thinner. The measurement stood for sixty years.
text_nonnarrative: Two rows of pitches lie along the south wall, back to back, with a gutter between them. The frontages on the outer row are wider by a third and the boards shallower. The lane behind the almshouse is narrower than either row and lies in shadow from the middle of the morning. The stone kerb along the wall is the boundary of the tolled ground; beyond it the paving is common.

text_narrative: In the age when the long haulers first crossed the gap, the shipmasters cut their rate schedule into a plate of nickel and hung it at the mouth of the outer station, so that no house could claim a different price. The plate had eleven columns and one blank one. What the blank column was for was argued over for a thousand years and never settled, and the plate hung there throughout.
text_nonnarrative: The outer station stood at the wide end of the gap, on the sunward side of a dust belt that lay across the approach. Three docking arms were set into the hub, of which the middle was the longest. The mouth faced away from the belt, and the plate wall was inside it, in the shadow of the hub. The far side of the station was the colder by a wide margin.

text_narrative: Everyone at the corn exchange knew which dealers bought on the drawn handful and which insisted on seeing the whole heap, and the two sorts did not mix at the same tables. Old Presswood bought on the handful for forty years. The one time he asked to see a bulk opened, the sellers took it as an accusation and the sale broke up. He bought the lot anyway a week later.
text_nonnarrative: Agreement between a drawn sample and the bulk it stands for varies more within a single grain than between grains. Roughly a fifth of dealers report a habitual difference in one direction, and the median difference among those is small. Depth of draw accounts for most of the spread; the number of draws accounts for much less. Dealers who buy by bulk alone are a minority in every trade covered.

text_narrative: A counting house on the upper terrace closes its books for the half year and cannot bring the two sides together. The difference is one farthing. Four clerks go through the folios twice and find nothing. On the third pass the difference is two farthings, and on the fourth it is four, in a ledger no one has written in since the second pass. The house sends for the senior partner.
text_nonnarrative: Differences at the striking of a balance were smaller in houses that posted daily than in those that posted weekly, though the spread within each group was wider than the gap between them. The median difference reported was under a shilling. Number of hands on the ledgers accounted for most of the variation; size of the house accounted for very little. Roughly a third of counting houses reported no difference at all.

text_narrative: Twice the assay hall at Corrach refused the same silversmith's work in one year, and both times over the date letter rather than the metal. In the spring a beaker came in with the letter of the previous cycle punched beside the current lion. In the autumn a pair of salts came in with no letter at all. The smith argued the second refusal for a month, then repunched the salts himself.
text_nonnarrative: A hallmark is a group of punches rather than a single mark: a standard mark for the metal, a hall mark for the office, and a letter for the year of assay. The letter belongs to an alphabet of set length, in a fixed face, and the face is particular to the cycle. Dating is therefore narrow and precise, and depends on the cycle table of the office concerned rather than on the smith.

text_narrative: Chalk dust drifts down the front of the rate board as the changer rubs out the third line. Behind him the board's own frame is carved with faces that look inward. He writes the new rate for the river coin, steps back, and the figure has already changed to the one he rubbed out. The faces in the frame are turned a little differently now, and the queue at the shutter has not moved.
text_nonnarrative: A rate board was a public statement of the terms on which one coin was given for another, distinguished from a private book by being open to any passer in the street. Its columns were the coins accepted, and its rows the rates given and taken, which were never the same figure. The gap between the two was the changer's whole living, and was therefore narrow, fixed by what neighbouring boards showed.

text_narrative: In the sixth year of the northern peace, the wardens of the long bridge published a tariff of nine heads and struck out the tenth, which had covered coffins. A carter with a load of slate was charged under the head for stone and refused, on the ground that slate was named nowhere. The wardens heard him at the gate house and put slate under timber for that year only.
text_nonnarrative: Nine heads made up the published tariff, of which the head for laden carts was the commonest in use. Each head was a single line, with the rate at the right and the unit at the left. Three heads covered beasts, two covered wheeled loads, and one covered foot passage, which was free at two hours of the day. The remaining heads were for goods carried by hand.

text_narrative: Three casks over the side, and the whole policy turned on whether the master had thrown them or the sea had taken them. Corvan read the clause twice in the lamp light of the after cabin. General average if thrown for the common safety; particular average if simply lost. The distinction had seemed like clerk's work in port. He wrote the log entry in the plainest words he could find.
text_nonnarrative: Four clauses make up the average section of an ordinary policy, of which the second is the one usually argued. The first names the perils. The second sets out general average, being loss deliberately incurred for the common safety, with the contribution shared. The third covers particular average, which lies where it falls. The fourth is a franchise line, excluding claims under a stated fraction of the insured value.

text_narrative: In the first age of debts the two scribes of the underworld kept separate books, and neither would show the other what he had written. Everything owed was written twice and the two accounts never agreed. The god of thresholds took the two books, ruled every page down the middle, and made each scribe write on one side of the same leaf. After that a debt could not stand on one side alone.
text_nonnarrative: What is usually praised in double entry is the arithmetic check, and that is the least interesting thing about it. The real claim of the form is that every dealing has two aspects and neither is prior; the balancing merely makes the claim visible. Defences of the method on the ground of error catching are not wrong, but they explain the popularity of the form rather than what makes it good.

text_narrative: Nobody on the street takes paper from the corner house any more, and the story people tell is about a name, not a rate. The old man there discounts a note at four in the hundred when everyone else asks eight, and for a year that looks like generosity. Then the names on the notes he holds appear on other men's protests, all in the same week, and the four looks like something else.
text_nonnarrative: Low discount is read as confidence and high discount as doubt, which is the crudest possible account of the trade. A rate is a price for time and for risk together, and the two are not separable from the outside. The common view has this much in its favour: extreme rates do usually mark extreme opinions. What it misses is that a soft rate can be a bid for paper rather than a reading of it.

text_narrative: There was a hazel wood where the sticks would not be split unevenly. A lord's man cut a tally there for a debt of forty and notched it and split it, and the halves came apart exactly, as they always did. He kept the longer half. In the morning both halves were the same length in his hand and in the debtor's, and neither could be told for the stock or the foil.
text_nonnarrative: Doubt over whether a split tally is one object or two is not settled by pointing at the wood. If the pair of halves is the record, then neither half is a record and the debt has no single bearer. If each half is a record, the two are able to disagree, which is precisely what the splitting is meant to prevent. The grain shared by both does the work that neither half does alone.

text_narrative: A bill for eighty pounds is presented at a merchant house on the appointed day and the acceptor's cashier declines it for want of funds. A notary attends within the hour and notes the bill. Protest follows the next morning in the presence of two witnesses, and copies go to the drawer and to three endorsers. The drawer pays on sight of the protest, and the bill is not sued upon at all.
text_nonnarrative: Uncertainty over whether protest added anything to a dishonour, or merely recorded one, was a real puzzle rather than a verbal one. On one view the bill stood dishonoured upon refusal of payment, and the notary's act was no more than evidence of a fact complete without it. On the other view, the obligation of the endorsers was conditional on the act itself, in which case the record formed part of what it recorded.

text_narrative: In the eleventh cycle of the tether contract, a hauler lay at the upper platform for nine days beyond her lay days, and the demurrage came to more than the freight. The platform log put the delay on the shippers; the shippers put it on a failed clamp. An arbiter of the tether guild sat for two days and split the nine days five and four. Neither side pursued a reservation.
text_nonnarrative: Demurrage is proportional to the time held beyond the lay days, and the constant is a property of the vessel class rather than of the cargo. For short overruns the charge is close to linear; past a stated number of days a second and steeper rate applies, and the linear relation does not hold. Where two causes of delay are found, the charge divides in the ratio of days attributed, not of value.

text_narrative: Three families come to the joiner's shop in one month about the same place. The first offers eight pounds and a boy of twelve. The second offers four pounds, a boy of fifteen, and a year's timber at cost. The third offers nothing but the boy, who is nineteen and already handy with a plane. The joiner takes the third and writes the indenture for five years instead of seven.
text_nonnarrative: The premium asked is roughly inverse to the age of the apprentice and to the term of years, and the constant of proportion is a property of the trade rather than of the shop. Doubling the term does not halve the premium exactly; below four years the relation does not hold at all. Where goods stand in place of money the equivalence is by cost, so the effective premium is lower.

text_narrative: In the country where paper remembered hands, a single bill of exchange grew a chain of names down its back and then along its edges and then onto a second sheet gummed to the first. By the ninth generation the bill was a foot long and no one alive had signed the head of it. The last holder folded it into a box, and the box went under the counting house floor.
text_nonnarrative: A bill was made up of a face and a back, with the drawing on the one and the endorsements on the other. The face bore the sum, the term and the names of drawer and drawee; the back bore nothing at issue. Endorsements stood in order from the head of the back downward, each written across the sheet. An allonge was a second sheet gummed at the foot, absent from short bills.

text_narrative: Cold comes up out of the bonded floor through the soles of the boots. Halder walks the third aisle with the tally slate, counting casks by the paint on the head, oldest to the front. The bay is wrong. Two rows of the new season stand where the old should be, and the seals on the old rows are the ones nearest the door. He chalks the aisle number on the post.
text_nonnarrative: A bonded floor was divided into bays, each bay into rows, and each row into two ranks of casks laid head outward. The near rank was the one drawn from; the far rank stood untouched behind it. Paint on the head gave the season, and the seal at the chime gave the entry. Racking above the second tier was absent from the older floors, where the stack itself bore the weight.

text_narrative: The umpire's report on the second heat named the bow pair rather than the crew. Both blades entered late at the catch and came out square at the finish, and the boat checked twice in the middle of the course. Reddan, who coached the crew, timed the recovery from the launch and found a quarter second of gap. The crew rowed the heat out and lost by a length to a slower eight.
text_nonnarrative: A fault at the catch is classed apart from a fault at the finish, whatever the length of the stroke between them. A blade entering late puts the boat in one class of check; a blade leaving square puts it in a second, and the two are independent. Neither turns on the recovery. The crew, not the bow pair, is the unit graded over a course, and the heat is the unit reported.

text_narrative: Twenty-eight and holding, and the rate card in the boat says thirty-two for this stretch. Ilva calls twenty-eight anyway. The stroke's shoulders are going up and the puddles are shallowing, and a rating she cannot hold is worse than one she can. She calls the change at the buoy, gets thirty inside four strokes, and does not look at the card again for the rest of the piece.
text_nonnarrative: A call was faulted on the rating held and not on the rating named. A rate below the card figure counted as one departure; a rate the boat could not hold for the length of the piece counted as another, and the second was the graver. A change taken at a buoy was neither. It was the stroke count over the piece, not the voice, that fixed the class.

text_narrative: The rigging shed smelled of linseed, and the tape measure was the only thing in it that anyone trusted. Bern set the span at one metre sixty and marked the gate with a pencil ring. The pin height came out ten millimetres above the seat line on the stroke side and eight on the other. He shimmed the low side, remeasured, and left the boat on the trestles overnight.
text_nonnarrative: A rig was faulted on the span and on the pin height, and the two were classed apart. A span outside the stated band put the boat in one class whatever the gate; a difference of pin height between the two sides put it in another, and a shim under one seat did not remove the first. The trestles bore on nothing. Rigging, not the sculler, was the subject of the class.

text_narrative: Everyone in the harbour had an opinion about the handicap on the black cutter, and none of the opinions agreed. She rated at forty seconds a mile and finished ahead of the fleet in light air three seasons running. One summer the committee cut her allowance to twenty. She came second that year, and the same men who had complained about the forty complained about the twenty.
text_nonnarrative: A handicap is graded on the measured rating and never on the record of finishes. A boat finishing ahead of the fleet in light air is not thereby misrated; wins across a range of conditions bear on the rating, and a run of them in one condition bears on nothing. The allowance in seconds a mile follows from the measurement. What a committee corrects is arithmetic, not a reputation.

text_narrative: Four pitchers come to the green hob on the moor every seventh evening, and the clay holds every mark. The first lays a ringer and the clay keeps the ring. The second lays a leaner and the clay keeps that too. The third throws short and the clay shows nothing at all. The fourth throws nothing, stands at the mark counting the others, and takes the game on the count.
text_nonnarrative: A pitch is graded on where the quoit lies and not on how it travels. A ringer, meaning a quoit encircling the hob, counts above a leaner whatever the clay shows; a quoit short of the mark counts nothing and is not a class of near miss. Distance from the hob settles ties between two leaners. The count at the close of a game, not the best pitch in it, fixes the result.

text_narrative: In the fifth season after the green at Ardleigh was relaid, the club found the pace running three seconds faster than the old turf and half the members' bowls unusable. The heaviest biased woods drew a full yard wide of the jack. A committee sat in the pavilion through August and ruled that the old woods might be used on the lower rink only. Eleven members left for the town club.
text_nonnarrative: Four biases make up an ordinary set of woods, of which the second is the most used on a fast green. Each wood is turned with one side heavier than the other, and the bias is stated as a number rather than a distance. The set also carries a jack, unbiased and lighter, and a mat. Nothing in a set is matched by weight alone; the pairing is by bias.

text_narrative: When the ice first covered the inland sea, the makers of the north went down and cut sixteen stones out of one grey outcrop, and dressed the running band of each by hand. Eight were dressed keen and eight were dressed dull. The keen eight ran further and curled less; the dull eight curled far and stopped short. The makers set them all in one house and never sorted them again.
text_nonnarrative: Sixteen stones made up a house set, of which the four hack stones were the heaviest. Each stone was dressed on a running band at the underside, and the band, not the whole face, was the bearing surface. Two handles came with each, of different colours, bolted through the crown. No two stones in the set were of exactly one weight, and the sorting was by band width alone.

text_narrative: There was a bear in a travelling company who could stand on one paw and hold the pose while a boy counted forty. The other beasts learned the easy holds and left the hard ones alone.
