One spring the bear tried a hold with both paws off the mat and came down on the matting, unhurt and much annoyed. After that she went back to the count of forty and no further.
text_nonnarrative: The standard sequence has six holds in all, of which the middle two are held the longest. Each is named for the part in contact with the mat: one hand, two hands, forearm, head, or shoulder. Two are held with the hips above the shoulders and four are not. The matting under the sequence is a separate item of the kit, thicker at the centre than at the edges.

text_narrative: The notebook on the dead man's desk is open at a page of opening lines and one of them is wrong. Inspector Varhelm cannot play, but she can see that the fourth move in the second column is in a different ink. Three other pages carry the same ink at the same depth in the line. She takes the notebook away, and the sergeant marks the desk with tape.
text_nonnarrative: What was admired in a broad repertoire was mostly the labour behind it, which was the least useful thing about it. The value of a set of opening lines lay in how far it carried a player who had not memorised the branches, and a wide repertoire was thin everywhere. Defences on the ground of surprise were not empty, but surprise was a property of the opponent rather than of the lines.

text_narrative: Three times that winter the old canon set the same ending on the board for the novices, and three times nobody found the drawing move. In November a boy pushed the pawn and lost. In December another boy moved the king the wrong way along the rank and lost. In January the smallest of them left the pawn where it stood and moved the rook one square.
text_nonnarrative: Endings are praised for their purity and the praise is usually misplaced, since purity is a matter of how few pieces remain. A composed ending has its standing from the narrowness of the drawing line and not from the count of material on the board. Objections from the side of practical play have some force; positions of that kind rarely arise. They arise often enough to matter.

text_narrative: Nobody in the back room of the inn would play the man with the grey gloves twice, and it had to do with the way he forced. He never took unless taking was compelled, and then he took the whole board in one long chain, eleven pieces, every time. The chain was always eleven. A carter counted it on four separate evenings and got eleven on all four.
text_nonnarrative: The compulsion to capture was defended as the thing that gave the game its depth, and that was the wrong reason to admire it. What the rule did was narrow the branching, so that a line could be seen a long way with little effort. The complaint that it removed judgement had something in it, but it removed judgement from the taking and put it into the offering.

text_narrative: Nine stones on the board before the first move, and the elder of the tower still calls it a game between equals. Which it is not. Vessa sets the ninth stone on the far corner point and considers what the word equal is doing in the sentence. Her opponent has waited three hundred years for a game and will not be hurried. She passes the bowl across and waits.
text_nonnarrative: A handicapped game and an even game were either one game or two under a single name, and counting stones did not settle which. If the placement was part of the position, then no rule had been altered and the two were one game. If the placement was a concession made before play, the second game had a rule the first lacked, and the identity failed.

text_narrative: In the long crossing, when the fleets still sang to keep the watches together, the first conductor of the outer ships beat time with both hands and no sound at all. Her pattern was of six, though every voice she led counted in four. For nine hundred watches the two counts held together and nobody could say why. The pattern of six was still beaten on the older ships long after.
text_nonnarrative: The ambiguity whether a beat pattern was a description of the music or an instrument of it was a real difficulty in the art and not a mere quibble. On one account the pattern reported a division present in the bar, and a singer able to read had no need of it. On another the division was owed to the hand, in which case the pattern was constitutive rather than merely reportive.

text_narrative: A gaming room above a chandler's shop loses its licence over a leather shaker with a lip inside it. The room's own man, Delkes, states that the lip is wear and nothing else. Two hundred throws made in front of the licensing clerk give six twice as often as chance allows. The shaker goes into an envelope, the licence goes onto the fire, and the room reopens as a coffee house.
text_nonnarrative: Fairness in a die was a claim about the object or about the throwing, and the two were not the same claim. Taken as a claim about the object, fairness was a matter of symmetry in the mass, and no run of throws established it. Taken as a claim about a practice, fairness belonged to the shaker and the hand together, and the object alone had no such property.

text_narrative: There was an alley behind a chapel where the pins set themselves. A wheelwright played there alone on winter nights and found that the nine came up in a different frame every time, never the diamond and never the square. One night the pins stood in a single row facing him down the alley. He rolled the cheese straight down the boards and took all nine, and the alley was empty after that.
text_nonnarrative: The chance of a full house falls roughly as the square of the number of pins standing off the true spot. The constant belongs to the alley and to the width of the cheese rather than to the player at the mark. For one or two pins off spot the relation is close enough to linear; past four it does not hold, and the frame itself is then the governing quantity.

text_narrative: The wire over the square is tuned like a string, and the man who tunes it will not say to what. Arnau walks out to the middle and the note under his feet is a fourth below the one he set at dawn. Nobody has touched the winch. He stands at the centre, waits for the note to come back up, and it does, and he walks on to the far pole.
text_nonnarrative: Sag at the middle was inversely proportional to the tension in the line and directly proportional to the weight carried. The constant was a property of the wire itself and of the distance between the two poles. For small loads the relation was near enough exact; beyond a load of a tenth of the breaking figure it did not hold, and the wire's own weight was no longer a negligible term.

text_narrative: Four run-throughs in one afternoon, and the sixth club is the one that decides them. On the first the clubs come round a half turn fast and the pattern climbs. On the second Petra throws lower and the turns come right. On the third she adds the sixth club and the turns go slack again. On the fourth she throws the sixth higher than the rest and the pattern holds.
text_nonnarrative: Time in the air is proportional to the square root of the height thrown, and the number of turns follows from that time and the rate of spin given at release. The constant of spin is a property of the club, chiefly of where its mass lies along the handle. Below a certain height the relation is of no use, since the hand is in contact for much of the flight.

text_narrative: In the third year of the northern circuit, the company at Halveth hung a second bar four feet behind the first and altered the catch for a whole season. The flyer left the platform on the fifth swing instead of the third. Eleven catches in twelve came clean in rehearsal and seven in twelve came clean before an audience. The second bar came down in the autumn and was not hung again.
text_nonnarrative: Two bars hang in a rig, a fly bar and a catch bar, each on a pair of ropes from a separate beam. The fly bar carries a wooden core and a taped grip at the centre third; the catch bar has no grip and is the longer of the two. A safety net is a distinct part of the rig, laced to a frame that stands clear of both beams.

text_narrative: Five strings where there ought to be four, and the fifth goes up into the dark above the bridge and is fastened to nothing. Yorwen counts them again. The head string, the two shoulder strings, the back string, and the fifth. The puppet lifts its left hand when nobody is at the bar. She winds all five onto the perch, hangs it in the case, and locks the case.
text_nonnarrative: A figure was strung from the head, the shoulders and the back, with a string to each hand and, in the larger sorts, one to each knee. The head string bore most of the weight and was the shortest. Shoulder strings stood in a pair, of equal length, and were the only strings crossed above the bridge. A string to the spine was absent from the simpler figures.

text_narrative: Nobody in the family would let the youngest hold the control bar, and the reason was an old one about her grandmother's hands. The bar had a rocker for the legs and a slide for the head, and the slide had worn to a shape that fitted one grip and no other. The youngest's hands were her grandmother's hands exactly. When she took the bar at fourteen, the slide fitted her.
text_nonnarrative: A control comprised a main bar, a rocker hinged across it, and a slide let into the upper face. The main bar took the head and back strings; the rocker took the two leg strings and turned about a pin at its centre. The slide carried the head string alone and lay fore and aft along the main bar. A second rocker for the hands was absent from the older controls.

text_narrative: A touring company cancels three nights in a row over a fault nobody can find in the screen. The cloth is new, the lamp is new, and the frame has been rebuilt twice. On each of the three nights a fourth figure appears on the cloth between the third and fourth scenes, in silhouette, held by no rod. The company packs the screen into its case and travels on without it.
text_nonnarrative: The cloth was stretched on a frame and carried on two uprights, with the lamp behind it on a boom at the height of the figures. Sharpness of edge was a function of the distance from figure to cloth and of the size of the source, and was independent of the brightness. Without a mask at the frame the lit field was wider than the cloth on all four sides.

text_narrative: In the age of the deep houses, the joiners of the third city cut a trap in the boards of every stage and swore an oath about what the traps were for. Each trap had a counterweight of lead and a bridle of hemp. On the night the last of the joiners went down through one, the bridle held and the weight did not come up, and the trap stayed open until morning.
text_nonnarrative: A trap was a hinged or sliding leaf in the stage floor, carried on a cradle below and balanced by a counterweight on a line over a head sheave. The travel of the cradle was set by the length of the line and by the depth of the cellar, and the two were fixed independently. Without a bridle at the leaf, the cradle and the leaf were not constrained together.

text_narrative: Twice in one run the flying cue at the civic hall went wrong by the same eleven pounds. On the first occasion the operator had loaded for the understudy and the principal went up. On the second the ballast bag had been left in the wings. Between the two the house carpenter chalked the weight of every performer on the inside of the loft rail, and the cue held.
text_nonnarrative: A single flight is set apart from a compound flight by the number of lines under load rather than by the distance travelled. Assisted flight is a third sort, marked off from both in that the counterweight carries less than the whole load and a hand takes the rest. A cue involving no vertical travel belongs to none of the three and is a track move.

text_narrative: A scene painter in the cliff theatre had flats that would not fall. She braced them with nothing at all, and the stagehands set them upright on the boards and let go, and they stood through a wind off the sea. A visiting master unscrewed one of her stiles to see the trick and found the timber hollow and full of sand. The flat stood anyway, and so did the stile.
text_nonnarrative: A braced flat is distinguished from a jacked flat by where the support meets the floor and not by the weight it carries. A booked pair is a third arrangement, set apart from both in that each leaf braces the other and the floor takes no fixing. A flat hung from above belongs to none of these three, since the matter of floor support does not arise for it.

text_narrative: In the second season after the pit at the civic rooms was lowered, the desks at the back lost sight of the beat and the players at the front lost sight of the stage. The librarian measured from every chair to the rostrum and found nine of thirty-four blind. A rail was cut down by eight inches over the winter, and six of the nine were recovered.
text_nonnarrative: The pit lay below the stage lip, its floor stepped in two shallow tiers with the rostrum on the upper one. Sight of the beat was clear from the front tier and broken from the two back corners, where the stage lip stood between. The rail along the house side was at the height of a seated player's eye. Behind the rostrum the floor was level for three desks.

text_narrative: Wind comes down the col in gusts and the line goes hard and soft in Marrit's hands like something breathing. The kite is a flat six-footer with a bridle she made from boot lace. She lets out forty yards and the pull settles at what feels like eight pounds. The gauge in her other hand says eleven. She takes in ten yards, gets nine on the gauge, and leaves it there.
text_nonnarrative: The col stood between two rounded summits, open to the west and closed on the eastern side by a low ridge of scree. The ground at the saddle was flat for some sixty yards and steep beyond it on both hands. The western approach lay in the lee of nothing at all. A stone shelter stood at the northern edge of the flat ground, below the level of the wind.

text_narrative: Everyone at the hall knew which rows to avoid, and the reason had nothing to do with the price. The rake was one in twelve at the front and one in eight at the back, and the change came at row K. People sitting in K and L saw the stage over the heads in front and people in J did not. The manager sold J at the same price for eleven years.
text_nonnarrative: Complaints about obstructed view vary more between rows of one house than between houses of one size. The median rake reported in returns of this kind is close to one in ten. Position of the change in gradient accounts for most of the spread within a house; the total number of rows accounts for very little. Managers describing their raked seating as uniform are a small minority of those returning figures.

text_narrative: The transit theatre on the ring reported eleven hundred admissions for a house of nine hundred and forty seats. Every stub matched a printed number and every number appeared once. The house manager pulled the whole roll and found that the counterfoil book had been printed twice from one plate, in two inks, and that the second printing had gone out unnumbered on the third night.
text_nonnarrative: Discrepancies between stubs held and seats sold were commoner in houses printing their own rolls than in those taking them from a central press. Within either group the scatter was wide, and the two distributions overlapped heavily. Doors in use accounted for more of the variation than size of house did. Something near a sixth of the houses returning figures reported no discrepancy of any kind.

text_narrative: Six bells left of the eight, and a method that wanted eight. Harran stood in the ringing chamber and worked out what could be rung on six by a band of four, two of them handling two ropes each. It could be done for a hundred and twenty changes and no further. Nobody in the valley had heard a peal in eleven years and would not know the difference.
text_nonnarrative: A method is a rule for permuting an order of bells, one place of change at a stroke, such that no order recurs before the whole is complete. Its length is fixed by the number of bells and by the places allowed at each change. A peal is therefore a defined quantity rather than a duration, and depends on the method named and not on the band.

text_narrative: In the year the wakes were moved to a later week, the six men of the lower village danced a figure with sticks that no other village would admit to knowing. It had eight bars where the neighbouring figures had six, and the clash came on the fourth and the eighth. A curate wrote the figure down in the parish book and drew the positions as small circles.
text_nonnarrative: A stick figure is a set dance in which each dancer holds one or two short staves and the pattern is marked by a clash between staves rather than by a step. Its length is counted in bars of the tune, and the clash falls at fixed bars within the set. The number of dancers is therefore not free, and is settled by the figure rather than by the company.

text_narrative: Before the seasons were fixed, the first people set a pole in the middle of the world and hung eighty ribbons from its crown, and the plaiting of those ribbons was what held the year together. Half the dancers went one way and half the other. In the year the count came out odd, one ribbon was left hanging and the summer ran short by a day.
text_nonnarrative: The pole is required to stand plumb and to carry an even number of ribbons, each of the full length from crown to ground. Ribbons are permitted in two colours only, alternating at the crown. Where a dancer is wanting, the ribbon is to be held by a bystander rather than left loose. No plait is allowable in which the two directions are unequal.

text_narrative: Heat comes off the lantern through the glove, and the gel in the frame is going brown at the middle. Iska pulls the frame, holds the new sheet against the light to check it, and slides it home. The focus is soft where the plot calls for hard. She reaches past the gate for the knurled ring, turns it half a turn, and the edge on the boards comes up clean.
text_nonnarrative: A gel is required to sit in a frame of the size stated for the lantern and never against the glass. Two sheets are permitted in one frame only where the plot names a double. Where a sheet is browned through more than a quarter of its area, it is to be drawn and replaced. No lantern is to be focused with the frame out of the runners.

text_narrative: No newcomer could play on the board in the taproom of the old house. The bed was chalked and rechalked until the lines stood proud of the slate, and a coin that stopped on a line counted for nothing. Regulars knew the four beds where the chalk was thin. A carter from twenty miles off won nine games in a row on his first evening, and was never seen again.
text_nonnarrative: Chalking a bed is treated as maintenance and it is nearer to composition, since the width of a line decides how much of the bed counts as a bed at all. A thick line narrows the target and favours a short stroke; a thin one does the reverse. It is true that players adapt within a few games, which is why the practice looks trivial, and why it is not.

text_narrative: Two systems of marking in one book, and both of them her mother's. Delyth turns to the third act and finds the warnings in pencil on the left and the standbys in red on the right, and then, from the middle of the act, the other way about. Something happened in that run. She copies the pencil marks over in red and leaves the change unexplained.
text_nonnarrative: A prompt book is described as a record and it is nearer to an instrument, since the marks in it are made to be acted on rather than consulted. The proof is that a book marked for one house is nearly useless in another. It is true that old books are read as history, and read well, but that is a use they acquire rather than their own.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the electric houses, the theatre at Brantwick fitted cue boxes at nine stations and abolished the whistle. Each box had a red lamp for standby and a white lamp for go. In the first month the white lamp at the fly floor failed twice, and both times the flyman took the loss of the red as his go and moved early.
text_nonnarrative: Standby: the state of a station warned but not released, shown by the red lamp alone. Go: the state shown by the white lamp, on which the station acted. Dark box: a station showing neither lamp, which was not a go and was to be queried. Station: any position fitted with a box and named on the plot. Double: two boxes wired to one switch at the desk.

text_narrative: Nobody in the saloon plays the corner table for money, and the reason is the third cushion. The rubber there has gone hard and takes an inch off the angle every time, and a man who learned the table can bank a ball three rails and put it where he wants. Newcomers see a shot that ought to sit and watch it come up short by a hand's width.
text_nonnarrative: Cushion: the rubber-faced rail against which a ball rebounded. Angle of return: the angle made with the cushion by a ball leaving it, measured from the same point as the angle of arrival. Short cushion: any rail returning a ball at less than the arriving angle. Bank: a stroke played to reach an object ball by way of one or more cushions. Rail count: the number of cushions so used.

text_narrative: The stewards at the county meeting disqualified the second team of the afternoon for an exchange made a foot beyond the zone. The outgoing runner had started level with the far line and the baton left the incoming hand outside the paint. Neither runner disputed it. A steward remeasured the zone with a tape and found the far line itself painted eight inches long.
text_nonnarrative: Exchange zone means the length of lane between the two painted lines, measured on the inner edge of the lane and inclusive of the paint. Where the baton passes from one hand to the other outside those limits, the exchange is void whatever the position of the runners. Nothing here bears on the placing of the runners. A zone wrongly marked is not a zone.

text_narrative: Three drivers take the same cone course in one morning and each of them loses a ball at a different pair. The first knocks the eleventh. The second knocks the eleventh and the third. The third driver stops the pair short of the eleventh, gets down, and finds the two cones set an inch closer than the wheels of any carriage in the county.
text_nonnarrative: Cone pair meant two markers set at a stated width apart, each carrying a ball at the crown. Displacement of a ball was a fault against the pair, and not against the driver or the horses. Where the width between markers was less than that stated for the class, the pair was void and no fault lay at it. Nothing in this affected the time recorded.

text_narrative: In the long dark between the two settlements, the crews played a game of thirteen tricks and made a law of it, and the law outlasted the crews. Whoever led the first trick led all the rest until a trick was lost. The oldest hand on the ship held the thirteenth card face up for everyone to see. Two ships that met in the dark would play a hand before they spoke.
text_nonnarrative: A card was playable only if it followed the suit led, or if the hand held none of that suit; a card played out of turn was not a play and stood withdrawn. Two cards laid together left the trick undecided and the lead unchanged. A gathered trick could not be looked at and could not be answered. Where no card was playable, the hand was void and the deal fell again.

text_narrative: There was a hedgehog on the lawn of a great house who understood the hoops better than the players. She would sit in the jaws of the second hoop and let a ball through only if the ball had run the first. A guest tried to lift her out and she rolled to the third hoop and sat there instead. That season no ball ran a hoop out of order on that lawn.
text_nonnarrative: A ball is through a hoop only if no part of it stands within the jaws with the stroke complete; a ball resting between the uprights is not through, and the point does not stand. Two balls in one hoop leave the order of play unchanged. A ball played out of turn is not a stroke and cannot be answered. Where a hoop is out of order, the point is not available.

text_narrative: Past the third peat hag the mist closed in, and Ivar counted forty paces before the next cairn showed. He set two stones on its top, wedging the flatter one against the wind, and looked back for the one behind. Nothing. The moor gave him only heather and a run of black water. He walked back sixty paces, found the cairn half fallen, and rebuilt it to knee height before going on.
text_nonnarrative: Cairn spacing on open moor is graded on visibility, not on the height of the stones. A gap that hides the next cairn in mist counts as a fault whatever the paces between them. Heather and peat bear on the siting and never on the class. Wind is a cause of collapse, not a category. Knee height is the floor for a marker; anything lower falls into the same class as standing water.

text_narrative: Nobody on the low road would cut a blaze after dusk, and there was a reason for it. Old Merrin had done it once, three slices in the bark of a rowan, and by morning the tree carried four. The fourth was deeper, and it pointed off the path towards the wet ground. Two carriers followed it as far as the alder scrub and came back without their packs. After that the blazes were cut at noon.
text_nonnarrative: A blaze counts as a waymark only by its cut, never by the tree that carries it. Three slices in sound bark is the standard mark; a fourth slice, or one deeper than the rest, is a disqualifying fault whatever the road. Rowan and alder are graded alike, bark thickness aside. Direction bears on the cause of a bad blaze and not on its class, so a mark pointing at wet ground is faulty for its depth alone.

text_narrative: A crew of four reaches the lower ford at midday and finds the gravel bar shifted twenty feet downstream. The lead hand steps in with a pole, feels for the shelf, and stops at mid-thigh where the current begins to press sideways. She signals the others back. The party moves upstream to the wide reach, where the water is shallower and slower over sand, and crosses there in a line, packs held high.
text_nonnarrative: A ford was classed by the behaviour of the current, not by depth alone. Water at mid-thigh over gravel was passable; the same depth over sand, with the flow pressing sideways, was not. A shifted bar was a cause of a bad crossing and never a class of one. Width bore on the grading only through speed: the wide reach was the safer for being slower, whatever the length of the line.

text_narrative: The front points are too long for this, and Halvard knows it before the second step. Forty millimetres, filed square last season for hard ice, and here the crust is soft over rubble, so each point drives through and finds nothing. Better to have brought the shorter set. He kicks a platform instead, edges the boot flat, and works across on ten points rather than two, which is slow and which is fine.
text_nonnarrative: Point length was graded against the surface, never against the boot. Forty millimetres counted as a hard-ice fitting; on soft crust over rubble the same length was a fault, since the points found no purchase at depth. Filing the points square bore on wear and not on the class. Ten-point technique was the standard for such ground, and a front-point ascent there was disqualified whatever the ice above it. Length alone was not decisive.

text_narrative: Three seasons on the gritstone edges and Nesta had built stances in every awkward place the crag offered. On the first she braced across a chimney with the rope over one shoulder and both feet on rounded footholds. On the second she sat in a notch with a sling round a spike, and the pull came from below all afternoon. On the last she stood, no anchor above her, and took the rope in with a bight round her waist.
text_nonnarrative: Stances are classed by the direction of pull they hold, not by how comfortable they are. A sitting stance in a notch counts as directional; a standing one with no anchor above is graded lower whatever the quality of the footholds. Rounded gritstone bears on the cause of a slip and never on the class. A rope taken round the waist is a separate matter, and a chimney brace, a spike and a sling are all admissible where the crag allows.

text_narrative: There was a drover who owed a stance-keeper for four nights of grass. Being short of coin, he brought his beasts in over the high wall at dusk and out again before the horn, three nights running. On the fourth the keeper had laid thorn along the gap, and the herd would not take it. The drover stood in the wet until light, counting heads he could not move, and paid what the grass came to.
text_nonnarrative: Grass at a drove stance is held in three enclosures of unequal size, the largest to the road. Capacity is a function of the sward and of the number of nights a herd stands, not of the walled area alone. Water lies at the low corner of each, so drainage and grazing order are coupled. The thorn gap in the boundary wall is a keeper's device: without it the enclosures are independent of the road.

text_narrative: In the ninth year of the salt road works, the train out of the lower depot carried crates of unequal weight. The clerk set the heavier crate on the near side of each pony and the lighter with a stone to balance it. By the second bend four loads had shifted and one pony had gone down on the scree. Sand bags were entered in the tally that winter.
text_nonnarrative: A packhorse load was carried on a wooden saddle tree with two side hooks of equal reach. Its stability was a function of the difference between the two side weights and of the height of the load above the tree, not of the total. Ballast in the lighter crate was one remedy; a shorter hook was another. Without a breast strap the two sides were mechanically independent of the girth.

text_narrative: Before the peoples had houses, the sky was pitched like a tent over the flat of the world, and its cords ran down to four hills. The maker of it had set the cords too near the walls, so the fabric drummed and let in cold at the seams. A daughter of the north hill drew each cord out to the length of its own height, and pegged it there. The drumming stopped, and the seams held.
text_nonnarrative: A guy line stands at an angle set by the ratio of peg distance to attachment height. Its tension is a function of that ratio and of the stretch in the fabric, not of the pull applied at the peg. At forty-five degrees the vertical and horizontal components are equal; nearer the wall the vertical dominates and the seam carries most of the load. Without a taut ridge the two side lines are independent of each other.

text_narrative: The proofing shed smells of wax and cold linseed, and the tent that hangs at the far end is not the one brought in. Kirsa checks the tally chalked on the beam. Nine panels went into the vat; ten hang dripping now, and the tenth is dry to the hand and marked with a seam pattern nobody in the shed cuts. She leaves it hanging and works down the row from the other end.
text_nonnarrative: Oil proofing and wax proofing were two classes of the same trade, and paraffin dressing a third. The first was distinguished by what it filled rather than what it coated, since linseed lay within the weave and not on it. Wax was the opposite case, a surface class, soft to the hand and reversible. Paraffin belonged to neither, since its distinguishing mark was smell rather than either stiffness or gloss. Weave count bore on all three.

text_narrative: Anyone digging in on the ridge road cuts two holes, and the old hands will tell whoever asks why. The family in the third winter cuts one, a good wide shaft straight up, and banks the door tight against the wind. Nobody on the ridge speaks of them without care. So the rule on the ridge is a roof hole and a low vent at the door, and a stick left standing in each.
text_nonnarrative: Two classes of snow shelter were recognised, and a third was marginal. A vented shelter was distinguished by the number of openings rather than by their size: a roof hole above and a low door vent below were the pair. A single-shaft shelter was the other class, marked by what it lacked. The trench with an open end belonged to neither, since the distinguishing feature there was the absence of a banked wall.

text_narrative: A survey team on the second ice shelf lost four hours to a runner fault on the ninth traverse. The rear sledge had been fitted with flat-bottomed runners from the depot store, and the crust that morning was granular and dry. Drag readings on the tow bar ran to twice the figure logged for the cambered pair ahead. The team swapped the load forward, cached the flat runners at a marker post, and reached the shelf edge after dark.
text_nonnarrative: Rocker runners were a third class, set between flat and cambered forms rather than outside them. A cambered runner was distinguished by curvature along its length; a flat one by the absence of it, and not by width or by the material of the shoe. The rocker class was marked by curvature at the ends only, so it stood nearer the flat form under load and nearer the cambered form on turns. Sole polish was common to all three.

text_narrative: There was a weaver of snowshoe webbing who would not sell the close pattern to strangers. A traveller from the birch country came in the black month and asked for it three times, and three times was given the open lattice instead. On the fourth asking the weaver cut the close web and laced it, and the traveller went out over the drifts and did not sink. He also did not come back.
text_nonnarrative: Across the oval frame the webbing lies in two zones. The forward zone, under the ball of the foot, is close-laced, its cords crossing at three-inch intervals; the tail zone behind is open, with gaps twice that. The toe hole sits forward of centre, its long axis fore and aft. The rawhide is thickest at the two side rails and thinnest at the tail, where the frame is narrow and the load light.

text_narrative: In the fourth season of the northern route, the works party drove eleven pitons into the great slab above the second ledge. Nine went into a single crack that ran diagonally, and two into blind pockets near the arete. At the winter inspection the two pocket pins stood proud by half an inch and the crack line held sound. The route book for that year records the slab as pinned throughout and the arete as left bare.
text_nonnarrative: The slab above the second ledge stands at seventy degrees, wider at the base than at the top. One crack runs across it diagonally from the left corner to a point two thirds of the way up the right edge. Blind pockets lie in a scattered band below that line, none deeper than two inches. The arete is on the right, undercut at its foot, and the rock there is sound where the slab is not.

text_narrative: In the age when the cliff roads were made, the anchor rings of the descent were set by the hand of a giant who worked downward from the rim. Each ring was driven into the living rock at the length of one rope from the last, and the lowest was set in the pool itself. The giant's daughter came after and doubled every ring, for she did not trust a single point of iron.
text_nonnarrative: Eight anchor stations lay on the cliff face between the rim and the pool, one below the other. The spacing was a rope length, so no station was out of sight of the two nearest it. Each stood on a ledge wide enough for two, set back from the fall line and to the left of it. The rock at the third and fourth stations was banded and damp; the lower face was drier and steeper.

text_narrative: Over one summer on the timber run, Brannagh lashed rafts at four different landings. At the first the poles were green larch and the withies short, so the frames came out slack and needed a second wrapping. At the third the crew had wire, and the work took half the time and held twice as long. At the last landing there was neither wire nor withy, and she bound the corners with plaited bark.
text_nonnarrative: Lashing practice varies more within a single river than between rivers. Of the rafts in the sample, some sixty percent are bound with wire at the corners and the rest with withy or bark. The median number of turns at a corner joint is seven, with a wide spread among the smaller crews. Pole species accounts for most of that spread; landing and season for very little of it. Frame slackness is reported in three grades.

text_narrative: The path is worn wrong, and Ottilie cannot stop looking at it. Two ruts, both smooth, both the width of a canoe gunwale, and both running uphill away from the water rather than down to it. Nobody carries a hull up from a lake and leaves nothing at the top. She follows the left rut to the ridge and finds moss unbroken, and the ruts continuing into it, and no boats anywhere.
text_nonnarrative: Wear on portage trails was reported unevenly across the survey. Rut depth varied more between adjacent sections of one trail than between whole trails, and the median depth at the crest was four inches. Ground cover accounted for most of the spread; length of carry for surprisingly little. Among the trails in the sample, rather more than half showed a single rut and the remainder two, with paired ruts commonest on the wider portages.

text_narrative: In the boat shed behind the house, two hulls sit upside down on trestles, and Ludo runs a string from stem to stern of each. The old one clears the keel line by two fingers amidships. The new one touches. He writes both figures on the doorframe under a dozen others in the same hand, then stands back and looks at the flat one for a long while.
text_nonnarrative: Rocker in small craft is distributed narrowly. In the recorded sample the rise at the stem above the amidships keel line is between one and three inches in nine hulls of ten. The median is a little under two. Variation within a single builder's output is greater than variation between builders, and hull length accounts for most of what remains, waterline width for almost none of it.

text_narrative: Every caravan out of the well town has one man who will not ride a forked tree, and in this one it is the cook. The word among the drivers is that his father sat a forked saddle for eleven days across the red ground and would never sit a saddle straight again. So the cook rides the flat pad behind the second beast, cushions piled, and takes the shifting as it comes. Nobody argues with him about it.
text_nonnarrative: A saddle tree for the dromedary is a rigid frame that bears on the ribs to either side of the single hump rather than on the hump itself. Its class is fixed by the number of arches: two in the forked pattern, one in the ring pattern, none in the flat pad, which counts as a tree only by courtesy. Load capacity depends on arch height and on the width of the side bars. Padding is therefore thin and evenly laid.

text_narrative: There was a keeper of a road inn who had no water and sold shade instead. Travellers paid a coin for a place along the north wall of his court, where the arcade threw its shadow all afternoon, and paid nothing for the south. One year a wanderer bought the south side for a season and planted it with figs, and the court had both shade and fruit. The keeper never sold a place along the north wall again.
text_nonnarrative: A road inn of the arid belt was a walled court with a single gate, characterised by an arcade on all four sides and stalls behind it. Its depth was fixed by the span of the vaulting and rarely exceeded four paces. Beast standing was on the ground floor, human lodging above, and the well or cistern at the centre of the court. Shade was therefore the principal asset of the north range, and rents were graded accordingly.

text_narrative: In the eleventh year of the palm court, the well rota was kept on a tally board of eight pegs, one for each holding. That summer the third holding moved its peg twice in one night and drew at the hour of the fifth. The elders of the court struck the third holding from the board until the next flood and gave its water to the sixth. The board was afterwards kept under a lock of two keys.
text_nonnarrative: A well rota is a schedule of entitlement rather than of labour, characterised by fixed shares and movable hours. Each holding is entitled to a share defined as a stated number of bucket lifts, not as a length of time at the head. Its position depends on the standing of the holding and on the level in the shaft, which is lowest before the flood. Transfer between holdings is possible; the total is not divisible below one lift.

text_narrative: When the long walkers first crossed the dark side of the plain, they were given no lamps and no marks on the ground. Each was taught the seven fixed lights of the northern crown and the two that stand behind it, and each carried a knotted cord for counting the nights. The eldest of them walked with her head back and her feet in the dust for eleven seasons. The road she wore was the road the others kept.
text_nonnarrative: Walkers on the night stages are required to hold two fixed lights at all times, one ahead and one at the shoulder. Substitution of a low light for a high one is permitted only where cloud stands above forty degrees. Knotted cord counts are to be made at each halt and are not to be relied on beyond nine nights. Lamps are not permitted on the plain at all, and no mark is to be cut in the dust.

text_narrative: The second party leaves the depot at first light and works east on a bearing of eighty-two degrees. Two counters walk abreast, one telling hundreds on a string of beads and the other keeping a tally in a wax book, and their figures part by nine paces in the first mile. The leader takes the lower of the two. At the fourth mile the counters agree again, and the party turns north for the ridge without a fix from the sky.
text_nonnarrative: Two counters were required on every leg of more than a mile, and their tallies were to be recorded separately. Where the figures parted by more than ten in the hundred, the lower was to be entered and the leg walked again. Bead strings were permitted for hundreds; knots and notches were not, except on ground where a string was liable to snag. No count was to stand as a fix without a bearing taken at each end of the leg.

text_narrative: Hedda copies itinerary strips for the guild, and each one teaches her something about what the road will not hold. On the first she draws the river crossings to scale and runs out of vellum at the third town. On the second she drops the scale and keeps the order, and the strip fits. On the fourth she adds a spur that no rider has asked for, and the master crosses it out with a single stroke.
text_nonnarrative: The strip itinerary was the weaker form of map and the more useful one, and not for economy of skin. A strip could not be wrong about the shape of a country, since it made no claim about shape; it asserted order and distance only. Against this it may be said that a rider off the line was left with nothing. True enough, and beside the point: the strip was addressed to a rider who stayed on it.

text_narrative: The bell had rung the whole of the previous night and Aldric had counted it, and the count was wrong. Nineteen strokes to the quarter hour, always, and the rope in the tower loft hung slack and dry. No brother slept above the porch that winter. He had gone up twice with a lamp and found the wheel still and the frost unbroken on the sill, and had come down both times without waking anyone.
text_nonnarrative: Fog bells at the mountain hospices of the old passes were defended on the wrong ground. The argument for them rested on audibility, which was the weakest part of the case, since sound in fog was as often reflected as direct. The better defence was that the bell fixed an interval rather than a direction, and an interval was enough to hold a line. That the two were often confused was no argument against the bell.

text_narrative: The hut door was drifted shut and it took Verity twenty minutes with the shovel blade to clear the lower half. Inside, the shelf held four tins, a bag of salt with the corner gnawed, and a candle stub in a lid. The book on the nail said the winter store had been made up in the autumn to twelve tins. She wrote the date and the count, put back one of her own tins, and shut the inner door behind her.
text_nonnarrative: Winter store: the fixed quantity of tinned food, salt and light held in a refuge hut through the closed season. Standing store: the part of that quantity which is not to be drawn on except when the hut is snowed in. Replacement: any equivalent left in place of what is taken, in kind or otherwise. Deficit: the difference between the entry in the hut book and the count on the shelf. Idle tin: one on the shelf past its second closed season.

text_narrative: Everyone on the eastern sectors knew which line Torvald walked, and it was not the one on the board. He had a loop of his own that took in the two high tarns and left out the whole of the forestry block, and the office never queried a return in eleven years. The odd thing was that his sector had the fewest lost walkers of any. The loop stayed on the board, drawn in a hand nobody claimed.
text_nonnarrative: Sector: the ground for which a single patrol return is made, bounded by watercourses rather than by fence lines. Standing line: the route drawn on the sector board, which is the route of record. Working line: any route actually walked, whether or not it coincides with the standing line. Dead ground: the part of a sector visible from no point on either line. Return: the single entry in which a sector, a line and a date are held together.

text_narrative: There was a marten who could read, and she lived under the floor of a summit shelter where the register was kept. Whatever name was written last, she would gnaw it out before the next party came, so that every walker found a book ending in someone else's hand. The wardens blamed damp, then blamed each other, then chained the book to the beam. The marten took to gnawing the chain instead, and the shelter kept no register after that.
text_nonnarrative: A trail register meant, under the old shelter rules, any bound book kept at a shelter in which parties entered their passage. Loose sheets did not fall within the definition, nor did a book kept elsewhere and brought in. Where a register was chained, the chain was part of the register and its removal was a removal of the whole. Nothing in the rules touching registers affected the separate duty of the warden as to the shelter itself.

text_narrative: In the third edition year the club altered the contour interval of its guidebook plates from fifty feet to twenty-five. The engraver, working from the same plates, thinned every fifth line rather than cutting new ones, and the printer read the thin lines as blanks. Four hundred copies went out with the high corries flattened. The committee recalled none of them and issued a slip of errata for the loose end papers instead.
text_nonnarrative: Contour interval meant the vertical distance between successive lines on a plate, and not the horizontal spacing of them. A line was an index line where its weight exceeded that of its neighbours, and index status was a matter of weight alone, whatever the height it stood for. Where an interval was stated on a plate, the plate governed; where it was stated only in the text, the text was of no effect.

text_narrative: The high road above the cloud line had a rule of its own, and it was older than the men who kept it. A traveller who gained more than a thousand feet between one shrine and the next found the next shrine gone from its place, and the path level, and the day no further on. The old women of the valley called it the road keeping its own count, and they walked slowly, and they arrived.
text_nonnarrative: A stage was legal only where the gain between shrines was under a thousand feet. A day in which two such stages stood consecutively was void, and no shrine could be counted twice within it. Descent was not a stage and could not be answered by one. A position in which the traveller stood above the last shrine but below the next was undefined, and the count was taken from the lower. Rest bore on no rule.

text_narrative: The freight string out of the flats halts at the second creek an hour before noon, as the contract allows, and the ponies are turned loose on the bottom grass. One mare crosses to the far bank and stands in the willow scrub, out of sight of the wrangler. The string is short a head at the count and the halt runs to two hours. The wrangler brings her back at a walk and the load goes on unshifted.
text_nonnarrative: A grazing halt is admissible only where the ground carries loose feed and the water is within a hundred paces. A halt on a made road is not a grazing halt whatever its length. Two halts inside one hour count as one, and the shorter of them cannot be claimed against the day's allowance. A string standing short at the count is not in halt, and no head may be entered as grazing while it is out of sight.

text_narrative: Maru crosses the tide causeway four times in the one week and the stones are never the same count. On the first crossing there are nineteen, and the ninth is loose under the heel. On the second there are nineteen and the loose one is sound. On the third there are twenty, and the new one is dry on top though the tide has been over it. On the fourth she counts to eighteen and turns back to the bank she came from.
text_nonnarrative: Of the three sizes of causeway stone in use, the middle was the commonest: a block two feet square and eighteen inches deep, set with the grain across the flow. The largest were reserved for the two ends and for the deepest part of the channel, and were half again as thick. The smallest were fillers, laid in threes where a single block would not bear. Each carried a chisel mark on its landward face, and the marks ran in sequence.

text_narrative: Three strokes meant a cart, and Sile had heard three strokes at a quarter past two with no cart on the slip. She had gone down anyway, because the rope end was wet and the bell wheel warm, and a warm wheel in that cold meant a hand on it inside the hour. Nobody on the far bank owned to ringing. The ferry log for that night carried her initials against a crossing that had not happened.
text_nonnarrative: Four signals stand in the ferry code, and no more. One stroke is a foot passenger; two, a passenger with a beast; three, a cart or a load requiring the ramp. The fourth is a double pair, rung slowly, and belongs to the ferryman rather than the bank. Repetition is not a fifth signal but a mark of impatience, and the code is silent on it. Each stroke is a full swing of the wheel.

text_narrative: The print in the yard mud is a clinker pattern, eleven nails, and the outer row worn to nothing on the left side. Ferrand squats over it with the lamp and does not touch it. Half the men on this coast walk in clinkers, and half of those wear the outside row down, and the eleventh nail is common as rain. He measures the stride instead, heel to heel, and finds it short for the height of the wall.
text_nonnarrative: Too much is claimed for nail patterns as marks of identity. What passes for a distinguishing pattern in the trade literature is usually a pattern of wear, and wear is a property of ground rather than of a boot. The best work on the subject is the work that treats a print as evidence of weight and stride and nothing else. It is fair to say that clinker counts narrow a field; it is not fair to say they close one.

text_narrative: Nobody at the shore station would carry a glass-sided lantern after the third autumn, and the reason was always given the same way. The glass ones showed a face in them at certain angles, a face nobody could account for, and the mica ones did not. It was said the difference was in the reflection, and the men who said so were the men who carried mica. The store issued glass for another two winters and the store's lanterns came back unlit.
text_nonnarrative: Mica screens are underrated and glass overrated, and the literature has the comparison backwards. What is praised in glass is brightness, which is a property of the flame and not of the screen; what is dismissed in mica is diffusion, which is the whole point of a screen in wind. The soundest writing on lanterns is the writing that treats the screen as a wind device rather than an optical one. Cost is a poor argument either way, and durability a worse one.

text_narrative: There was a stonecutter in the border marches who was paid by the letter and so cut the longest names he could find. Where the road passed a hamlet of one syllable he cut the old name of the valley instead, in full, and the post stood twice the height of its neighbours. Riders learned to read the marches by height rather than by word, and the cutter's pay was fixed by the yard from that year on.
text_nonnarrative: Nothing cut on the stone settled whether a milepost named a place or merely pointed at one. If naming was the function, then a post bearing a valley name and no distance was a milepost still, and a bare arrow was not. If pointing was the function, the reverse held and the letters were ornament. The two accounts were not rivals so much as answers to different demands, one of the reader and one of the road.

text_narrative: In the second winter of the shelter's use the visitors' book filled to the last page, and the margins after that. Entries of the ordinary kind, dates and names and weathers, ran down the centre; the margins carried something else, arguments about the roof and a running dispute over the woodpile. The keeper of the ground bound in twenty fresh leaves in the spring. By the following autumn the margins of those were full and the centres half empty.
text_nonnarrative: Marginalia in a shelter book and entries in it are alike in medium and unlike in kind, which is why one word for both misleads. An entry is addressed to the keeper and is complete in itself; a marginal note is addressed to whoever comes next and is a half of something. If that difference is real, then a book of margins only is not a register at all but a correspondence. Either way the paper is the same paper.

text_narrative: In the first age of the dry roads, water was carried in skins of hide that let nothing through, and it was hot at the end of every stage. A woman of the salt villages took a bag of coarse-woven flax and hung it on the shady side of her beast, and the bag wept all day and the water in it stayed cool. The hide makers of the plain never forgave her.
text_nonnarrative: Cooling in a porous bag was proportional to the rate of loss through the wall. The constant of proportion was a property of the weave rather than of the water, so a coarse cloth and a fine one of equal area were not comparable. The rate itself was proportional to the vapour deficit of the air outside, and to nothing in the water. Beyond saturation the relation did not hold at all.

text_narrative: A convoy on the southern sand route lost the line of poles at the ninth kilometre and spent the night stationary. The poles there had been set at two hundred metre intervals when the route was new; the dunes had since risen to within a metre of the tops. The lead driver walked forward on a bearing and found three in a row buried entirely. The convoy dug out four and doubled the height of two before moving on.
text_nonnarrative: Visible spacing on a dune track is inversely proportional to the height of the poles above the crest line. Where that height is halved, the interval at which a pole can be picked up is halved with it. The constant depends on the eye level of the driver and on haze, not on the colour of the pole. Below a quarter metre of standing height the relation fails, since the pole is then a feature of the sand.

text_narrative: Yannek runs the traction sledge on the ice plain three times in the short season, and each run teaches him a different lesson about the bridle. On the first the kite flies steady and the sledge tracks a hand's width off the wind line. On the second the front lines stretch and the whole rig sits nose down and slows. On the third he shortens the rear pair by a span and the sledge lifts a runner on every gust.
text_nonnarrative: A traction rig consisted of a kite, a bridle of four lines, and a sledge with two runners. The bridle attached at the sledge nose in a single ring, and the four lines were unequal: the forward pair longer than the rear by a hand's width. Rear lines were absent in the earliest single-line forms, which had no means of trim. The runners stood outside the frame rather than under it, and a fin between them was proper to the larger sizes.

text_narrative: The pole is wrong for this river and Ines knows it at the second step. A rubber shoe on the end, good on rock, useless in a gravel bed where it skates and finds no seat, and the spike is somewhere in the depot. Two more steps and the shoe rides up over a cobble. She turns the pole and uses the butt end, which is bare wood and bites, and crosses on three points with the water at her belt.
text_nonnarrative: The wading pole had three parts: a shaft, a ferrule at the lower end, and a wrist loop at the upper. The ferrule was seated on a shoulder turned in the shaft and pinned across, so shaft and ferrule stood as separate members rather than one. A spike ferrule ended in a point; a shoe ferrule in a flat disc of rubber. The wrist loop was absent in the shorter river poles, where the butt itself served as a second foot.

text_narrative: In the fourteenth year of the reckoning, the tally-keeper Aunwe set the nameless day after the short month instead of before it, and wrote the change into the ledger in the same brown ink as the rest. The market wardens kept the old order. For nine days the town held two dates at once. On the tenth the wardens gave way, and Aunwe cut the older column out of the ledger with a knife.
text_nonnarrative: A nameless day was placed by rule and not by preference. Position in the reckoning was the whole of the matter: a day set after the short month was one class of insertion, a day set before it another, and the two were never held to be the same. Ink and hand in the ledger bore on the record and never on the class. Two dates in a town counted as a defect of the wardens.

text_narrative: Before the two lights agreed, the Weaver of Tides hung twelve moons on a cord and found the cord too short for the sun's circuit. She knotted a thirteenth moon into the slack at every third turning, and the knot showed itself as a night of double shadow. The first people counted the knots and called them stolen nights. The Weaver let the name stand, and the cord has held ever since, uneven and sufficient.
text_nonnarrative: Twelve lunar months are shorter than one solar circuit by about eleven days, and a lunisolar calendar is the arrangement that absorbs the shortfall. Intercalation is a function of the accumulated deficit and of the rule chosen to discharge it, never of any single month. A thirteenth month is the usual instrument. Without a fixed rule the two counts are independent, and the seasons stand in no settled relation to the named months.

text_narrative: The clerk of the almanac had both tables in front of her and still could not make the feast fall where the council wanted it. Two rules, both old, both written in the same hand, put the date a week apart. Whichever she chose, half the parishes would keep the wrong day and blame the almanac for it. She thought about the printer waiting downstairs, and set the earlier date, and left the later one in a footnote.
text_nonnarrative: A movable date is less a calculation than a choice of authority, since the arithmetic is trivial and the disagreement is about which rule governs. Two defensible rules yield two defensible dates, and no computation settles between them. The usual defence offered for the older rule is continuity, which is a real consideration and not by itself a decisive one, because continuity favours whichever rule a given district has kept longest, and districts differ among themselves.

text_narrative: There was a village with eight days to its week and no name for the last of them. The old carter said a nameless day was a day nobody owed anything on, and he saved his debts for it. One spring the reeve named the day after the hill above the barley, and the carter paid what he owed on the morning of it, and never spoke to the reeve again as long as either lived.
text_nonnarrative: Named days and numbered days are two systems of equal length, distinct in what they anchor to. A named day is fixed to something outside the cycle, a place or a trade or a season. A numbered day is fixed only to the day ahead of it in the count. Blank days are a third kind, belonging to the count but bearing no name and no number, and obligations of every sort lapse on them.

text_narrative: Rain on the parapet, and the third watch has another hour in it. Ondrej counts the bell strokes twice because the wind takes the fourth one away from him. He walks the north face to the corner tower, sets a hand on the cold stone, walks back. The relief is late. Somewhere below, a dog works itself into a temper and gives up on it. He counts again at the half, and gets it right.
text_nonnarrative: The watch stations lay at four points of the wall, one to each face, with the corner towers between them. The north face was the longest, some ninety paces, and the parapet there stood a foot lower than elsewhere. The bell hung in the gate tower, above the level of the walk. Sound from it was clear along the east face and poor along the north, where the wind was off the water.

text_narrative: The tower bell struck twenty-five at midday on the second of the month, according to three separate accounts taken from the square below. A pin in the striking train had worn through and let the hammer run free. The bellringer on duty, a woman of nineteen named Corvish, climbed to the chamber and stopped the train by hand at the twenty-sixth stroke. The clock kept correct time throughout, and the fault lay only in the count.
text_nonnarrative: An hour bell is struck by a hammer held clear of the rim and freed by a locking pin in the striking train. Count is a function of the notched wheel, which the pin rides, and of nothing in the going train. The two trains share a weight and are otherwise separate. A worn pin therefore affects how many strokes sound, and the time shown at the dial is untouched by any of it.

text_narrative: Three winters the sacrist Ilve kept the long vigil by candle. The first winter the candle burned out an hour short and she sat in the dark and did not report it. The second she trimmed the wick too often and the mark ran late. The third she let it alone, and the flame took the ring at the exact turn of the watch, and that troubled her more than either failure before it.
text_nonnarrative: Burn rate in a marked candle was proportional to the cross-section of the wick and very nearly independent of the diameter of the wax. Doubling the wick halved the interval between rings. The constant of the relation was a property of the tallow and differed by batch, so a candle from one pouring was comparable only with others of that pouring. Beyond about a third of the length consumed, the relation held poorly.

text_narrative: They still argue about the year the tanners walked ahead of the dyers. The route was the same as always, up the long street and round by the fish steps, but the marshal put the tanners forward because the dyers were short of banner-bearers. Nobody objected on the day. It was a week later, at the settling of accounts, that a dyer refused to pay his share of the candles, and it took two seasons to mend.
text_nonnarrative: Precedence in a procession is held by company and not by person, so a substitution of bearers of any kind is without effect on order. A company short of its full complement keeps its place; a company absent altogether forfeits it for that occasion only. Two companies may not occupy one rank. An order altered by a marshal on the day is good for that day and is no precedent for the day that follows.

text_narrative: Fog in the yard, and the banners are laid out on trestles in the order they will walk. The keeper of the poles, an old man with a cracked thumbnail, shifts the green one two places down and nobody stops him. The green company folded four years back and its banner walks anyway, out of habit. He weights the cloth with lead shot against the wind and stands back to look along the line.
text_nonnarrative: Nine banners make up the full set, of which the three field banners are the largest and the only ones hung from double poles. Each is wool, dyed in a single ground colour, with the company device in appliqued linen at the centre and a fringe on three sides. The four ward banners are half that size and single-poled. Two mourning banners are plain black, undevised, and kept apart from the rest.

text_narrative: Everyone in the trades knows which company holds the best day and knows it will never come back. The coopers have their patron in the second week of the warm month, which is when the fair is, and the ropers have theirs in the wet. The rota is supposed to turn every seven years. It has not turned in thirty. The ropers put a claim in each spring, the clerk files it, and that is the whole of it.
text_nonnarrative: Attendance at a patron day varied more between trades than between years within a trade. The median turnout across the twelve companies was near four in ten of those enrolled on the books, though the two largest accounted for most of the spread. Days in the warm months drew roughly twice the numbers of days in the wet, and proximity to a fair explained more of that difference than the size or the age of a company did.

text_narrative: In the third year after the spring was cleared, the wardens of the water took up the offerings from the basin and found among them a bronze pin of a make nobody could place. The pin lay under the silt at the outflow rather than at the head, where offerings were laid. The wardens set it back at the head. By the following spring it had worked down to the outflow again, and they let it stay.
text_nonnarrative: An object counts as votive by its placing and not by its worth, so a bronze pin at the head of a basin and a worked stone in the same position fall in one class. Whatever lies in the silt at the outflow is of doubtful class, since water alone accounts for a thing in that position. Depth bears on the age of offerings and never on whether they were laid. The wardens' record is no criterion.

text_narrative: Every year of the four she has done it, Meriel builds the board the same way and gets a different picture out of it. The clay takes petals differently in a dry spring. This year the border of alder cones sits proud and the field of yellow behind it sinks, so the whole panel reads hollow from the lane. Her aunt says nothing about that. The stewards say nothing either, and the board hangs nine days regardless.
text_nonnarrative: A dressing board consisted of a plank backing, a bed of puddled clay some half an inch deep, and the applied material pressed into the clay face. The backing was framed on three sides and open at the foot for drainage. Petals, seeds, cones and bark were the four classes of material. A border of coarse material at the edge was general in every district; a border of petals was absent in the older boards.

text_narrative: There was a binder who could not make the last sheaf into any figure but a bird. She tried the horn shape her mother made, and the lantern, and the plain knot, and each one came out of her hands with a head and a beak on it. The farm took this for a sign and hung the bird over the door. It hung there nine years, and in the tenth it was found facing the wall.
text_nonnarrative: Four figures were common at the close of harvest, of which the horn was the smallest and by some way the most often made. The lantern form was hollow, built on a frame of six straws, and stood about a hand high. The knot was solid and had no frame at all. A fourth, the bird, was local to a few valleys and was made from the last sheaf only, never from gleanings or from straw bought in.

text_narrative: The custom at Hollowmere is that the oldest tree hears the song first, and the oldest tree has been dead for eleven years. They sing to it anyway. The cider goes on the roots, the bread goes in the fork of the branches, and every year the dead tree puts out one green shoot on the south side by the middle of the warm month. Nobody in the parish finds this remarkable, which is the strange part.
text_nonnarrative: What was least persuasive in orchard custom was never the singing but the accounting attached to it: the claim that a tree sung to bore more fruit than one left unsung. Such comparisons were made between trees of unequal age and unequal soil, and were worth nothing. The customs that lasted best were the ones that advanced no claim of the sort, and asked only for noise and cider, which nobody had to defend.

text_narrative: A company of mummers lost its doctor two nights ahead of the season and put the smith's daughter into the coat. She played it straight, no gagging, and the play ran nine minutes shorter than in any year before. The parish liked it that way. The company kept her in the coat for six seasons, and by the end of them nobody could remember what the doctor had been for in the first place.
text_nonnarrative: Stock figures in a mumming play sort into three kinds by what they are permitted to do. The combatants exist to be matched against each other and have no lines outside the challenge. The restorer stands apart from the fight and is the only figure who may undo its result. Attendant figures belong to neither kind, take no part in the action, and are the ones a company may cut when short.

text_narrative: The rule is one mask to a face and no face bare after the lamps are lit, and Tobar knows the rule better than the wardens do. What he does not know is whether the second mask counts, the small one sewn inside the first, against the cheek. It belonged to his grandmother. She wore it under a hare's head for forty years and nobody ever asked. He ties the outer one on and walks toward the noise.
text_nonnarrative: A face was covered or it was not; there was no partial state, and a mask pushed up onto the brow counted as a bare face. Two masks worn together were a single covering provided the outer one was whole. A covering taken off inside the ring could not be resumed there, and the wearer stood outside the custom for the remainder of the night. Recognition by name was no offence and required no answer.

text_narrative: The fire on the eastern ridge was built to twice the sanctioned height and was visible from the coast road for the first time in forty years. The builders, a party of eleven from the settlement below, gave the reason as a shortage of hands for the usual four smaller fires. No damage followed. The ridge council recorded the breach, allowed the fire to burn, and set a marker at the sanctioned height for the following year.
text_nonnarrative: Each fire is required to stand no higher than two and a half times the height of a person, measured to the crown in its unlit state. Spacing of not less than thirty paces between fires is required on level ground and forty on a slope. A single large fire is permitted only where hands are short and the ridge council has been notified. Water is to be held within reach of every third fire.

text_narrative: Down at the slipway the floats are going out one at a time, and the fourth will not sit level. Ferrin kneels in the shallows with the frame across his knees and shifts the ballast stone an inch aft. The paper glows orange from inside, then blue, which is not a colour the candles make. He puts it in the water anyway. It rides level to the bend and does not come back with the others.
text_nonnarrative: A float is a light frame of split cane, a paper shell over it, a ballast stone lashed at the base, and a candle seat amidships. The frame is six hoops to a side, tied at the crossings and nowhere glued. The shell is one sheet, lapped at the stern only. Smaller floats have no seat and take a taper wedged into the base instead, and the ballast in those is loose sand.

text_narrative: A mason once cut the threshold mark on a house at the wrong depth, too shallow by half, and would not go back to deepen it. He said a mark was a mark or it was nothing, and depth was a thing masons had invented so as to be paid twice for one job. The house stood ninety years and no ill came of it. When it was pulled down, the stone went whole to the door of the next.
text_nonnarrative: A threshold mark means a cut figure in the sill stone of a dwelling, made at the raising of that dwelling and at no later time. Where a mark is cut to less than the customary depth, it is a mark in full, and the shortfall is a matter between the mason and the householder alone. Nothing in the depth requirement affects a mark inherited with a stone taken from an earlier building on the same ground.

text_narrative: In the year the west tower was raised, the builders left the foundation niche empty and mortared the cover stone over nothing at all. The clerk of works wrote it down plainly. Three masters in succession refused to open the course and put the matter to the one who came after. The tower stood four hundred years and was taken down in the fifth century of the city for a road, and the niche was empty.
text_nonnarrative: A foundation niche was a void left in the lowest course of a wall, closed by a single cover stone and intended to hold a deposit. Its size was fixed by the course height and rarely exceeded a hand's span in any direction. Contents were various and of no structural consequence. An empty niche was accordingly a defect of custom rather than of building, and the distinction was maintained in the clerks' records.

text_narrative: The gate had a roof and two benches and a rule that nobody could explain: the bearers waited under it for the length of one hundred counted breaths. Sivrin had counted for the parish eleven times. What troubled him was that the count ran long in the dark and short at midday, and the gate seemed to know the difference, because the cold came up through the boards at exactly the hundredth breath either way.
text_nonnarrative: A gate pause meant the interval during which a bearing party remained under a covered gate and was not in motion. Where the interval was measured by counted breaths, the count and not the elapsed duration was the measure, and a slow count was a good count. Nothing in the custom required a covered gate; where none stood, the pause was made at the boundary mark, and the interval was unaltered by that.

text_narrative: A stone cut this spring at the yard on the mill road carries its lettering in two sizes, which the parish register does not allow. The cutter, an apprentice in her second year, says the name would not fit the panel at the single size. The family accepts the stone. The register keeper notes the departure and lets it stand, on the ground that the alternative is a blank panel and a second stone at the family's cost.
text_nonnarrative: Lettering on a memorial stone was required to be of one size throughout the panel, and of one face throughout. Abbreviation was permitted in the dating line alone and nowhere else. A name too long for the panel at the required size was to be set over two lines rather than reduced. Departures were permitted only on the written note of the register keeper, and that note was to be kept with the stone's entry.

text_narrative: The tailor on Kell Street has taken a grey band back four times this year and given out a black one instead, which is the wrong direction entirely. People go from black to grey to nothing, never the reverse. He does not ask. The fourth is a woman he has served since the shop opened, and she puts the grey on the counter and waits, and he wraps the black and marks the ledger.
text_nonnarrative: Deep mourning: the first period, of six months, in which black is worn without relief of any kind at all. Half mourning: the period following, of equal length, in which grey and violet are admitted and black is optional. Reversion: any return to a deeper grade from a lighter one, which the custom does not recognise. Standing mourning: the wearing of a single band with no term set to it whatever.

text_narrative: Two Halvasts live in the lane and there is one name day between them, and the register will not add a second. The older one keeps the day. The younger keeps a day of his own choosing in the cold month, which nobody official recognises and everybody on the lane observes, with a cake and the same three neighbours. The register keeper lives four doors down and comes to it every year without fail.
text_nonnarrative: Entered name: a name held in the parish register with a fixed day set against it. Shadow day: a day kept in a household for a name with no entry, or for a name sharing an entry with another holder. Doubling: the condition in which two living holders share one entered name. Release: the striking out of an entry, permitted on removal from the parish and on no other ground whatever.

text_narrative: When the first binding was made there were no words for it, only a stone held in both hands until the hands were warm and the stone was warmer. The Nine who witnessed it agreed that warmth was the whole of the form. Later ages added words, and the words grew long, and a school arose to argue their order. The stone stayed in the hall and nobody could say which of the two now held the oath.
text_nonnarrative: An oath in the strict sense means a form of words spoken in the presence of at least one witness competent to hold it. A binding of the older kind, made by gesture and without words, is an oath for every effect of custom, and the absence of words is no ground of challenge. Where both forms attend one undertaking, the gesture governs, and nothing in the wording of the spoken part limits it in any way.

text_narrative: Anwel had been left at the first grade of the cut for two years while novices half his term went up to the second. Nobody would say what the second grade required. It was not learning; he had the whole house recitation by heart. It was not conduct either. He had begun to think the grade was simply the master's memory of a face, and that his face was one the master did not keep.
text_nonnarrative: Advance between grades of the cut was settled by term and by conduct and by nothing a novice could show. Length of term was counted from entry to the house and not from the first cut, so two novices of equal years stood at different grades.
