Conduct was a bar and never a qualification: it held a novice where he was and could not lift him. Recitation, learning and the master's regard bore on none of it.

text_narrative: The great silence runs from the last bell to the first, and in the north walk it runs a little longer. Osk keeps to the south walk for that reason. Tonight the lamp in the north walk is lit and somebody is standing under it, not moving, at an hour when nobody should be there at all. He does not go and look. He counts the flags of the south walk to the door, forty-one, and goes in.
text_nonnarrative: Silence was to be kept from the last bell of the evening to the first of the morning, in all four walks and on the stair between them. Speech was permitted in that interval only at the gate and only to a person outside the house. Lamps were required to be out in three walks, and one lamp was to be left burning in the fourth. Passage through the walks was permitted without limit of any kind.

text_narrative: Five times that winter the reading fell to Halde, and five times the book was open at a different place than the rota said. The first time he read what was in front of him. The second he corrected it aloud and the room went still. By the fifth he had stopped looking at the rota altogether, and read whatever the book showed, and the kitchen sent up an extra dish that night without explanation.
text_nonnarrative: A reading is valid whatever the passage, provided the reader is the one the rota names for that meal. Substitution from the floor is not permitted; an absent reader means the meal stands without reading, and the rota is unaltered by the omission. Correction aloud by the reader is not itself a reading and does not answer the obligation. Two readers at one meal is a position the rota cannot produce and has no remedy for.

text_narrative: A band of six at the tower on the ridge completes a full extent on Thursday evening, two hours and eleven minutes, the first there in sixty years. The conductor, a schoolmistress of thirty-four, calls the whole of it from the treble. One change is disputed by a listener in the yard below and stands after the band's own account is taken. The bells are rung down at once and the ringers go home.
text_nonnarrative: The number of changes in a full extent was the factorial of the number of bells, so six bells gave seven hundred and twenty and seven gave five thousand and forty. Duration was proportional to that number and to the interval between strokes, which was fixed by the weight of the heaviest bell. Adding one bell to a band therefore multiplied the labour by the new count and by no smaller factor.

text_narrative: Once a pedlar sold badges for a road he had never walked, and every badge he sold was of a shape nobody had seen at the shrine end of it. Walkers came back and found their badges did not match. Instead of complaint there was pride, and within a generation the pedlar's shapes were the ones the road was known by, and the true ones were taken for counterfeits and thrown in the ditch.
text_nonnarrative: A road badge is a cast token, usually of a lead and tin alloy, worn to show that a route has been walked to its end. Its form is proper to a single road and is never shared, which is what makes the type a mark of route rather than of custom. Weight is low by design, under half an ounce, and the pin is integral to the casting rather than soldered on.

text_narrative: In the second season of the new road, the staging post at the high col issued four hundred tokens and took back only two hundred and ninety at the far end. The keeper, a woman who had held the post since the road was cut, wrote that the missing hundred and ten were in the pockets of walkers who had turned back at the snow line and kept them. No count was ever reconciled.
text_nonnarrative: Staging posts sit at the three cols and at the ford, which is the only one on level ground. The col posts stand above the tree line, in the lee of the ridge on the northern side, with a shelter wall at the west end of each. Distance between the second and third posts is the greatest, a full day in poor weather. The ford post is the lowest and the wettest.

text_narrative: When the long dark ended, the first builders set a wheel of stone in the plain and cut sixty notches around its rim, one for each interval of the returning light. They aligned the wheel to the horizon and not to the pole, which the later builders held to be an error. The wheel kept true nine thousand years regardless, and the wheel of the later builders, aligned to the pole, drifted out inside a century.
text_nonnarrative: A calendar wheel was sound or unsound by its drift and by nothing else. Wheels aligned to the horizon and wheels aligned to the pole were two classes of construction, and neither was a fault in itself; a wheel of either class answered only to the interval it was cut for. Notches out of true on the rim were a defect of the stone and of the builders' hand, and bore on the reading and not on the class.

text_narrative: The box took nine lots and gave back three, and the three that came were supposed to be random. Ilsa had cast it four hundred times over the winter and kept a tally on the inside of the lid. The pale lot came up in seven casts of ten. She did not think the box was speaking. She thought somebody had shaved the pale lot thin, and she could not decide which of those two was the worse thing.
text_nonnarrative: A cast is void or good by the state of the box and the lots, never by the result the lots show. Nine lots in the box and three drawn is the whole of a good cast; a short box voids it. A lot shaved thin is a defect of the lot and not of the box, and either defect voids alike. A pale lot drawn oftener than the rest is a matter for the tally kept on the lid.

text_narrative: Four times a year the fast fell, and four times Dremen the baker had to decide what the house would do about bread. In the spring fast he baked as usual and sold nothing at all. In the summer he baked half and threw half away. In the autumn he shut the oven and lost the week. In the winter he baked at night for the day after, and those loaves were the best of the year.
text_nonnarrative: Whether a fast was an abstention or an observance mattered to the baker and not to the faster. On the first account the fast was constituted by what was not eaten, and a house that produced food stood outside the matter entirely. On the second the fast was a state of the whole settlement, and production was itself participation or its refusal. Neither account was derivable from the other, and custom held both of them together.

text_narrative: The first bucket out of the well after the turn of the year is worth something, and the young people in Aiverd sit up all night to be the one who draws it. This year the winner is a child of nine who was asleep at the well head and woke when the others arrived. Nobody disputes it. The rule is who draws first, not who waits longest, and the rule has never been written down.
text_nonnarrative: An unwritten rule was more stable than a written one in matters of this kind, precisely because nobody could point to a text and argue from its wording. Disputes were settled by what everybody in the place remembered, and memory converged where reading diverged. The obvious objection, that memory was the less exact of the two, held in general and bore very little here, since exactness was not what the rule was for.

text_narrative: Long after the shadow first crossed the second sun, the watchers on the station rings held a vigil of four hours and named it for the older sun rather than the eclipsed one. Their reason was lost inside three generations. What survived was the practice, kept to the hour, by people who had drifted so far out that neither sun showed as more than a bright point on the hull glass.
text_nonnarrative: Identity of an observance is not settled by pointing at the practice, since the practice is itself what stands in dispute. On one account identity is continuous transmission, and a vigil kept for no remembered reason is the same vigil. On another it is content, and the thing kept is a different observance under an inherited name. The hour is common to both accounts and decides between them not at all.

text_narrative: The cord had ninety-nine knots and Bettel had worn the ninth one smooth in a way she could not account for, since she was careful to work the whole length evenly. She laid it out on the table under the lamp and went along it with her thumb. The ninth was smaller than the rest by half. She counted the cord twice more, found ninety-nine both times, and put it back in the drawer.
text_nonnarrative: Cords in household use showed uneven wear at a small number of positions, and the ninth and the fortieth were the commonest of these. Wear was greater among older holders, though the difference between households was larger than the difference between ages inside one household. Of those who kept a cord daily, about a third had one knot noticeably reduced, and its position was consistent within a family and not across families.

text_narrative: A trail clock on the orbital keeps the hour six minutes long for the third cycle running, and the fault is traced to the pressed powder rather than to the tray. The station's timekeeper, an engineer named Sooren, declines to replace the batch. She marks the trays with the six-minute correction in white paint and files the drift with the ring authority. The authority accepts the correction and orders no new batch.
text_nonnarrative: Trail clocks are defended on the ground that they need no power, which is true and beside the point, since what is unreliable in them is never the power. Consistency of the pressed material is the whole of the problem, and no design addresses it. The best instruments of the class are the ones that abandon accuracy outright and mark only the order of intervals, which they do very well indeed.

text_narrative: In the year the fence line was moved, the boundary walk took eleven hours instead of the usual seven, and the marshal of the walk, an old rider named Coy Ondrast, refused to let the party cut the corner at the dry wash. Two of the young ones went round by the road anyway. Their names were struck from the roll of walkers that year, and both were restored the year after without comment.
text_nonnarrative: Walking a boundary was a poor way of recording one and a good way of keeping one, and the two ends were regularly confused. A walk fixed nothing that a survey did not fix better. What it did was distribute knowledge of the line among people who had no document, which no survey achieved. The objection that memory was unreliable was correct and did not bear, since the walk was annual.

text_narrative: Among the animals the door custom held all winter, and the badger who ruled the sett decreed that every entrance wear a ring of holly and nothing else. The fox brought ivy and was turned away. The fox brought ivy again the year after that, and the year after that, until the badger was old and the ring at the sett door was half ivy and nobody remembered the decree.
text_nonnarrative: Ring: a closed garland hung flat against a door, of one material throughout. Swag: the same material hung open at the ends, which is not a ring and does not stand for one. Mixed ring: a closed garland of two materials, admitted at some doors and refused at others. Lapse: the condition of a door bearing no garland at midwinter, which carries no penalty and is simply noted.
